items.caption: Finally, we coembed all 4,096 features from A/1 and all 512 features from A/0 into the plane using UMAP to allow for interactive exploration of the space of features:
items.title: The UMAP Feature Browser
items.takeaway: A screenshot of the interactive map the authors publish alongside the article: every dictionary direction from two autoencoder runs — 4,608 of them — projected onto a plane, with a searchable list of human-written feature labels beside it. It establishes that the qualitative families of features the paper describes in prose are also tight geometric clumps, and that features from the small run and the large run land in the same clumps. It is a browsing tool, not a measurement: the clusters carry the meaning, the coordinates do not.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

This is a screenshot of a live page, not a static plot. Each dot in the right pane is one learned [[feature]] — more exactly one [[feature-direction]], a single column of the decoder matrix $W_d$ that the paper also calls the [[dictionary-decoder]].

Those columns live in the 512-dimensional space of MLP neuron activations of the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]]. Each is held to unit length, so a column is a pure direction with no magnitude of its own.

Two [[dictionary-learning-run]]s are drawn together here. All 512 features of run A/0 and all 4,096 of run A/1 go into the same embedding, giving $512 + 4096 = 4608$ dots. Names follow the paper's [[feature-notation]]: `A/1/776` means transformer A, run 1, feature number 776.

### How to read it

The right pane is a two-dimensional [[umap]] embedding of those 4,608 vectors, fit with cosine distance. Both axes are UMAP coordinates. They carry no units, no scale and no meaning of their own.

What the embedding tries to preserve is neighbourhood. Two dots sit close when their dictionary vectors point in nearly the same direction. So read the clumps, not the positions — and do not read the gap between two clumps as a distance.

The left pane is the same set as a scrollable list. Each row shows a feature id and a short human-written label. Rows are grouped under a cluster number produced by [[hdbscan-feature-clustering]], and the list order comes from [[one-dimensional-umap-ordering]]; the cluster numbers themselves are just tags.

### What it shows

The three visible groups are thematic. Cluster #49 gathers citation features, #42 section references, #43 formatting and figure references. Several labels have the shape `"ref" in [context]`, which is the paper's notation for [[token-in-context-features]].

Two things follow. Each cluster mixes A/0 and A/1 ids, so a coarse feature from the small run sits beside the finer run-1 features covering the same ground — the geometric face of [[feature-splitting]]. And the families the paper argues for in prose show up as [[feature-geometry-clusters]], meaning conceptually similar features have small angles between their vectors.

One row reads `[Ultralow density cluster]`, a stand-in label for a member of the [[ultralow-density-cluster]] the authors treat as a training artifact rather than a real feature.

terms.definition: A dimensionality-reduction method that places high-dimensional points in a low-dimensional space while trying to keep each point near the same neighbours it had before. Here it takes 512-dimensional feature directions down to two coordinates for display.
Fitting one UMAP to the features of two different runs at once, rather than one map per run. It is what lets an A/0 dot and an A/1 dot be compared for closeness on the same picture.

The first field of a feature id: which of the two one-layer transformers the features were learned from. The paper trains transformers A and B with identical hyperparameters and different random seeds, and studies A throughout.
The second field, naming a dictionary learning run: the 512-feature autoencoder trained on transformer A's MLP activations. It is the smallest run in the A/0…A/5 sequence.
The 4,096-feature autoencoder trained on the same activations, eight times wider than A/0. It is the run the paper discusses most and recommends readers start with.
The full three-field identifier: transformer, run, then feature index inside that run. The paper writes transformer neurons differently, as A/neurons/32, so the two are never confused.
One learned direction in MLP activation space, produced by the sparse autoencoder and hoped to correspond to a single human-interpretable thing. Each dot on the map is one.

The unit vector in the 512-dimensional neuron space along which a feature writes when it fires — one column of the decoder matrix $W_d$. These columns, not the feature's activations, are what UMAP is run on here.
The autoencoder's output weight matrix. The paper uses "decoder" and "dictionary" for the same object, and its columns are the feature directions plotted here.
The distance UMAP is given: it compares vectors by the angle between them and ignores their lengths. Since the dictionary columns are already unit-norm, this is the natural choice.
The column holding the group heading for each block of rows. Every listed feature belongs to exactly one such group, or to none.
Group identifiers assigned by HDBSCAN run on a separate 10-dimensional UMAP of the same features. The numbers are arbitrary labels, not a ranking or an ordering.
The column holding each row's feature id. The unlabelled column to its right holds that feature's written explanation.

A short human-written description of what the feature appears to respond to, such as "Years in some citation notation". These are interpretations attached by the authors for browsing, not measured quantities.
A text box that filters the left-hand list by the words in those written labels. It is how a reader finds, say, every feature whose description mentions "citation".
The label shape used for a feature that fires on one particular token but only inside a particular kind of surrounding text. [context] is a placeholder standing in for whatever that context is.

A placeholder label rather than an interpretation: it marks a feature that fires on roughly one token in ten million and that the authors say is almost never interpretable. They treat such features as an artifact of autoencoder training.
Labels that are just a literal string mean the feature mainly fires on that token. These sit in the same clusters as the longer prose labels, which is the point being made.
Fragments of Markdown section-anchor syntax appearing in cluster #42's labels. They show that the cluster is organised around a specific textual convention, not a broad topic.
Fragments of Markdown citation syntax appearing in cluster #49's labels. Features keyed to different pieces of the same citation format end up adjacent on the map.

A label naming what the feature does to the output as well as what it responds to: it fires in a citation and pushes up the probability of a year token. The paper notes every feature in a one-layer model can be read both as an input detector and as an action.
One feature's dictionary direction, placed at its two UMAP coordinates. All dots are drawn identically; nothing about a dot's size or colour encodes information here.
The two UMAP output coordinates. They are unnamed and unnumbered on purpose — the embedding has no preferred orientation, origin or scale, so the numbers would mean nothing.
Evenly spaced reference lines in the scatter pane. They help judge relative separations while panning and zooming; they do not mark meaningful values.

The subset of dots printed with their feature id, so a viewer can read identities without hovering. Labels are placed where there is room and can overlap, so some of the printed ids collide and are hard to read.
Toggles whether the mouse wheel zooms the scatter. Off by default so the wheel scrolls the page instead of the plot.
View controls for the scatter pane. "home" restores the full view of all 4,608 points after a reader has zoomed into a cluster.
A density-based clustering algorithm that finds groups of varying shape and leaves outlying points unassigned. It supplies the cluster numbers in the left pane.

The observation that as the dictionary grows, one broad feature is replaced by a family of narrower ones covering roughly the same ground. On this map it appears as A/0 and A/1 features sharing a cluster.

numbers.meaning: The number of features in run A/1, all of which are plotted. It is the dictionary size chosen for that run — eight times the width of the MLP being decomposed, which is what makes the dictionary overcomplete.

The number of features in run A/0, all of which are also plotted. This run is deliberately set to exactly the number of MLP neurons, so it is the smallest dictionary that is not compressing the layer.

The length of every dictionary column before UMAP, because the autoencoder reconstructs the 512 MLP neuron activations of the one-layer transformer. Same number as A/0's size, but a different quantity.
The total dot count in the scatter, from $512 + 4096$. Both runs go into one embedding so that features from different dictionary sizes can be compared for proximity.
The number of UMAP output dimensions, which is why the display is a plane. The paper also fits a 10-dimensional embedding, but only for clustering, and a 1-dimensional one for list order.

The UMAP hyperparameter setting how many nearest neighbours define each point's local structure. Larger values preserve more global shape at the cost of local detail; 15 is the value the paper reports for this embedding.
The UMAP hyperparameter controlling how tightly points may pack together in the output. A small value like this lets clusters compress into dense blobs, which is why the clumps here look solid.
Not a count but the distance setting: similarity is angle between dictionary vectors. This is the choice that makes "nearby on the map" mean "similar feature direction".
The HDBSCAN setting for the smallest group that counts as a cluster. Three is permissive, so even a small family of two split features plus their parent can be named a cluster.
The separate UMAP embedding that the clustering is actually run on, and its packing parameter. Clustering in 10 dimensions rather than 2 avoids letting the flattening to a plane decide the groups.

numbers.value: 0 and 1 (the middle field of an id)
numbers.meaning: The run index. A/0…A/5 form a sequence at fixed L1 coefficient with increasing dictionary size, so a larger index means a wider dictionary here.

The range of the third field of a feature id, one per hidden unit of the corresponding autoencoder. An index like 3898 is only a slot number and carries no ordering — feature 3898 is not in any sense larger or later than feature 357.

The three group headings visible in the left pane. They come from HDBSCAN's arbitrary labelling, so 42 and 43 being adjacent numbers is not why they are adjacent in the list — the list order comes from a one-dimensional UMAP.

numbers.value: about $10^{-7}$ (roughly one token in ten million)
numbers.meaning: The firing rate that defines the ultralow density cluster referenced by one row's label. The paper reports almost none of these features are interpretable, in contrast with the high density mode around $10^{-5}$.

items.caption: We aim to take its MLP activations – the activations we can't avoid needing to decompose – and decompose them into "features":
items.title: Where the Dictionary Attaches
items.takeaway: This schematic names the exact tensor the paper decomposes: the 512-dimensional post-ReLU MLP activation vector at a single token position of a one-layer transformer. It shows that vector being sent out to a sparse, overcomplete autoencoder and coming back, and that the thing the autoencoder returns is a set of between 512 and 131,072 feature activations rather than the 512 neuron values.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

The whole model under study, drawn as one vertical column, with a single tensor pulled out to the right.

Read the column bottom to top. `tokens` enter, `embed` turns them into vectors, and the tall vertical line is the [[residual-stream]] — 128-dimensional in this model. Each small circled junction on that line is a point where a block's output is added back in.

The lower junction is fed by the attention heads $h_0$, $h_1$, and so on. Above it, `MLP (ReLU)` reads from the stream and its output rejoins at the upper junction. Then `unembed` maps the stream to `logits`. That is the entire [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]]: one attention block, then one MLP block.

### How to read the pulled-out part

`acts (512)` is the MLP's hidden layer after the ReLU, for one token position — 512 numbers. This is the tensor being decomposed.

The caption's phrase, "the activations we can't avoid needing to decompose", is the reason it was chosen. A one-layer attention-only transformer can be rewritten so its hidden states never appear; adding a ReLU MLP closes that route off ([[mlp-activations-as-target]]).

The two arrows form a round trip. The lower arrow, `acts` to `"features"`, is the encoder: a linear map, a bias, a ReLU, producing one non-negative [[feature-activation]] per dictionary element ([[autoencoder-encoder]]). The upper arrow runs back: the decoder rebuilds the 512-vector as a weighted sum of unit [[feature-direction]]s ([[dictionary-decoder]]).

Training minimizes reconstruction error on that loop plus an [[l1-sparsity-penalty]] on the middle layer, which drives most feature activations to exactly zero. Sparsity is what makes the middle layer readable rather than just another dense recoding.

### What it shows

The count on the right box carries the claim. The dictionary holds 512 to 131,072 elements, so at the wide end there are 256 times more feature slots than neurons — [[overcompleteness]] ([[dictionary-learning]]).

The paper's stated reason for going wide is [[superposition]]: it takes the MLP to represent more features than it has neurons, which would leave individual neurons [[polysemanticity|polysemantic]] and not the right unit to interpret. So the output is a sparse set of [[feature]] activations, not neuron activations. The scare quotes around "features" are the authors' own hedge that these are learned objects, not confirmed ones.

terms.definition: The integer token ids fed into the model, produced by a byte-pair-encoding tokenizer, so a token need not correspond to a whole character or word.
The lookup that maps each token id to its initial vector in the residual stream. Drawn here only to show where the column starts.
The residual stream: the running 128-dimensional vector that each block reads from and adds its output back into.
The two points where a block's output is summed back into the residual stream — the lower one for the attention heads, the upper one for the MLP block.
The individual attention heads of the single attention block. The ellipsis stands for the remaining heads; the paper does not state how many there are.

The model's one MLP block, whose elementwise nonlinearity is a ReLU. The elementwise nonlinearity is what makes the neuron basis a privileged basis, which is why neurons were ever a plausible unit of analysis.

The MLP's hidden activation vector at one token position, taken after the ReLU. This is the tensor the paper decomposes; the schematic elides the output weight matrix that maps it back down into the residual stream.

The autoencoder's hidden layer: one non-negative activation per dictionary element. The quotation marks are the authors' hedge — these are what the method returns, and whether they correspond to anything the model itself uses is the question the rest of the paper argues.

terms.term: the two arrows between the shaded boxes
terms.definition: The autoencoder's round trip. Lower arrow: the encoder mapping the 512-vector to feature activations. Upper arrow: the decoder rebuilding the 512-vector from them.
Only a small number of the feature activations are non-zero on any given token, enforced by an L1 penalty on the hidden layer during training.

The dictionary has more directions than the dimension of the space it decomposes. The paper insists this is what separates its setting from ordinary disentanglement work, and it is what makes recovering the activations a hard inverse problem solvable only because the answer is sparse.

The specific approximation to dictionary learning used here: a one-hidden-layer network trained with MSE reconstruction loss, chosen over classical dictionary learning algorithms because it scales to billions of datapoints and is no more computationally capable than an MLP layer itself.
The final linear map from the residual stream to one logit per vocabulary token.

The model's unnormalized next-token scores. In a one-layer model these are close to linear in the feature activations, which the paper later uses to check features against the model's actual behavior.

numbers.meaning: The width of the MLP hidden layer, and therefore the length of the activation vector being decomposed. It is a design choice of the transformer the authors trained, paired with a 128-dimensional residual stream.

The range of dictionary sizes trained, shown on the features box. The low end matches the number of neurons exactly; the high end is 512 multiplied by 256. The paper sweeps this range rather than picking one size because how many features you ask for changes what you get.
The largest expansion factor: 256 times more dictionary elements than neurons. 512 × 256 = 131,072, the upper number printed in the figure.

The smallest expansion factor, giving 512 features — exactly as many features as neurons. Included as the floor of the sweep, so the effect of going overcomplete can be seen against a matched-size baseline.

Not printed in the figure, but the run the paper actually analyzes in detail, called A/1. 512 × 8 = 4,096. The authors describe it as a deliberately modest expansion compared with what they trained at the top end.

The residual stream dimension of the transformer — the width of the vertical line in the schematic. Stated in the appendix, not printed on the figure. Note it is smaller than the 512-wide MLP layer that sits on it.

The whole column contains one attention block and one MLP block. The paper picks this size because it is, in its words, the simplest language model it does not understand: a one-layer attention-only model could be handled without decomposing hidden states, and adding the MLP is what forces the problem.
Index labels on the attention heads, not quantities. They serve only to indicate that the attention block has several parallel heads writing into the residual stream.

items.caption: In fact, in our largest experiments we'll expand to have 256 times more features than neurons, although we'll primarily focus on a more modest 8× expansion.
items.text:
| Transformer | Sparse Autoencoder
Layers | 1 Attention Block 1 MLP Block (ReLU) | 1 ReLU (up) 1 Linear (down)
MLP Size | 512 | 512 (1×) – 131,072 (256×)
Dataset | The Pile [cite: gao2020pile] (100 billion tokens) | Transformer MLP Activations (8 billion samples)
Loss | Autoregressive Log-Likelihood | L2 reconstruction + L1 on hidden layer activation
items.title: The Two Models, Side by Side
items.takeaway: The table is the paper's specification sheet for both models it works with: the small transformer under study on the left, and the sparse autoencoder trained on that transformer's MLP activations on the right. It establishes that the transformer is an ordinary language model trained in the ordinary way, and that the only unusual thing about the autoencoder is its width and its sparsity penalty. The paper flags that although it trains dictionaries up to 256 times wider than the MLP, the analyses it presents mostly use an 8x expansion.
items.walkthrough:
This is a two-column specification sheet, not a results table. The left column, headed **Transformer**, describes the model the paper is trying to understand: the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]]. The right column, headed **[[sparse-autoencoder]]**, describes the tool the paper builds to understand it.

Four rows run across both: Layers, MLP Size, Dataset, Loss. Read across a row to compare the two models on one dimension. Read down a column to get one model's full recipe.

### The transformer column

Layers: one attention block, one MLP block with a ReLU. That is the entire model. It is chosen as the smallest network whose MLP cannot be analysed away by rewriting ([[mlp-activations-as-target]]).

MLP Size: 512 neurons. Those 512 post-ReLU activations are the vectors everything else in the paper decomposes. The appendix adds that they sit on a 128-dimensional [[residual-stream]].

Dataset: [[pile-dataset|The Pile]], 100 billion tokens. The Pile is public, so the run can be reproduced. 100 billion tokens is far more than a model this small needs; the paper calls this [[overtraining]] and hopes it produces cleaner representations.

Loss: plain autoregressive log-likelihood. Nothing in the training was changed to make the model easier to read. That matters — the interpretability work has to take the model as it comes.

### The autoencoder column

Layers: a ReLU up-projection, then a linear down-projection. The encoder maps a 512-dimensional activation to $m$ hidden units; the decoder maps back down to 512. The decoder's columns are the [[dictionary-decoder]] — one direction per learned [[feature]].

MLP Size: 512 at $1\times$, up to 131,072 at $256\times$. Since the input is 512-wide, $m/512$ is the [[expansion-factor]]. Multiply: $512 \times 256 = 131{,}072$. A hidden layer wider than its input is [[overcompleteness]], and the paper wants it because it believes the MLP packs more features than neurons via [[superposition]].

Dataset: 8 billion sampled MLP activation vectors, harvested by running the transformer over Pile text.

Loss: squared reconstruction error plus an [[l1-sparsity-penalty]] on the hidden activations. The L1 term is what pushes most feature activations to exactly zero.

The last line of the caption is the caveat. The $256\times$ run exists, but the detailed analyses use $8\times$ — 4,096 features — because wider dictionaries keep splitting features into finer ones ([[feature-splitting]]).

terms.definition: The left-hand column, specifying the one-layer language model the paper is trying to interpret. Everything in it describes an ordinary model trained in an ordinary way.

The right-hand column, specifying the analysis tool: a one-hidden-layer autoencoder with a wide ReLU hidden layer and an L1 penalty on that layer, trained to reconstruct the transformer's MLP activations. Its hidden units are what the paper calls features.
The row giving each model's structural depth. It is where the reader sees that both models are about as small as they can be.
The row giving the width of the hidden layer in each model. For the transformer this is the neuron count; for the autoencoder it is the number of learned features, which the paper varies.
The row naming what each model is trained on. Note the dependency: the autoencoder's dataset is produced by running the transformer, so the transformer must be trained first.
The row giving each model's training objective. The two objectives have nothing in common, which is the point — the autoencoder is fitted to the transformer's activations, not co-trained with it.
The transformer's single attention layer, which moves information between token positions. The paper does not decompose it; it decomposes only what the MLP produces.
The transformer's single feedforward layer with a ReLU nonlinearity. Its post-ReLU activations are the target of the whole decomposition effort.

The autoencoder's encoder: a linear map with a bias followed by a ReLU, projecting a 512-dimensional activation vector up to the wider hidden layer. Its output vector is the set of feature activations for that token.

The autoencoder's decoder: a linear map with a bias projecting the hidden layer back down to 512 dimensions. Its weight matrix columns are the feature directions, which is why the paper also calls the decoder the dictionary.

The public text corpus the transformers are trained on. The paper says it chose it over Anthropic's internal dataset so the experiments would be reproducible, while noting that some features are likely idiosyncratic to whatever dataset is used.

The autoencoder's training data: the 512-dimensional post-ReLU vectors produced by the transformer's MLP, one per token, collected by running the trained transformer over Pile text. The autoencoder never sees the text directly.
The transformer's ordinary next-token prediction objective. Listing it here signals that no interpretability-friendly modification was made to the model's training.

The first half of the autoencoder's loss: the squared error between the original MLP activation vector and the autoencoder's reconstruction of it. The paper takes a mean over vector elements for this term.

The second half of the autoencoder's loss: a penalty on the sum of the absolute hidden activations, weighted by a coefficient the paper calls $\lambda$. It is what forces most features to be exactly zero on any given token, which is what makes the decomposition sparse.

The multiplier written after each autoencoder width, equal to the hidden-layer size divided by the 512-dimensional input. It says how many times more features the dictionary has than the MLP has neurons.

The vector produced by the encoder's ReLU, one entry per dictionary element. The paper treats each nonzero entry as one feature firing on that token, and each corresponding decoder column as that feature's direction in activation space.

numbers.meaning: The transformer's layer count. The paper wants the simplest model it cannot already analyse: a one-layer attention-only network can be rewritten without reference to its hidden states, but adding a ReLU MLP makes that impossible, so the MLP has to be decomposed.

The autoencoder's layer count. It is a one-hidden-layer MLP trained as an autoencoder, with the input weights serving as encoder and the output weights as decoder; the ReLU is what allows most feature activations to be exactly zero.

The transformer's MLP width — the number of neurons whose post-ReLU activations are being decomposed. This is also the input and output dimension of the autoencoder, since the autoencoder reconstructs those same vectors.
The transformer's residual stream dimension, given in the appendix rather than in the table. The MLP is four times wider than the residual stream, which is standard.

The smallest dictionary trained: exactly as many features as the transformer has neurons. This is the degenerate end of the sweep, where the autoencoder has no room to represent more features than neurons at all.

The largest dictionary trained. It is 512 multiplied by 256, so the autoencoder has 256 times more features available than the MLP has neurons. The paper trains this wide because it believes the MLP represents more features than neurons through superposition.

The expansion factor and feature count the paper says it primarily focuses on, corresponding to the dictionary learning run it labels A/1. It is a compromise: wide enough to unpack superposition, narrow enough that a person can review the features.

How much Pile text the transformer is trained on. This is far more than compute-optimal for a 512-neuron model; the paper hypothesizes that heavy overtraining lets the model learn cleaner representations in superposition.
The number of MLP activation vectors used to train the autoencoder. The paper says scale mattered: training on more data made features subjectively sharper and more interpretable.

The total size of the collected activation dataset, of which just over 8 billion are actually consumed. The surplus exists because the paper samples without replacement and never repeats a data point.

How the activation dataset was built: the transformer is run over 40 million Pile contexts and activation vectors are sampled from 250 tokens in each. Multiplying gives the 10 billion total, and the vectors are shuffled so a batch draws from many different contexts.
The autoencoder's training schedule. Multiplying 8,192 by 1,000,000 gives 8.192 billion activation vectors, which is the 'just over 8 billion' figure the table rounds to.

The size of run A/2, the next dictionary up from A/1, mentioned in the feature splitting section. Going 512 to 4,096 to 16,384 takes the number of base64-specific features from 1 to 3 to many more, which is the evidence for feature splitting and the reason the paper does not simply use its widest dictionary.

The paper trains two one-layer transformers with identical hyperparameters and data, differing only in initialization seed. A is the model studied throughout; B is used to check whether the same features reappear, which the paper calls universality.

items.caption: We think this happens via a kind of “noisy simulation”, where small neural networks exploit feature sparsity and properties of high-dimensional spaces to approximately simulate much larger much sparser neural networks .
items.title: The Simulated Larger Network
items.takeaway: The figure states the paper's working picture of superposition: the network we can actually inspect is a squeezed-down projection of a much larger, much sparser network whose neurons would each be one clean feature. Because that projection packs more feature directions than there are neurons, the directions can only be almost orthogonal rather than orthogonal, and a single real neuron ends up sitting on several feature directions at once — which is what polysemanticity looks like from the neuron's point of view.
items.walkthrough:
You are looking at two cartoon networks stacked one above the other, with three orange dashed arrows running from the top one to the bottom one, and three lines of explanatory text down the right side.

### The two panels

The top panel is labelled HYPOTHETICAL DISENTANGLED MODEL. It is a network that does not exist. It has three columns of six dots each, densely wired together in grey. Each dot is a neuron, and in this imagined network every neuron is exactly one [[feature]] — one interpretable thing, cleanly separated from everything else. Nothing is shared, nothing is mixed.

The bottom panel is labelled OBSERVED MODEL. This is the network you can actually load and run. Same three columns, but only three dots each. These are real neurons.

### How to read it

Read the picture downward, following the arrows. There is one arrow per column, and each carries the same operation: the six idealized units of that column are pushed down into the three real units below it.

Six things into three slots is the whole point. In three dimensions you can only have three mutually orthogonal directions, so six directions cannot all be perpendicular; some pairs must overlap. The figure's middle caption names the compromise — the idealized neurons are *projected* onto the real network as "almost orthogonal" vectors over the neurons. This is [[superposition]], and the mechanism the paper proposes for it is [[noisy-simulation]]: a small network approximately simulating a larger, sparser one.

### Why the packing is tolerable, and what it costs

Two properties make the overlap survivable. First, [[feature-sparsity]]: on any given datapoint only a few features are active, so most overlapping pairs are never lit at the same time. Second, high dimensionality: the number of directions you can fit at small pairwise angles grows very fast with the number of dimensions, far faster than the dimension itself.

The cost is [[interference]]. Reading a feature off its almost-orthogonal direction also picks up a little of every other feature sharing space with it.

Now read the picture upward. One bottom dot lies along several top-panel feature directions, so it fires for several unrelated things. That is [[polysemanticity]] — a consequence of the projection, not a separate fact about neurons.

The panel is an illustration of a hypothesis, not a measurement; the 6-to-3 squeeze is drawn for legibility, and the real ratio the paper works with is far larger.

terms.definition: The label on the top panel. It names a network that is not observed and may not exist as a literal object — the larger, sparser network that the real one is hypothesized to be approximating.
The label on the bottom panel. It names the network that actually exists and can be run — here standing in for the paper's one-layer transformer and its MLP layer.

In the top panel's caption, a feature that occupies one unit all by itself, with no sharing. Every neuron in the hypothetical model is one of these, which is what makes that model interpretable neuron by neuron.
Neurons. In the top panel each dot is simultaneously a neuron and a feature; in the bottom panel each dot is a real neuron that may carry parts of several features.
Connections, i.e. weights between units in adjacent columns. They are drawn dense and unlabelled — the picture is about how many units there are and what they mean, not about specific weight values.
Successive layers of each cartoon network, three in each panel. They exist only to make the drawing look like a network; nothing in the figure depends on there being three.
The mapping from the hypothetical model to the observed one, one arrow per column. They run downward, meaning the larger network is expressed inside the smaller one, not recovered from it.

The word set in orange in the middle caption. It means the idealized neurons are written as vectors in the smaller network's activation space — a linear map into fewer dimensions than there were units.
Named in the first caption line. The claim that networks want to represent more features than they have neurons, and do so by giving each feature its own direction rather than its own neuron.
The bolded phrase in the first caption line. The claim that the observed network's computation approximately reproduces what a much bigger, much sparser network would compute.

The phrase in the middle caption, in scare quotes in the original. Each feature is a vector spread across many neurons, and any two such vectors have a small but nonzero dot product because there is not room for them all to be perpendicular.
The bolded phrase in the bottom caption. It restates what the arrows do: many feature directions are compressed into an activation space with fewer dimensions than there are features.

The bottom caption's closing word. What the projection looks like if you examine one real neuron: it responds to a mixture of apparently unrelated things, because several feature directions have weight on it.
The phrase from the sentence that introduces this figure. The simulation is noisy because the packing is imperfect — the larger network is reproduced approximately, not exactly.
Not drawn, but the property that makes the packing work: only a small number of features are active on any one datapoint, so most overlapping pairs are rarely on together.

Not drawn, but the price of the packing: because feature directions are not orthogonal, activating one feature slightly activates others, and reading one off its direction picks up traces of the rest.

numbers.meaning: Dots per column in the top panel — the number of features in the hypothetical disentangled network's layer. Chosen for legibility, not measured; it just needs to exceed the bottom panel's count.

Dots per column in the bottom panel — the number of real neurons available to hold those six features. In three dimensions at most three directions can be mutually orthogonal, so six directions must overlap.

The implied expansion ratio, 6 features into 3 neurons. This is the figure's illustration of overcompleteness — more directions than dimensions — at the smallest ratio that still makes the point visible.
Layers drawn in each panel. This number carries no argument; the figure would say the same thing with one column or ten.
One orange arrow per column, indicating the projection applies at every layer rather than at one special place.
Not in the figure, but what the bottom panel stands for in the paper: the MLP of the one-layer transformer under study has 512 neurons, and this is the space into which features must be packed.
Not in the figure. The expansion factor the paper mainly works with when it fits a dictionary to those 512 activations, giving 4,096 features — a far bigger squeeze than the drawn 2×.
Not in the figure. The largest expansion the paper runs, 131,072 features over 512 neurons, indicating how much larger the hypothesized top panel may be than the drawing suggests.

items.caption: This includes examples of when they activate, what effect they have on the logits when they do, examples of how they affect the probability of tokens if the feature is ablated, and much more:
items.title: Anatomy of a Feature Page
items.takeaway: A labelled tour of one page of the paper's published feature browser, which puts four kinds of evidence about a single learned feature side by side: where it fires, what it does to the next-token logits, whether any single neuron matches it, and whether a parallel training run found the same thing. For the feature shown, no neuron correlates with it above 0.09, while a feature from the parallel run correlates at 0.75.
items.walkthrough:
This is one page from the [[feature-exploration-interface|feature exploration interface]], the published tool that has a page like this for every [[feature|feature]] in every [[dictionary-learning-run]]. Everything outside the grey box is annotation added for the paper. The tool itself prints none of it.

Read the page in four columns.

**Identity.** The header gives the feature's index within its run, `#3923`, and a human-written label, `Latin: ?`, whose question mark records that the labeller was not confident. Below sits an [[automated-interpretability|automated]] explanation, written by Claude from activating examples alone, and a score of $0.305$. That score is the rank correlation between the activations Claude later predicted from that explanation and the true ones.

Three tables follow. NEURON ALIGNMENT writes the [[feature-direction|feature direction]] out in the [[neuron-basis-coefficients|basis of the 512 MLP neurons]] and lists the three largest coefficients. CORRELATED NEURONS instead ranks neurons by how closely their activations track the feature's across the dataset, which is the paper's preferred way of hunting for a [[most-correlated-neuron|neuron counterpart]]. CORRELATED B FEATURES runs the same comparison against the parallel run on the second transformer, the paper's measure of [[universality|universality]] by [[activation-similarity|activation similarity]].

**Statistics.** The upper histogram counts nonzero activations by size, and its header reports [[feature-density|feature density]] — the fraction of all tokens on which this feature fires at all. Beneath it are the ten most negative and ten most positive [[logit-weight|logit weights]], the linear estimate of how firing shifts each next-token logit, with the whole distribution plotted below.

**Examples.** The third column holds the [[top-dataset-examples|top 20 activating examples]]. The fourth holds subsample intervals: [[activation-interval|evenly spaced bands]] stepping down from the maximum, so a reader can check whether the story still holds at weaker activations. In every snippet the bold token is the selected one, four tokens of context sit on each side, orange shading is activation strength, and the underline colour reports a [[feature-ablation|feature ablation]] — blue where deleting the feature raised the model's loss on that token, red where it lowered it.

**What it shows.** The layout is the paper's per-feature argument in one screen. Here the two neuron tables stay near zero while the parallel-run feature reaches 0.75, which is the shape of evidence the paper wants: not a neuron, but not a fluke either.

terms.definition: The index of this feature within its dictionary learning run, printed as a clickable link so a page can be cited by URL. Under the paper's naming scheme a full name would also carry the transformer letter and run number, as in A/1/3923.
A free-text label written by one of the paper's authors after looking at the page. The trailing question mark is the labeller flagging that the reading is tentative, not a fixed part of the format.
The automated interpretability panel: an explanation of the feature generated by Claude from activating examples alone, with no access to the human label.

How well that generated explanation predicts unseen activations. Claude is given the explanation and fresh token sequences, predicts an activation for each token, and the score is the correlation between predicted and true values.

terms.term: "The neuron attends to common Latin words and short phrases."
terms.definition: The text Claude produced for this feature. It says "neuron" because the same prompt is used for real MLP neurons and for autoencoder features, so the wording is generic rather than a claim that this feature is a neuron.

A table decomposing the feature's direction into the 512 MLP neurons and showing the three neurons with the largest coefficients. It answers whether dictionary learning simply handed back one neuron under a new name.
Which MLP neuron the row refers to, numbered within the transformer's 512-unit hidden layer. Clicking it opens that neuron's own page in the same interface.
The feature direction's coefficient on that neuron. The decoder columns are constrained to unit length, so this is a component of a unit vector and can be signed either way.

That coefficient's share of the total absolute mass of the direction, that is |value| divided by the sum of |coefficient| over all 512 neurons. The paper does not define the column in text, but the printed numbers are consistent with this reading. It is a spread-out-ness gauge: a one-neuron feature would read near 100%.

A table ranking MLP neurons by how well their activations track this feature's across a large sample of dataset tokens. The paper says it trusts this more than neuron alignment for finding a neuron counterpart, because neurons differ in activation scale.
The ordinary linear correlation between the feature's activation vector over sampled tokens and the neuron's (or the other feature's), after subtracting each one's mean.

The same comparison without mean-subtraction: the cosine of the angle between the two activation vectors. Because activations are non-negative and mostly zero, it usually lands close to the Pearson value, which is what the printed columns show.

The same activation comparison, but against features from the matched dictionary trained on the second transformer. Both transformers use identical hyperparameters and data and differ only in random seed, so a high value means two independent runs found the same thing.
The second one-layer transformer and the dictionary learned on it. The paper keeps it aside specifically to test whether features recur across seeds.

A histogram of this feature's activation values, built by sampling tokens at random and keeping only those where the feature is nonzero. Zeros are excluded, so the plot describes the shape of firing, not how often it fires.

The fraction of all sampled tokens on which the feature has a nonzero activation. The paper uses the distribution of this quantity across features as a quick proxy for whether an autoencoder trained well.
The scalar output of the feature on a token, the coefficient the autoencoder assigns to this dictionary direction. It is non-negative because the encoder ends in a ReLU.

The ten vocabulary tokens the feature pushes down hardest and the ten it pushes up hardest, by logit weight. Logit weight is computed by pushing the feature direction through the MLP output weights, a linearized layer norm, and the unembedding.

The logit weight value, plotted over the whole vocabulary. Softmax is shift-invariant, so there is no absolute zero; the paper shifts each feature's weights so the median is zero, and the listed tokens are the tails of this distribution.

The 20 dataset snippets on which this feature fires most strongly, the standard first look at what a unit responds to. The paper notes elsewhere that judging a unit only from its maximal examples flatters it.
The largest activation among the examples shown in that panel. In the top panel it is the feature's maximum over the sampled corpus; in each subsample interval it marks the top of that band.

One band of the activation range, with examples drawn from it at random. Interval 0 sits just below the top activations and the numbering counts downward, so higher-numbered intervals show progressively weaker firings.
The feature's activation on that token, with darker orange meaning a larger value. It marks where the feature fired.

The token that caused this snippet to be selected for display, that is the one whose activation placed it in this panel or interval. Everything around it is context, not part of the selection criterion.

Ablating the feature raised the model's loss on predicting that token, so the feature was helping that prediction. Ablation means recomputing the forward pass with this feature's contribution subtracted out of the MLP activations.
Ablating the feature lowered the loss on that token, so the feature was hurting that prediction. In the paper's Arabic case study this happens mostly on punctuation shared with other scripts.
A flag that this exact snippet has already been shown in another interval on the same page. It exists so a reader does not mistake a duplicate for independent evidence.
Holding the cursor on any token for two or more seconds reveals its numeric activation and ablation effect, since the shading and underline colour only encode these approximately.

terms.term: Latin-ending tokens (ibus, orem, ips, aliqu, ea, imus, orum, ulum, itor, nostr)
terms.definition: The top positive logit tokens. They are word fragments from pseudo-Latin filler text, several of them genuine Latin case and verb endings, which matches the lorem-ipsum boilerplate visible in the example snippets.

terms.term: English sports and place tokens (Rangers, Center, NBA, CW, WF, League, watch, Hockey, West, sville)
terms.definition: The top negative logit tokens: the things the feature makes less likely when it fires. They read as ordinary English proper-noun and sports vocabulary, the opposite of pseudo-Latin filler.

numbers.meaning: The feature's index inside its dictionary learning run. The run being shown is A/1, which has 4,096 features, so indices run from 0 to 4,095 and this one sits near the top of that range purely by ordering, not by importance.

The autointerp score: the correlation between the activations Claude predicted from its own written explanation and the true activations, over sixty nine-token examples. The paper reports Spearman rank correlation as its main scoring throughout, so this is a middling result, well above zero but far from a clean match.

The feature's density: it is nonzero on about 1.44 tokens in a thousand. That places it in what the paper calls the high density cluster, whose right-hand mode sits around one in a hundred thousand to one in a thousand, and well clear of the ultralow density cluster around one in ten million that the paper treats as a training artifact and excludes.

The top row of NEURON ALIGNMENT: MLP neuron 138 carries a coefficient of +0.40 in the feature's direction, which is 3.6% of the direction's total absolute mass. Neuron indices run 0 to 511 because the transformer's inner MLP dimension is 512.

The second and third alignment rows. Both print +0.27 yet differ in the percentage column, which means the underlying values differ in a decimal place the display rounds away (roughly 0.274 versus 0.269).

The implied L1 norm of the feature direction, recoverable from the table: 0.40 divided by 0.036 gives about 11.1, and 0.27 divided by 11.1 gives 2.4%, so the column is internally consistent. This is the number that makes the non-alignment argument. A direction sitting entirely on one neuron would have L1 of 1; a unit vector spread evenly over all 512 neurons would have L1 of about 22.6. At 11.1, this feature is spread across dozens of neurons, closer to the even case than to the single-neuron case.

The single most correlated MLP neuron. A Pearson correlation of 0.09 is very weak: no neuron in the layer fires in anything like the same pattern as this feature. This is the number that would have to be large for the feature to be a relabelled neuron.

The second and third most correlated neurons, weaker still. Neuron 138 is worth noticing: it is the largest single contributor to the feature's direction, yet its activations correlate with the feature's at only 0.05, which is exactly why the paper prefers the correlation table over the alignment table when checking for a neuron counterpart.

The closest feature in the parallel B run, correlating at 0.75. Across all of A/1 the median correlation with the best-matching B feature is 0.72, so this feature is a typical case of the paper's universality result. The comparable median for the closest matching neuron between the two transformers is 0.46.
The next two B-run features. The sharp fall from 0.75 to 0.10 means the match is a single specific counterpart rather than a diffuse cluster of similar features.

Counts of sampled nonzero activations per bin. The leftmost bin is the tallest at about 250, so most firings are weak; the paper's activation interval analysis exists precisely because weak firings are where interpretations tend to break down.
The activation range, ticked at 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12. It runs just past the observed maximum of 11.54.
The ten negative logit weights, from Rangers at −0.37 to sville at −0.29. The narrow spread means no single token is strongly suppressed; suppression is broad and shallow.

The ten positive logit weights, from ibus at +0.48 to nostr at +0.36. The positive tail is slightly larger in magnitude than the negative tail, consistent with the feature pushing toward a specific vocabulary rather than away from one.

The plotted range of logit weights over the vocabulary. The bulk sits in a single mode at zero because the weights are shifted so that each feature's median is zero; the listed tokens are the thin tails.
The largest activation seen anywhere in the sampled corpus, reported at the head of the TOP ACTIVATIONS column. All interval boundaries are fractions of this number.

The maximum activations inside subsample intervals 0, 1 and 2. The steps between them are about 0.87 and 0.83, so bands are close to evenly spaced. Extrapolating that step down to zero implies roughly a dozen bands, which fits the appendix's mention of a top-activations panel plus twelve further intervals but sits awkwardly with the callout's stated ten. The paper's own counts of intervals are not consistent across sections.
The number of top activating examples shown. Elsewhere the paper uses the same count when searching neurons for a given behaviour, so the two displays are comparable.
Rows in each of the three comparison tables. Only the top three neurons or features are listed, which is enough to show whether a match exists but not enough to characterise the full distribution.
The number of logit weights shown on each side, and the number of subsample intervals the callout names.
Tokens of context displayed on each side of the selected token, giving nine tokens per snippet. The same nine-token window is what Claude is scored on in the automated evaluation.
The hover dwell time before the tooltip with exact activation and ablation numbers appears, long enough that it does not fire while a reader is scanning.
Tokens in the subset used to build these visualizations, with only 10 tokens taken from each context so that the examples are not clustered inside a few documents.
Dataset examples used when computing the feature-to-neuron activation correlations reported in the CORRELATED NEURONS table.

The transformer's inner MLP dimension and the number of learned features in the A/1 run. The dictionary is eight times overcomplete, which is what makes it possible for a feature to have no neuron counterpart at all.

items.caption: Our interface also allows users to search through features:
items.title: The Feature Search Bar
items.takeaway: A screenshot of the search strip in the paper's public feature browser, with its four dropdowns opened. It carries no results, so what it establishes is only the shape of the query the authors built for themselves: pick a matching mode, pick which part of a feature's record the query is matched against, pick a sort key over all features in a run, and pick which per-token loss difference is drawn as underlines.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

One strip of controls from the [[feature-exploration-interface]], the published viewer that covers every [[feature]] in every [[dictionary-learning-run]]. The four menus are shown opened, stacked below the bar they belong to. The three arrows and their captions at the top, and the two paragraphs at the right, are annotations the paper added to the screenshot.

No feature, no dataset example and no number appears here. Read it as a description of a query, not as evidence.

### How to read it

Left to right, the row builds one search. The first box takes a string, and the menu beside it says how that string is matched: literally, ignoring case, as a regular expression, or as a whole-field match rather than a substring.

The "in" menu says which part of a feature's record the string is matched against. Options span the [[top-dataset-examples]] a feature fires on, the tokens of those examples on their own, the feature's [[logit-weight]] entries, its index and name, and the explanation written for it by [[automated-interpretability]].

"Sort by" then orders the features. Some keys are plain bookkeeping — index, random. Others are properties the paper measures elsewhere: how strongly a feature fires at most, its [[feature-density]], and how close it sits to a single neuron, which is the check behind [[feature-neuron-nonalignment]].

### What it shows

The last menu is the one that carries real content. Under "Feature Ablation", each token's underline is coloured by the change in that token's predicted log-likelihood when this one feature's contribution is subtracted from the MLP activation — replacing $\mathbf{x}$ with $\mathbf{x} - f_i(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{d}_i$ and finishing the forward pass. That is [[feature-ablation]], read per token.

Under "Residual Ablation", nothing is switched off. The whole MLP activation is replaced by the autoencoder's reconstruction from all learned features, and the underline shows the resulting loss difference. It is the per-token view of the global claim that the dictionary recovers most, not all, of what the MLP contributes; see [[loss-recovered-by-features]].

So the strip mostly tells you what the authors wanted to be able to ask: find features by their behaviour, then look at what each one is worth to the loss.

terms.definition: The free-text box at the far left, with a "Go" button. The string typed here is matched against whichever part of a feature's record the "in" menu selects.

The default matching mode: the query string must appear in the searched field with exactly the capitalisation typed. Relevant here because many features in this paper key on case and on script, so "the" and "The" can belong to different features.
Matching mode that ignores capitalisation, so a query matches upper- and lower-case occurrences alike.
Treats the query as a regular expression rather than a literal string, matching with capitalisation respected. Useful for finding character classes, such as runs of digits or non-Latin script.
The same regular-expression matching, with capitalisation ignored.
Requires the searched field to equal the query in full, rather than merely containing it. Distinguishes a token that is exactly the query from any longer token containing it.
The label above the second menu. It selects which part of each feature's stored record the query is matched against.

Search field option: match the query against the text of the dataset examples on which a feature activates most strongly. These top-activating examples are the standard first-pass way of guessing what a unit responds to.

Search field option: match against the individual tokens of those top examples rather than the surrounding text, so a hit means the feature fired on or near that specific token rather than somewhere in the same passage.

Search field option: match against the vocabulary tokens a feature pushes up or down when it fires, rather than against the contexts where it fires. This searches by what a feature does instead of when it activates.
Search field option: match against both the top activating examples and the logit-affected tokens, returning features that hit in either.
Search field option: match against the individual tokens of the top examples together with the logit-affected tokens.
Search field option: match against a feature's numeric index within its run and any name attached to it, which is how you jump straight to a feature you already know, such as A/1/3450.

Search field option: match against the natural-language explanation a language model wrote for the feature from examples of its activations. Searching this field means searching the machine-written descriptions rather than the raw data.
The label above the third menu. It chooses the ordering applied to the features listed, independently of the search itself.

The default sort key, and the interface's own label for some measure of how consistently a feature fires on similar inputs. The paper's text does not define it, so treat the name as the only description available.

Sort keys ordering features by the largest value the feature ever reaches, descending or ascending. A feature's maximum activation is the scale the paper uses elsewhere when it divides a feature's range into intervals.

Sort keys ordering features by feature density, the fraction of tokens on which the feature is nonzero. "Min Dense" surfaces the rarest features, which the paper associates with an ultralow-density cluster that is mostly uninterpretable.

terms.term: Max Neuron Aligned / Min Neuron Aligned
terms.definition: Sort keys ordering features by how close a feature is to being a single MLP neuron. This is the property the paper checks when it argues a feature is not merely a relabelled neuron; the exact statistic behind the menu entry is not stated in the text.
Sort key ordering by the ratio of a feature's maximum activation to its density, which favours features that fire rarely but hard.
Sort key ordering features by their position in the dictionary, which is arbitrary with respect to meaning and serves as a stable default ordering.
Sort key giving an arbitrary shuffle. It matters for evaluation, because judging features only by the most striking ones is the bias the paper's blinded scoring is designed to avoid.
Sort key ordering by how well each feature matches the typed query. It is greyed out in this screenshot because the search box is empty, so no relevance ranking exists yet.
Sort key ordering features by how well a machine-written explanation predicts the feature's true activations, scored as a rank correlation between predicted and actual values.
The label above the fourth menu. It selects which quantity is used to colour the underline drawn beneath each token in the displayed text examples.

Underline mode: colour each token by the change in its predicted log-likelihood when this single feature's contribution is subtracted from the MLP activation and the forward pass is completed. It shows which predictions depended on this one feature.

Underline mode: colour each token by the loss difference when the MLP activation is replaced wholesale by the autoencoder's reconstruction from all learned features. It shows where the dictionary as a whole fails to reproduce the layer.
Underline mode that draws no underlines, leaving only the activation highlighting on the text.
The unit vector in MLP activation space along which a feature writes when it fires, written $\mathbf{d}_i$. Ablation subtracts the activation times this direction.

terms.term: "Search among the features" / "Where the search query is matched" / "Which ablation is used to color the underlines of tokens"
terms.definition: The three arrow captions across the top. They are labels the paper added to the screenshot, not text present in the interface.

numbers.meaning: Matching modes offered for the query string: case sensitive, case insensitive, two regular-expression variants, and exact (not substring).
Fields the query can be matched against: top examples, top example tokens, logits, the two combinations of those, index and name, and autointerpretation.
Sort keys listed, of which one (Search Relevance) is disabled because no query has been entered.
Underline modes: Feature Ablation, Residual Ablation, and None.
The number of features switched off under "Feature Ablation" — exactly one, the feature currently being viewed. This is what separates it from Residual Ablation, where no feature is removed at all.

The fraction of the MLP's log-likelihood loss reduction recovered by the features in run A/1, the run the paper focuses on. "Residual Ablation" is the per-token picture of the remaining 21%: the loss the reconstruction fails to account for.
The complementary share — the extra loss incurred by replacing the MLP activations with the autoencoder's output, measured against the loss from zero-ablating the MLP entirely.

The higher recovery figure for run A/5, which uses 131,072 learned features and an L1 coefficient of 0.004. Given as evidence that the residual shrinks with a larger dictionary or a weaker sparsity penalty, so what a Residual Ablation underline shows depends on which run you are browsing.
The number of tokens in the subset of the training dataset from which the interface's displayed examples are drawn, with only 10 tokens taken from each context.
Tokens of context shown on each side of the selected token in the interface's text windows — the span across which these underlines are drawn.
The count of results, activations, features or measurements visible in this screenshot. The figure documents the query controls only.

items.caption: Additionally, we provide a second interface displaying all features active on a given dataset example. This is available for a set of example texts.
items.title: Text-First Feature Browser
items.takeaway: A second published interface that inverts the usual view: instead of picking a feature and seeing the texts it fires on, you pick a text and see every feature active anywhere in it, ranked, each with a machine-written label. Hovering a token re-ranks the list for that token; hovering a feature paints its activation back onto every token. This is tooling for auditing the decomposition, not evidence for any claim.
items.walkthrough:
Three screenshots of one browser tool, in the three states it moves through as you move the mouse. This is the [[data-oriented-interface]], and it inverts the main [[feature-exploration-interface]], which starts from a single feature and shows the texts it fires on. Here you start from a text.

### The resting state

The left panel fixes one dataset example — the closing stanza of Keats's "Ode on a Grecian Urn", preceded by the `<EOT>` token that opens the context. Every token carries an orange shade.

Below the text sits a table of every [[feature]] the [[sparse-autoencoder]] finds active somewhere in this stanza: `Index`, `Act`, `% of Max`, `Autointerpreted Label`.

The label column is written by a language model from examples of when the unit fires; that pipeline is [[automated-interpretability]]. The prompt frames the unit as a neuron, which is why every label opens "This neuron…" even though these rows are learned features.

### Reading the two activation columns

Feature #447 shows $1.281$ and $19.03\%$. Dividing, $1.281 / 0.1903 \approx 6.73$. In the middle panel the same feature shows $3.026$ and $44.95\%$, and $3.026 / 0.4495 \approx 6.73$ again.

So `% of Max` normalises each [[feature-activation]] by that feature's own largest activation over the dataset — the same normalisation behind the paper's [[activation-interval]]s. The percentages are per-feature, so they are not comparable across rows as raw strengths.

### The two hovers

The middle panel hovers the token `generation`. The list re-sorts by activation at that token, and the top row turns deep orange: #447 at $3.026$, then #174, #227, #496. Feature #448, second in the whole-text list, has dropped out of the top four. One archaic-language feature dominates that token; the rest are weak.

The right panel hovers row #504, labelled as firing on "a comma followed by the word 'and'". Its activation is painted across the stanza. Commas light up, including commas that are not followed by "and", so the written label looks approximate rather than exact.

That is the use of the tool. You can check a label against a text token by token, in either direction. No number in the figure is a result.

terms.term: "For a selection of texts, we show all the active features." (left panel heading)
terms.definition: The resting state of the interface: a fixed piece of text with a table below it listing every feature that fires anywhere in that text. The paper offers this view for a set of chosen example texts, not for arbitrary input.

terms.term: "Hovering over a token will reveal the top activating features for that token" (middle panel heading)
terms.definition: The first interaction: pointing at one token re-sorts the table so the features are ranked by how strongly they fire on that token specifically, rather than on the text as a whole.

terms.term: "Hovering over a feature will show its activation on each of the tokens" (right panel heading)
terms.definition: The second interaction: pointing at one table row shades every token in the text by that single feature's activation there, so a written label can be checked against the text.

The column giving each active unit's number inside the dictionary, shown as a blue link (#447, #448, …) that presumably opens that unit's own page in the main feature interface. All six visible indices fall below 512; the figure does not name which dictionary learning run is on screen.

The column giving the activation value — the scalar the autoencoder's ReLU hidden unit takes. In the resting and feature-hover states it is a per-text number; when a token is hovered it becomes that feature's activation on that token.

The column giving the activation as a percentage of that feature's own maximum activation over the dataset. It rescales each feature onto its personal 0–100% range, so it says how strongly a feature is firing relative to itself, not relative to other rows.
The column holding a natural-language description of the unit, written by a language model from examples of tokens where the unit fires. It is a guess about the unit, not a verified property of it.

terms.term: "This neuron …" (the opening words of every label)
terms.definition: The autointerpretability prompt describes whatever unit it is shown as a neuron, so the generated labels say "neuron" even when the row is a learned feature rather than an MLP neuron. The paper elsewhere keeps the two strictly apart in notation.

The strongest unit on this text, labelled as firing on elevated, formal or old-fashioned language — "thou", "hast", "thy", "verily", archaic verb forms like "knowest", and titles like "lord" and "sir". It tops both the whole-text list and the list for the hovered token.

Labelled as attending to formal or archaic religious language: worshipping, professing belief, preaching, praying, invoking God. Second on the whole-text list, but absent from the top four for the token "generation".

Labelled as attending to medical and biomedical terminology — conditions, treatments, procedures, diagnoses, anatomy. Its presence on a Keats stanza is a reminder that a weakly firing unit's label need not describe why it fired here.
Labelled as firing when there is a comma followed by the word "and". This is the row hovered in the right panel, and its painted activation lands on commas generally, not only on commas before "and".
Labelled as firing on the term "here" and on words about stating facts or sharing information. It appears only in the token-hover list, ranked second for the token "generation".
Labelled as firing on present participle verb forms (-ing) and similar-sounding endings such as -ington and -ation. It ranks fourth for the token "generation", whose ending matches that description.
The end-of-text token that begins the context window, marking the start of a fresh document. It is heavily shaded in the first two panels and unshaded under feature #504.

The background colour on each token in the text pane, darker for more activation. In the resting state it summarises the total feature activity on a token; under a feature hover it shows that one feature's activation.
The highlight on #447 in the middle panel, marking the top-ranked feature for the hovered token. The remaining rows keep the pale background.
The small popup naming the token currently under the cursor, so it is unambiguous which token the re-ranked list belongs to. Tokenization means the displayed unit need not be a whole word.
The end-of-line marker shown at the close of each verse line, making newline tokens visible as tokens rather than as invisible whitespace.
The dataset example under inspection: the final stanza of Keats's "Ode on a Grecian Urn". It is a piece of text chosen for display, not a result about poetry.

A partly visible row below #504 ("This neuron seems to fire for examples of words or…") showing that the table scrolls. The figure therefore does not reveal how many features are active on the text in total.

numbers.meaning: Panels in the figure — one interface in three states: resting, token hovered, feature hovered.
Feature #447's whole-text activation and the same value as a share of its dataset maximum. The two together imply a maximum of about $1.281/0.1903 \approx 6.73$.
Feature #448's whole-text activation. Implied maximum $0.451/0.076 \approx 5.93$, so this feature is firing at well under a tenth of its usual peak.
Feature #227's whole-text activation. Implied maximum $0.291/0.0333 \approx 8.74$ — a weak firing of a feature whose label is about biomedical text.
Feature #504's whole-text activation, unchanged between the left and right panels because hovering a row paints the text without re-computing the row. Implied maximum $0.211/0.0242 \approx 8.72$.

The same feature evaluated at one token instead of the whole text. It is more than twice the resting value, and the ratio again gives $\approx 6.73$, confirming that % of Max divides by a fixed per-feature constant.
Second-ranked feature for that token. Implied maximum $0.825/0.1375 = 6.00$.
Third-ranked feature for that token, up from 0.291 in the whole-text list. Implied maximum $\approx 8.74$, matching its resting-state ratio.
Fourth-ranked feature for that token; the -ation ending of "generation" matches its label. Implied maximum $0.340/0.052 \approx 6.54$.

Not printed in the figure, but recoverable by dividing Act by % of Max. They differ from feature to feature, which is why the percentage column is needed at all: a raw activation of 0.5 means something different for each row.
Every feature active on this stanza is firing far below its own peak. The paper notes elsewhere that most real activations are small, and that low activations are the harder ones to interpret.
Identifiers within the dictionary, not quantities — the numbering carries no ordering or meaning. Every visible index is below 512, which the figure leaves unexplained.
The table is cut off by the screenshot rather than exhausted; a fifth row is partly readable in the left and right panels, so the true count of active features on this text is not shown.

items.caption: If our proxy shows that a feature only activates in some relatively rare and specific context, that would exclude the typical form of polysemanticity.
items.title: Ruling Out Polysemanticity With a Proxy
items.takeaway: A schematic of the paper's argument for specificity: if an independently computed proxy marks out a small, specific region of the data, and a feature only fires inside that region, then the feature cannot be firing on the mix of unrelated things that makes a neuron polysemantic. The third panel adds the paper's own caveat: a feature is often narrower than its proxy, with other features covering the rest.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Three cartoon panels, not plots of measured data. In each one the large grey circle stands for the whole set of tokens in the training distribution. Black dots mark tokens where a single learned [[feature]] is active. The orange ring, in the second and third panels, encloses the tokens that a [[computational-proxy]] flags as belonging to some hypothesized context.

The proxy is a score you can compute from the text alone: $\log(P(s\mid\text{context})/P(s))$, the log-likelihood ratio of a string under a hand-written model of the context against its likelihood under the empirical data distribution. Nothing about the autoencoder enters that number. That independence is the point — it gives a yardstick the learned feature was not fit to.

### How to read it

Read each panel as a question about overlap. Do the black dots sit inside the orange ring, or scatter across the grey circle?

Panel one is what [[polysemanticity]] looks like: one unit firing on several clearly unrelated kinds of input, dots spread with no common region.

Panel two is the case the paper wants. Every dot falls inside the ring, so whenever the feature is on, the proxy says the context is present. The paper calls this [[activation-specificity]], and treats it as the more important half of its case.

Panel three is the honest complication. The feature's dots cover only part of the ring, and a second, paler feature covers the rest. When features are finer-grained than the proxy, several of them share the territory — the paper's [[multiple-features-for-one-context]] observation.

### What it establishes

The figure is an argument shape, not evidence. It says what a specificity result would rule out; the actual numbers arrive later, when [[feature-activation]] is histogrammed against proxy score for particular features.

Two hedges belong with it. A proxy built from Unicode blocks or character sets has false negatives — shared punctuation, whitespace, tokens split mid-character — so dots outside the ring are not automatically polysemanticity. And the panels say nothing about the reverse direction, whether the feature fires everywhere in the ring.

terms.definition: The label on the large grey circle: the full set of tokens in the model's training distribution, drawn as the universe inside which everything else lives.
The label on the black dots: the tokens where one learned feature has a nonzero value. Each dot is a place in the data where the feature fires, not a magnitude.

The label on the orange ring: the region of the data that a cheaply computable score marks as belonging to the hypothesized context. Here it is drawn as a hard boundary, though the underlying score is continuous.
The caption inside the third panel's ring, marking that region as the one the proxy flags — the same orange region as in panel two, now shown containing more than one feature.
The label on the two overlapping dots in panel three: separate learned features that each cover part of the proxy's region and together fill it. The paper reports this for Arabic and base64.
The failure mode panel one depicts: a single unit responding to a mixture of clearly unrelated contexts, so no one interpretation covers when it fires.

The paper's proposed unit of interpretation — a direction in activation space with a scalar activation, recovered as one hidden unit of the sparse autoencoder rather than as a neuron of the transformer.

The proxy's actual definition, $\log(P(s\mid\text{context})/P(s))$: how much more likely a string is under a model of the context than under the data as a whole. The paper motivates the log form by noting features act linearly on logits, so they should be incentivized to track log-likelihoods.

A string — in practice a prefix of tokens ending at the token being scored. The paper maximizes the ratio over the different prefixes leading up to and including that token, since a feature's activation can depend on what preceded it.
The likelihood of the string under the full empirical data distribution, estimated as a unigram product $\prod_{t\in s}p(t)$ over token frequencies.
The likelihood of the string under a hand-built generative model of the hypothesized context — random draws from a character set, or a Unicode-block test combined with Bayes' rule.
The claim panel two supports: when the feature is on, the context is usually present. It is one of the five claims the paper tries to establish for each feature it studies in depth.
The converse claim, not shown here: when the context is present, the feature is usually on. Panel three is where its failures get patched by other features.
The worked instance of this scheme, $\log(P(s\mid\text{Arabic Script})/P(s))$, built by checking whether characters fall in Arabic Unicode blocks.

numbers.meaning: The number of panels: the failure case (scattered polysemanticity), the target result (feature inside proxy), and the complication (several features sharing one proxy region).
Dots drawn in panels one, two and three. These are illustrative counts only — the figure is a schematic, and no count corresponds to a measured number of tokens or features.
The per-character probability the base64 proxy assigns to any character in [a-zA-Z0-9+/], modeling a base64 string as uniform draws from its 64-symbol alphabet.
The per-character probability the DNA proxy assigns to each of A, T, C and G, modeling a DNA sequence as uniform draws from four letters.

The tiny probability assigned to a character outside the context's alphabet, or to $P(\text{Arabic}\mid s)$ when $s$ contains any non-Arabic character. It makes the log-ratio collapse for off-context strings rather than going to $-\infty$.
Two of the Unicode blocks the Arabic proxy tests membership in. Working from block ranges is what makes the proxy cheap, and also what makes it miss shared punctuation and whitespace.

The share of training tokens that are Arabic script — from the Arabic case study, not printed in this figure. It is the size of the orange ring relative to the grey circle in that instance, and small rarity is what gives panel two its force.
The share of tokens on which the Arabic feature is active that are actually Arabic script. This is the measured version of panel two: most dots fall inside the ring, though not all.
How that 81% varies with activation strength — 25% when the feature is barely on, 98% above an activation of 5. Panel two's clean containment holds at high activations and degrades at low ones.
The activation level above which the Arabic feature's specificity reaches 98%. The paper argues large activations matter most because a feature's effect on the logits is linear in its activation.
