A break in both axes: the value exactly zero gets its own narrow lane, and the continuous positive range begins at this marker. Without the break, the enormous zero bin would swamp the plot.

terms.term: 0 (the separate lane and the dot at the corner)
terms.definition: The bin holding tokens where the feature, the neuron, or both are exactly off. The narrow strips between the marginals and the scatter hold the points with one coordinate at zero.
An annotation with a dotted leader pointing at the origin bin, noting that the overwhelming majority of tokens sit there because both the feature and the neuron are inactive almost all the time.

A hand-drawn ring around the small cluster of Arabic-script vocabulary tokens sitting high on the feature's logit-weight axis. This is the far-right second mode of the feature's logit weight distribution seen edge-on.

A hand-drawn ring around the large near-zero cloud, with a question mark. The paper's tentative reading is that this mass is unwanted cross-talk imposed by superposition rather than anything the model uses.

Because feature directions in superposition cannot all be orthogonal, activating one feature slightly activates and slightly moves the logits of others. That leakage is what "interference weights" would be.

The hypothesis that a network encodes more features than it has neurons, giving each feature its own linear combination of neurons. It is why a feature like this one need not line up with any single neuron.

terms.term: Mixture of non-English languages (the neuron's actual role)
terms.definition: The paper's description of what neuron 489 responds to. It offers this as a sensible superposition strategy, since languages are close to mutually exclusive and so are cheap to pack together.

terms.term: The feature is not a neuron
terms.definition: The check this figure serves: confirming that dictionary learning found something the neuron basis does not already expose, rather than handing back a conveniently clean neuron under a new name.
Reference lines marking zero logit weight on each axis, so the reader can see that the blue bulk is centred on no-effect and the red cluster is not.
Annotation drawn over the scatter by the authors to pick out two point populations. They are not fitted contours and carry no statistical claim.

numbers.meaning: Pearson correlation between the feature's activations and neuron 489's activations across the dataset. It is the headline number of the left panel: the most feature-like neuron in the model still barely tracks the feature.

Pearson correlation between the feature's logit weight vector and the neuron's, over the vocabulary. Slightly larger than the activation correlation — the tilt of the blue cloud — but the paper calls the similarity minimal.
The index of the feature within dictionary learning run A/1. It carries no meaning beyond identifying the feature.
The index of the neuron within transformer A's MLP, which has 512 neurons. It was selected by correlation search, not by position.
The dictionary learning run the feature comes from. Runs A/0 through A/5 share a fixed L1 coefficient and increase in dictionary size, so the run index fixes how many features were learned.
The number of dataset examples over which the paper searched for the neuron most correlated with the feature. A large sweep is needed because the feature fires on a very small fraction of tokens.
The range of activation values for the feature and the neuron. Both are post-ReLU, so neither goes below zero, and the axes are broken so exact zero sits in its own lane.
The level above which the paper reports the feature is 98% specific to Arabic script. In the left y-marginal this is roughly where the bar becomes solid red with no blue left.
Where the bottom histogram flattens into a single pale band. Beyond this point so few tokens fall in each bin that the composition stops varying.

The share of training tokens that are Arabic script, from the specificity section. It is the base rate, and it is why red is a thin sliver in every x-marginal bin: at a typical neuron activation the composition is close to the background distribution.
The share of tokens on which the feature is active that are Arabic script. Against a 0.13% base rate, this is what "specific" means for this feature.

The Arabic share when the feature is barely active versus when its activation is above 5. The gap between them is exactly the gradient you see running up the left y-marginal, from mostly blue at the bottom to solid red at the top.
The plotted range of logit weights. Values are median-centred per feature, so zero means no effect on that token's logit and the scale is relative, not absolute.
Roughly where the right panel's y-marginal flips from almost entirely blue to majority red. Above this the tokens the feature promotes are predominantly Arabic script.

The band holding the ringed "Arabic Token Logits" cluster. These are the vocabulary tokens whose probability the feature raises most, and they sit spread across the neuron's axis, showing the neuron does not single them out.

From the same section: searching every neuron's top 20 dataset examples for Arabic script turned up one neuron with a single Arabic example; eighteen of its remaining examples were English and one Cyrillic. This is the separate check that no neuron is an Arabic neuron.

numbers.value: 3 (largest coefficients, all negative) and 27 (coefficients at least 0.1 in magnitude)
numbers.meaning: The feature's decomposition in the neuron basis, reported just before this figure. The feature is spread over dozens of neurons, and its three strongest components point the wrong way, which is what motivated looking at the correlated neuron instead.
The number of ReLU neurons in the one-layer transformer's MLP, the pool from which neuron 489 was selected.

sections.title: The feature is not a neuron

items.caption: We search for the feature with the highest activation correlation and find B/1/1334 (corr=0.91), which is strikingly similar:
items.title: The Arabic Feature Found Again in Model B
items.takeaway: A second, independently seeded one-layer transformer, given its own independently seeded dictionary-learning run, produces a feature (B/1/1334) whose per-token activations correlate 0.91 with the Arabic-script feature A/1/3450 from the first model, and whose activation distribution looks like the same Arabic feature drawn again. The paper offers this as its per-feature evidence for universality: the feature appears to be a fact about how these models represent this data, not an accident of one training run.
items.walkthrough:
You are looking at one feature's activation distribution, drawn in exactly the format used earlier for [[arabic-script-feature]] A/1/3450. The point of the figure is that the two pictures can be laid side by side.

Start with the name in the title. Under the paper's [[feature-notation]], "B" is the second one-layer transformer ([[transformer-a-and-b]]) — same architecture, same Pile data, same hyperparameters, different random seed. The "1" is a [[dictionary-learning]] run matched in size and [[l1-coefficient]] to A/1, but trained on activations from different tokens. "1334" is the index of one feature inside that run's 4,096.

Now the axes. The horizontal axis is the feature's activation on a token, from a hard zero at the far left out to about 7.1. The vertical axis is density: how many sampled tokens land in that activation bin. Colour encodes the [[arabic-script-proxy]] score for the token, a [[computational-proxy]] of the form $\log(P(s\mid\text{Arabic Script})/P(s))$, blue at $-5$ and red at $+5$.

Exact zeros are broken out separately, at the "0" and ">0" marks: the sparsity penalty makes most tokens exactly zero, which would otherwise be a spike of infinite density. The strip under the main panel renormalizes each column to full height, so it shows the colour mix conditional on that activation level. The four boxes on top are dataset examples sampled near activation 0.75, 2.7, 4.75 and 6.8, with the scored token shaded orange.

What it shows: red fills the whole right side, and the mass piles into a mode peaking near 9K density around activation 5.3–5.7. That is Arabic script. Below 1, red still holds most of the column, where A/1/3450's low range was largely blue — the text's claim that B's version is "more specific in the 0–1 range."

B/1/1334 was not picked by hunting for Arabic. It is the feature in B/1 whose per-token activation vector has the highest [[pearson-correlation]] with A/1/3450's across 40,960,000 shared tokens, the paper's [[activation-similarity]] measure. That correlation is 0.91.

Two seeds, two dictionaries, one Arabic direction: that is the [[universality]] claim, here for a single feature. The systematic version, a median of 0.72 across all of A/1, comes later.

terms.definition: The plot type: a density histogram of one feature's activation values over sampled dataset tokens, with each token colour-coded by an independent proxy score. It is the paper's standard first exhibit for a feature, used here so B/1/1334 can be compared against the same plot for A/1/3450.
The feature this figure shows: feature number 1334 in dictionary-learning run 1 on transformer B. The paper picks it out as the closest match in B to the Arabic-script feature in A.
The paper's lead case-study feature, from the first transformer, which fires on Arabic script. This figure exists to be read against A/1/3450's version of the same plot.

Two one-layer transformers trained with identical hyperparameters, architecture and dataset, differing only in the random seed used for initialization. A is the model studied throughout; B exists mainly to test whether features recur.

terms.term: The middle number in a feature name (the "1" in B/1)
terms.definition: An index for which dictionary-learning run the feature came from; runs vary in dictionary size and L1 coefficient. B/1 is the run matched to A/1 in hyperparameters, but trained on activations from a different transformer and different tokens.

A direction in the MLP activation space recovered by the sparse autoencoder, treated as an interpretable unit in place of a neuron. Its activation on a token is the corresponding hidden unit's value in the autoencoder.
The value the feature takes on a given token, after the autoencoder's ReLU. Higher means the feature is firing more strongly on that token.

How many of the sampled tokens fall into each activation bin, stacked by proxy colour. It is a count-shaped density, so the total area over an interval is the number of tokens activating in that range.

The Arabic-script proxy's score for each token, $\log(P(s\mid\text{Arabic Script})/P(s))$ — how much more likely the string is under the hypothesis that it is Arabic than under the general data distribution. Positive means the proxy thinks the token is Arabic script.

The label telling you which end of the colour scale is Arabic: red, at the right of the bar, is high log-likelihood ratio for Arabic script. Blue is the other end, where the proxy judges the token unlikely to be Arabic.

The specific proxy behind the colours, built by checking whether a character falls in the Arabic Unicode blocks and dividing by a unigram estimate of the token's baseline probability. It is a yardstick that is independent of the model, so agreement between it and the feature is evidence rather than circular.

Generally, a cheaply computable score for "is this string in the hypothesized context", used as an outside check on a feature's interpretation. The paper's proxies are imperfect and it says so, which matters for reading the low-activation end of this plot.

The same colour breakdown as the main panel, but with every column stretched to full height. It answers "of the tokens at this activation level, what fraction score as Arabic", independent of how many tokens there are.

terms.term: Hard zeros (the "0" and ">0" marks left of the axis)
terms.definition: Exact-zero activations are pulled out into their own marker rather than plotted as a bar. The L1 sparsity penalty makes the feature exactly zero on the vast majority of tokens, which would be a delta spike in the density.

The four boxes across the top, each a handful of short text snippets drawn from a bin of the activation axis, with the scored token shaded. Orange intensity marks how strongly the feature fired on that token.
They tie each dataset-example panel to the activation level it was sampled from, so you can see what text looks like at that strength of firing.

terms.term: \xd8, \xaf, \xa9 and similar escape sequences in the snippets
terms.definition: Byte-level tokens shown when an Arabic Unicode character is split across several tokens by the tokenizer. The feature in A typically fires only on the last token of such a character, which is why partial byte strings appear highlighted.
The Pearson correlation between B/1/1334's activation vector and A/1/3450's, both indexed by the same tokens. It is the criterion by which B/1/1334 was selected, not a property discovered afterwards.

The paper's model-independent way of matching features across models: represent each feature as the vector of its activations over a fixed token set, then correlate. Two features count as the same feature if they fire on the same tokens to the same degree.

The claim that the same features form in separately trained models and are recoverable by separate dictionary-learning runs. It is one of the five things the paper tries to establish for each feature it studies in depth.
Whether the feature being on implies the context is present — read here as how much red there is at each activation level. The paper says B/1/1334 is more specific than A/1/3450 in the 0–1 range.
The L1 term on the autoencoder's hidden activations that produces the hard zeros this plot separates out. It is what makes only a few features active per token.

numbers.meaning: Pearson correlation between the activations of A/1/3450 and B/1/1334. B/1/1334 is by construction the highest-correlating feature in B/1, so 0.91 is the maximum achievable match, not a typical one — the median across all A/1 features is much lower.

The number of tokens the activation correlation is computed over: both features are evaluated on the same shared text, giving two vectors of that length which are then correlated. The paper states this size and does not break down how the tokens were sampled.
The feature's index within run B/1. Indices are arbitrary labels assigned by the autoencoder, so 1334 in B has no relation to 3450 in A — that they match at all is the finding.
The dictionary-learning run index. A/1 and B/1 are the matched pair: same dictionary size and L1 coefficient, different transformer and different training activations.

The number of features in the A/1 dictionary, and so in its matched B/1 counterpart. It is an 8x expansion over the transformer's 512 MLP neurons, the size the paper does most of its detailed analysis on.

numbers.value: x-axis 0 to about 7.1, ticks at 1.0 through 7.0
numbers.meaning: The range of activation values B/1/1334 takes on the sampled data; the axis stops where the feature's largest observed activation is. A/1/3450's version of this plot runs to about 9.0, so the two features are on different scales and only their shapes are directly comparable.
Token counts per activation bin. The A/1/3450 plot tops out at 5K, so heights across the two figures should not be compared without noticing the different scales.
The bulk of the feature's firing, and it is almost entirely red. This is the Arabic mode: when the feature is strongly on, the proxy nearly always agrees the token is Arabic script.

The flat low plateau of weakly-activating tokens. The paper's three hypotheses for such weak activations are an imperfect proxy, a calibrated-but-wrong model, and an autoencoder too narrow to hold every true feature.

numbers.value: about 4K at the far left of the axis
numbers.meaning: The spike of just-above-zero activations. Its top band is blue, meaning the tokens that barely activate the feature are the ones least likely to be Arabic — the same shape A/1/3450 shows, but with a larger red share here.

The log-likelihood ratio in nats: 0 means the token is exactly as likely under the Arabic hypothesis as under the general distribution, +5 means about 150 times more likely, -5 about 150 times less. The scale is clipped at both ends.

The activation levels the four dataset-example panels are drawn from, chosen to span weak, middling, strong and near-maximal firing. They let you read what the text actually looks like at each height of the curve.

numbers.value: 151, 3148, 59.55, 22, 1/2 and similar numerals inside the snippets
numbers.meaning: Incidental content of the sampled text, not measurements. They appear because Arabic-script passages in the Pile contain digits and prices, and their presence shows the feature fires on the Arabic tokens around them rather than on the numerals.

From the specificity analysis of A/1/3450: Arabic script is 0.13% of training tokens but 81% of the tokens on which that feature is active. They set the baseline against which the red mass in this plot should be judged as far above chance.

The correlation between A/1/3450's activations and the thresholded Arabic proxy, over 40 million tokens — a feature-versus-proxy number. It is lower than 0.91 partly because several features in A/1 share the job of representing Arabic script.

Median best-match activation correlations across all of A/1: 0.72 when matching features to B/1 features, 0.46 when matching the two transformers' neurons instead. The 0.91 here is a strong case, and the paper's systematic claim rests on the medians, not on this feature.

The logit weight correlation between A/1/3450 and B/1/1334, reported later. The two features fire on nearly the same tokens (0.91) but their output weight vectors agree far less, which the paper attributes to a central mode of near-zero weights it calls interference.

numbers.value: 100 million tokens, 10 per context, 4 tokens of window either side
numbers.meaning: The sampling behind the dataset-example panels: visualizations use a 100M-token subset of the training data, taking only 10 tokens per context, and show four tokens of context on each side of the scored token.

items.caption: This feature clearly responds to Arabic script as well. If anything, it's nicer than our original feature – it's more specific in the 0–1 range. The logit weights tell a similar story:
items.title: The Same Arabic Feature in Model B
items.takeaway: A dictionary trained on a second, separately seeded one-layer transformer contains a feature, B/1/1334, that behaves like the paper's Arabic script feature: its activations are dominated by Arabic-script tokens, and its logit weights show the same shape — one big mode at zero plus a small right-hand mode made almost entirely of Arabic and Arabic-byte tokens. The paper reads the low 0–1 activation band as slightly cleaner here than in the original feature, which is an eyeball comparison rather than a measured one.
items.walkthrough:
Two plots, one feature: **B/1/1334**. "B" is a second one-layer transformer, trained on the same data with a different random seed. "1" names the [[dictionary-learning-run]] on it, and "1334" the feature inside that run. It was not hand-picked by eye: it is the feature whose activations have the highest [[pearson-correlation]] (0.91) with the [[arabic-script-feature]] A/1/3450 over 40,960,000 tokens. The question being asked is [[universality]] — does the same feature reappear in a model trained from scratch?

### The activation histogram

The x axis is activation level, running from 0 to about 7.1. The y axis is how many sampled tokens land at that level.

Each slice is colored by the [[arabic-script-proxy]], a [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]] scoring $\log(P(s|\text{Arabic})/P(s))$. Deep red means the token looks Arabic; deep blue means it does not. The thin strip beneath rescales every column to full height, so it reads directly as "what fraction of tokens here are Arabic."

Watch the 0–1 band. That is where the original feature was murkiest: only about 25% of its barely-active tokens scored Arabic, against 98% above activation 5. That murk is why [[activation-specificity]] gets argued band by band rather than in one number.

Here the blue non-Arabic wedge collapses sooner, and the sampled examples at roughly 0.75 are already mostly Arabic script. That is the entire content of "more specific in the 0–1 range." The paper gives no percentage for B, so treat this as a visual claim.

### The logit-weight histogram

A [[logit-weight]] is one number per vocabulary token: how much this feature firing pushes that token's next-token logit up or down. It is computed by pushing the [[feature-direction]] through the MLP output weights, a linearized layer norm, and the unembedding. Softmax ignores constant shifts, so the weights are [[logit-weight-median-centering|shifted to put the median at zero]].

The x axis spans $-0.6$ to $0.6$. One tall blue mode sits at zero.

The inset magnifies the right tail. It is nearly all red, labelled with Arabic letters and with `\xd8`, `\xd9`, `\xda`, `\xdb` — first bytes of [[utf8-multi-token-characters|Arabic characters split across tokens]]. This is the [[logit-weight-second-mode]] again, in a different model.

The paper's guess about the central blue mode is [[weight-interference]]: weights the model would prefer to be zero, but cannot make zero under [[superposition]].

terms.definition: The feature this figure is about: feature index 1334, from dictionary learning run 1, trained on transformer B. Under the paper's notation the three slots are model / run / feature index.

The second of two one-layer transformers the paper trained with identical hyperparameters, data and architecture, differing only in the random seed used at initialization. It exists mainly so features can be compared across models.
The original Arabic script feature from the main model, which B/1/1334 is being compared against. It is the paper's lead case study.
Title of the lower figure. It plots, over the whole vocabulary, how strongly this feature pushes each token's next-token logit up or down.

terms.term: Distribution of weights from feature to logit for each vocab element
terms.definition: The figure's subtitle, stating what each counted item is: one vocabulary token contributes one weight value to the histogram.

The signed strength with which this feature's firing raises or lowers a given token's logit, obtained by multiplying the feature direction through the MLP output weights, a linear approximation of layer norm, and the unembedding matrix.
The x axis sub-label. It restates that this is a weight along the direct path from the feature to the output logits, not a measured effect on real text.
How many vocabulary tokens fall at each logit-weight value, smoothed into a curve. The paper does not state the normalization, so read the height as relative rather than as a literal token count.
Title of the upper figure. It plots how often the feature takes each activation value across sampled dataset tokens, colored by whether the token looks Arabic.
The scalar output of this feature — the post-ReLU hidden unit of the sparse autoencoder — on a given token. Zero means the feature is off.

Tokens where the feature is exactly off are drawn as their own point rather than folded into the curve, because the L1 sparsity penalty makes exact zero enormously common and would otherwise put a spike of infinite density at 0.
The color scale for the Arabic proxy score, from blue at low values to red at high. It is applied identically in both plots.
The legend's direction label: moving right along the color bar, toward red, means the token is more likely to be Arabic script under the proxy.

A cheap per-token score $\log(P(s|\text{Arabic Script})/P(s))$ built by checking whether characters fall inside Arabic Unicode blocks. It is an independent yardstick, computed without looking at the model at all.

The thin band under each main plot, where every column is rescaled to full height. It shows the proportion of Arabic versus non-Arabic tokens at that x value, independent of how many tokens are there.
The four boxes above the activation histogram, each showing text sampled from a band of activation levels, with token background shaded by how strongly the feature fired.
The magnified panel over the right tail of the logit-weight histogram, connected by dashed lines to the region it expands. Without it the second mode would be invisible next to the central peak.
Raw byte tokens that are the first halves of UTF-8 encodings of Arabic-block characters. They carry high logit weight because predicting them is the model's way of starting an Arabic character.
Other byte tokens appearing at the low end of the second mode. \xe0\xa6 is a prefix for Bengali-block characters, so these are not Arabic and sit in the mixed, bluer part of the tail.

terms.term: Arabic letter tokens (و, ل, ب, ك, م, د, ر, ا, ص, ال, ة, ز, ى, ط)
terms.definition: Whole Arabic letters and short Arabic strings that receive the largest positive logit weights. These are the tokens the feature most raises the probability of when it fires.
Hebrew tokens appearing near the left edge of the zoomed tail. They get mildly positive weight but score low on the Arabic proxy, so they are drawn blue.
Latin-script tokens sitting inside the positive tail. They are examples of weight that does not fit the Arabic interpretation, which the paper attributes to interference rather than intent.
Assorted Greek, accented-Latin, punctuation, currency and Arabic-presentation-form tokens at the low end of the tail. Their presence shows the second mode is not perfectly pure.
The paper's hypothesis for the large central mode: the model would ideally set these weights to zero, but because features share directions in superposition it cannot, so noise leaks through.

Because softmax is invariant to adding a constant to all logits, logit weights have no absolute zero. The paper shifts each feature's weight vector so its median is zero, which is what puts the main mode at 0.0.
Weights for vocabulary elements that are extremely rare or never used are dropped before plotting, since their weights are untrained noise.
The criterion used to pick B/1/1334: the Pearson correlation between two features' activation values over a fixed large token sample. The match was found by search, not chosen by eye.

The claim these two plots support: that dictionary learning on an independently trained model recovers the same feature, suggesting the feature is a fact about the task rather than an accident of one training run.
Whether the feature being on implies Arabic script is present. It is what the color breakdown of the activation histogram is testing, and the 0–1 band is where it is weakest.

numbers.meaning: Pearson correlation between the activations of A/1/3450 and B/1/1334. B/1/1334 was selected precisely as the highest-correlation feature in run B/1, so this is the value of the maximum, not a value drawn at random.
The number of tokens over which that activation correlation was computed. A large sample is needed because the feature fires on a rare slice of the data.
The activation band the caption's claim is about. This is the low end of the range, where a feature is barely on and where the original A feature's activations were least purely Arabic.

The right-hand edge of the activation axis, i.e. the largest activation this feature reaches on the sampled data. The original A/1/3450 ran to about 9, so the two features are on different activation scales; only the shape is comparable.

The y-axis ticks of the activation histogram — the sampled-token density at each activation level. The curve peaks near 9K at an activation around 5.3–5.5, which is the feature's characteristic 'on' level.
The four activation levels the dataset-example panels are drawn from, marked by dotted lines dropping into the histogram. They sample the low, middle, high and extreme parts of the range.

The logit-weight axis range. Because weights are median-centered, 0.0 means 'this feature leaves that token's logit where the median token sits', and the axis is symmetric to show that almost nothing is strongly negative.

Ticks on the density axis of the logit-weight plot, with the central mode peaking near 0.43M. The height is large because nearly the whole vocabulary is packed into a narrow band around zero; the paper does not state the normalization, so treat these as relative.
The slice of logit weight that the inset magnifies. Everything the paper cares about in the second mode lives here, at a density thousands of times below the central peak.

The range of the log-likelihood-ratio color scale. A score of 0 means the token is equally likely under Arabic and under the general data distribution; +5 means about e^5 times more likely under Arabic; -5 the reverse.

For the original feature A/1/3450, the share of barely-active tokens that scored as Arabic by the proxy. It is the low-band number that B/1/1334 is being informally compared against — and the paper reports no matching figure for B.
For A/1/3450, the share of tokens with activation above 5 that scored as Arabic. The gap between this and 25% is exactly why the low band is worth arguing about separately.
For A/1/3450, the share of all tokens on which the feature is active at all that scored as Arabic, pooling every activation level.
The share of training tokens that are Arabic script. This is the base rate; against it, 81% is the size of the specificity result.
The run index in both A/1 and B/1. Matched runs on the two transformers used the same dictionary size and L1 coefficient, so this is a like-for-like comparison; A/1 has 4,096 features.

items.caption: To more systematically analyze the similarities between A and B, we look at scatter plots comparing the activations or logit weights:
items.title: Arabic Feature Across Two Models
items.takeaway: Dictionary learning on a second, independently trained transformer produces a feature whose firing pattern closely tracks the original Arabic script feature (Pearson correlation 0.91), while the two features' effects on output token logits agree much less (0.23). The agreement sits in a small cluster of Arabic tokens that both features push up; the disagreement sits in a large, roughly round cloud of small weights near zero, which the paper guesses is interference rather than anything the model cares about.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Two scatter plots, both comparing the same pair of features. One is [[arabic-script-feature]] A/1/3450. The other is B/1/1334, its closest match in a [[dictionary-learning]] run on a second one-layer transformer, trained on the same data with different random seeds. Under [[feature-notation]], the first slot names the model, the second the autoencoder run, the third the feature index. This pair is the paper's [[universality]] test for this feature.

The left plot puts one point at each **token position** in a large sample of data. Its x coordinate is the [[feature-activation]] of B/1/1334 there; its y coordinate is A/1/3450's activation. Colour carries the Arabic-script proxy: red for tokens the proxy scores as Arabic script, blue for the rest. The strips along each axis are marginal distributions, and the note "Most probability mass is at zero" with the `>0` break exists because the feature is off on nearly every token.

The right plot puts one point at each **vocabulary token**. Its coordinates are the two features' [[logit-weight]] for that token — how much the feature firing pushes that token's next-token logit up or down. Each vector is shifted so its median is zero ([[logit-weight-median-centering]]), which is why the cloud sits on the origin.

### How to read it

A point on the diagonal means the two runs agree about that token. The number above each panel is the [[pearson-correlation]] of all the points: 0.91 for activations ([[activation-similarity]]) and 0.23 for logit weights ([[logit-weight-similarity]]).

### What it shows

On the left, a red band runs up the diagonal into a dense clump near $(5.5,\,6.5)$. Both features fire on the same Arabic tokens, at similar strengths.

On the right, two populations. A small red group sits top right — Arabic tokens that both features upweight, the [[logit-weight-second-mode]] again, now in two dimensions. Around the origin sits a much larger blue cloud, roughly circular and untilted.

Correlation is a count-weighted average over points. The central cloud holds nearly the whole vocabulary; the Arabic cluster holds a few dozen tokens. A round cloud contributes essentially nothing to correlation, so the bulk drags the number down to 0.23.

The paper's guess, hedged with a question mark on the label, is that the cloud is [[interference]] — weights the model would prefer to be zero but cannot zero out, because [[superposition]] leaves feature directions non-orthogonal.

terms.definition: The paper's lead Arabic script feature: feature number 3450 in dictionary learning run 1 on transformer A. It supplies the y coordinate in both panels.

Feature 1334 in run 1 of dictionary learning on transformer B, a separately trained one-layer model. It was picked as the feature in B/1 whose activations correlate most strongly with A/1/3450's, and supplies the x coordinate in both panels.

Shorthand in the axis labels for the two dictionary learning runs being compared, one per transformer. "Run" here means an autoencoder fit, not a training run of the transformer, though each run here sits on a different transformer.
The scalar value the sparse autoencoder's hidden unit takes for that feature at a given token — how strongly the feature fires there. The left panel's y-axis is printed with a typo, "Activaitons".

One entry of the vector giving how much the feature, when active, raises or lowers each vocabulary token's next-token logit. It is computed by pushing the feature direction through the MLP output weights, a linearised layer norm, and the unembedding.
The subtitle above each panel, giving the Pearson correlation of the plotted point cloud. On the left it is the activation similarity; on the right the logit weight similarity.
Treating a feature as a vector of values over a fixed set of data points, and comparing two features by correlating those vectors. This is what the left panel measures.
Treating a feature as a vector indexed by vocabulary token — its effect on outputs rather than its firing pattern — and correlating those vectors across models. This is what the right panel measures.
The red annotation and shaded ellipse marking the small group of vocabulary tokens, mostly Arabic script characters and their UTF-8 byte fragments, that both features push up strongly.

The blue annotation and shaded circle marking the large central cloud of small logit weights. The question mark is the paper's own hedge: it hypothesises these are cross-talk the model would rather not have, not deliberate effects.

The cross-talk that follows from superposition: because more features are packed in than there are dimensions, feature directions cannot all be orthogonal, so one feature's firing leaks small amounts onto others and onto their output weights.
The hypothesis that the network represents more features than it has neurons, each as its own direction, tolerating some interference because features are rarely active at once.

The annotation pointing at the isolated bin at the left/bottom end of the activation marginals. The feature is inactive on the overwhelming majority of tokens, so that bin is split off to keep the rest of the distribution readable.
The tick just after the axis break on each activation marginal, showing where the strictly positive activations begin. Everything left of it is the exact-zero spike.

The stacked coloured bands running alongside each axis, showing the one-dimensional distribution of that axis's variable with its composition by colour. Reading a marginal shows whether that axis alone separates Arabic from non-Arabic.

terms.term: Red points and red marginal regions
terms.definition: Tokens the Arabic script proxy scores high, meaning it judges them likely to come from Arabic script text. In the right panel red marks Arabic vocabulary tokens.

terms.term: Blue points and blue marginal regions
terms.definition: Tokens the proxy scores low: everything the proxy does not judge to be Arabic script. These dominate both panels by count.
A cheap independent score, the estimated log likelihood ratio $\log(P(s|\text{Arabic Script})/P(s))$ built from Arabic Unicode blocks, used to colour points without consulting the feature itself.
The horizontal and vertical dashed lines at zero on the logit weight axes, marking no effect on a token's logit. Their intersection is where the interference cloud is centred.

The unit of a point differs between panels: on the left each point is one occurrence of a token in the data, on the right each point is one entry of the vocabulary. The same feature pair is plotted over two different index sets.

numbers.meaning: Pearson correlation between the two features' activations, printed above the left panel. It is high because both features are essentially off outside Arabic script and both ramp up together on Arabic tokens; this is also the criterion by which B/1/1334 was selected as A/1/3450's counterpart, so it is the maximum over B/1, not a random pairing.

Pearson correlation between the two features' logit weight vectors, printed above the right panel. It is far lower than 0.91 because nearly every vocabulary token sits in the round central cloud, which is close to uncorrelated, while the tokens the two features agree on are a small cluster far out.

The number of tokens over which the paper says activation correlations are computed when searching for a matching feature. The left panel plots a sample of that; the 0.91 figure is the correlation over the full set.

Feature indices inside their respective dictionaries. They are arbitrary labels assigned by the autoencoder, and carry no meaning beyond identity — matching features across runs never lines up indices.

The dictionary learning run index. Runs differ in dictionary size and L1 coefficient; A/1 and B/1 use identical hyperparameters, so the only difference between them is the random seed of the transformer and of the autoencoder.

The range of feature activation values. Zero means the ReLU hidden unit is off; the observed maximum sits somewhat above 8 for both features, so the panel is square over a shared range and the diagonal is meaningful.

numbers.value: about 5.5 on x and 6.5 on y
numbers.meaning: Where the dense red clump sits: the main Arabic mode, the activation level both features reach on clear Arabic script. It sits slightly above the diagonal because A/1/3450 runs a little hotter than B/1/1334 on the same tokens.

The range of logit weights plotted. Weights are median-centred per feature because softmax is shift-invariant, so only differences between tokens matter; the sign says whether the feature makes a token more or less likely.

The approximate radius of the shaded interference cloud in logit weight units. A weight of that size is small relative to the 0.4 to 0.6 range where the Arabic cluster sits, which is why the paper treats the cloud as incidental.

The corner both axes reach in the Arabic token cluster. These are the tokens whose probability both features raise most when active, and the only region where the two models clearly agree about effects.

Background figures from the specificity section that give the colouring its weight: Arabic script is 0.13% of training tokens, yet 81% of the tokens on which A/1/3450 is active. Red is rare in the data and common wherever the feature fires.

Context from the global universality analysis: the median activation correlation between an A/1 feature and its best match in B/1 is 0.72, while the same procedure on transformer neurons gives 0.46. The 0.91 here is well above the typical feature.

The paper's most extreme case of the same gap, for features A/1/3949 and B/1/3321. It shows the 0.91-versus-0.23 split in this figure is not a one-off, and that logit weight correlation can disagree with activation correlation entirely.

items.caption: This binarized proxy then has a Pearson correlation of 0.8 with the feature activations.
items.title: DNA Activations Split by Proxy
items.takeaway: Every token in a sample of the data is sorted by how strongly the DNA feature A/1/2937 fires on it, and colored by whether a hand-built "is this DNA" score fires on it too. The strong activations are almost entirely DNA and the weak ones are mixed, and across the whole range the feature and the yes/no score reach a Pearson correlation of 0.8.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

The large panel is a histogram over tokens. Each token from a sample of the training data is placed on the horizontal axis by how strongly the [[dna-feature]] A/1/2937 fires on it. That number is the [[feature-activation]] — the ReLU output of one hidden unit of the [[sparse-autoencoder]] — and it runs from 0 to about 11.5 here. The vertical axis, "Density", is simply how many sampled tokens land in that bin, peaking near 25K just above zero.

Each token is also scored by a second, independent thing: the [[dna-proxy]]. This is a [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]], $\log(P(s|\text{DNA})/P(s))$. The numerator treats the string as a random draw over A, T, C and G, each with probability $1/4$. The denominator is a plain [[unigram-p-s-estimate]] of the string under the corpus. A positive value means DNA explains the string better than ordinary text does.

Tokens like `CAT` are both nucleotide triplets and English words, so the score is always taken over groups of at least two tokens, maximizing over prefixes ([[prefix-maximization]]). Those log-ratios come out strongly bimodal, so the paper throws away the magnitude and keeps only the sign — [[proxy-binarization]]. Red means the binarized proxy says DNA; blue means it does not.

### How to read it

Exact zeros are pulled out into the thin sliver left of the axis, marked `0` versus `>0`. The [[l1-sparsity-penalty]] makes most tokens exactly zero, which would otherwise be a spike swamping the plot.

The narrow band below the histogram restretches every column to full height, so you can read the red fraction even where the raw counts are almost nothing. The four boxes on top are five random dataset examples each, tied by dotted lines to roughly 1.3, 4.5, 6.7 and 11.4.

### What it shows

At the top of the range the columns are solid red, and the examples are unbroken nucleotide strings. The paper reports that all 10 random examples above activation 6.0 are DNA. Low down there is a lot of blue.

Across the whole range the two signals correlate at 0.8 ([[feature-proxy-correlation]]). Read that as a ceiling-limited number: one variable is graded and the other has two values, so even perfect ordering could not reach 1.0. The paper also argues most disagreements are the proxy's fault, not the feature's.

terms.definition: The plot's title, and the paper's standard chart for a single feature: a histogram of that feature's activation values over a token sample, broken down by color into whether the feature's proxy fires. It is the paper's basic evidence for activation specificity.

The identifier of the feature being plotted. "A" is the transformer (one of two identically trained one-layer models), "1" is the dictionary learning run, and "2937" is the index of the feature within that run's dictionary.

The name the paper gives A/1/2937 after inspecting it: a feature that fires on long uppercase strings of A, T, C and G used to write nucleotide sequences. The paper says it is the only feature in this dictionary devoted to the DNA context.
How strongly the feature fires on a token — the value of that autoencoder hidden unit after its ReLU. Zero means the feature is off; larger means more strongly on.
The number of sampled tokens whose activation falls in a given bin. It is a raw count of tokens, not a probability density that integrates to one.

The scale the coloring is drawn from: the DNA proxy's score $\log(P(s|\text{DNA})/P(s))$, running from -5 (blue) to +5 (red). Because the paper binarizes on the sign, the histogram reads as two flat colors rather than a gradient.

The legend's arrow, saying which end of the color scale means DNA. Red, the positive end, is where the proxy judges the string more likely under the DNA hypothesis than under the general text distribution.
Tokens whose binarized DNA proxy is positive — the surrounding string looks like a nucleotide sequence by the ATCG character model.
Tokens whose binarized DNA proxy is negative — the string is better explained by ordinary text statistics than by a random ATCG string.

The cheaply computable "is this a DNA sequence" score used as an independent yardstick for the feature. It models DNA as a uniform random string over [ATCG] and is evaluated on groups of at least two tokens.
The paper's general device: a hand-built numerical score for a hypothesized context, computed without reference to the model, so that a feature's behavior can be checked against something external.
The proxy reduced to a yes/no value by taking its sign. The paper does this here because the DNA log-probabilities come out strongly bimodal, so the magnitudes carry little extra information.
The probability of the string under the DNA hypothesis, modeled as an independent draw of each character from {A, T, C, G} with probability 1/4 each.
The probability of the string under the general data distribution, estimated as the product of independent per-token unigram probabilities from the corpus.

The ordinary linear correlation coefficient, here computed between the feature's continuous activation and the proxy's binary 0/1 value. The paper uses it as one number combining sensitivity and specificity.

The separate sliver at the far left holding tokens where the feature's activation is exactly zero, split off from the tokens with any positive activation. The note explains that sparsity puts a spike (a dirac delta) of probability mass at exactly zero, which would dominate the plot if left in.
The property, enforced by the L1 penalty on the autoencoder's hidden layer, that the great majority of features are exactly off on any given token. It is what creates the hard-zero spike.

The same red/blue breakdown with every column stretched to full height, so it shows the proportion of proxy-positive tokens at each activation level rather than the count. It makes the far right readable, where raw counts are near zero.

The four boxes along the top, each holding five randomly drawn text snippets from a band of activation values, tied to their place on the x-axis by dotted lines. They let you check by eye what the feature is firing on at that strength.
Within each snippet the bold token is the one whose activation places it in that band, and the orange shading marks where the feature is active across the window of context shown.
Example snippets from the high-activation boxes: uninterrupted uppercase nucleotide strings, which both the feature and the proxy agree on.

Example snippets from the lowest box, where the feature is weakly on. Some contain A/T/C/G letters inside ordinary English words; these are the false-positive-looking cases the paper attributes partly to an imperfect proxy and partly to an imperfect model or autoencoder.

terms.term: AG ACA GAT TGG, '-GTC CGT GAG, AAA TGT AAA G
terms.definition: Snippets from the middle boxes: nucleotide triplets broken up by spaces or preceded by a 5'- prefix. The proxy's strict ATCG character model fails on these even though they are DNA, which is the paper's main example of the proxy being wrong rather than the feature.
The claim this chart is built to test: that when the feature is on, the hypothesized context is usually present. It is read off the right-hand side of the histogram.
The complementary claim: that when the context is present, the feature is usually on. Correlation across the whole plot mixes this with specificity into one number.

numbers.meaning: The Pearson correlation between the binarized DNA proxy and the feature's activations. The paper offers it as a joint summary of sensitivity and specificity that, unlike a hit rate, takes activation magnitude into account. It is not 1.0 partly because the proxy misses DNA written with spaces, punctuation or missing bases, and partly because a two-valued variable cannot fully track a graded one.

The proxy's sign is the cut point: positive log-likelihood ratio counts as DNA, negative as not. The paper picks the sign rather than a tuned threshold because the log-probabilities come out bimodal, so the exact cut barely matters.

The proxy is never evaluated on a single token, because vocabulary tokens like CAT are legitimate English words as well as nucleotide triplets. Requiring at least two tokens makes the ATCG hypothesis actually discriminating.

The probability assigned to each of A, T, C and G under the DNA hypothesis $P(s|\text{DNA})$ — a uniform random nucleotide string. This is what makes a long ATCG run score very high: each character contributes $\log(0.25/p_{\text{unigram}})$, and the ratio compounds with length.

The tiny probability the paper's parallel character-set proxy (stated for base64) gives to characters outside the allowed set. It is what makes a single stray character collapse the score, and it is why spaces inside TGG AGT push the DNA proxy negative.
The activation level above which the paper reports all 10 randomly sampled dataset examples are DNA. It is the paper's cutoff for calling the feature's upper register clean.
The number of random dataset examples checked above activation 6.0. It is a small sample, and the paper's claim of specificity in the high register rests on it plus the red fraction of the histogram.

The span of activation values this feature takes. There is no fixed scale for feature activations; the range is whatever the autoencoder unit happens to output, so the axis is only comparable within this feature.
Token counts per bin. The peak of roughly 23K sits just above zero, showing that most tokens where the feature is at all on are barely on — the long weak tail is where the blue lives.

The range of the underlying log-likelihood ratio shown in the legend. Because the scores are bimodal and the paper only uses the sign, tokens effectively sit at the two ends and the plot reads as two colors.
Four activation bands are sampled for illustration, at roughly 1.3, 4.5, 6.7 and 11.4 on the axis. They are chosen to span the spectrum, including one band where the feature is only weakly on.

Each band shows five randomly drawn snippets. Random rather than top-activating sampling is the point: the paper argues that judging a unit by its maximum-activating examples makes anything look monosemantic.
The context window shown around the highlighted token in each snippet, per the paper's visualization appendix. It is why the DNA strings appear truncated at both edges.

The subset of the training data used to build these visualizations, sampling only ten tokens from any single context. Sampling sparsely across many contexts avoids letting one long DNA document dominate the picture.

The corresponding correlation for the Arabic script feature A/1/3450 against its own proxy, thresholded at 0 over 40 million tokens. It gives a sense of scale for what 0.8 means in this paper: both are called substantial, and neither is close to 1.

"A" names the transformer, "1" names the dictionary learning run (runs differ in dictionary size and L1 coefficient), and "2937" is the feature's index inside that run's dictionary. The index carries no meaning of its own.

items.caption: Below we show a grid of random examples at four activation levels (including feature off) where the proxy does and doesn't fire.
items.title: The DNA Feature-Proxy Disagreement Grid
items.takeaway: A random-sample grid crossing the DNA feature's activation level against whether the hand-built DNA proxy fires, used to audit the cases where the two disagree. The authors read all 24 disagreements and attribute 22 of them to the proxy's strict ATCG vocabulary rather than to the feature, leaving one genuine miss and one genuine false alarm. It is a hand-judged count of 48 examples, so it supports the claim that the feature is sensitive and specific for DNA rather than measuring it.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Eight boxes of text sit in two rows and four columns, above a thin colored strip.

The strip is the activation histogram for the [[dna-feature]] A/1/2937, which fires on long uppercase runs of A, T, C and G. Its horizontal axis is activation level, from the feature being off at 0 out to about 11.5. Each vertical slice is split by color: red is the share of tokens at that level where the [[dna-proxy]] fires, blue the share where it does not.

That proxy is a hand-built score, not a second model. It models DNA as a random string over ATCG, each base with probability $1/4$, and asks how much more likely a string is under that story than under ordinary text: $\log(P(s|\text{DNA})/P(s))$. The continuous score is then [[proxy-binarization]] — reduced to yes or no by its sign.

Red grows with activation across the strip. That growth is the [[activation-specificity]] claim. The blue at low activations is what the grid above exists to examine.

The four columns are four sampled activation levels, each joined to its place on the axis by a dotted line: off (0), then roughly 4.8, 7.1 and 11.4. The two rows are the proxy's verdict — pink on top for proxy active, blue below for proxy not active.

Each of the eight cells holds six dataset examples drawn at random from that combination, not the strongest ones, which is the point of the design: unlike a list of [[top-dataset-examples]], a random draw can show failures. Within an example, the bold token is the one being scored, four tokens of context sit on either side, and orange shading gives the feature's activation on each token.

### How to read it

Agreement lives in the bottom-left cell, where feature and proxy are both off, and in the top row of the three active columns, where both are on.

Disagreement lives in the other four cells. The top-left cell holds six cases where the proxy fires and the feature is off. The bottom row of the three active columns holds eighteen cases where the feature fires and the proxy does not.

### What it shows

The authors walk those 24 cases and blame the proxy in 22 of them. Spaces (" AAG"), dashes ("5'-"), square brackets and missing bases all break the strict ATCG model, though the text is plainly DNA. The feature also fires on "5'-", where DNA is about to start.

Two errors are marked as real. A red star flags one [[activation-sensitivity]] miss: genuine DNA the feature stays off for, though it starts firing on the next token. A blue star flags one false positive, "sgRNA target", which is DNA talk but not a nucleotide string.

terms.definition: The feature under study: feature number 2937 from dictionary learning run 1 on transformer A. The paper says it is the only feature in that run devoted to modeling DNA context.

The independently computed score for "is this a DNA sequence", equal to the log-likelihood ratio of the string under a DNA model versus under ordinary text. It is the yardstick the feature is checked against, and it is written by hand rather than learned.
The row of cells holding examples where the binarized DNA proxy came out positive. Its cells are shaded pink.
The row of cells holding examples where the binarized DNA proxy came out non-positive. Its cells are shaded blue.
The scalar value the sparse autoencoder's hidden unit takes on a token, after the ReLU. Here it both labels the histogram axis and selects which column of examples you are reading.
The leftmost column and the isolated bar at 0: tokens where the feature's activation is exactly zero. It is shown as its own bucket rather than folded into the low end of the continuum.
Within each slice of the bottom strip, the portion of tokens at that activation level for which the proxy fired. Red climbing toward the right is the specificity story in one picture.
The complementary portion of each slice: tokens at that activation level where the proxy did not fire. Blue at low activations is what the example grid is auditing.

The small filled dot and open circle just under the axis, separating the exactly-zero bucket from the continuum of positive activations. They mark that the leftmost bar is not part of the smooth distribution.
The four dashed lines running from each column of cells down to a point on the activation axis. They say which activation level the six examples in that column were sampled from.
Per-token shading inside an example, darker where the feature activates more strongly. It lets you see the feature switching on partway through a string.
Within each example, the single token whose activation put that example in this column. The surrounding tokens are context, four on each side.
The mark on the one case the authors count as a genuine failure of sensitivity: real DNA ("for: ATCGTGCGTGACATT") that the proxy flags and the feature misses.
The mark on the one case the authors count as a genuine failure of specificity: "sgRNA target BBL_gRNA_", where the feature fires on text about DNA that is not itself a nucleotide string.
Here, a token that really is part of a DNA sequence but on which the feature stays off. One such case is marked in the grid.
Here, a token on which the feature fires that the authors judge is not DNA. One such case is marked in the grid.
Snippets pulled at random from the tokens meeting a cell's condition, rather than the ones with the highest activation. Random sampling is what makes the grid capable of exposing errors.

terms.term: GCAT strings that are contextually not DNA
terms.definition: The column-1 caption's name for text such as "PISCATAWAY" or "GRETTA LEVINS", where letters from the ATCG alphabet happen to line up and the proxy fires even though no DNA is present. These are proxy errors, not feature errors.

The formatting the captions blame for the proxy going silent on real DNA — " AAG", "AC-3'", "5'-AAG", "AG[AG...]". Any character outside ATCG collapses the proxy's likelihood, while the feature keeps firing.

Standard biochemistry notation for the two ends of a nucleotide strand, appearing in examples like "5'-TCT". The feature fires on the prefix itself, which the authors read as it predicting the DNA that follows.

Guide RNA, terminology from gene editing that appears in the blue-starred example. It is molecular-biology vocabulary rather than a nucleotide sequence, which is why the authors count the feature's activation there as a real false positive.
The end-of-text token visible in one of the both-off examples. It appears only as ordinary tokenizer output in a random snippet.

The proxy reduced to a yes/no by taking the sign of its log-likelihood ratio, justified because the ratio's distribution turned out strongly bimodal. Every red/blue split in this figure is a split on that binary value.
The figure's term for a disagreement where the authors judge the feature to be at fault, as opposed to the many where they judge the proxy at fault.

numbers.meaning: The grid's shape: proxy active versus proxy not active, crossed with four sampled activation levels. Every cell is one combination of feature state and proxy verdict.
Random dataset examples shown in each cell. Six is enough to read quickly and small enough to fit eight times on a page; it is not a sample size chosen for statistical power.
Total examples on display, being 8 cells times 6 examples. This is the full evidence base for the figure's conclusion.
The activation level of the leftmost column, drawn as its own isolated bar: the feature is entirely off. It also serves as the threshold for the binarized proxy, whose sign decides red versus blue.

The three positive activation levels the other columns were sampled at, read off where their dotted lines meet the axis. They span the low-middle, middle and top of the feature's range so that purity can be compared across registers.
The range of the activation axis, i.e. the largest value this feature takes on the sampled data. The red share of the strip approaches all of it at the far right.
Examples in the top-left cell: cases where the proxy fires but the feature is off. All six sit in the feature-off column, so this cell is the entire sensitivity audit shown here.

Examples in the bottom row across the three active columns (3 x 6): cases where the feature fires but the proxy does not. The summary text on the right calls these "flagged by the proxy", which reads as loose wording, since the proxy is precisely what did not fire on them.
Disagreements the authors count as real errors of the feature, out of the 24 disagreements shown. The remaining 22 they attribute to the proxy's strict ATCG vocabulary.
The false negative rate implied by the top-left cell: one of the six proxy-positive, feature-off examples is genuine DNA the feature missed. The other five are strings the proxy misread.
The false positive rate implied by the bottom row: one of the eighteen feature-on, proxy-off examples is judged not to be DNA. The other seventeen are DNA the proxy's character model could not score.
The Pearson correlation between the binarized DNA proxy and the feature's activations, reported in the surrounding text. It is the single-number summary the grid is meant to explain the gaps in.
From the text just above: all ten random dataset examples with activation above 6.0 were DNA. This is why the figure spends its attention on the lower registers instead.

The probability the proxy assigns each of A, T, C and G under its DNA model, treating a sequence as uniform random bases. Any other character therefore drives the likelihood ratio sharply negative, which is the mechanism behind the spaces-and-dashes failures.

The minimum number of tokens the proxy is evaluated over, because single tokens such as CAT occur in ordinary English as well as in DNA. Grouping tokens is what keeps the proxy from firing on every stray codon-like word.
Tokens of context displayed on each side of the scored token in every example, per the paper's visualization appendix. It is why each snippet is a nine-token window rather than a full sentence.
The visualization dataset: a 100 million token subset of training data, taking only 10 tokens from each context. The random examples in the grid are drawn from this pool.
The number of learned features in run A/1 and the number of MLP neurons in transformer A. The feature shown, A/1/2937, is one of those 4,096 directions living in a 512-dimensional activation space.

items.caption: The downstream effect of the DNA feature being active, as measured by logit weights, make sense, with all the top tokens being combinations of nucleotides like AGT and GCC.
items.title: The DNA Feature's Logit Weights
items.takeaway: Plotting how much the DNA feature A/1/2937 pushes each vocabulary token's next-token logit up or down, the paper finds the usual shape: a tall mode of near-zero weights, plus a tiny bump far out in the right tail. Every token in that bump is a short uppercase string of A, T, C and G — 'ATCC', 'GCC', 'AGT', 'TTTT' and so on. What the feature does to the model's predictions therefore matches what makes it fire, and logit weights are never shown to the dictionary learning, so this is independent of how the feature was found.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

A [[logit-weight|logit weight]] is one number per vocabulary token: how much that token's next-token logit moves when a feature fires.

The paper reads it off a single linear route from the [[feature-direction|feature direction]] through the [[mlp-output-weights|MLP output weights]], a [[layer-norm-linearization|linearised layer norm]], and the [[unembedding-matrix|unembedding matrix]] — the [[path-expansion-logit-attribution|path expansion]] $d_i W_{down} \pi L W_{unembed}$.

Here the whole vector for the [[dna-feature|DNA feature]] A/1/2937 is drawn as a smoothed histogram: one point per vocabulary token, with [[anomalous-token-exclusion|never-used tokens dropped]].

### How to read it

The horizontal axis is the logit weight, from $-0.6$ to $0.6$. The vertical axis, Density, is tokens per unit of logit weight, so an area under the curve is a token count. The curve peaks near $0.37$M, so a slice $0.01$ wide there covers roughly $3{,}700$ tokens.

The zero point is arbitrary. Softmax is shift-invariant, so the paper [[logit-weight-median-centering|slides each feature's weights until the median is zero]].

Colour carries separate evidence. Each token is tinted by the [[dna-proxy|DNA proxy]] — the [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy|log-likelihood ratio]] $\log(P(s|\text{DNA})/P(s))$ — blue at $-5$ for non-DNA, red at $+5$ for DNA.

The inset magnifies roughly $0.2$ to $0.6$. The strip under the axis shows, at each position, the blue/red split of the tokens sitting there.

### What it shows

A single tall mode sits at $0.0$: almost every token barely moves. The label "Interference Weights?" is the paper's suggestion, question mark included, that this bulk is [[weight-interference|unwanted cross-talk]] forced by [[superposition]] rather than intended behaviour.

Far out in the tail is a [[logit-weight-second-mode|second, tiny mode]] near $0.46$, too small to see at the main scale.

The inset names who sits where. At about $0.26$ the tokens are ordinary text — ' TT', 'ARIES', 'clonal', 'ICAL', 'AGS', 'IAL', ' shooter', 'AX', `'↵\n '`, 'AK'. At about $0.35$ they are mixed: 'CU', 'TAC', ')~', ' GAG', "'-", ' ADVISED'.

At the bump every token is nucleotides: 'ATCC', 'GGC', 'AGCC', 'GAT', 'GCT', 'TTTT', 'GTT', 'ATC', 'ATT', 'AG', 'AAT', 'CCT', 'GAG', 'GTC', 'CTC', 'ATCT', 'GT', 'ACCT', 'ACC', 'CCCC', 'GG', 'GCC'. Above about $0.48$ a brace collects 'CACT', 'AGC', 'GAC', 'AGG', 'AGT', 'CTT'.

The strip says the same without reading tokens: all blue below $0.30$, mixed between $0.31$ and $0.41$, solid red from about $0.42$ on.

The output side matches the input side. The paper's wording — "all the top tokens" are nucleotide combinations — holds at the top; at the $0.35$ shoulder the listed tokens are not all DNA.

Nothing about logits enters the [[dictionary-learning]] objective, which sees only MLP activations. That is what makes this a [[feature-downstream-effects|downstream check]] rather than a restatement.

terms.definition: The chart's title. It is a smoothed histogram over vocabulary tokens of the single feature's logit weight vector, not a distribution over features or over data.

The feature being plotted, in the paper's naming scheme: transformer A, dictionary learning run 1, feature index 2937. It fires on long uppercase runs of A, T, C and G, and the paper says it is the only feature devoted to the DNA context.

terms.term: "Distribution of weights from feature to logit for each vocab element."
terms.definition: The subtitle, which fixes what a single data point is: one vocabulary token, and the weight running from this one feature to that token's logit.

How much this feature firing adds to (positive) or subtracts from (negative) that token's next-token logit, before softmax. It is a weight, not a probability change, and its effect scales with the feature's activation.

Vocabulary tokens per unit of logit weight, smoothed into a curve rather than binned into bars. Area under the curve over an x-interval is approximately the number of tokens whose logit weight falls in that interval.
One entry of the model's token vocabulary — the unit indexed by the logit weight vector. Extremely rare or never-used entries are excluded from the plot.

An annotation pointing at the tall central mode. It marks the paper's hypothesis, stated with a question mark, that these near-zero weights are noise the model is forced to carry because features share directions, not behaviour it wants.

terms.term: "Note the bump in the right tail, which corresponds to DNA tokens."
terms.definition: The instruction printed above the inset. It tells you the point of the figure is the small far-right mass, not the central peak.

The colour scale, running blue through white to red. It encodes the DNA proxy's score for a token, and it is independent of the logit weights: the x-position comes from the model's weights, the colour comes from an outside string statistic.
The arrow label on the colour legend, saying which direction is DNA-like. Red (high ratio) means the token looks like it came from a nucleotide string; blue (low ratio) means it does not.

The string being scored by the proxy $\log(P(s|\text{DNA})/P(s))$. The numerator models DNA as a uniform draw over A, T, C and G; the denominator is a unigram estimate of how likely the string is in general text.
The magnified copy of the right tail, shown because the second mode is far too short to see against a peak of 0.37M. Its vertical scale is stretched enormously relative to the main plot.

The thin horizontal band beneath the main plot. At each logit weight it shows the blue/red proportions of the tokens sitting there, rescaled to full height, so it reports composition rather than count.
The tall blue peak centred on zero, holding essentially the whole vocabulary. Its tokens are neither pushed up nor down by any appreciable amount when the feature fires.
The small red mass out near 0.46. It is the recurring second mode the paper finds for interpretable features: the tokens whose likelihood the feature most increases.
The tokens at the bump, all two- to four-character uppercase strings over the alphabet A, T, C, G. These are the fragments a byte-pair tokenizer produces when it chews through a nucleotide sequence.

The tokens collected by the curly brace at the extreme right, above roughly 0.48 — the very highest logit weights of all. They are again pure A/T/C/G strings, which is the paper's claim that the top tokens are nucleotide combinations.

The tokens labelled at the shoulder around 0.35, where the composition strip is still mixed. Some are DNA-compatible ('TAC', ' GAG') and some are not ('CU' contains U, a base of RNA rather than DNA; ' ADVISED' is ordinary English).
The tokens labelled at about 0.26, still inside the blue slope. They are ordinary uppercase-ish text fragments, not DNA, showing where the tail stops being generic and starts being nucleotides.
The two example tokens the paper names in its sentence introducing the figure. Both are three-base codon-length strings, and both sit at the far right of the tail.

A token that is spellable in the ATCG alphabet but also occurs in ordinary text. The paper flags exactly this ambiguity elsewhere (its example is 'CAT'), and handles it by scoring the proxy on groups of at least two tokens rather than single tokens.
Four-character single-base runs. Homopolymer stretches are common enough in nucleotide text that the tokenizer gave them their own tokens.
Two-character nucleotide tokens in the bump. Their presence shows the feature upweights DNA fragments at several token lengths, not just triplets.

terms.term: Leading-space tokens (' TT', ' GAG', ' shooter', ' ADVISED')
terms.definition: Tokens whose printed form begins with a space, a byte-pair encoding convention marking word-initial position. They are distinct vocabulary entries from their unspaced counterparts and get their own logit weights.
The newline token, drawn with a return glyph so it is visible. It appears among the non-DNA tokens partway up the tail.

A direction in the MLP's activation space recovered by the sparse autoencoder, which the paper treats as the interpretable unit in place of a neuron. Its logit weight vector is what this figure plots.

numbers.meaning: The three parts of the feature's name. 'A' is the transformer (the paper trains two identical one-layer models differing only in seed, A and B). '1' is the dictionary learning run, which fixes the dictionary size and L1 coefficient. '2937' is the index of this particular feature within that run.

The horizontal range of the plot, with ticks every 0.1. Logit weights are small in absolute terms because the softmax only cares about differences between logits; the whole story is in the sub-unit spread, not in large values.

The vertical ticks, in tokens per unit of logit weight, evenly spaced every 50,000. The axis has to reach hundreds of thousands because the whole vocabulary is squeezed into a peak only about a tenth of a logit-weight unit wide.

The height and position of the central peak. Reading it as a density: a window 0.01 wide at the peak holds roughly 0.37M times 0.01, about 3,700 tokens. Integrating the whole curve gives a few tens of thousands, which is the vocabulary size after excluded tokens are dropped; the paper does not state that size.
The slice of the horizontal axis the inset magnifies. It starts where the central mode has essentially died out, so the inset contains only tail.
Where the pointer for ' TT', 'ARIES', 'clonal', 'ICAL', 'AGS', 'IAL', ' shooter', 'AX', the newline token and 'AK' lands. This is still on the descending blue slope, and the tokens there are not DNA.
Where the pointer for 'CU', 'TAC', ')~', ' GAG', "'-" and ' ADVISED' lands. It sits on the shoulder where the composition strip first turns substantially red, which is why the list is a mixture.
The centre of the second mode, the small red bump, and where the large nucleotide token list points. It is the densest point of the DNA tail.
The span the curly brace covers, holding 'CACT', 'AGC', 'GAC', 'AGG', 'AGT', 'CTT'. These are the highest logit weights this feature assigns to anything, roughly 0.5 above the median.

Ticks on the colour legend, the value of the DNA log-likelihood ratio. Zero means the string is equally likely under 'this is DNA' and under general text; positive favours DNA. The paper does not say whether these are nats or bits, and the sign alone is what it uses when it binarises this proxy elsewhere.

Not printed here, but the number the colour depends on: the proxy models DNA as a random string in which each of A, T, C and G has probability 1/4. The denominator P(s) is a product of per-token unigram probabilities.

The three regimes of the composition strip. Below 0.30 essentially every token there is blue, so upweighted tokens are ordinary text. Between 0.31 and 0.41 the red fraction climbs unevenly. From about 0.42 to the right edge the strip is entirely red, meaning every token the feature upweights that strongly scores as DNA.

The sizes of the two nucleotide token lists — 22 tokens named at the bump and 6 at the extreme tail. Together they are the concrete content behind the caption's claim that all the top tokens are nucleotide combinations.

The character length of the nucleotide tokens shown, from 'AG' and 'GG' up to 'ATCC' and 'ACCT'. The tokenizer was not built for DNA, so a nucleotide sequence gets cut into short, irregular pieces rather than clean codons.

Not in this figure, but the number it is being read against: the Pearson correlation between the binarised DNA proxy and this feature's activations, reported one subsection earlier. That number is about when the feature fires; this figure is about what it then does.

items.caption: The neuron whose coefficient is the highest in our feature's vector, A/neurons/227, also has no DNA sequences in its top activating examples.
items.title: The DNA Feature's Nearest Neuron
items.takeaway: The neuron that comes closest to the DNA feature is not a DNA neuron: across its whole activation range, and in random examples drawn from the top of that range, the DNA proxy fires on only a thin sliver of tokens and no nucleotide strings appear. The paper reads this as evidence that dictionary learning found something the neuron basis does not already contain, rather than relabelling an already-clean neuron.
items.walkthrough:
**What this is.** A histogram of one neuron's activations, drawn in the same format the paper uses for its learned features ([[feature-activation-distribution-plot]]). The title names the unit: A/neurons/67. Under the paper's [[neuron-notation]], "A/neurons/" marks an MLP neuron of transformer A — one of the 512 in the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]] — not one of the 4,096 dictionary entries in run A/1.

**Why a neuron is on the page.** The [[dna-feature]] A/1/2937 fires on long uppercase runs of A, T, C and G. Before crediting [[dictionary-learning]] with finding it, the paper checks whether the feature is just a neuron under a new name ([[feature-neuron-nonalignment]]). One route in is the [[most-correlated-neuron]]: the neuron whose activations track the feature's most closely over roughly 40 million dataset examples. For A/1/2937 that neuron is A/neurons/67.

**How to read it.** Left to right is the neuron's activation on a token, from just above zero out to about 6.4. Exact zeros are pulled out to the two ticks at the far left, because sparsity would otherwise put a spike at 0. Height is how many tokens land at that activation.

Color is not activation. It is the [[dna-proxy]], the [[computational-proxy]] score $\log(P(s|\text{DNA})/P(s))$ ([[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]]). Red means the string is far likelier under a DNA model than under ordinary text; blue means it is not. The band underneath renormalizes each column to full height, so even a small red fraction stays visible.

The four boxes hold random dataset examples at the four activation levels the dotted lines mark. Each line is one sampled token, bolded, with four tokens of context on either side; orange shading tracks how hard the neuron fires there.

**What it shows.** Blue, all the way across. The red sliver along the bottom never grows into a majority, even at the neuron's highest activations. The top box, near activation 6.2, holds GDHVRSKVFKQEKGKE and TTSAVAAQRGYST — protein-style letter runs — plus FIS3, SPSS and TRY_RUN. Capital letters of many kinds, no nucleotide strings. That mixture is ordinary [[polysemanticity]], the condition [[superposition]] predicts.

The feature's own version of this plot peaks near 23K tokens and reaches activation 11.4, going mostly red at the top. This neuron peaks near 0.8M, about thirty-five times denser.

**One caveat about the pointer.** The sentence introducing this item names a different neuron, A/neurons/227 — the one with the largest [[neuron-basis-coefficients]] in the feature's direction vector — and makes the same claim about it. The panel printed here is the correlation check, not the coefficient one, and the paper prints no numeric value for that coefficient. It says elsewhere that it trusts the correlation route more, since neurons differ in activation scale.

terms.definition: The plot's title and its type: a histogram over tokens of how strongly one unit fires, with dataset examples pinned above chosen activation levels. Here it is applied to a neuron rather than to a learned feature.
The unit plotted: neuron 67 of the 512-neuron MLP in transformer A. It is here because its activations correlate more strongly with the DNA feature's than any other neuron's.

A different neuron, named in the sentence that introduces this item: the one with the largest coefficient in the DNA feature's dictionary vector. The paper says it too has no DNA in its top activating examples; it is not the neuron drawn here.
