The DNA feature this whole check is about: feature 2937 of the 4,096 learned in dictionary run A/1 on transformer A. It fires on long uppercase strings of A, T, C and G.
The paper's way of writing a transformer MLP neuron, as against the run/size/index form used for learned features. It keeps the two kinds of unit distinguishable in a sentence.
The label on the row of four boxes: text snippets sampled from the corpus at the activation levels the dotted lines mark, showing what the neuron actually fires on there.
How many tokens in the visualization sample fall at each activation level. It is a count, not a probability, and it excludes the tokens where the neuron is exactly off.
The scalar post-ReLU value of the neuron on a token. Higher means the neuron fires harder on that token.

The quantity the colors encode: how much likelier the surrounding string is under a DNA model than under a general text model. It is the paper's independent yardstick, computed without reference to the model.
The concrete score used here, $\log(P(s|\text{DNA})/P(s))$, with DNA modelled as a random string over the characters A, T, C and G and evaluated on groups of at least two tokens.
The paper's general device: a cheap, hand-built score for "is this the hypothesized context", used to test a unit's interpretation instead of trusting eyeballed examples.
Reads the color bar's direction: moving right along the bar, toward red, means more DNA-like. Blue is the other end.
The continuous scale mapping proxy values onto the filled area of the histogram. It is not binarized here, unlike the version of this plot used for the feature's specificity check.

terms.term: Renormalized band (the strip below the histogram)
terms.definition: The same red/blue split with each activation column stretched to full height, so proportions can be read where the raw density is nearly flat. It is what makes the thin DNA fraction at high activations visible at all.

terms.term: 0 and >0 ticks (far left of the axis)
terms.definition: Markers separating tokens where the neuron is exactly off from tokens where it is on. Zeros are held out of the density because sparsity would otherwise put a spike at the origin.
Vertical lines connecting each example box down to the activation level its snippets were sampled from.
Inside the example boxes, how strongly the neuron fires on each token; darker orange is a stronger activation, no shading is off.
The token each example line is centered on — the one the sample was drawn for. The four tokens on either side are context.
A run of the letters A, T, C and G representing DNA, such as AGTTTCGTTTAC. The claim of this item is that none appear among this neuron's top examples.
An entry of a feature's direction vector, which lives in the 512-dimensional space of MLP neurons. Its size says how much that one neuron contributes to the feature's direction.

terms.term: The feature is not a neuron
terms.definition: The check this item belongs to: showing that dictionary learning did not simply hand back a neuron that was already clean, since that would make the result trivial.
One unit responding to a mixture of unrelated inputs. The mixture of protein fragments, acronyms and code identifiers in the top box is what it looks like here.
The hypothesis that the model packs more features than it has neurons by giving each a direction spread across many neurons, which is why a feature can have no neuron of its own.

numbers.meaning: The index of the plotted neuron among the MLP's 512. It was picked not by hand but by search: it is the neuron whose activations correlate most with the DNA feature's.

The index of the neuron named in the introducing sentence, selected by a different criterion — the largest coefficient in the DNA feature's dictionary vector. The paper makes the same negative claim about it but prints no plot of it here and no value for that coefficient.
The DNA feature's index within run A/1. Feature indices carry no order or meaning; they are just slots in the dictionary.
The width of the MLP layer being decomposed, and so the number of neurons any such comparison can draw from. It is also the dimension of the vector whose coefficients pick out A/neurons/227.
The number of features in run A/1, the dictionary the paper analyses in detail. It is 8 times 512, the expansion factor chosen so the dictionary can hold more features than the layer has neurons.
The expansion factor of run A/1: features per neuron. The paper trains dictionaries from 1x up to 256x, but focuses its detailed work on this one.
The span of the x-axis: the neuron's activation range over the visualization sample. The right edge is roughly where its largest observed activation falls.
The x-axis ticks. They are plain activation units with no normalization, so they are comparable only within this one unit — a neuron's scale need not match a feature's.
The y-axis ticks, in millions of tokens. The curve peaks just under 0.8M immediately above zero activation, meaning the great majority of the neuron's firing is weak.

numbers.value: 23K (peak of the feature's own version of this plot)
numbers.meaning: For comparison: the DNA feature's activation distribution peaks near 23 thousand tokens where this neuron peaks near 800 thousand. The neuron is roughly thirty-five times denser, which is the ordinary situation — features are sparse by construction, neurons are not.
The DNA feature runs to roughly activation 11.4, and its high end turns mostly red. That contrast is the point of putting the two plots near each other.

The color bar's ticks, in log units of the likelihood ratio. Zero is the break-even point where the string is equally likely as DNA or as ordinary text; +5 means about 148 times likelier as DNA, -5 about 148 times less likely.

The four activation levels the dotted lines mark, and so the levels the example boxes sample from. They are spread across the range, with the last near the top, so the reader can see whether purity improves as the neuron fires harder.

numbers.value: 5 lines per box, 20 examples in total
numbers.meaning: How many random snippets are shown at each level. It is a small sample, which is why the paper also reports the full colored distribution rather than resting on the boxes alone.
The window drawn around each sampled token, per the paper's activation-visualization appendix. It is narrow, so a long DNA run would still be recognizable but a long-range context cue might not be.
The size of the training-data subset used to build these visualizations, taking only 10 tokens from each context so the sample spans many documents.
The number of examples over which the feature-to-neuron activation correlation was computed to select A/neurons/67. A large sample matters because both units are off on most tokens.

The Pearson correlation between the binarized DNA proxy and the DNA feature's activations, reported one section earlier. It is the number this neuron's picture is implicitly measured against: the feature tracks the proxy, the neuron does not.

From the parallel Arabic case, the only place the paper prints coefficient magnitudes: 27 neurons had coefficients of at least 0.1 in that feature's direction, and the three largest were negative. It is offered as the shape of what a top coefficient means — one entry among many, not a stand-in for the feature.

sections.title: The Feature Is Not A Neuron

items.caption: A/1/2937 has a correlated feature (corr=0.92) in run B/1, B/1/3680. Their top logit weights agree, and are DNA tokens (e.g. AGT) forming a separate mode (circled on the right) than the bulk of the logit weights for both.
items.title: The DNA Feature in a Second Model
items.takeaway: A separately trained transformer, given its own dictionary learning run, yields a feature that fires on almost exactly the same tokens as the DNA feature (activation correlation 0.92) and pushes up the same nucleotide tokens. Their logit weights agree only weakly overall (0.46), but the disagreement lives in a large near-zero central mode that the paper hypothesizes is interference noise, while the small circled DNA-token mode is shared.
items.walkthrough:
Two scatter plots sit side by side. Both compare the same pair of features: the [[dna-feature]] A/1/2937, plotted on each panel's vertical axis, against B/1/3680 on each horizontal axis.

B is a second transformer, trained on the same dataset with a different random seed, and then given its own [[sparse-autoencoder]] run with identical hyperparameters. Asking whether the same feature turns up there is the paper's test of [[feature-universality]].

### The left panel: when they fire

This is [[activation-similarity]]. Each dot is one token position from the sample corpus. Its horizontal position is how strongly B/1/3680 fired there, its vertical position how strongly A/1/2937 fired.

Color comes from the [[dna-proxy]], reduced to yes/no by its sign: red means the surrounding text scores as a nucleotide sequence, blue means it does not.

The strips outside the frame are marginals — the distribution of each axis on its own, each bar split red and blue by what fraction of the points at that level are which. The note "Most probability mass is at zero" points at the break both axes carry, separating an exact-zero bucket from the ">0" range. Features are sparse, so nearly every token lands in that bucket.

The dots that do fire lie roughly along the diagonal, and the red mass sits together in the far upper right. The [[pearson-correlation]] is 0.92.

### The right panel: what they do

Here each dot is a vocabulary token, not a corpus position, and its coordinates are the two features' [[logit-weight]]s for it — how far each feature's firing pushes that token's next-token logit. This is [[logit-weight-similarity]].

There are two modes. The small red-circled one at the top right, near $0.35$ to $0.55$ on both axes, holds DNA tokens such as "AGT": both models push these up, and by similar amounts.

The large blue-circled one is centered on the origin and holds every other token, with weights small in both models and only loosely related. Its label reads "Interference Weights?", question mark included. The paper's guess ([[weight-interference]]) is that these weights are unwanted, forced by [[superposition]] rather than chosen.

That bulk dominates the count, so the overall correlation is only 0.46. The agreement the paper is pointing at is in the circled minority.

terms.definition: The DNA feature: feature number 2937 in dictionary learning run 1 on model A. It fires on long uppercase strings of A, T, C and G, and the paper says it is the only feature in that run devoted to the DNA context.

The identifier actually printed in both plot headers of this figure. It does not match the prose, which names A/1/2937; elsewhere in the paper A/1/2357 is the base64 feature. Everything else in the figure (the 0.92 correlation, B/1/3680, the DNA tokens) matches the DNA feature, so the header appears to be a typo.

Feature 3680 in dictionary learning run 1 on model B, the counterpart the paper found for the DNA feature. It was selected as the feature in B/1 whose activations correlate most highly with A/1/2937's.

The two one-layer transformers the paper compares, trained on the same dataset with different random seeds. Each has its own sparse autoencoder run, so features found in one are not tied by construction to features found in the other.
The paper's naming scheme: model (A or B), then dictionary learning run (1), then the index of the feature within that run's dictionary.
The panel comparing the two features by when they fire, one point per token position in the sampled corpus.
The panel comparing the two features by what they do, one point per vocabulary token.

For a given feature, a vector with one entry per vocabulary token, giving how much that feature's firing raises or lowers that token's next-token logit. In this one-layer model it can be read straight off the weights, without running the model.
The subtitle on each panel: the Pearson correlation of the two coordinates being plotted in that panel. On the left it is over token activations; on the right it is over per-token logit weights.
The two axes of the left panel: the scalar activation of A/1/2937 (vertical) and of B/1/3680 (horizontal) at the same token position.
The two axes of the right panel: how much A/1/2937 (vertical) and B/1/3680 (horizontal) each push up the same vocabulary token.
Points where the binarized DNA proxy says yes — the text around that token scores as a nucleotide sequence, or in the right panel the token itself is a DNA-like token.
Points where the binarized DNA proxy says no. In the left panel these are ordinary non-DNA contexts; in the right panel, the bulk of the vocabulary.

The narrow bands outside each axis. They show the distribution of that one axis alone, with each bar split into blue and red by the share of points at that level that the proxy calls DNA. Reading them tells you whether an axis on its own separates DNA from non-DNA.

An annotation in the lower left of the activation panel, pointing at the dense band sitting exactly at activation zero. It states that the overwhelming majority of tokens do not activate either feature at all.

A break in both activation axes. The exact-zero bucket is drawn as its own segment, separate from the continuous range of positive activations, so that the sparse nonzero values are not crushed against the axis.
The label on the small red circle in the right panel. AGT is a vocabulary token made of nucleotide letters; the circle gathers tokens of that kind, which both features push up strongly.
A three-letter nucleotide triplet that exists as a single token in the model's vocabulary. It stands in for the family of tokens made from A, T, C and G.

The label on the large blue ellipse in the right panel, question mark in the original. It marks the paper's hypothesis, not a measurement: that this near-zero central mode is cross-talk the model would rather not have, forced on it because features in superposition cannot all be orthogonal.

The hypothesis that the network represents more features than it has neurons by giving each a direction in activation space, at the cost that those directions cannot all be orthogonal and so leak into each other.
Hand-drawn shading over the two clusters in the right panel. They are annotations added to point at the modes; they are not fitted contours or confidence regions.
The dashed vertical and horizontal lines in the right panel, marking logit weight zero on each axis. They show that the bulk mode straddles zero in both models.

numbers.meaning: The Pearson correlation between the activations of A/1/2937 and B/1/3680, printed above the left panel. It is high because the two features fire on essentially the same token positions; the paper reports the same style of number for the Arabic feature (0.91), so this is the level of agreement it treats as a match.

The Pearson correlation between the two features' logit weight vectors, printed above the right panel. It is far below 0.92 because the correlation is computed over all vocabulary tokens, and the near-zero central mode contributes most of them while agreeing only loosely between the two models.
The range of both activation axes in the left panel. Activations are ReLU outputs, so they are non-negative; roughly 11 is the largest value either feature reaches on the sampled data.

The approximate activation level above which the left panel is dominated by red. The paper reports separately that all ten random dataset examples above activation 6.0 for this feature are DNA sequences, so the red concentration in the upper right is consistent with that.
The range of both logit weight axes in the right panel. Logit weights are signed: positive means the feature pushes that token up, negative means it pushes it down.

Where the circled DNA-token cluster sits on both axes. The value is read off the plot, not stated in the text; the point is that these weights are several times larger than the bulk and positive in both models at once.
The span of the dense central mode on both axes. These are the weights the paper suspects are interference: small, centered on zero, and only weakly aligned between the two models.

Context, not in this figure: the Pearson correlation between the binarized DNA proxy and A/1/2937's activations, reported in the specificity section. It is the basis for treating red-vs-blue coloring here as a reasonable stand-in for whether the context really is DNA.

Context: the number of tokens over which the paper defines activation correlation when searching another run for a feature's counterpart. B/1/3680 was chosen as the highest-correlating feature over a sample of that size.

Context from the global universality analysis: matching every A/1 feature to its best B/1 counterpart gives a median activation correlation of 0.72, while matching neurons between the same two transformers gives 0.46. The 0.92 here is well above the feature median, so this pair is a good case rather than a typical one. Note the coincidence that the neuron median equals this figure's logit weight correlation; they measure different things.

Context: the Arabic script feature's activation correlation and logit weight correlation between the same two runs. The same gap appears there, which is why the paper treats the low logit weight correlation as a property of the measure rather than a failure of this particular match.

The dictionary learning run index. Runs differ in dictionary size and L1 coefficient; run 1 is the one used for the individual feature case studies throughout the paper, and both sides of this comparison use it so the hyperparameters match.

items.caption: The activation distribution colored by the corresponding computational proxy, together with the random dataset examples from each activation level, shows that this feature is quite specific to base64.
items.title: Base64 Activations Coloured by Proxy
items.takeaway: The figure is the paper's specificity check for its base64 feature A/1/2357: it stacks every sampled token by how strongly the feature fired, and colours the stack by an independently computed base64 score. The higher the activation, the more completely the column is filled by tokens the score calls base64, which is what the authors mean by calling the feature "quite specific" — though they give no percentage here, and the score itself is admittedly too broad.
items.walkthrough:
You are looking at the entire firing record of one learned feature, spread out along the axis of how hard it fired.

The title names the feature in the paper's [[feature-notation]]: transformer **A**, [[dictionary-learning-run]] **1** (the run with 4,096 learned features), feature index **2357**. That is the [[base64-feature]].

The horizontal axis is the [[feature-activation]] value on a token, running from just above $0$ to about $12.5$. The vertical axis, Density, counts how many sampled tokens fall in each activation bin — nearly 40K in the leftmost bin, thinning to a shelf near 5K between roughly 3.5 and 7, then trailing to nothing.

Note the small break at the left. Tokens where the feature is exactly zero are pulled out of the plot and shown only as the separate stub at $0$; the [[l1-sparsity-penalty]] forces most activations to be hard zeros, so leaving them in would put a spike at the origin taller than everything else. The plotted region begins at the mark `>0`.

Now the colour, which is where the actual claim lives. Every token also gets a [[computational-proxy]] score for base64, computed without reference to the model. It is a [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]]: $\log(P(s\mid\text{base64})/P(s))$. The numerator models base64 as a uniform draw over the 64 characters `[a-zA-Z0-9+/]`, each at $1/64$, with anything else at $10^{-10}$ ([[base64-proxy]]). The denominator is a [[unigram-p-s-estimate]]. The score is taken as the maximum over prefixes ending at the token ([[prefix-maximization]]). Blue is $-5$, red is $+5$, and the legend's arrow marks red as the base64 end.

So each vertical slice is a stack of that bin's tokens sorted by score, and the band underneath redraws the same stacks as proportions. Height tells you how often the feature fires that hard; colour tells you what those tokens were ([[feature-activation-distribution-plot]]).

Reading left to right: at the weakest activations roughly half the column is deep red, with a clear blue and white band on top. By about 2.5 the blue is a sliver. Above about 4 the column is essentially solid red — that is the [[activation-specificity]] claim.

The four panels sample five random examples each at the marked levels, four tokens of context on either side, drawn from a 100-million-token subset ([[activation-visualization-sampling]]). The weakest panel is ordinary web text; the rest are base64 strings.

Two cautions the paper states itself. Red means the proxy fired, not that the text is base64 — hexadecimal scores red too and has its own feature, A/1/3817 ([[hexadecimal-feature]], [[proxy-limitations]]). And the digits left unhighlighted inside these strings belong to a separate feature ([[base64-digit-feature]]).

terms.definition: The plot title. It means the histogram of how strongly this one feature fired across a large sample of dataset tokens, with each bin broken down by the proxy score of the tokens in it.

The identifier of the feature being plotted, in the paper's three-part scheme: transformer A, dictionary learning run 1, feature number 2357 within that run. It is the feature the paper calls the base64 feature.
One of the two one-layer transformers the paper trained with identical hyperparameters and different random seeds. A is the main model studied; B is used mostly for universality checks.
The dictionary learning run, meaning one trained sparse autoencoder. Run A/1 has 4,096 learned features; runs differ in dictionary size and L1 coefficient.
The scalar value this feature takes on a token, i.e. the ReLU hidden-unit value of the sparse autoencoder for dictionary element 2357. Larger means the feature fired harder on that token.
The number of sampled tokens whose activation falls in that bin, labelled in thousands. It measures how often the feature fires at that strength, not how base64 those tokens are.

terms.term: Hard zeros (the note under the axis)
terms.definition: Tokens where the feature's value is exactly zero, excluded from the density curve and shown only as the separate stub at 0. The note explains that sparsity puts a dirac delta of probability mass at zero, which would swamp the rest of the plot.
The axis mark showing where the plotted region begins, immediately above zero. Everything to the right of it is a token on which the feature is actually active.

The quantity the colour encodes: log of the probability of the string under the base64 hypothesis divided by its probability under the general data distribution. It is the paper's standard form for every feature proxy.

The encoding whose alphabet is [a-zA-Z0-9+/], used to write binary data as text; it shows up in web pages, URLs and embedded assets. The paper models a base64 string as a random sequence of those characters.

terms.term: base64 → (label at the red end of the legend)
terms.definition: Marks which direction of the colour scale means base64-like. Red is a high ratio, meaning the surrounding string is far more probable under the base64 model than under ordinary text.
The continuous scale mapping proxy score to colour, blue at -5 through white at 0 to red at +5. Within each vertical slice, tokens are stacked by this score with the reddest at the bottom.

terms.term: Proportion band (the strip below the main plot)
terms.definition: The same stacks rescaled so each activation bin fills the full height. It shows the colour composition at each activation level without the histogram's shape getting in the way, and it is the only place the hard-zero column appears.

Randomly drawn text snippets from the levels marked by the dotted lines, showing what the feature was actually looking at when it fired that hard. They are random at that level, not the top-activating examples, which is what makes them evidence about specificity.
Connect each example panel to the activation level its samples were drawn from, at roughly 0+, 4.7, 8.25 and 11.85.
Shows the feature's activation on each token in the snippet, darker for stronger. The bold token in the middle is the one whose activation places the example in that panel.
Rendered newline characters inside the sampled text. They appear because the visualizer prints the raw token stream, including whitespace tokens.

The claim that when this feature is on, the hypothesized context is present. It is the property this figure is built to test, and the paper treats it as the more important half of the case that a feature is not polysemantic.

A cheaply computed score for whether a string looks like it came from the hypothesized context, built by hand and not from the model. It gives an independent yardstick to compare feature activations against.
The numerator of the proxy: the probability of the string under the assumption it is a random base64 string, computed as a product over characters.
The denominator of the proxy: the probability of the string under the general data distribution, estimated as a product of independent per-token unigram probabilities.

A separate feature in the same run that fires on hexadecimal strings. It matters here because hexadecimal also scores high on the base64 proxy, so some red in this plot belongs to a different feature's territory.

numbers.meaning: The feature's index within dictionary learning run A/1. It is just an identifier; the run's features have no meaningful ordering.
The number of learned features in run A/1, the run this feature comes from. The paper's run sequence goes 512 features in A/0, 4,096 in A/1, 16,384 in A/2.
The range of the activation axis, i.e. the smallest positive to the largest observed value of this feature. The upper end is set by the data: no sampled token drove the feature past roughly 12.5.

The density ticks, in thousands of sampled tokens per activation bin. The curve peaks just under 40K at the smallest positive activations, sits on a shelf near 5K between roughly 3.5 and 7, and falls to zero past about 12.

The ticks on the log-likelihood-ratio colour scale. Zero means the string is equally likely under the base64 model and under general text; +5 means about e^5, roughly 150 times, more likely under base64; -5 the reverse.
The size of the base64 alphabet [a-zA-Z0-9+/], which is what the proxy's model of a base64 string draws from uniformly.
The probability the proxy assigns to each character that is in the base64 alphabet, under the assumption that a base64 string is a uniform random sequence over those characters.

The probability the proxy assigns to any character outside the base64 alphabet. It is a small floor rather than zero, so that a single stray character drives the score down sharply without making it undefined.
The activation levels the four example panels are sampled from, spread across the range so the reader can see how the text changes from the weakest firings to the strongest.
The number of random dataset examples shown per panel. They are sampled rather than cherry-picked from the top, which is what lets them speak to specificity at each level.
The number of tokens of context displayed on each side of the selected token in every snippet, per the paper's visualization settings.
The size in tokens of the training-data subset the visualizations are drawn from, taking only 10 tokens from every context so the samples are spread across many documents.

The Pearson correlation between this feature's activation and its base64 proxy, reported in the text. The authors call it low and attribute it mainly to the proxy being too broad, since hexadecimal and similar strings also score high while being handled by other features.

Digits the text singles out as visible in this figure's snippets without highlighting, because A/1/2357 fires preferentially on letters in base64. The digits are covered by a companion feature, A/1/2364.
The index of the hexadecimal feature in the same run, which handles strings made of [0-9A-F]. It is named to explain why some red in this plot is not really base64.

items.caption: (If we look at the conditional below, we see a more continuous transition to base64-specific tokens.)
items.title: Base64 Logit Weights and Their Conditional Strip
items.takeaway: For the base64 feature A/1/2357, the tokens whose logits it raises shade gradually from ordinary text tokens into base64-specific ones, rather than separating into two clean groups. The narrow strip below the histogram makes this visible by showing, at each logit weight, only the mix of token types and not how many tokens there are.
items.walkthrough:
You are looking at one figure with two panels sharing an x-axis. The tall panel is a histogram over the vocabulary. The thin band underneath is the "conditional" the surrounding text points to.

### What is being counted

Every vocabulary entry gets one number: the [[logit-weight]] of the base64 feature [[base64-feature]] A/1/2357 on that token. It says how much that token's output logit moves when the feature fires. The tall panel plots the distribution of those numbers, with horizontal position the weight and height the number of vocabulary entries there.

Color is a property of the *token*, not of the feature. Each token string $s$ is scored by the [[base64-proxy]], a [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]] $\log(P(s\mid\text{base64})/P(s))$. Deep blue is $-5$: the string is much likelier in ordinary text than in a base64 dump. Deep red is $+5$: the reverse. Each histogram bar is stacked by that score, reddest at the bottom.

Read the tall panel first. The bulk sits at zero and is solid blue, and the authors tag it "Interference Weights?" — a hedged guess that these tiny weights are cross-talk forced by [[superposition]] rather than anything deliberate [[weight-interference]]. To the right there is a shoulder and a small bump near $0.3$, magnified in the inset.

### What the strip adds

The strip has the same x-axis, but each vertical slice is stretched to fill the height. It throws away the count and keeps only the composition: among tokens with this logit weight, what fraction has which proxy score. Regions holding a handful of tokens get the same visual weight as the peak.

So read it left to right. It is solid blue out to roughly zero, then slides through pale blue, then pink, and only reaches saturated red near $0.35$–$0.4$.

That slide is the point. The same strip for the [[arabic-script-feature]] is blue and then abruptly red — a step. The paper's reading is that a token is Arabic or not, close to binary, while base64-ness is graded: `fr` is a French abbreviation *and* a legal base64 pair, so the model has reason to raise it only a little.

terms.definition: The figure's title. It names the object plotted: the spread of one feature's influence on next-token logits, taken across every vocabulary entry.
The feature being plotted, in the paper's naming scheme: transformer A, dictionary-learning run 1, feature index 2357. This is the base64 feature.

terms.term: "Distribution of weights from feature to logit for each vocab element"
terms.definition: The subtitle. It states the unit of the histogram: one data point per vocabulary element, not per token occurrence in the corpus.

For one feature and one vocabulary token, a linear estimate of how much the feature firing pushes that token's logit up or down. It is computed by multiplying the feature's direction through the MLP output weights, a linearized layer norm, and the unembedding matrix.
The horizontal axis of both panels, in logit units. Positive means the feature makes that token more likely; negative means less likely.

The vertical axis of the tall panel: how many vocabulary entries per unit of logit weight sit at that position. Its integral over the axis is the number of vocabulary entries included, so the tick values are far larger than the vocabulary itself.
One entry in the model's token vocabulary. The histogram has one sample per element, so a token that is common in text counts exactly as much as a token that almost never appears.

An annotation, with the question mark left in, pointing at the large blue mode centered on zero. The authors suspect these near-zero weights are unwanted cross-talk from packing many features into few dimensions, not anything the feature is trying to do.

The material to the right of the central peak — the shoulder near 0.1 and the bump near 0.3. For every feature the paper studies in depth, this far-right group turns out to be tokens specific to the feature's context.

terms.term: "Note the bump in the right tail, which corresponds to base64 tokens."
terms.definition: The note above the inset. It asserts that the small far-right hump is made of base64-specific tokens, which the coloring is meant to support.

The magnified box at upper right, redrawing the region from logit weight 0.2 to 0.6 on a vertical scale of roughly the bottom 45K of the main panel. Without it the second mode is only a few pixels tall.
The color scale. It maps each token's base64 proxy score to a color, running blue through white to red.
The arrow on the legend, saying which end of the color scale is which. Red is the base64 end; blue means the token is more characteristic of ordinary text.

The score coloring every token here: log of P(string | base64) over P(string). The numerator models base64 as characters drawn uniformly from [a-zA-Z0-9+/]; the denominator is the string's probability under the ordinary data distribution.
The denominator of the proxy, estimated as the product of independent unigram token probabilities over the string. A string that is common in the corpus gets a large P(s) and therefore a blue score.
The flat band below the histogram. At each logit weight it stretches the color stack to full height, so it shows the proportions of proxy scores at that weight and discards how many tokens are there.

The leftmost label group in the inset, listing tokens found around logit weight 0.24. The stack there is still part blue: these are short strings that occur freely in ordinary text, and '=-' is not even legal base64.

The middle label group, around logit weight 0.35. These are two-character letter pairs, several mixing cases, that are rare in English but ordinary inside base64 — the stack there is almost entirely red.
The label group at the far right tail, the tokens this feature raises most. They are short base64-legal strings with low unigram probability, so the proxy scores them at the red end.

The comparison case, whose version of this same plot appears earlier in the paper. Its conditional strip switches from blue to red abruptly, which is what makes the base64 gradient worth pointing out.
Cross-talk between features whose directions cannot all be orthogonal, so activating one slightly moves others. It is the paper's proposed source of the large central mode of near-zero weights.
Softmax is shift-invariant, so logit weights have no absolute zero. The paper shifts each feature's weights so the median is zero, which is why the central mode sits at the origin.

numbers.meaning: The feature identifier, read in three parts: the transformer it came from (A), the dictionary-learning run (1, which fixes the dictionary size and L1 coefficient), and the index of the feature within that run (2357).
The x-axis range in logit units, tick-marked every 0.1. The weights are small because they are one feature's linear contribution to a logit, not the logit itself.

The y-axis ticks of the tall panel, in vocabulary entries per unit logit weight. They are in the hundreds of thousands because the distribution is squeezed into a range about 0.2 wide, so the height times that width recovers a vocabulary of tens of thousands.
The height of the central peak, the tallest point in the figure. Almost the whole vocabulary is barely affected by this feature, which is what the peak's height encodes.
Where the central peak sits, just right of zero. Zero is the median weight by construction, and the mode landing slightly above it reflects the right skew the text describes.
The median logit weight, set by the paper's centering convention rather than measured. Because softmax ignores a constant added to all logits, only differences between these weights carry meaning.
Where the shoulder of paler blue and pink begins in the tall panel. The text calls this side base64-neutral or slightly base64-leaning, not yet base64-specific.
Where the small bump in the right tail sits, the mode the inset's note attributes to base64 tokens.
The x-range redrawn by the inset. It starts where the central mode has essentially died out, so the inset is showing only the second mode.

The approximate top of the inset's vertical scale, read off the dashed guide in the main panel — roughly the bottom fifth of the 0.25M axis. The second mode is small enough that it needs this much magnification to be legible.

The range of the color scale, in nats of log-likelihood ratio, with ticks at -2.5, 0 and 2.5. Zero (white) means the string is equally likely under base64 and under ordinary text; +5 means about 150 times likelier under base64.
The probability the proxy assigns to each character inside a base64 string, since base64 uses 64 characters. A two-character token that is entirely base64-legal therefore gets a numerator of 1/4096.
The probability the proxy assigns to a character outside [a-zA-Z0-9+/]. It is a stand-in for impossible, and it is what drives a token like '=-' deep into the blue.
Where the conditional strip becomes saturated red — the point past which nearly every token is base64-specific. The transition into it is gradual rather than sudden, which is the figure's claim.

By contrast, where the Arabic feature's conditional strip flips from solid blue to solid red in one step. The two strips are drawn the same way, so the difference in shape is the comparison the text is making.

The Pearson correlation between the base64 proxy and this feature's activations, reported in the same section. The authors read the low value as a fault of the proxy, which also fires on hexadecimal strings that have a feature of their own.
The number of tokens listed in the inset's three label groups, left to right. The rightmost group is short because very few vocabulary entries reach the extreme of the tail.

items.caption: A/1/2357 has a correlated feature (corr=0.85) in run B/1, B/1/2165. It also has high activation specificity for base64 strings:
items.title: The Base64 Feature Found Again in Model B
items.takeaway: A separately trained transformer, decomposed by a separately trained dictionary, yields a feature (B/1/2165) whose activations correlate 0.85 with the base64 feature from the first model, and which fires almost exclusively on base64-looking strings at high activation. The paper offers this as evidence that the base64 feature is a property of models trained on this data rather than an artifact of one dictionary learning run.
items.walkthrough:
This is the specificity plot the paper drew for its [[base64-feature]], redrawn for a feature in a second model. The title names B/1/2165. In the paper's [[feature-notation]], the `B` says the feature comes from the second of two one-layer transformers ([[transformer-a-and-b]]), trained on the same data with the same hyperparameters and a different random seed; the `1` names the [[dictionary-learning-run]]; `2165` is the feature's index inside that run's dictionary.

### How to read it

The horizontal axis is the [[feature-activation]] value, running from just above zero to about 9.5. Exact zeros are pulled out and shown as the separate mark at the far left, because a sparse code puts a large spike of mass at exactly zero. The vertical axis counts tokens at each activation level, taken from a sampled hundred-million-token slice of the training data ([[activation-visualization-sampling]]).

Each vertical slice of the shaded region is then split by color. The color is not the feature's own output. It is an independent score computed from the text alone, a [[computational-proxy]]: the [[base64-proxy]] $\log(P(s\mid\text{base64})/P(s))$, whose numerator treats the string as random characters each of probability $1/64$ and whose denominator is a unigram estimate. Red means base64 is far more likely; blue means far less. The legend says "Prefix String" because the score is maximized over the prefixes ending at that token ([[prefix-maximization]]).

The narrow band under the histogram renormalizes each column to full height, so it reads as the proxy's conditional distribution given activation. The four boxes are five sampled examples from the four activation levels marked by dotted lines; orange shading marks activation, and the bold token is the one being measured.

### What it shows

Below roughly 2.0 the columns carry visible blue — the feature fires weakly on strings the proxy rejects, like `nrk,nrk,` and `Cpz`. Above roughly 4.0 the columns are essentially all red and the sampled examples are unbroken base64. That pattern is what the paper calls [[activation-specificity]].

The figure exists for [[universality]]. The quoted 0.85 is [[activation-similarity]]: the [[pearson-correlation]] between the two features' activation vectors over a shared set of tokens. B/1/2165 is A/1/2357's nearest counterpart by that measure, and neither dictionary saw the other.

The paper quotes no specificity number for B and offers the picture instead. Note also that it calls this proxy too broad — against A's feature it reached only 0.38 — so low-activation blue is weak evidence of a false positive.

terms.definition: The paper's standard specificity picture: a histogram of how often a feature takes each activation value, with each column split by an independently computed text score. It is the same plot type used for the Arabic, DNA and base64 features.
The feature this figure is about: feature number 2165 in dictionary learning run 1 trained on transformer B. It is the base64 feature as found in the second model.
The base64 feature in the first model, studied in detail earlier in the paper. It is named in the caption as the feature B/1/2165 is being matched against; it does not appear in the plot itself.

The second of the paper's two one-layer transformers. A and B share architecture, dataset and hyperparameters and differ only in the random seed used for initialization, so B is used to test whether features recur across models.

The index of the dictionary learning run — one trained sparse autoencoder. Runs differ in dictionary size and in the L1 coefficient; run 1 on B is the matched pair of run 1 on A, trained with the same hyperparameters but on activations from a different transformer.
The feature's index within that run's learned dictionary. Indices carry no meaning and are not comparable between runs; feature 2165 in B has nothing to do with feature 2165 in A.

A direction in the MLP activation space recovered by the sparse autoencoder, together with the scalar coefficient it takes on each token. It is the unit the paper proposes to analyze the model in, instead of neurons.
The scalar value this feature takes at a given token — the coefficient the autoencoder's encoder assigns to this dictionary direction, after ReLU. Larger means the feature is firing more strongly.
How many sampled tokens fall in each activation bin. It is a raw count over the sampled corpus, labeled in thousands, not a normalized probability density.

terms.term: 0 and >0 marks at the left of the axis
terms.definition: A separator showing that hard zeros are excluded from the plot body. Sparsity means most tokens give this feature exactly zero, which would be a spike of mass at the origin swamping everything else.

terms.term: Prefix String Log-Likelihood Ratio (color legend title)
terms.definition: The quantity the colors encode: how much more likely the text ending at this token is under a base64 hypothesis than under the general data distribution, in log space. It is computed from the text only and never sees the model.

A reminder that the score is evaluated on several prefixes ending at the token in question, and the largest value is kept. This matters because a feature can fire more strongly deeper into a base64 run.

The specific score behind the colors: base64 is modeled as an independent random draw from the 64 characters [a-zA-Z0-9+/], and P(s) from a unigram token model. The paper judges it too broad, since things like hexadecimal strings also score high.

A cheap, model-independent guess at whether the hypothesized context is present, used as an outside yardstick against which the feature's firing is checked. Coloring by the proxy is how the paper avoids grading the feature by its own top examples.
The text encoding that writes binary data as characters drawn from [a-zA-Z0-9+/]. In a text corpus it shows up as long runs of mixed-case letters and digits with no word structure.

terms.term: Blue end of the color bar
terms.definition: Strongly negative log-likelihood ratio: the string is much less likely under the base64 hypothesis than under ordinary text. Blue area therefore marks tokens where the feature fires but the proxy says no base64.

terms.term: Red end of the color bar
terms.definition: Strongly positive log-likelihood ratio: the string looks far more like base64 than like ordinary text. Red is the color of agreement between feature and proxy.

The same data with every column stretched to full height, so it shows the mixture of proxy scores conditional on activation level rather than absolute counts. It makes the high-activation behavior readable where the raw counts are near zero.

Five randomly sampled text snippets drawn from each of four activation levels, connected to the histogram by dotted lines. They are sampled at that level rather than picked as top examples, which is what makes them evidence about typical behavior.
The token whose activation places that example at this point on the axis. The surrounding characters are context, shown four tokens either side.

Per-token feature activation across the whole snippet: darker orange means the feature fires more strongly there. It lets you see the feature switching on across a base64 run rather than at a single point.

The Pearson correlation between the activation vectors of A/1/2357 and B/1/2165 over a shared set of dataset tokens. It is the paper's activation similarity measure, and B/1/2165 is the feature in run B/1 that maximizes it against A/1/2357.

Representing a feature as the vector of values it takes over a fixed set of data points, and comparing features across models by correlating those vectors. It gives a model-independent handle on 'the same feature' when the two models share no weights or basis.

Ordinary linear correlation, between -1 and 1, computed here between two features' activation vectors. It is invariant to the arbitrary scale of each dictionary's activations, which is why the differing activation ranges of A and B do not matter.
The claim that when the feature is on, the hypothesized context is present — the direction that argues against the unit being polysemantic. This figure is the specificity evidence for B/1/2165.
The question of whether the same features arise in separately trained models. The paper treats it as evidence that recovered features are not artifacts of one dictionary learning run.

The autoencoder whose hidden units are the features and whose decoder columns are the feature directions, trained on model activations with a reconstruction term and an L1 penalty. The two dictionaries compared here were trained separately, on activations from different transformers.

A separate feature in model A that handles hexadecimal strings. It is why the paper says the base64 proxy is too broad: hex scores high on the proxy but is covered by its own feature, not by the base64 feature.

numbers.meaning: The Pearson correlation between the activations of A/1/2357 and B/1/2165 over a shared set of dataset tokens. B/1/2165 is the highest-correlating feature in run B/1, so this is the best available match, not a typical one.

Context from the paper's global analysis, not printed on this figure: the median activation correlation between a feature in A/1 and its best match in B/1 is 0.72, while matching neurons between the two transformers gives only 0.46. Against those, 0.85 is a well-matched feature.

The Pearson correlation between the base64 proxy and the activations of A/1/2357. The paper attributes the low value mostly to the proxy being too broad rather than to the feature being impure, which is why the blue material at low activation here should be read cautiously.

The character probabilities in the base64 hypothesis: each of the 64 base64 characters gets 1/64, everything else gets 10^-10 so that a single non-base64 character crushes the score. This is what makes the red-blue split near-binary on long strings.
The size of the base64 alphabet [a-zA-Z0-9+/], which sets the 1/64 uniform probability above.

The observed activation range of B/1/2165. The comparable plot for A/1/2357 runs to about 12.5; the two dictionaries were trained separately, so activation scale is not comparable between them, and the 0.85 correlation is scale-invariant for exactly this reason.
Token counts per activation bin over the sampled corpus. The units are counts, so the absolute height depends on the sample size, not just on the feature.
The peak of the histogram, at the smallest nonzero activations. Weak activations are by far the most common nonzero case, which is generic to sparse features.

numbers.value: about 7K to 8K, roughly flat from 2.0 to 5.5
numbers.meaning: The long plateau in the middle of the distribution. It says a substantial number of tokens drive this feature to mid and high values, so the specificity claim is not resting on a handful of examples.
The activation level above which visible blue largely disappears from the columns. Below it, the feature fires on some strings the proxy scores as non-base64.
The level above which the columns read as essentially all red and the sampled snippets are unbroken base64 — where the paper's specificity claim is strongest.

The log-likelihood ratio scale, in natural log units of how much more likely the string is under the base64 hypothesis than under the data distribution. It is clipped at the ends, so deep red means 'at least 5', not exactly 5.

Four activation levels sampled, five randomly drawn snippets each, connected to the histogram at roughly 0.75, 3.5, 6.9 and 8.55. Random sampling at a level, rather than showing top examples, is what lets these snippets speak to specificity.

numbers.value: 100 million tokens, 10 per context, 4 tokens each side
numbers.meaning: The visualization sampling scheme: examples come from a 100M-token subset of the training data, only 10 tokens are taken from any one context so the samples are not dominated by a single document, and each snippet shows four tokens of context on either side of the measured token.

items.caption: Like A/1/2357, B/1/2165's logit weights have a second mode corresponding to base64 tokens:
items.title: B/1/2165's Base64 Logit Mode
items.takeaway: In the second model's dictionary, the feature that matches the base64 feature does the same thing to the output that the original does: its logit-weight histogram has a small second mode, centered near +0.32, made almost entirely of tokens that would continue a base64 string. This is the downstream half of the universality claim — the two features do not just fire on the same text, they push up the same vocabulary.
items.walkthrough:
### What is plotted

One histogram over the whole vocabulary. A [[logit-weight]] is what you get by pushing a feature's direction through the MLP output weights, a linearized layer norm, and the unembedding: one number per vocabulary entry, saying how much that entry's next-token logit rises when the feature fires. The plot bins those numbers for a single feature, B/1/2165.

The horizontal axis is that weight, $-0.6$ to $+0.6$. Because softmax is shift-invariant there is no absolute zero, so each feature's weights are shifted until their median is $0$ (see [[logit-weight-median-centering]]). The vertical axis, "Density", is a smoothed count of vocabulary entries; only relative area means anything.

### How the color works

Every column is stacked and shaded by a [[computational-proxy]] applied to the token itself. The proxy is a [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]]: $\log\!\big(P(t\mid\text{base64})/P(t)\big)$. The numerator treats base64 as characters drawn uniformly from a 64-symbol alphabet ([[base64-proxy]]); the denominator is the token's plain unigram frequency ([[unigram-p-s-estimate]]). Deep blue is $-5$, deep red is $+5$.

So red means: this token is far likelier inside a random base64 string than in ordinary text. Those are the tokens that would continue a base64 string.

The narrow strip under the plot is the same data with every column stretched to full height — the composition at each weight, ignoring how many tokens are there.

### What it shows

The bulk is one tall mode, peaking near $0.27\text{M}$ at a weight of about $+0.02$, and it is solid blue. The paper reads this mass as [[weight-interference]]: noise the feature is forced to carry because directions in superposition are not orthogonal, not deliberate prediction.

The inset magnifies the box from $0.20$ to $0.60$. The curve dips to a trough around $0.27$, then rises again into [[logit-weight-second-mode]] peaking near $+0.32$ — roughly a twentieth as tall as the main mode — and dying out by about $0.45$.

Reading the color across that stretch: at $0.205$ about three-fifths of the column is still blue, at $0.27$ about a sixth, and at the peak essentially none. The transition is gradual rather than a clean break, which the paper attributes to base64 tokens also occurring in ordinary text.

Since B/1/2165 was picked only for firing when A/1/2357 fires, matching logit modes is separate evidence for [[feature-universality]].

terms.definition: The chart title. It says the figure is a histogram whose data points are the individual logit weights of one feature, one per vocabulary entry.
The feature being plotted. Read the notation as model B, dictionary learning run 1, feature index 2165 within that run.
The base64 feature from the first model, named in the sentence that introduces this figure. B/1/2165 is its counterpart, and this figure exists to show the two behave alike downstream.

The amount a token's next-token logit changes per unit of the feature's activation, computed along the linear path from the feature direction through the MLP output weights, a linearized layer norm, and the unembedding.
The figure's own gloss on the axis. It names the quantity as a weight on a path, not a measured effect on real data.
A smoothed count of how many vocabulary entries fall at each logit weight. It is a kernel density scaled to counts, so the absolute values are only meaningful relative to each other.

terms.term: "Distribution of weights from feature to logit for each vocab element" (subtitle)
terms.definition: States the population being histogrammed: one weight per vocabulary element, not per dataset token.
One entry of the model's token vocabulary. Extremely rare or never-used entries are dropped from these plots.
The colour variable. For each token it is the log of how much likelier that token is under the base64 hypothesis than under ordinary text.

terms.term: "base64 vs token unigram distribuiton" (legend subtitle, typo in the original)
terms.definition: Names the two distributions in the ratio: base64 as the hypothesis in the numerator, the corpus-wide per-token unigram distribution as the baseline in the denominator.
An encoding that writes arbitrary bytes as characters from the 64-symbol alphabet [a-zA-Z0-9+/]. Here it is modelled as a string of characters drawn uniformly from that alphabet.

In this figure, a vocabulary entry that would plausibly come next inside a base64 string — short mixed-case alphanumeric fragments that occur far more often per character in base64 than in ordinary text.

terms.term: Blue end of the colour bar
terms.definition: Log-likelihood ratio at or below -5: tokens much likelier in ordinary text than in a base64 string.

terms.term: Red end of the colour bar
terms.definition: Log-likelihood ratio at or above +5: tokens that essentially only appear inside base64 strings.
The tall blue hump centred just above zero, holding almost the entire vocabulary. The paper reads it as interference rather than intended prediction.
The small bump in the right tail. It is the set of tokens the feature actively pushes up, and here it is made of base64 tokens.

A magnification of the region of the main plot from logit weight 0.20 to 0.60 and density 0 to roughly 44K, connected to the main axes by dotted lines. It exists because the second mode is invisible at the main plot's vertical scale.

terms.term: Conditional strip (band below the main plot)
terms.definition: The same stacked colours with every column stretched to full height, so it shows the mix of proxy values at each logit weight independently of how many tokens sit there.
Five labels in the inset, each attached by a thin vertical line to a particular logit weight, sampling which vocabulary entries live at that point in the distribution.

The tokens sampled at the left edge of the zoom, around weight 0.22. They are alphanumeric but also ordinary English fragments ('ixel' from pixel, 'avascript' from JavaScript), which is why the column there is still mostly blue.

The tokens sampled just past the peak of the second mode, around weight 0.35. Nearly all are two-character mixed-case fragments of the kind a BPE tokenizer produces on random base64, and the column there is uniformly red.
The tokens sampled on the falling right side of the second mode, around weight 0.44 — the same character-pair pattern, at the weights the feature pushes hardest.
Two labels at the extreme right of the zoom, near weights 0.50 and 0.54, where the density has fallen almost to the axis. These are the individual tokens the feature up-weights most.

The paper's name for logit weights a feature carries without meaning to, because features are packed into more directions than the space has dimensions and so are not orthogonal. It is the proposed explanation for the large central mode.
Softmax only cares about logit differences, so logit weights have no absolute scale; the paper subtracts each feature's median weight to fix one.
A cheaply computed score standing in for the hypothesis about what a feature is for, used here as an independent label on tokens rather than as a fit to the feature.

The question of whether separately trained models learn the same features. B/1/2165 was found by looking for the feature in run B/1 whose activations correlate most with A/1/2357's, so its logit weights are a second, independent test.

numbers.meaning: The plotted range of the horizontal logit-weight axis, with ticks every 0.1. The range is a display choice; weights outside it, if any, are not shown.
The labelled density ticks. Since density here is a smoothed count over vocabulary entries, the area under the curve is on the order of the vocabulary size rather than 1.
The height of the main mode at its peak, read off the plot. It is where the great majority of vocabulary entries sit.
The logit weight at which the main mode peaks, read off the plot. It sits just above zero because the weights are centred on their median, not their mode.
The median logit weight, by construction: the paper shifts every feature's weights so the median lands here.
The horizontal span of the region the inset magnifies, marked in the main plot by a dotted rectangle.
The top of the magnified box in density units, roughly a sixth of the main peak. Everything in the inset is smaller than this.
The logit weight where the curve bottoms out between the two modes, read off the plot. It is the dip that makes the second mode a separate mode rather than a shoulder.
The logit weight at the peak of the second mode, read off the plot. This is the figure's main location claim: the base64 tokens cluster here.
The density at the second mode's peak, read off the plot — roughly one twentieth, about 5%, of the main mode's peak height. The second mode is a small population.
Where the second mode has fallen back to near the axis, read off the plot. Beyond it only a thin sliver of tokens remains out to 0.6.
The approximate logit weights the five token labels point to, measured from the leader lines. They walk from the transition zone, through the peak, out to the extreme tail.
How many tokens each of the five labels lists. The counts shrink toward the right because there are fewer tokens out there to name.

The ticks on the colour bar, in log-likelihood-ratio units. The scale is clipped at both ends, so a token at 5 is at least that base64-specific and may be far more so; the paper does not state the log base.
A token equally likely under the base64 model and under the ordinary unigram distribution. The white middle of the bar is the neutral point.

The fraction of each column that is blue at weights 0.205, 0.25, 0.27 and 0.32, measured off the image. It quantifies the gradual handover from ordinary tokens to base64 tokens as you move right, rather than a sharp boundary.

The probability the proxy assigns to each character of a base64 string, one over the size of the base64 alphabet [a-zA-Z0-9+/]. A token's probability under the base64 hypothesis is this raised to its character length.

The probability the proxy assigns to a character outside the base64 alphabet. One space or punctuation mark in a token therefore drives its ratio far negative, which is why the main mode is uniformly deep blue.

The activation correlation between A/1/2357 and B/1/2165 reported in the surrounding text. It is how B/1/2165 was identified as the counterpart, and it involves no logit weights — which is what makes this figure independent evidence.

The median activation correlation between an A/1 feature and its closest B/1 match, from the paper's global universality analysis. It is the yardstick against which the 0.85 for this pair counts as high.

items.caption: Correlations and scatter plots are also consistent with them being very similar features:
items.title: Base64 Feature, Matched Across Two Runs
items.takeaway: The base64 feature found in model A (A/1/2357) and the one found in a separately seeded model B (B/1/2165) line up on both axes the paper uses to compare features: their activations across text correlate at 0.85, and their per-vocabulary-token logit weights correlate at 0.82. The paper offers this as consistent with the two being the same feature discovered twice, not as proof of it.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Two scatter plots, each comparing one pair of features. The [[base64-feature]] A/1/2357 comes from a [[dictionary-learning-run]] on model A; B/1/2165 comes from a run on model B, a transformer trained on the same data with a different random seed. In both panels, run B is the horizontal axis and run A is the vertical axis, so each point is (value in B, value in A).

The left panel puts one point per token of text, at that token's [[feature-activation]] in each run. The right panel puts one point per vocabulary token, at that feature's [[logit-weight]] for it — how much the feature firing pushes that token's next-token logit up or down. These are the paper's two ways of comparing features across models: [[activation-similarity]] on the left, [[logit-weight-similarity]] on the right.

### How to read it

A tight diagonal band means the two runs assign nearly the same number to the same thing. A round, untilted cloud means the two numbers are unrelated. The [[pearson-correlation]] printed above each panel summarizes the tilt: 0.85 for activations, 0.82 for logit weights.

The strips along each axis are marginal distributions, red where the token is base64-like and blue where it is not, following [[base64-proxy]]. The left panel's note applies to its axes: most probability mass sits at exactly zero, so the axis has a separate zero column before the ">0" region, and the plotted points are the rare tokens where the feature fires at all.

### What it shows

The right panel separates into two circled modes. The small red one at top right is the [[logit-weight-second-mode]] — base64-specific tokens like 'q' and 'ZX' that both features upweight. The large blue cloud near zero is labeled "Interference Weights?", the paper's guess ([[weight-interference]]) that these small weights are unwanted noise forced by [[superposition]].

Both numbers are high. Median activation correlation across all of A/1's features is 0.72 ([[feature-vs-neuron-universality]]), so 0.85 is above typical, and 0.82 is far above the Arabic pair's 0.23. Here even the interference cloud tilts diagonally; the paper does not explain that, saying only that the overlap between the two modes follows from base64 tokens also occurring in ordinary text. It reads the pair as evidence for [[universality]].

terms.definition: Feature number 2357 from dictionary learning run 1 on model A — the base64 feature the paper studies in detail. It supplies the vertical axis of both panels.
Feature number 2165 from dictionary learning run 1 on model B, the feature whose activations correlate most highly with A/1/2357. It supplies the horizontal axis of both panels.
The two separately trained one-layer transformers, each with its own sparse autoencoder run over its MLP activations. Same dataset and hyperparameters, different random seeds.
The vertical axis of the left panel: how strongly A/1/2357 fires on a given token of text. Zero means the feature is off there.
The horizontal axis of the left panel: how strongly B/1/2165 fires on the same token. Each point pairs the two runs' readings on one token.

The vertical axis of the right panel: how much A/1/2357, when active, changes the logit of one particular vocabulary token. Computed by tracing the feature direction through the MLP output weights, a linearized layer norm, and the unembedding.
The horizontal axis of the right panel: the same quantity for B/1/2165, for the same vocabulary token. Points are indexed by vocabulary entry, not by text position.
The subtitle of each panel: the Pearson correlation of the two coordinates plotted there. It is a summary of how tightly the cloud hugs a straight line.

The label on the small red cluster at the top right of the right panel — vocabulary tokens characteristic of base64 strings, which both features push up. These are the weights the paper takes to be the feature's deliberate effect.

The label, with the paper's own question mark, on the large blue cloud of near-zero logit weights. The suggestion is that these are cross-talk the model would set to zero if it could, not intended behavior.

Cross-talk between features whose directions in activation space are not orthogonal, so activating one slightly activates or affects others. The paper invokes it to explain the central blob rather than treating those weights as meaningful.
The hypothesis that the model packs more features than it has neurons by giving each its own direction rather than its own neuron. It is the reason the paper expects unavoidable interference weights.
The annotation under the left panel, pointing at the exact-zero column of the axis. It says the feature is inactive on the overwhelming majority of tokens, so the visible points are a small tail.
An axis marker on the left panel separating the exact-zero column from the region of small positive activations. Without the break, the zero spike would swamp the rest of the axis.

The colored bands along the left and bottom edges of each panel, showing the one-dimensional distribution of each axis on its own. Red marks base64-like tokens, blue marks the rest, following the paper's proxy coloring convention.
The thin outlines drawn around the red and blue clusters in the right panel. They mark the extent of the two modes so the reader can see them as separate populations.
The faint horizontal and vertical lines through 0.0 in the right panel. They separate tokens the feature upweights from tokens it downweights, in each run.
A text encoding that writes binary data as strings drawn from [a-zA-Z0-9+/]. It is the content both features respond to.
The paper's first cross-model comparison: treat a feature as the vector of values it takes over a fixed set of tokens, and correlate those vectors. It is what the left panel plots.
The paper's second cross-model comparison: treat a feature as the vector of logit weights it has over the vocabulary, and correlate those. It is what the right panel plots.

numbers.meaning: Pearson correlation between the two features' activations, printed above the left panel. It is high because both features fire on base64 text and stay near zero elsewhere, so their values rise and fall together token by token.

Pearson correlation between the two features' logit weight vectors, printed above the right panel. It is high partly because the shared base64 mode sits far from the origin and partly because, unusually, the central interference cloud is itself tilted along the diagonal here.

The activation range on both axes of the left panel. Feature activations are non-negative because the autoencoder's hidden layer is ReLU, and roughly 12 is the largest value either feature reaches on the sampled text.

The logit weight range on both axes of the right panel. Weights run both ways because a feature can suppress tokens as well as promote them, and the scale is small since a single feature makes a modest linear contribution to any one logit.

The origin of the logit weight axes. Softmax is shift-invariant, so logit weights have no absolute zero; the paper shifts each feature's weights so that its median weight is zero, which is what makes 0.0 a meaningful reference.
Where the red base64-token cluster sits on both logit axes. These are the tokens whose probability both features raise most when they fire.
Roughly where the blue interference cloud centers on both axes, slightly below zero. With the median pinned at zero and a positive second mode pulling upward, the bulk mode sits a little negative.

The number of tokens over which the paper computes activation correlations when searching for a feature's counterpart in the other run. It is the sample behind the 0.85 figure and behind the choice of B/1/2165 as the match.
The median activation correlation between a feature in A/1 and its best match in B/1, across all features. It is the baseline that makes 0.85 read as better than typical rather than merely nonzero.
The same median when matching transformer neurons across the two models instead of features. The paper reports it to argue that features are more consistent between models than neurons are.

The activation and logit weight correlations for the equivalent Arabic script pair earlier in the paper. The contrast matters here: the Arabic logit weights agreed only weakly because the central mode was near-isotropic noise, whereas the base64 pair reaches 0.82.
The dictionary learning run index within each model, distinguishing runs that differ in dictionary size and L1 coefficient. Both features come from run 1, so the comparison is like-for-like.
The index of each feature within its run, an arbitrary identifier assigned by training order. They carry no meaning beyond naming the two features being compared.

items.caption: A/neurons/470 (corr=0.18), we find that while it does notably respond to base64 strings, it also activates for lots of other things, including code, HTML labels, parts of URLs, etc.:
items.title: The Base64 Feature's Nearest Neuron
items.takeaway: The MLP neuron whose activations track the base64 feature most closely, A/neurons/470, correlates with it at only 0.18, and its own activation distribution stays mostly blue — mostly non-base64 — at every activation level. Its sampled examples are code, XML namespaces, pandoc `label="…"` markup, URL fragments and citation keys, categories with nothing in common but a punctuation-heavy texture. The paper reads this as the feature not being a neuron in disguise.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

A/neurons/470 is an actual MLP neuron inside transformer A, not one of the [[feature]] directions the autoencoder learned. The paper found it by scanning roughly 40 million dataset examples for the neuron whose activations track the [[base64-feature]] A/1/2357 most closely. That search is the [[most-correlated-neuron]] check.

The plot is the [[feature-activation-distribution-plot]] used earlier for the feature itself, redrawn for the neuron so the two shapes can be compared.

### How to read it

The horizontal axis is the neuron's activation on a token, running from just above $0$ to about $7.2$. Hard zeros are excluded — sparsity would put a spike at zero that dwarfs everything else — and the small "0 / >0" control at bottom left is that switch. The vertical axis is density, the number of tokens landing in each activation bin, peaking near 1.4M just above zero.

Color carries a second variable. Each token gets a [[base64-proxy]] score, the [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]] $\log\big(P(s\mid\text{base64})/P(s)\big)$, which is large and positive for strings that look like random base64 and negative for ordinary text. The legend runs from $-5$ (blue) to $+5$ (red). Within each vertical slice the tokens are stacked reddest-at-the-bottom. The thin strip beneath the main plot is the same stack renormalized to full height, so proportions stay readable where the raw density has fallen to nothing.

The four boxes are random dataset examples drawn from the activation levels marked by the dotted leader lines. Orange shading shows the neuron's activation per token; the bold token is the sampled one, with four tokens of context on each side.

### What it shows

Dark red never takes over. It stays a thin band along the bottom at every activation level, including the far right. The same plot for A/1/2357 is essentially solid red above roughly activation 4.

The samples say why. One box holds a PHP error, a JSON `"slug":null`, and `{data-label="tabest"}`. Another holds an XML namespace, a wiki URL and a citation key `[@bib43]`. A third is figure labels and `\[subsect:Moment\]`. The top box, near activation 6.7, is nothing but `label="…"}` markup and citation keys.

No visible sample is base64, though the paper says the neuron does respond to base64 notably. The categories share no meaning, only a machine-written, punctuation-dense texture.

The [[pearson-correlation]] between neuron and feature is 0.18, against 0.85 for the feature's counterpart in the second run. The neuron carries some base64 and much else — [[polysemanticity]], the outcome [[superposition]] predicts, and the thing this whole check exists to rule out for the learned features.

terms.definition: The plot title. It means a histogram over the ~100M-token visualization corpus of how often this unit takes each activation value, here broken down by color into how base64-like the underlying token was.

Neuron number 470 in the MLP layer of transformer A. The `neurons` slot in the paper's naming scheme marks this as a real unit of the transformer rather than a direction learned by a dictionary-learning run.

The base64 feature this neuron is being compared against: feature 2357 from dictionary-learning run 1 on transformer A. It is not drawn in this figure, but the 0.18 in the caption is its correlation with the neuron.
The label for the row of four text boxes above the plot. Each box holds random dataset examples sampled from one slice of the neuron's activation range, not the top-activating examples.
The vertical axis: how many tokens in the sampled corpus fall into each activation bin. It is a raw count, which is why it reaches millions.
The horizontal axis: the value the neuron outputs on a given token. Higher means the neuron fired harder on that token.

The color legend's title. Each token is scored by $\log(P(s\mid\text{base64})/P(s))$ — how much more likely the surrounding string is under a random-base64 model than under the paper's unigram model of ordinary text.
The hypothesis the color scale tests. The paper models a base64 string as a random sequence over the 64 characters [a-zA-Z0-9+/], the encoding used to embed binary data inside text.

The stacking key. Blue tokens score low on the base64 proxy (ordinary text), red tokens score high (base64-like). Inside each vertical slice the reddest tokens are stacked at the bottom, so a red band hugging the axis is the base64-like share.

The small control at the bottom left of the axis. The plot shows only nonzero activations; because the unit is off for most tokens, including exact zeros would produce a spike at 0 that flattens the rest of the curve.

The short band below the main plot. It is the same color stack with every column stretched to full height, so the proportion of base64-like tokens stays legible out in the tail where the raw density is near zero.
The four vertical dotted lines connecting each example box to the activation level its examples were drawn from — roughly 1.05, 2.15, 4.3 and 6.7.
Inside an example box, the background shade on each token shows how strongly the neuron activated there. Darker orange means a larger activation.
The token that was actually sampled at that activation level. The paper shows four tokens of context on either side of it.
Shorthand in the caption for the Pearson correlation between the neuron's activation and the feature's activation, computed token-by-token over a large sample of dataset examples.
One sampled example: an XML namespace declaration. It is markup plus a URL, and represents the "code and HTML labels" category the caption names.
Sampled examples of pandoc-style attribute markup used to label figures and tables in converted academic documents. These dominate the neuron's highest activation bin.
Sampled examples of citation keys in pandoc/BibTeX-converted text. Another unrelated category the neuron fires on.
A sampled example from a PHP error message. It stands for the general "code" category the caption lists.

Sampled examples from a JSON blob and a hexadecimal-looking identifier. The hex-like strings matter because the base64 proxy scores them high even though the paper says a separate feature, A/1/3817, handles hexadecimal.
A sampled example that is a fragment of a URL path — the "parts of URLs" category from the caption.
A sampled example of an escaped LaTeX-style cross-reference in converted text. It is neither code nor base64, and shows how wide the neuron's response range is.

numbers.meaning: The index of the neuron in transformer A's MLP layer. It has no meaning beyond identification; the paper selected it because it was the neuron most correlated with the base64 feature, not because of where it sits.

The Pearson correlation between A/neurons/470's activations and A/1/2357's activations. This is the highest such correlation over all neurons in the model, so 0.18 is a ceiling, not a typical value — no neuron tracks this feature closely.
