For contrast, from the preceding subsection: the correlation between A/1/2357 and its counterpart feature B/1/2165 in a second, independently trained model. A feature in another model matches far better than the best neuron in the same model.

From the same case study: the correlation between A/1/2357 and the base64 proxy itself. The paper attributes the low value to the proxy being too broad — hexadecimal strings, for example, score high on it but belong to a different feature.
The index of the base64 feature within dictionary-learning run A/1. Feature indices are arbitrary labels assigned by the autoencoder.

The ticks on the Log-Likelihood Ratio color legend, in log units. Zero means the string is equally likely under the base64 model and under the ordinary-text unigram model; +5 means about $e^5$ times more likely under base64; -5 the reverse. The scale is clipped at these ends.
The density axis ticks, counting tokens per activation bin. The scale reaches millions because this neuron is active on a large share of tokens.
The peak density, at the smallest nonzero activation bin. The distribution falls monotonically from there, the ordinary shape for a unit that mostly fires weakly.

The range of the activation axis, so roughly 7.2 is the largest activation this neuron reaches in the sample. The feature A/1/2357's own plot runs out to about 12.5, so the neuron's dynamic range is narrower.

The peak density on the corresponding plot for the feature A/1/2357 — about thirty-five times smaller than this neuron's 1.4M peak. The feature fires on far fewer tokens, which is what the sparsity penalty is buying.

The activation level above which the feature A/1/2357's version of this plot is essentially solid red. This neuron's plot never reaches that state at any level, which is the contrast the figure is making.

The four activation levels the dotted leader lines mark, and from which the example boxes were sampled. They spread across the range so a reader can see whether the neuron's meaning sharpens as it fires harder. Here it does not.
Two things: the number of example boxes, and the number of context tokens shown on each side of the sampled token in every snippet.
The size of the token subset from the training data used to build these visualizations, with only 10 tokens taken from each context so the samples are not dominated by a few documents.
The number of dataset examples over which the paper computed activation correlations when searching for the neuron most correlated with a feature.
The probability the base64 proxy assigns to each of the 64 characters in [a-zA-Z0-9+/] under the base64 hypothesis, treating a base64 string as uniform random over that alphabet.
The probability the base64 proxy assigns to any character outside the base64 alphabet. It is a near-zero floor rather than exactly zero so the log-likelihood ratio stays finite.

sections.title: The Feature Is Not A Neuron

items.caption: The logit weights suggest it somewhat increases base64 tokens, but is much more focused on upweighting other tokens, e.g. filename endings.
items.title: Neuron 470's Mixed Logit Weights
items.takeaway: The neuron most correlated with the base64 feature does push base64 tokens up a little, but the tokens it pushes up hardest are filename endings like 'htm', 'png' and 'pdf', which are not base64-specific. The paper reads this as a neuron that helps carry the base64 feature while mostly doing other work, so it is not a clean base64 unit the way the learned feature is.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

This is the output side of a single MLP neuron, not a learned feature. Under the paper's [[neuron-notation]], `A/neuron/470` is neuron 470 of the 512-neuron MLP in transformer A, the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]] under study.

Every unit in that layer has a [[logit-weight]] vector: one number per vocabulary token, saying how much the unit firing raises or lowers that token's next-token logit. It is obtained by pushing the unit's direction through the MLP output weights, a [[layer-norm-linearization]], and the unembedding. The plot is a histogram of those numbers.

Neuron 470 is on stage because it is the [[most-correlated-neuron]] to the [[base64-feature]] A/1/2357, at correlation 0.18. The question being asked is whether that neuron was already doing the feature's job.

### How to read it

The x-axis is the logit weight, from $-0.6$ to $+0.6$. Softmax only cares about differences between logits, so the paper applies [[logit-weight-median-centering]]: each unit's weights are shifted so the median sits at zero.

The y-axis is density in vocabulary tokens per unit of logit weight, so the area under the curve is the vocabulary count, not the height.

Color is the extra ingredient. Each token is tinted by its [[base64-proxy]] score, $\log(P(s|\text{base64})/P(s))$: deep blue at $-5$ means the token is far likelier in ordinary text, red at $+5$ means far likelier inside base64.

The thin band below the axis re-draws the same data with each column normalised to full height, so you can read the color mix at a logit weight where the density is too small to see.

### What it shows

One broad mode sits near zero, which the paper elsewhere treats as [[weight-interference]] rather than deliberate behavior.

A red sliver of base64 tokens does ride the positive side, cresting around $+0.10$ to $+0.15$. That is the "somewhat increases base64 tokens" part.

But the red thins out by about $+0.3$. The largest weights, out near $+0.55$, are `'htm'`, `'png'`, `'pdf'` — filename endings — and the strip there reads pale and blue, not red.

So the second mode this neuron has is not a base64 mode. That is the evidence for [[feature-neuron-nonalignment]] on the output side: a mixed effect, consistent with [[polysemanticity]].

terms.definition: The plot title. It means a histogram over vocabulary tokens of how much this unit's firing changes each token's next-token logit.
Neuron 470 of the 512-unit MLP in transformer A. The 'neuron' segment marks it as an actual MLP neuron rather than a dictionary-learned feature, which would be written A/1/2357.
For one vocabulary token, the linear estimate of how much this neuron firing at unit activation adds to that token's logit. Positive means the neuron makes the token more likely.
How many vocabulary tokens fall per unit of logit weight, plotted as a smoothed curve. Area under the curve counts tokens; height on its own does not.
The base64 proxy score assigned to each token, $\log(P(s|\text{base64})/P(s))$. It says how much more likely the token is under a random-base64 model than under the model's general text distribution.

terms.term: Blue end of the color scale
terms.definition: Tokens with strongly negative proxy scores, meaning they are much likelier in ordinary text than in base64. Most of the vocabulary sits here.

terms.term: Red end of the color scale
terms.definition: Tokens with strongly positive proxy scores, meaning they are much likelier inside a base64 string than in ordinary text. These are the tokens a genuine base64 unit ought to be upweighting.
At each logit weight the total density is split into colored sub-bands by proxy score, so the vertical thickness of the red band is the number of base64-leaning tokens receiving that weight.

terms.term: The narrow strip below the plot (the conditional)
terms.definition: The same stacked coloring with every column stretched to full height, showing the proportion of each proxy score at a given logit weight regardless of how few tokens are there. It is the only way to see the color of the sparse right tail.
The tokens annotated at the far right, the ones this neuron upweights most. They are filename endings, and the paper names them as the neuron's dominant downstream group rather than base64.
An encoding that writes binary data as strings over the 64 characters [a-zA-Z0-9+/]. The paper models a base64 string as a uniform random draw from that alphabet.
Because softmax is shift-invariant, logit weights have no absolute zero. The paper subtracts each unit's median weight, which is why the bulk of this histogram sits at zero.
The dictionary-learned base64 feature this neuron is being compared against. Its own logit weight plot, drawn the same way, has a right tail that is solidly red.
The paper's label, used on the companion feature plot, for the large near-zero central mode: small logit effects it reads as unwanted cross-talk from superposition rather than intended behavior.

numbers.meaning: The index of the neuron being plotted, inside transformer A's MLP. It was picked by searching for the neuron whose activations correlate most with the base64 feature, not chosen for its logit weights.
The width of the MLP in the one-layer transformer under study, so neuron 470 is one of 512 candidates. The residual stream is 128-dimensional.

The Pearson correlation between this neuron's activations and the base64 feature's, over roughly 40 million dataset examples. It is the highest such correlation any neuron achieves for this feature, which is the paper's reason for showing this neuron and not another.

The plotted range of logit weights, with ticks every 0.1. Everything the neuron does to the output distribution is contained in a band of this width because logit weights are small compared with the logits themselves.

The density axis ticks, in vocabulary tokens per unit of logit weight. They are large because the vocabulary is tens of thousands of tokens and almost all of them are packed into a mode about 0.2 wide.
The peak height of the histogram, reached just right of zero. It is the top of the central near-zero mode the paper attributes to interference rather than to intended upweighting.
Where the central mode peaks. Since the median has been shifted to zero by construction, the mode sitting slightly above zero means the weight distribution has a somewhat longer left tail.
Where the red base64-leaning band is thickest, at about 10K density against a local total near 0.15M. This is the visual content of the claim that the neuron 'somewhat increases' base64 tokens.
The logit weight beyond which the red band has essentially vanished. Base64 tokens stop appearing well before the neuron's strongest positive weights are reached.

The logit weight of the annotated top tokens 'htm', 'png' and 'pdf'. It is roughly four times the weight at which base64 tokens peak, which is why the paper calls the neuron 'much more focused' on these.

The color bar ticks for the proxy's log-likelihood ratio. Zero means the token is equally likely under the base64 hypothesis and under the general text distribution; +5 means about $e^5$ times likelier under base64.

The probability the proxy assigns to each character of a base64 string, since base64 uses a 64-character alphabet drawn uniformly. The numerator $P(s|\text{base64})$ is the product of these over the string.

The probability the proxy assigns to any character outside the base64 alphabet, a stand-in for 'essentially impossible'. It is what drives ordinary punctuation and non-Latin tokens to the deep blue end of the scale.

sections.title: The Feature Is Not A Neuron

items.caption: The activation and logit correlations are consistent with this neuron helping represent the same feature, but largely doing other things.
items.title: Base64 Feature Against Neuron 470
items.takeaway: The neuron whose activations most resemble the base64 feature's shares only part of its behaviour: an activation correlation of 0.18 and a logit-weight correlation of 0.64, with most of the mass in both plots sitting off the diagonal. The paper reads this as consistent with the neuron helping represent the feature while largely doing other things, which is what it needs in order to say dictionary learning did not simply hand back an already-monosemantic base64 neuron.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Two scatter plots comparing the same pair of objects, and the pair does not change between panels. On both y axes sits the [[base64-feature]] A/1/2357. On both x axes sits A/neurons/470, the [[most-correlated-neuron]] to that feature among the transformer's 512 MLP neurons.

The left panel plots activations. One point is one dataset example: how hard the neuron fired, against how hard the feature fired.

The right panel plots [[logit-weight]]s. One point is one vocabulary token: how much the neuron pushes that token's next-token logit, against how much the feature does.

One label is wrong. The left x axis reads "Feature Activations (Run B)", left over from the template that compares two [[dictionary-learning]] runs; the panel title and subtitle both say the x axis here is the neuron.

### How to read it

Color is the [[base64-proxy]], a score for how base64-like a string or token is. Red is base64-looking, blue is not, and orange sits between, because that score is graded rather than binary.

The colored strips outside each axis are marginals, stacked by color, so you can read what fraction of the mass at each level is base64.

Activations are non-negative and usually exactly zero. The exact-zero row, the exact-zero column and the both-zero corner are pulled out into thin rugs and one dot, labelled "Most probability mass is at zero."

### What it shows

Left panel, [[pearson-correlation]] $0.18$. The cloud is a wide vertical smear rather than a diagonal. The feature reaches past $12$ while the neuron tops out near $6$, and the feature's strongest activations sit at middling neuron values. The y-marginal is almost all red above about $2$; the x-marginal keeps a blue majority until the neuron's top bin. The neuron does respond to base64, more than the Arabic case's neuron responds to Arabic — but not only to base64, which is [[polysemanticity]]. The thin strip where the neuron is exactly zero still carries many red points.

Right panel, correlation $0.64$. Two modes: a red ellipse of base64 tokens near $(0.17,\,0.32)$, and a much larger blue ellipse centred near the origin. The red mode is displaced up and to the right, so both raise base64 tokens. But the blue bulk is itself tilted along the diagonal, and the paper elsewhere reads that central bulk as [[weight-interference]] rather than deliberate behaviour — so a good share of $0.64$ comes from the mode it trusts least ([[feature-neuron-nonalignment]]).

terms.definition: The left panel compares how strongly two things fire on the same dataset examples. Each dot is one token position sampled from the dataset.
The right panel compares what two things do to the model's output. Each dot is one vocabulary token.
The base64 feature: feature number 2357 in dictionary learning run A/1, a 4,096-feature sparse autoencoder trained on the MLP activations of transformer A. It fires on base64-encoded strings.
Neuron 470 of transformer A's 512-unit MLP layer. The N in the title is shorthand for the paper's "neurons" slot in its identifier scheme, which keeps neurons visibly distinct from learned features.

The main one-layer transformer the paper studies, and the source of both objects plotted here. The feature is on the y axis and the neuron on the x axis, so despite the axis labels, everything in this figure comes from run A.

terms.term: Run B (in the left x-axis label)
terms.definition: A leftover from the template used for the run-A-versus-run-B universality plots, where the x axis really is a second transformer. Here it is a mislabel: the x axis is A/neurons/470, as the panel title and correlation subtitle both state.
The subtitle of each panel: a Pearson correlation between the feature's values and the neuron's values, computed over dataset examples on the left and over vocabulary tokens on the right.

terms.term: Feature Activaitons (Run A) — y axis, left panel
terms.definition: The activation of A/1/2357, i.e. the coefficient the sparse autoencoder assigns to that feature when reconstructing the MLP activation vector at a token. Spelled with a typo in the original figure.

terms.term: Feature Activations (Run B) — x axis, left panel
terms.definition: Despite the label, the post-ReLU activation of A/neurons/470 at the same token. Non-negative, like the feature's activation.

terms.term: Logit Weight (Run A) — y axis, right panel
terms.definition: For each vocabulary token, how much the feature's firing changes that token's output logit, computed by pushing the feature direction through the MLP output weights, a linearized layer norm, and the unembedding.

terms.term: Logit Weight (Run A Neuron) — x axis, right panel
terms.definition: The same quantity computed for neuron 470's direction instead of the feature's direction: how much that neuron firing changes each token's logit.

terms.term: Red points and red marginal regions
terms.definition: High base64-proxy score: dataset examples that look like base64 strings, or vocabulary tokens that occur far more often in base64 than in text generally.

terms.term: Blue points and blue marginal regions
terms.definition: Low base64-proxy score: ordinary text examples, or tokens with no base64 lean.

Middling proxy scores. The paper notes that base64-ness is a continuous distinction rather than a binary one, since any string of English letters has some chance of appearing inside a base64 blob, so the color scale has a populated middle.

The score doing the coloring: the log ratio of the probability of a string under a model of base64 (uniform over [a-zA-Z0-9+/]) to its probability under the empirical data distribution. The paper judges this proxy too broad, since hexadecimal also scores highly.

terms.term: Marginal density strips (the tall strip left of each panel, the wide strip below)
terms.definition: The one-dimensional distribution of each axis variable, drawn as stacked bands so that at each level you see the fraction of mass in each color. They are how the paper reads specificity: a strip that is red at high values means high values imply base64.

terms.term: Thin rug strips beside the scatter
terms.definition: The exact-zero row and column, drawn separately because activations pile up at zero. The narrow vertical strip holds examples where the neuron is exactly zero but the feature is positive; the narrow horizontal strip holds the reverse.
A break in the activation axes separating the exact-zero bin from the strictly positive range, so the enormous zero spike does not swamp the rest of the plot.

An annotation pointing at the single dot in the bottom-left corner, which stands for all examples where both the feature and the neuron are exactly zero. Features are sparse, so this is the overwhelming majority of tokens.
A contour drawn around the mode of base64-specific token logits, up and to the right of the origin. It marks the tokens both the feature and the neuron push up.
A contour around the main mode of ordinary tokens, centred near the origin and stretched along the diagonal. The paper's guess is that this bulk is interference rather than intended behaviour.
Reference lines marking zero logit weight on each axis. Zero is set by convention: logit weights are shifted so each vector's median is zero, since softmax is shift-invariant.

The paper's method for finding a neuron counterpart to a feature: take the neuron whose activations have the highest Pearson correlation with the feature's over roughly 40 million dataset examples. It prefers this to reading off the feature's largest coefficients in the neuron basis.
The paper's name for the large central mode of near-zero logit weights, which it hypothesizes is unwanted crosstalk forced by superposition rather than something the model wants.
A neuron that fires for a mixture of unrelated things. Neuron 470 fires on base64 but also on code, HTML labels and parts of URLs, which is why it is a poor unit of explanation on its own.

numbers.meaning: Pearson correlation between the feature's activations and neuron 470's activations, printed above the left panel. It is low because the neuron fires on plenty of non-base64 material and the feature does not track its magnitude; the paper cites this same number in the text when introducing the neuron.

Pearson correlation between the two logit-weight vectors, over vocabulary tokens, printed above the right panel. It is much higher than 0.18 because both vectors raise base64 tokens and, additionally, the large central mode of small weights is itself tilted along the diagonal.

The shared range of both activation axes on the left panel. It is shared because the panel reuses the feature-versus-feature template, so the neuron gets the same scale as the feature even though the two quantities have no common unit.
Roughly the largest feature activation reached in the scatter, on the y axis. The feature's activation scale runs well past the neuron's.
Roughly where neuron 470's activations stop in the scatter, on the x axis. Everything above about 6.5 in the bottom marginal is one merged tail bin, drawn as a uniform block.

The feature activation above which the y-marginal is essentially solid red. Below it, blue creeps in: the feature's weak activations are less reliably base64, the same pattern the paper reports for its other features.
The shared range of both logit-weight axes on the right panel. Logit weights are median-centred, so the scale straddles zero and the units are logits.
Roughly where the red base64-token mode sits: neuron weight around +0.17, feature weight around +0.32. Both are positive, so both push base64 tokens up, but the feature pushes about twice as hard.
Roughly where the blue bulk of ordinary tokens is centred: close to the origin on both axes, as expected for weights the paper reads as interference around a median of zero.
The index of the feature within run A/1. It carries no meaning beyond identity; features are numbered arbitrarily within a dictionary.
The index of the neuron within transformer A's MLP layer, between 0 and 511.
The dictionary learning run index. A/1 is the 4,096-feature run, an 8x expansion over the 512 neurons, and the run all the paper's detailed feature analyses use.
The number of neurons in the transformer's MLP layer, and so the number of candidates searched when looking for the most correlated neuron.

The number of features in run A/1, eight times the neuron count. Having more features than neurons is the point: it is what lets the decomposition pull apart directions that share neurons under superposition.
The size of the dataset sample over which the paper computes activation correlations like the 0.18 here, large enough for a rare feature to fire on a usable number of tokens.

Reported in the surrounding text, not on this figure: the Pearson correlation between the base64 proxy and the feature's activity. The paper blames the shortfall on the proxy being too broad, since hexadecimal strings score as base64 but are handled by a separate feature, A/1/3817.

The comparison values from the matching figure for the Arabic script feature and its most correlated neuron. Base64's 0.18 and 0.64 are both higher, which is why the paper says this neuron does notably respond to base64 rather than dismissing it outright.

The activation and logit-weight correlations between A/1/2357 and its counterpart feature B/1/2165 in a second transformer, from the universality figure. They set the scale for what a genuine match looks like, and 0.18 falls far short of it.

sections.title: The Feature Is Not A Neuron

items.caption: There is also some blue in strong activations; this appears to significantly be on "common characters", such as whitespace or punctuation, which are from other unicode blocks (see more discussion of similar issues in the Arabic feature section).
items.title: The Hebrew Feature's Activation Spectrum
items.takeaway: A histogram of how often feature A/1/416 takes each activation value, with each slice split by an independent Unicode-based score for "is this Hebrew". Strong activations are almost entirely Hebrew, which is the paper's specificity claim for this feature. The blue that survives at strong activations is mostly shared punctuation and whitespace, which the proxy scores as non-Hebrew by construction, so the paper reads it as a fault in the proxy rather than in the feature.
items.walkthrough:
The article prints no caption here; the sentence quoted alongside is the text that points at the figure, not the authors' own label.

### What you are looking at

This is the specificity picture for the [[hebrew-feature]], written A/1/416 in the paper's [[feature-notation]]. The plot is the paper's standard [[feature-activation-distribution-plot]]: sample a large number of tokens, record what value this one feature takes on each, and build a histogram of those values.

Then colour it. Each token also gets a score from the [[hebrew-script-proxy]], a cheap independent guess at whether the token sits in Hebrew text, computed from Unicode blocks rather than from the model.

### How to read it

The horizontal axis is the feature's activation level, from $0$ to about $9$. Hard zeros are pulled out into their own marker at the far left, because the [[sparse-autoencoder]]'s sparsity penalty leaves most tokens at exactly zero and that spike would otherwise swamp the curve.

The vertical axis is density — how many sampled tokens fall in each activation bin, up to about 20K.

Colour is the proxy score, not the activation. It is the [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]] $\log(P(s|\text{Hebrew})/P(s))$, clipped to $\pm 5$: red means the proxy calls the token Hebrew, blue means it does not. Inside the four example panels, the orange highlight is a separate thing — there it marks activation strength.

The strip beneath the main plot renormalises every column to full height, so you read proportions instead of counts.

### What it shows

Two modes. A tall blue mass hugging zero, and a second bump near $7.5$–$8$ that is almost solidly red. Between about $2$ and $6$ there is very little mass at all.

So when this feature fires strongly, the text is Hebrew. That is [[activation-specificity]], and it is the half of the case that matters most, because [[large-activations-dominate]] the feature's effect on the logits.

### The blue at the top

Some blue persists even in the strong-activation bump. That is not counter-evidence. The proxy assigns any string containing a character outside the Hebrew Unicode blocks a probability of $10^{-10}$, so a space, a comma or a digit inside a Hebrew sentence scores deeply negative. The rightmost panel shows exactly that: punctuation and "230,000" embedded in Hebrew. This is the paper's general catalogue of [[proxy-limitations]], and one of its three [[weak-activation-hypotheses]] applied at the other end of the range. The paper hedges — the blue "appears to significantly be" common characters, unquantified.

terms.definition: The plot's title. It means a histogram over sampled tokens of the value one particular feature takes, not a distribution over features.
The identifier of the feature being plotted: model A, dictionary learning run 1, feature index 416 within that run. The paper calls it the Hebrew feature.
How many sampled tokens fall into each activation bin. Labelled in thousands, so 5K is five thousand tokens.
The scalar value the feature takes on a token — the post-ReLU hidden unit of the sparse autoencoder for this dictionary direction.

terms.term: 0 and >0 (the two small markers at the left)
terms.definition: Exactly-zero activations are separated from the merely small ones. Sparsity puts a large point mass at zero, and mixing it into the first bin would distort the curve.
The quantity the colour encodes: how much more likely the token's surrounding string is under the Hebrew hypothesis than under the general text distribution.
Tells you which direction along the colour scale means more Hebrew. Redder is more Hebrew by the proxy's judgment.

terms.term: Blue (negative end of the colour scale)
terms.definition: The proxy judges this token's string as unlikely to be Hebrew. It does not mean the feature is wrong — the proxy has its own failure modes.

terms.term: Red (positive end of the colour scale)
terms.definition: The proxy judges the string as Hebrew: characters drawn from the Hebrew Unicode blocks.

terms.term: White / pale band (middle of the colour scale)
terms.definition: A log-likelihood ratio near zero — the proxy is indifferent, the string is about as likely under Hebrew as under the general distribution.
A cheaply computable score standing in for the human hypothesis about a feature, used as an independent yardstick so the evaluation does not just consult the feature itself.
A contiguous range of Unicode codepoints. Hebrew has its own block, which is what makes a purely mechanical script detector possible here.
Whitespace, punctuation and digits shared across languages. They appear inside Hebrew text but live outside the Hebrew Unicode blocks, so the proxy scores them as non-Hebrew.

terms.term: Conditional distribution strip (the band under the main plot)
terms.definition: The same colour breakdown, renormalised so every activation level fills the full height. It shows the proportion of tokens of each proxy score at that activation, independent of how many tokens there are.

terms.term: Dataset example panels (the four boxes above the plot)
terms.definition: Snippets of real text sampled from activation levels marked by the dotted lines beneath them, so you can see what the feature is responding to at each strength.
Within the example boxes, background shade marks the feature's activation on that token. Darker orange is stronger. This is a different encoding from the blue-red of the histogram.
Connect each example panel to the activation level its snippets were drawn from.
Raw byte tokens shown where a Unicode character was split across several tokens. \xd7 is the first byte of most characters in the basic Hebrew block.
The claim that the feature being on implies the hypothesised context is present. This figure is the evidence for it — read right to left, high activations are red.
The converse claim: that the feature is on whenever Hebrew is present. This figure does not establish it, and the paper reports it as imperfect for this feature.
A separate feature that fires on the \xd7 byte and predicts the bytes completing Hebrew codepoints. The paper offers it as part of why A/1/416's sensitivity looks incomplete.

numbers.meaning: The three parts of the feature's name: model A (one of two one-layer transformers trained with different seeds), dictionary learning run 1, and feature 416 inside that run. Runs differ in dictionary size and L1 coefficient.
The span of activation values this feature actually reaches. Ticks are every 1.0. Nothing beyond about 9 appears because the feature simply never goes higher on the sampled tokens.
Token counts per bin, ticked every 5K. The scale is set by the near-zero spike; everything else is small by comparison.

Almost all sampled tokens sit at or just above zero activation. This is what sparsity looks like: the feature is off for the overwhelming majority of text, and that bulk is deep blue because the overwhelming majority of text is not Hebrew.

numbers.value: ~3.3K (height of the second mode, near activation 7.5–8.0)
numbers.meaning: The strong-activation bump. It is two orders of magnitude smaller in count than the zero spike, but it is where the feature does its work, and it is almost entirely red.

numbers.value: ~2 to ~6 (the flat middle of the x-axis)
numbers.meaning: The trough between the two modes. The feature is rarely partway on; it is mostly either off or firing hard. That gap is what makes the specificity claim clean at the top end.
The log-likelihood ratio is clipped at plus and minus five before colouring. Beyond that the colour saturates, so a very confident non-Hebrew judgment and an extremely confident one look the same.

The probability the script proxy assigns to P(script | s) when the string s contains any character outside the script's Unicode blocks. In log terms that is roughly -23, well past the -5 clip, which is why a single space or comma inside Hebrew text renders as saturated blue.

The approximate activation levels the four example panels are drawn from, marked by the dotted lines. They span the range deliberately: the leftmost panel is Latin, Japanese and Devanagari with no Hebrew at all; the rightmost is dense Hebrew.

numbers.value: 230,000 and 17 (numerals visible in the third and fourth panels)
numbers.meaning: Digits embedded in Hebrew sentences. They are the caveat made concrete — the feature fires on and around them, the proxy scores them as non-Hebrew, and the disagreement is the proxy's fault.

The Pearson correlation between the Hebrew proxy and A/1/416's activations, reported in the surrounding text. It combines specificity and sensitivity into one number, and it is well under 1 mainly because of sensitivity misses, not because of what this figure shows.
The activation correlation of the closest neuron, A/neurons/489. Given elsewhere in the section, it is the reason the paper says no single neuron encodes this.

The byte value that opens the UTF-8 encoding of most basic-block Hebrew characters. It explains why byte tokens litter the example panels and why a second feature exists just to handle the continuation bytes.

numbers.value: ~5 (the threshold the paper uses when talking about the 'upper spectrum')
numbers.meaning: For the analogous Arabic feature the paper quotes specificity of 98% above activation 5, against 25% when barely active. The Hebrew section does not give matching percentages, so the same threshold is being used qualitatively here rather than measured.

numbers.value: 100 million tokens, 10 per context, 4 tokens each side
numbers.meaning: How the visualisation was built: a 100M-token subset of the training data, sampled at ten tokens per context, with a four-token window shown around each displayed token. This is why the example snippets are short and disconnected.

items.caption: Note that \xd7 is the first token in the UTF-8 encoding of most characters in the basic Hebrew Unicode block.
items.title: Hebrew Feature Logit Weights
items.takeaway: The Hebrew feature's effect on the model's output is concentrated in a small second bump far to the right of the main mode, and the tokens in that bump are Hebrew letters plus the byte `\xd7`. Because `\xd7` is the shared first byte of the UTF-8 encoding of most basic-Hebrew characters, pushing up that one token amounts to pushing up the whole script — evidence that the feature does not merely co-occur with Hebrew but acts to produce it.
items.walkthrough:
The plot summarizes one thing: what a single learned feature does to the model's output when it fires. [[hebrew-feature]] A/1/416 is the Hebrew feature from [[dictionary-learning-run]] A/1, one of that run's 4,096 features. For every vocabulary element the authors compute a [[logit-weight]] — they push the feature's direction through the MLP output weights, then a linearized layer norm, then the unembedding, which gives how much that token's next-token logit moves per unit of [[feature-activation]]. The x axis is that number. The curve is its distribution across the whole vocabulary, and the y axis counts vocabulary elements per unit of logit weight, so area, not height, is a token count.

Two conventions come first. Softmax only cares about differences between logits, so the authors [[logit-weight-median-centering]] shift each feature's weights until the median is zero; the peak sitting at $0.0$ is therefore partly by construction. Weights for extremely rare or never-used vocabulary elements are [[anomalous-token-exclusion]] dropped from the plot.

Color carries a second variable. Each token is tinted by the [[hebrew-script-proxy]] score, a [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]] of the form $\log(P(s\mid\text{Hebrew})/P(s))$, which asks how much more likely that token is in Hebrew text than in the corpus at large. Deep red is $+5$, about $e^5 \approx 148$ times more likely; deep blue is $-5$.

Now the shape. Almost every token sits in the tall blue mode at zero, barely moved by the feature — which the paper elsewhere reads as [[weight-interference]] rather than as computation. The inset magnifies the right tail, invisible at the main plot's scale, and there the blue tail thins out into a separate low red bump around $0.45$. That bump is the [[logit-weight-second-mode]], and it is Hebrew.

The tokenization point is what makes the mode legible. [[utf8-multi-token-characters]] Hebrew letters are outside ASCII, so UTF-8 spends two bytes on each: the figure's example is ד (U+05D3), encoded as `\xd7` then `\x93`, and the [[byte-pair-encoding]] tokenizer leaves those as two tokens. Every letter from alef to tav shares that same leading byte `\xd7`.

So the most useful single move available to a model that expects Hebrew next is to raise `\xd7`. Upweighting one byte is upweighting the whole script.

That is what the mode holds: bare `\xd7`, Hebrew letters, and merged tokens like `ר\xd7` that end one character and open the next. A companion feature, [[hebrew-continuation-feature]] A/1/1016, fires on `\xd7` and predicts the bytes that finish the character.

terms.definition: The figure's title. It says the plot is a histogram/density over vocabulary tokens of the feature's linear effect on each token's output logit, not a histogram over dataset examples.
The feature being plotted: model A, dictionary learning run 1, feature index 416. It is the paper's Hebrew feature, one of the 4,096 features in the A/1 autoencoder.

terms.term: "Distribution of weights from feature to logit for each vocab element" (subtitle)
terms.definition: The subtitle restating the unit of the plot: one data point per vocabulary element, its value being the weight along the path from this feature to that element's logit.

How much the feature's firing raises or lowers one token's next-token logit, computed by multiplying the feature direction by the MLP output weights, a linearized layer norm, and the unembedding matrix. Positive means the feature makes that token more likely.
The number of vocabulary elements per unit of logit weight. The area under a stretch of the curve is a token count, so the tall central peak means most of the vocabulary sits there.
One entry of the tokenizer's vocabulary, i.e. one output logit. Here it includes whole words, word fragments, and single raw bytes such as `\xd7`.

The color variable: each token's Hebrew proxy score, $\log(P(s\mid\text{Hebrew})/P(s))$ — how much more probable that token is under the hypothesis that the text is Hebrew than under the corpus distribution.
Tells you which end of the scale is Hebrew: moving right along the bar, toward red, means more Hebrew-specific. The proxy itself is built by checking which Unicode block a character falls in.
Tokens with a negative Hebrew log-likelihood ratio — tokens that are evidence against Hebrew, such as English word fragments.
Tokens with a positive Hebrew log-likelihood ratio — tokens that occur far more often in Hebrew text than in the corpus overall.

terms.term: Inset (the boxed panel at upper right, connected by dashed guide lines)
terms.definition: A magnification of the right tail of the same distribution. It exists because the second mode is only about a thousandth the height of the central peak and would be a flat line at the main plot's scale; its own y scale is stretched and unlabeled.

terms.term: Color strip (the thin band directly under the main plot)
terms.definition: At each logit weight, the mix of token colors there, drawn as a stacked band rather than as a curve. It shows blue holding all the way up to roughly 0.3 and red taking over the far right, which is the same fact the inset shows in more detail.

The large blue bump centered at zero: the vast majority of tokens, whose logits the feature barely touches. The paper's reading elsewhere is that these small nonzero weights are interference from superposition rather than anything the model computes with.

The small red bump far to the right, the tokens whose probability rises most when the feature is on. Finding such a mode, and finding it interpretable, is the recurring pattern across the paper's case-study features.

A single-byte token for byte 0xD7. In UTF-8 it is the first of the two bytes encoding most characters in the basic Hebrew Unicode block, including every letter from alef to tav, so it is the model's generic "Hebrew character starts here" token.

A single-byte token for byte 0xD6, appearing at the low end of the red region. It is the leading byte for the codepoints just below the ones `\xd7` covers, which in the Hebrew block are the accent and vowel-point characters, so it is Hebrew-associated but less exclusively so.
The second byte of the figure's worked example: the continuation byte that, after `\xd7`, completes the character ד. It appears in the side note, not in the plotted labels.
A continuation-byte token appearing in the blue tail of the distribution, alongside English fragments. It is not part of the Hebrew mode; it sits in the region the plot treats as unremarkable.
The Hebrew letter dalet, used in the side note as the worked tokenization example: one character, one codepoint, two byte tokens.
Vocabulary entries that render as one or two complete Hebrew letters (qof, alef, ayin, yod, tav, pe, dalet, and vav-resh). These sit in the second mode: the feature raises their logits directly.

Vocabulary entries that pair a completed Hebrew letter (or a space) with the leading byte of the next character. Byte-pair merging created them because that sequence is frequent in Hebrew text, and the feature upweights them for the same reason it upweights bare `\xd7`.

Labeled tokens in the blue right tail — English word fragments plus one Cyrillic fragment. They get a mild positive logit weight from this feature with no Hebrew connection, which is what the tail below the second mode looks like.

The Unicode range U+0590–U+05FF holding Hebrew letters, points and marks. The paper's Hebrew proxy is defined by membership in this block, and the tokenization claim is about the UTF-8 encoding of its characters.

terms.term: "Many Hebrew unicode code points are split into two tokens" (side note)
terms.definition: The figure's own gloss on why byte tokens dominate the second mode: a Hebrew character is usually not one token, so predicting Hebrew means predicting its byte pieces in order.

terms.term: A/1/1016 (not in the figure; from the surrounding text)
terms.definition: A complementary feature that fires on `\xd7` and predicts the bytes completing Hebrew characters. It is the other half of the loop this figure's second mode sets up.

numbers.meaning: The plotted range of logit weights. The scale is arbitrary in absolute terms — logit weights are only meaningful as differences — but relative to it, the second mode near 0.45 is a large effect and the central mode is not.
Where the central peak sits. It sits there partly by construction: because softmax is shift-invariant, the authors subtract each feature's median logit weight, so the median is zero by definition.

The y-axis gridlines, in units of vocabulary elements per unit logit weight. The central peak reaches about 0.4M; multiplied by the roughly 0.1-wide core of that mode, that accounts for a vocabulary in the tens of thousands, which is the whole plotted vocabulary.
The stretch of x the inset magnifies. The paper's interest is entirely here — everything left of it is the mode it calls interference.
Roughly where the red second mode peaks, with the bump spanning about 0.35 to 0.6. These tokens are the ones the feature most raises: Hebrew letters and Hebrew-leading bytes.

Where the labeled blue tail tokens (' microscope', 'oms', '\x8b', 'stal', 'то', 'clerosis') sit. They get a positive but smaller weight than the Hebrew mode, and they show the tail is not clean — the separation between the two modes is a gap in density, not a total absence of non-Hebrew tokens.

Roughly where '\xd6', ' י' and 'נ' are labeled, at the left shoulder of the red mode. `\xd6` leads the lower part of the Hebrew block, so it is a weaker Hebrew signal than `\xd7` and is upweighted less.

The ticks of the color bar, in nats of log-likelihood ratio. 0 means a token is exactly as likely in Hebrew text as in the corpus at large; +5 means about $e^5 \approx 148$ times more likely; -5 means about 148 times less likely.

The byte written `\xd7`. In UTF-8 a two-byte sequence starting 110xxxxx carries the codepoint's top five bits, and 0xD7 corresponds to codepoints U+05C0–U+05FF — which contains the Hebrew letters. That is why one byte stands in for the script.

The figure's worked example. Dalet's codepoint 0x05D3 is 11 bits; the top five go into the first byte, giving 0xD7, and the bottom six into the second, giving 0x93. Every basic-Hebrew letter repeats the first half of that arithmetic.
The basic Hebrew Unicode block. It defines what the Hebrew proxy counts as Hebrew, and its upper part is exactly the range whose UTF-8 encodings begin with `\xd7`.

The number of tokens most Hebrew code points become. This is why the second mode contains raw bytes at all, and why a Hebrew feature's downstream job is partly a two-step sequence rather than a single prediction.
The number of features in the A/1 dictionary learning run that A/1/416 comes from. Context for reading the feature's name, not shown in the figure.

The Pearson correlation between the Hebrew script proxy and A/1/416's activations, stated in the surrounding text rather than in the figure. It is moderate; the paper attributes part of the shortfall to feature A/1/1016 covering the `\xd7` tokens instead.

items.caption: Consider the following activation and logit correlation plots:
items.title: The Hebrew Feature Against Its Closest Neuron
items.takeaway: The neuron whose activations track the Hebrew feature most closely does not behave like the feature: the correlation is 0.1 on activations and 0.38 on logit weights, and in both plots the feature's axis cleanly separates Hebrew while the neuron's axis does not. The paper takes this as evidence that dictionary learning did not simply hand back an already-Hebrew neuron under a new name.
items.walkthrough:
Two scatter plots, side by side. Both compare one learned feature against one neuron of the transformer's MLP. The feature is A/1/416, the [[hebrew-feature]]; in the paper's [[feature-notation]] that reads transformer A, [[dictionary-learning-run]] 1, feature number 416. The neuron is A/neurons/489, one of the MLP's 512 neurons.

That neuron was not picked at random. It is the [[most-correlated-neuron]] — the one whose activations track this feature's most closely over roughly 40 million dataset examples. If any single neuron were quietly doing this feature's job, it would be this one.

In both panels the feature is on the vertical axis and the neuron on the horizontal. Dots are colored by the [[hebrew-script-proxy]], a log-likelihood ratio for Hebrew text: red is Hebrew, blue is not.

### Left panel: activations

One dot per dataset token. Its height is the feature's activation there. Its horizontal position is neuron 489's activation on that same token. Both axes run 0 to 9, with a break separating exactly zero from the ">0" range, because most of the mass sits at zero.

The red cloud sits high, roughly 6.5 to 8.2 on the feature axis. Horizontally it spreads across about 1.5 to 3.5, mixed in with blue points at those same neuron values. The printed [[pearson-correlation]] is 0.1.

Now read the marginal strips along each edge. The strip beside the y-axis turns red toward the top. The strip under the x-axis stays blue across the whole neuron range, carrying only a thin red trace. Knowing the feature is high tells you the token is Hebrew; knowing the neuron is high does not.

### Right panel: logit weights

Here one dot is one vocabulary token. Its height is the feature's [[logit-weight]] on that token — how much the feature firing pushes that token's next-token logit up or down. Its horizontal position is the neuron's weight on the same token. Both axes run $-0.6$ to $0.6$.

A dense blue cloud sits at the origin, tilted slightly upward, ringed and labelled "Interference Weights?". That is the paper's guess that the shared near-zero mass is [[weight-interference]] forced by [[superposition]] rather than deliberate behavior; the question mark is the authors' own. The printed correlation, 0.38, comes largely from that cloud.

The red ellipse at the upper right holds the Hebrew tokens, sitting near 0.42 to 0.55 on the feature axis. The feature axis separates them from everything else. Their neuron weights, roughly 0.1 to 0.35, sit inside the blue cloud's own horizontal spread.

Both panels make the same point in the same way, which is the check the paper calls [[feature-neuron-nonalignment]].

terms.definition: Marks the left plot as comparing per-token activation values — how strongly the feature and the neuron each fire on the same piece of text. Each point is one token from the dataset.
Marks the right plot as comparing weights onto output logits rather than activations. Each point is one element of the model's vocabulary.
The Hebrew feature: transformer A, dictionary learning run 1, feature index 416. It is a learned direction in MLP activation space, not a neuron.
Neuron 489 of transformer A's 512-unit MLP. The 'neurons' slot in the notation marks this as an actual neuron of the transformer rather than an autoencoder feature.
The subtitle of each panel, giving the Pearson correlation between the quantity plotted on the y-axis (the feature) and the one on the x-axis (the neuron). 'A' here is the feature A/1/416.
The activation of feature A/1/416 on a given dataset token, as read off the sparse autoencoder's hidden layer. (The label carries a typo in the original.)
The post-ReLU activation of neuron 489 on that same dataset token.

For one vocabulary token, how much that token's next-token logit moves when feature A/1/416 is active, computed by pushing the feature direction through the MLP output weights, a linearized layer norm, and the unembedding.

terms.term: Logit Weight (Run A Neuron) — right x-axis
terms.definition: The same quantity computed for neuron 489 instead of the feature: how much that neuron's activity moves each token's logit.
The Hebrew script proxy score for the token, a log-likelihood ratio built from Unicode blocks. Red means the token scores as Hebrew, blue means it does not.

The narrow colored bands along the left edge and the bottom edge of each plot. Each collapses the scatter onto one axis, showing what fraction of points at each value along that axis is Hebrew (red) versus not (blue).

A break in both activation axes separating the spike of tokens at exactly zero from the continuous range above zero. Without the break, the zero atom would swamp the plot, since most tokens do not fire the feature or the neuron at all.

The labelled red ellipse in the right panel, marking the vocabulary tokens the Hebrew proxy scores as Hebrew — including the \xd7 byte that begins the UTF-8 encoding of most basic-block Hebrew characters.

The labelled blue ellipse around the central mass of near-zero logit weights. The paper's suggestion, with the question mark as printed, is that this mass is unwanted cross-talk forced by superposition rather than behavior the model intends.
Hand-drawn guides around the two clusters in the right panel, not fitted confidence regions. They are there to point the eye at the second mode and at the central cloud.

terms.term: Dashed crosshair at the origin (right panel)
terms.definition: Reference lines at zero logit weight on both axes. Zero is meaningful because logit weights are shifted so that each feature's median weight is zero; the softmax is shift-invariant, so only relative weights matter.

The selection rule that put neuron 489 in these plots: over roughly 40 million dataset examples, its activations correlate with this feature's more than any other neuron's do. It is the paper's preferred search for a neuron counterpart to a feature.

numbers.meaning: Pearson correlation between the feature's activations and neuron 489's activations, printed above the left panel. It is the highest such value over all 512 neurons, which is why the paper says there is no similar neuron.

Pearson correlation between the feature's logit weights and the neuron's logit weights, printed above the right panel. It is higher than the activation correlation, but the plot shows the agreement concentrated in the central near-zero cloud the paper tentatively calls interference, not in the Hebrew tokens.
The feature's index within dictionary learning run A/1. It carries no meaning beyond identifying the feature.
The dictionary learning run in the feature's name. Runs differ in dictionary size and in the L1 coefficient used.
The index of the neuron in the transformer's MLP. This is the same neuron that turned out to be most correlated with the Arabic script feature, which the paper reads as a multi-language neuron.
The number of neurons in the one-layer transformer's MLP, so the size of the pool searched for a neuron counterpart to the feature.
The residual stream width of the transformer being studied. Not printed on the figure, but it is the dimension the 512 MLP neurons write back into.
The number of dataset examples over which activation correlations were computed to pick the most correlated neuron. A large sample matters because Hebrew text is rare in the corpus.
The range of both axes in the left panel. It is set by the feature, whose activations reach about 9; the neuron's activations stop near 4.5 to 5, leaving the right half of the panel empty.
The vertical band where the red (Hebrew) points sit in the left panel — the feature's strong-activation regime, which the paper says is where its specificity to Hebrew is high.
The horizontal spread of those same red points, i.e. what neuron 489 was doing on Hebrew tokens. Blue non-Hebrew points occupy the same range, which is why the neuron's axis fails to separate Hebrew.
The range of both axes in the right panel, covering the logit weight distribution for both the feature and the neuron after the median-zero shift.
Where the Hebrew token cluster sits on the feature's logit weight axis. This matches the small second mode on the far right of the feature's own logit weight histogram.
Where those same Hebrew tokens sit on the neuron's logit weight axis. The range lies inside the bulk blue cloud, so the neuron's weights give no separated Hebrew mode.

The bulk of the blue cloud in the right panel on both axes. Nearly all vocabulary tokens get a small weight from both the feature and the neuron, which is what the 'Interference Weights?' label is pointing at.
The scale of the Hebrew log-likelihood ratio driving the red/blue coloring, as printed on the companion activation and logit histograms for this feature. Positive is Hebrew-leaning, negative is not.

Context from the surrounding section, not printed here: the Pearson correlation between the Hebrew script proxy and the feature's activations. It is the yardstick against which the neuron's 0.1 should be read.

The corresponding activation and logit weight correlations in the matching figure for the Arabic script feature, which uses the same neuron 489. The Hebrew numbers are slightly higher but the paper reads both cases the same way.

sections.title: The Feature Is Not A Neuron

items.caption: A/1/416 has a correlated feature in the B/1 run, B/1/1901 (corr=0.92) that has significant activation specificity:
items.title: Hebrew Feature Found Again in Model B
items.takeaway: A dictionary trained on a second, independently seeded transformer contains a feature, B/1/1901, whose activation histogram looks like the Hebrew feature's: the strong end of its firing range is dominated by tokens a Unicode-based Hebrew score calls Hebrew, and its activations correlate 0.92 with A/1/416's across a large token sample. The paper reads this as evidence that the Hebrew feature is not an accident of one training run, though it rests on one matched pair and one correlation number.
items.walkthrough:
You are looking at a single feature's activation histogram, for the feature named B/1/1901.

Read the name under the paper's [[feature-notation]]: model B, [[dictionary-learning-run]] 1, feature index 1901. B is the second of the [[transformer-a-and-b]] pair — same architecture, same data, same hyperparameters, different random seed. So this feature was learned from a model that never saw model A's weights.

### How to read it

The horizontal axis is activation level: how strongly the feature fired on a token, from 0 to just past 7. The vertical axis counts tokens falling in each bin.

Colour is the independent part. Each token is scored by the [[hebrew-script-proxy]], a [[computational-proxy]] of the [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]] form $\log(P(s \mid \text{Hebrew})/P(s))$ computed from Unicode blocks, not from the model. Deep red is $+5$: the token is far likelier under "this is Hebrew" than under text at large. Deep blue is $-5$.

Stacking those colours inside each bin gives the paper's standard [[feature-activation-distribution-plot]]. The thin strip underneath is the same stack normalized so every column sums to one, which keeps the sparse right tail legible.

### What it shows

At the left edge the bin holds about 4.3K tokens and is nearly all dark blue — weak firings on non-Hebrew text. Density falls to roughly 0.5K by activation 2, rises to a mixed shoulder near 3.9, then climbs to a second peak of about 4.3K near 5.9, of which roughly 3.5K is deep red.

That upper mode is the claim: above about 5, firing is almost exclusively on Hebrew. The paper calls this "significant [[activation-specificity]]" and does not claim purity lower down; its [[weak-activation-hypotheses]] — imperfect proxy, imperfect model, imperfect autoencoder — apply here as they did for Arabic.

The four boxes are sampled dataset examples at four activation levels, drawn under the paper's [[activation-visualization-sampling]] scheme, with orange shading marking per-token activation. The leftmost box holds a URL fragment and Hungarian; the rightmost is solid Hebrew. Byte tokens like \xd7 appear because Hebrew characters are split across tokens ([[utf8-multi-token-characters]]).

B/1/1901 was found by [[activation-similarity]]: the B/1 feature whose activations correlate most with A/1/416's. That correlation is 0.92, which the paper takes as [[feature-universality]].

terms.definition: The plot title. It means a histogram of how often the feature takes each activation value across a large sample of dataset tokens, not a distribution over anything the model outputs.
The feature this plot is about: feature number 1901 in dictionary learning run 1 trained on transformer B. It is the feature whose activations most closely track the Hebrew feature A/1/416.
The Hebrew feature in the main model, feature 416 of run A/1. It is the feature this plot's subject is being matched against; it is not itself drawn here.

The second one-layer transformer, trained with the same architecture, dataset and hyperparameters as A and differing only in random seed. The paper uses it specifically to test whether features recur.
The middle slot in the feature name identifies one trained sparse autoencoder. Runs differ in dictionary size and L1 coefficient, and the A/1 and B/1 runs are a matched pair with identical settings.

Shorthand in the caption for activation correlation: the Pearson correlation between two features' activation vectors over a fixed sample of tokens. It is the paper's working measure of whether two features from different models are the same feature.

The quantity the colour encodes: $\log(P(s \mid \text{Hebrew})/P(s))$ for the token's string $s$. Positive means the string is more probable under the hypothesis that the text is Hebrew than under the general text distribution.
Names the hypothesis in the numerator of that ratio, and the arrow says which way is more Hebrew. Redder tokens score higher on the Hebrew proxy.

terms.term: Blue end of the colour scale
terms.definition: Tokens the Hebrew proxy scores negatively — strings it considers unlikely to be Hebrew. In this figure blue dominates the weak-activation end.

terms.term: Red end of the colour scale
terms.definition: Tokens the Hebrew proxy scores positively, i.e. strings it reads as Hebrew script. Red dominates the strong-activation mode, which is the figure's point.
The count of sampled tokens whose activation falls in a given bin, labelled in thousands. It is a histogram height, not a probability density integrating to one.
The scalar value the feature takes on a token — the post-ReLU coefficient the sparse autoencoder assigns to this dictionary direction. Zero means the feature is off.

terms.term: 0 and >0 (the two markers at the axis origin)
terms.definition: A control separating the exactly-zero bin from the positive range. Because features are sparse, the zero bin would otherwise dwarf everything and hide the shape of the active distribution.

terms.term: Normalized strip below the main chart
terms.definition: The same colour stack rescaled so each activation bin sums to full height. It shows the composition at each activation level independently of how many tokens are there, so the thin right tail can be judged.
Four panels of sampled text, each tied by a dotted line to the activation level it illustrates. Each box holds several short token windows drawn from tokens whose activation is near that level.
Per-token feature activation, with darker orange meaning a stronger firing. The unshaded surrounding tokens are context, not places the feature fired.
The token the example is centred on — the one whose activation places this window at this point of the axis. The four tokens on each side are shown for context.

A raw byte token, written in escape notation because it is not a printable character on its own. It is the first byte in the UTF-8 encoding of most characters in the basic Hebrew Unicode block, so it prefixes most Hebrew characters.
Another lead byte appearing in the examples; it begins the UTF-8 encoding of Hebrew points and some other characters just outside the main Hebrew block.

Continuation bytes — the second half of a split Hebrew character, each of which selects a particular letter after a \xd7 or \xd6 lead byte. They appear as separate tokens because the tokenizer splits these characters.

terms.term: Hebrew letters shown in the examples (א, ת, מ, ם, ...)
terms.definition: The rendered Hebrew characters in the sampled windows, which is what the reader can check the proxy against by eye. The strong-activation boxes are almost entirely made of them.

terms.term: Non-Hebrew text in the weakest box (/gdk-pixbuf/+bug/6657, "ségünk véglegesíten", "t⏎ra môi")
terms.definition: A URL fragment, Hungarian and accented Latin text sampled at low activation. They are the visible face of the blue mass at the left of the histogram: the feature fires faintly on non-Hebrew, often on accented or non-ASCII characters.

The glyph used for a newline character inside an example window. The paper notes elsewhere that such common characters lie outside the script's Unicode block, so the proxy scores them low even where the feature fires.

terms.term: "ic translation:" fragment in the third box
terms.definition: An English fragment appearing beside Hebrew in a mid-to-high activation window. It illustrates that examples are windows of real text, so Latin context can sit next to the tokens that actually drove the activation.

The claim being tested here: when the feature is on, is the hypothesized context actually present. The caption asserts it holds significantly for B/1/1901, and the histogram's red upper mode is the evidence offered.
The question of whether the same features form in separately trained models. This figure is one instance of the paper's affirmative answer for a specific feature.

numbers.meaning: The Pearson correlation between the activations of A/1/416 and B/1/1901. The paper reports it as the reason to call B/1/1901 the counterpart feature; B/1/1901 was chosen precisely as the B/1 feature maximizing this quantity, so the number is a maximum over the run, not a random draw.
The index of this feature within the B/1 dictionary. Indices carry no meaning beyond identity, so 1901 and 416 being different tells you nothing about the features.
The index of the Hebrew feature within the A/1 dictionary — the feature this one is matched to.

The number of tokens over which activation correlations are computed when searching for a matching feature. The size is set so that even features firing on a small fraction of tokens still have enough active examples for a stable correlation.

The tick marks on the log-likelihood-ratio colour scale, in nats. Zero means the token is equally likely under the Hebrew hypothesis and under the general distribution; +5 means about $e^5 \approx 148$ times likelier under Hebrew; -5 the reverse. The scale is clipped at these ends, so the deepest red and blue are saturated bins.

The range of the activation axis. The upper end is set by the largest activations this feature reaches; the paper does not treat activation units as comparable across features, since the autoencoder's decoder directions are normalized but the coefficients are not otherwise calibrated.
The range of bin counts on the vertical axis. Absolute heights depend on the sample size and bin width, so what matters is the shape and the colour composition rather than the counts themselves.

The count in the lowest positive activation bins, almost entirely blue. Weak firings on non-Hebrew text are the single most common thing this feature does by token count — which is why the paper argues elsewhere that strong activations, not common ones, deserve the interpretive weight.
The trough between the weak non-Hebrew mass and the Hebrew mode. The bimodality is what makes a single threshold around 5 meaningful.
A middle shoulder where red and blue are roughly comparable. This is the mixed zone: the feature is clearly on, but the proxy agrees on only part of it.

numbers.value: about 4.3K near activation 5.9, of which roughly 3.5K is red
numbers.meaning: The Hebrew mode. Roughly four fifths of the tokens in the peak bins score positively on the Hebrew proxy, and the remaining blue is largely whitespace and punctuation, which sit outside the Hebrew Unicode block and so are scored as non-Hebrew even inside Hebrew text.

The four activation levels the dotted lines connect to, one per example box. They are spaced to span the distribution — one in the weak blue mass, two in the mixed middle, one in the Hebrew mode — so a reader can see the text change as activation rises.
The sampling shown. This is a small hand-sized sample per level, so it illustrates rather than measures; the histogram behind it is the quantitative claim.
The context window displayed around each selected token in the examples, per the paper's visualization settings.
The subset the visualization examples are drawn from, and the cap on how many tokens are taken from any one document. The cap prevents a single Hebrew document from supplying every example.

Reported in the main Hebrew section, not on this plot: the Pearson correlation of the Hebrew proxy with A/1/416's activations. It is lower than the 0.92 feature-to-feature figure partly because a complementary feature, A/1/1016, handles the \xd7 lead byte, so A/1/416 misses activations the proxy expects.
The corresponding activation correlation for the Arabic feature pair A/1/3450 and B/1/1334, given for comparison in the earlier universality section. Hebrew's 0.92 is in the same range.

Context from the global analysis: the median activation correlation between a feature in A/1 and its best match in B/1 is 0.72, while matching neurons between the same two transformers gives 0.46. Against that backdrop 0.92 is a well-matched feature, not a typical one.

items.caption: Logit weights have a second mode, as before:
items.title: B/1/1901's Hebrew Logit-Weight Mode
items.takeaway: For the Hebrew feature found in the second transformer's dictionary (B/1/1901), the distribution of logit weights over the vocabulary has the same shape reported for the first transformer's Hebrew feature: one large mode at zero, plus a small mode far to the right made of Hebrew-script tokens and the byte \xd7 that begins most Hebrew UTF-8 characters. The paper offers this as evidence that the matched features in the two runs do the same job downstream, not just fire at the same times.
items.walkthrough:
**What you are looking at.** B/1/1901 is a [[feature]] from run B/1 — [[dictionary-learning]] applied to a second one-layer transformer, trained identically to the main one but from a different random seed. For every element of the output vocabulary, the paper computes a [[logit-weight]]: it pushes the [[feature-direction]] through the MLP output weights, a linearized layer norm, and the unembedding ($d_iW_{down}\pi L W_{unembed}$), a [[path-expansion-logit-attribution]]. Each weight says how much that token's next-token logit moves when the feature fires.

The horizontal axis is that weight. The vertical axis is a smoothed density over vocabulary elements, in millions. Softmax is shift-invariant, so there is no absolute zero here; the paper shifts each feature's weights so the median is zero ([[logit-weight-median-centering]]). Extremely rare and never-used tokens are dropped ([[anomalous-token-exclusion]]).

Colour is not part of the histogram. Each token is tinted by its Hebrew [[computational-proxy]] score — the [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]] $\log(P(s|\text{Hebrew})/P(s))$ — blue for low, red for high.

**How to read it.** The inset is a magnifier on the right tail: roughly the region above weight $0.2$, with density below about $0.03$M. It has no ticks of its own. The narrow strip beneath the main panel shares the x-axis but shows *composition* — what fraction of tokens at that weight are Hebrew — rather than how many tokens are there.

**What it shows.** Almost the whole vocabulary sits in the blue mode at zero: firing this feature barely moves those logits. In the tail, a small red bump appears near $0.45$. This is [[logit-weight-second-mode]].

The labels say which tokens. Around $0.3$ the tokens are ordinary fragments — 'rosis', 'l', 'urion', 'bird', 'lichen', 'ч' — no Hebrew. At the red bump the labelled tokens are Hebrew letters and tokens containing \xd7, the first byte of the UTF-8 encoding of most basic-block Hebrew characters ([[utf8-multi-token-characters]]).

So the feature raises the probability of Hebrew script, matching what it fires on. The A-run feature A/1/416 gave the same picture ([[hebrew-feature]]), which the paper reads as [[universality]]. Note this is a linear estimate of effect, not a measured one ([[logit-weight-caveats]]).

terms.definition: The chart's title. It names what is being plotted: a histogram whose population is the vocabulary, and whose value per token is that token's logit weight for this one feature.
The feature being shown. Read as model B, dictionary learning run 1, feature index 1901 within that run's 4,096 learned features.
The second of the paper's two one-layer transformers. It has the same hyperparameters, dataset and architecture as the main model A, and differs only in the random seed used for initialization.

A dictionary learning run on model B's MLP activations, matched in hyperparameters to A/1 but trained on activations from a different transformer and different tokens. It is the run the paper uses to test whether features recur across models.
The Hebrew feature in the main model, whose logit-weight plot this one is being compared against. The introducing sentence's 'as before' points at it.
A direction in the MLP activation space recovered by the sparse autoencoder, treated by the paper as an interpretable unit in place of a neuron.
For one vocabulary token, the linear estimate of how much this feature's firing changes that token's next-token logit. Positive means the feature makes the token more likely; negative, less likely.
How many vocabulary elements fall near a given logit weight, smoothed into a curve and scaled in millions. It measures crowding of tokens, not strength of effect.
One entry of the model's output vocabulary, used here as the unit being counted. The subtitle says the histogram has one weight per vocab element.
The colour scale's variable: the Hebrew proxy score of each token, an estimate of log(P(s|Hebrew)/P(s)). It is an independently computed label, not derived from the feature.
The label above the colour bar, saying which end is which. Redder means more Hebrew-specific under the proxy; bluer means more typical of the dataset at large.
The visual encoding of the proxy score. Blue tokens carry a strongly negative Hebrew score, white near zero, red strongly positive.
The unlabelled magnified box on the upper right. It stretches the right tail of the main histogram — roughly weights above 0.2 at very low density — so the small second mode becomes visible.

The short bar directly under the main panel, on the same x-axis. Instead of density it shows the red/blue mix at each weight, so a mostly-red section means nearly every token at that weight scores as Hebrew.
The small separate hump far to the right of zero. It is the set of tokens whose likelihood this feature raises most, and the paper reads it as the feature's downstream 'meaning'.
The tokens labelled in the lower part of the right tail, around weight 0.3. None are Hebrew, which is why the curve there is still largely blue.

The list annotating the red mode. As printed it mixes Hebrew letters with escape sequences — 'ר', 'ת', 'ו', 'ש', '\xd7', 'ק', 'ות', 'י', 'ל', '\xd7מ', '\xd7ה', 'א' — and its exact ordering is hard to recover because right-to-left Hebrew and left-to-right escapes are rendered together.

A raw byte written in escape notation, decimal 215. It is the first byte of the UTF-8 encoding of most characters in the basic Hebrew Unicode block, so predicting it is how the model starts predicting a Hebrew character.

The single token annotated furthest right, at the highest labelled logit weight. It pairs a Hebrew letter with the \xd7 lead byte in one token — the kind of merge byte-level BPE produces on Hebrew text.

The convention that fixes the x-axis origin. Since softmax ignores a constant shift across all logits, the paper subtracts each feature's median logit weight, putting the bulk of the vocabulary at zero by construction.
Vocabulary elements that are extremely rare or never used, which the paper drops from these plots because their weights are unreliable.
The method behind the numbers on the x-axis: trace one linear route from the feature direction through the MLP output weights, a linearized layer norm, and the unembedding to the logits.
A cheaply computed score standing in for 'is this Hebrew', built here from Unicode block membership via Bayes' rule. It is the independent yardstick the colour uses.

numbers.meaning: The feature index within run B/1. It carries no meaning of its own; features are numbered arbitrarily inside a run.
Model B, dictionary run 1. Run 1 is the 4,096-feature setting the paper studies in most depth; B/1 is its counterpart on the second transformer.
The number of features in a run-1 dictionary, so the size of the pool B/1/1901 was picked from. It is an 8x expansion over the 512 MLP neurons.
The width of the transformer's MLP layer, and so the dimension of the activation vector the autoencoder decomposes. Feature directions live in this space.
The residual stream dimension of the one-layer transformers. It bounds how much the MLP output can write before the unembedding.
The full x-axis range of logit weights shown, with ticks every 0.1. The paper does not claim these are the extreme values; the axis is cropped to where the density is.

The y-axis range. The curve peaks at about 0.4M just below zero, meaning tokens are packed most densely there; multiplying that height by the roughly 0.13-wide bulk gives a count on the order of the vocabulary size, though the paper does not state the vocabulary size or the exact normalization.
Where the main mode sits. It sits there by construction, because each feature's logit weights are shifted so the median is zero.
The left edge of the region the inset magnifies. By this point the main mode has almost died out, which is why the tail needs its own panel to be visible at all.
The upper density limit of the magnified box, roughly one-thirteenth of the main peak. It is the ceiling that makes the second mode readable.
Where the non-Hebrew label ('rosis', 'l', 'urion', 'bird', 'lichen', 'ч') points. The moderate-positive region is not yet Hebrew-specific, so the curve there is still mostly blue.
Roughly where the small red second mode peaks. These are the tokens whose likelihood the feature raises most, and they are the ones the Hebrew proxy scores highest.

Ticks on the colour legend, in units of the Hebrew log-likelihood ratio. Zero means the token is as likely under the general data distribution as under the Hebrew hypothesis; +5 means about e^5 times more likely under Hebrew.

The byte value that opens most basic-block Hebrew characters in UTF-8. Its presence high in the second mode is the paper's explanation for why a Hebrew feature upweights an apparently meaningless byte token.

The activation correlation between A/1/416 and B/1/1901, reported in the preceding sentence of the paper. It is why these two are treated as the same feature found twice, and it is what makes this figure a matched comparison rather than a coincidence.

The Pearson correlation between the Hebrew script proxy and A/1/416's activations. The paper attributes part of that shortfall to a separate feature, A/1/1016, which fires on \xd7 and predicts the bytes completing a Hebrew codepoint.

Median activation correlation between best-matching features across the two models, against the same figure for best-matching neurons. The gap is the paper's general universality claim, of which this figure is one instance.

items.caption: Activation and logit weight correlations are again consistent:
items.title: Hebrew Feature Across Two Models
items.takeaway: The Hebrew feature from run A has a counterpart in a second, independently trained run that fires on nearly the same tokens (activation correlation 0.92) but whose effects on next-token logits agree far less (0.3). The paper reads that gap the way it read the same gap for the Arabic feature: the tokens the feature is actually about agree closely, while a large central cloud of near-zero logit weights, which the paper guesses is unwanted interference, drags the overall correlation down.
items.walkthrough:
Two scatter plots compare one feature against its match in a second model. The left panel compares when the two fire; the right panel compares what they do to predictions.

Both plots name the same pair, `A/1/416` vs `B/1/1901`. In the paper's notation the letter is the transformer, the middle digit is the [[dictionary-learning-run]], and the last number picks a feature out of that run. `A/1/416` is the [[hebrew-feature]]. `B/1/1901` comes from a run over a different transformer, trained on the same data with a different random seed — which is what makes this a test of [[universality]].

### How to read the left panel

Each dot is one token from the sampled data. Its horizontal position is the [[feature-activation]] of `B/1/1901` there; its vertical position is the activation of `A/1/416`.
