The measure that decides whether two features across runs get a line. Cosine similarity between their activation vectors, computed twice — once over only the tokens where the first fires, once over only the tokens where the second fires — keeping the larger value.
The phenomenon the figure illustrates: as the dictionary grows, a feature is replaced by a family of narrower features covering roughly the same territory.
Features firing on fewer than roughly one token in a million, almost none of them interpretable. The paper excludes them before building this graph.

numbers.meaning: The number of learned features in A/0, the leftmost column. It equals the transformer's MLP width, so this dictionary is not overcomplete — one learned feature per neuron, an expansion factor of 1x.
The number of learned features in A/1, the middle column. Eight times the MLP width.

The number of learned features in A/2, the rightmost column. Thirty-two times the MLP width. The three sizes are powers of two chosen as a sweep with the L1 coefficient held fixed, so column-to-column differences come from dictionary size alone.

The masked cosine similarity threshold above which a line is drawn between two features. The paper says plainly it was chosen for display — low enough to show some of the richness of splitting, high enough to keep the graph visualisable. Nothing about the value is derived.

The number of boxes drawn in the A/0, A/1 and A/2 columns. These are the features linked above threshold, not counts of all math-related features in each run; the surrounding text says the coarsest run has three features for technical settings, while the figure as printed traces two.

The feature indices inside each run. They are arbitrary identifiers assigned by the autoencoder's hidden-unit ordering, so index size carries no meaning — A/1/512 sharing a number with A/0's dictionary size is a coincidence.

The parallel count the paper gives for base64 features across the same three runs, quoted in the section this figure sits in. It is the same sweep read on a different feature family, and is why the paper treats splitting as general rather than particular to mathematics.
The widest autoencoder in the paper's full sweep, given for context. This figure stops at 16,384, so it shows part of the range rather than its end.

items.caption: At a sufficiently coarse level dictionary learning cannot tell the difference between these, but when we allow it to use more learned sparse features, the features split and refine into a zoo of different P features that fire in different contexts.
items.title: The P Feature Zoo
items.takeaway: One coarse feature that looked like a pointless "fires on the letter P" detector turns out, in wider dictionaries, to be a family of sixteen or more features that each fire on P in a different context — surnames, acronym patterns, biochemistry, LaTeX, legal citations. The paper offers this as its explanation for the strange single-token features that show up in small dictionaries: they are contexts the small dictionary could not tell apart, so widening the dictionary refines them rather than fragmenting them.
items.walkthrough:
### What the columns are

Five columns, one per [[dictionary-learning-run]] in the A sequence, from A/0 with 512 learned features to A/4 with 65,536.

All five [[sparse-autoencoder]] runs are trained on activations from the same one-layer transformer, with the same sparsity setting. Only the dictionary size changes. So the columns are five resolutions of one underlying picture, which is what the paper means by treating [[dictionary-resolution]] as a zoom level.

Each dark box names one feature in the paper's [[feature-notation]] — run, then index within that run. The grey text below is the authors' reading of what that feature fires on. Every feature shown fires on the token " P" where a word begins with a capital P; [[byte-pair-encoding]] makes that a token in its own right.

### How to read the links

A line joins a feature to its relatives one column over. Where several features connect, the lines merge into one vertical spine, so a bundle says the family carries over without saying which parent became which child.

Two cautions. The paper notes these P relatives were found by [[manual-inspection]], not by the [[masked-cosine-similarity]] score used in the mathematics-and-physics figure — so the links here are a hand-drawn reading, not a measured one. And the relation is not a clean tree anyway: [[splitting-is-not-a-tree]] is the paper's own statement that features both split and merge between sizes.

### What it shows

At A/0 there is a single box, A/0/395, "Misc. 'P' Feature", with a list of P-words. At A/1, still one. That is the apparent bug: a high-magnitude feature that fires on one token and seems to add nothing a bigram could not supply.

At A/2 it has become four: a leftover misc feature, surnames starting with P, P\*N\* acronyms, and PDE. At A/3 there are ten, at A/4 sixteen — Pokemon, PCB, PPAR, PEG, LaTeX $P\_\{$, the legal citation "P.".

The claim is that [[feature-splitting]] refines rather than fragments: the coarse feature was already covering all these contexts at once, and the specific ones are [[token-in-context-features]]. This fits the paper's conjecture about [[true-features]] held in tight [[superposition]]. The evidence here is the labels themselves, which are summaries of activating examples; no quantitative check appears in this figure.

terms.definition: The leftmost column header: the coarsest dictionary learning run on transformer A, with 512 learned features. It is the same width as the MLP layer being decomposed, so it has no room to spare.
The second column: the 4,096-feature run, which is the dictionary the paper analyses in most detail elsewhere. In this figure it still holds only one P feature.
The middle column: the 16,384-feature run. It is where the single P feature first visibly divides.
The fourth column: the 32,768-feature run. Ten P features are drawn here.
The rightmost column: the 65,536-feature run, the widest dictionary shown. Sixteen P features are drawn here.

The paper's identifier for a single learned feature: transformer (A), dictionary learning run (0–4), then the feature's index inside that run. The index carries no meaning beyond position in the dictionary.

The authors' label for a feature that fires on the token " P" across assorted words with no narrower pattern they could name. It is the coarse, unsplit form of the whole family, and it survives in reduced form even at A/4.

terms.term: Bolded P in the word lists
terms.definition: A typographic convention in the figure: within each example word, the P the feature actually fires on is bold. It marks that the activating unit is the token " P", not the whole word.

terms.term: Plastic, Possibly, Pioneer, Preliminary, Pseud-, Pregn(ant), Prairie, Patterns, Pension, Peking, Pseudo, Pulse
terms.definition: The example words listed under A/0/395 and A/1/1057. They are unrelated in meaning, which is the point: at these dictionary sizes the feature's only common thread is the letter itself.

terms.term: Ponce, PIPER, Pichon, Pell, Pioneer, Possibilities, Pronounciation, PNAS, PSA
terms.definition: The examples under A/2/7661, the misc P feature that survives into A/2. The mix of names, ordinary words and acronyms shows this box is still the unresolved residue. "Pronounciation" is printed with that spelling in the figure.

terms.term: First letter of last name, esp. beginning in P (Pabst, Pugh, Pays, Pryon, Pates, Pattinson)
terms.definition: The reading of A/2/7573: a feature that fires on the initial P of surnames rather than on P generally. It is one of the first genuinely contextual splits.

terms.term: Acronyms, esp. P*N* (PN, PNs, PNN, PPN, PND, PNP)
terms.definition: The reading of A/2/4318: a feature for P-initial acronyms whose following letters tend to include N. The asterisks are wildcards standing for any letters, so P*N* is a rough pattern rather than a strict string.

The same wildcard shorthand for sibling acronym features at A/3 and A/4 — A/3/32708 and A/4/49203 for P*V*, A/3/9092 for P*W*, and the P*E* note on the A/2 math/protein box. Each covers a different letter pattern inside P-initial acronyms.

The reading of A/2/4318, A/3/22720 and A/4/32210: a feature firing on the token P in the acronym PDE, which reads as "partial differential equation" in mathematics and "phosphodiesterase" in biology. The label keeps both because the feature does not separate them.
An additional acronym listed under A/3/22720 alongside PDE. In chemistry it names polybrominated diphenyl ethers; the figure lists it as a token the feature also fires on.
The reading of A/3/7399: a feature for the acronym PLD plus a grab-bag of other P-initial acronyms. This box is drawn as the parent of the boxed cluster of seven narrow A/4 features.
The reading of A/3/6439 and A/4/41489: a feature firing on P in PCB, printed circuit board, in electronics writing. It is one of the pairs joined by a single straight line across the two columns.
The reading of A/3/7313 and A/4/27099: a feature that fires on the P of Pokemon. It is a case where the split lands on one proper noun rather than a topic.
The reading of A/3/8618 and A/4/4598: a feature for the P in PPAR, a receptor protein family, in biochemical text.
The reading of A/3/20260 and A/4/12546: a feature for the P in PEG, polyethylene glycol.
The reading of A/4/32210 inside the boxed cluster: a feature for the P in cytochrome P450, a family of enzymes. It appears only at the widest dictionary size shown.
The reading of A/4/13120: a feature for the P in the journal name PLOS (Public Library of Science), in both capitalisations.
The reading of A/4/22642: a feature for the P of "Pitt", covering the university and the surname without distinguishing them.
The reading of A/4/29469: a feature for the P in PPI and assorted other acronyms. The "other acronyms" tail means even at 65,536 features some boxes remain partly unresolved.
The reading of A/4/43583: a feature firing on the P of a specific two-word organisation name. It is the narrowest kind of split shown.
The reading of A/4/10255: a feature for P in LaTeX markup, where it is followed by subscript or superscript syntax. The context is a typesetting format rather than a subject area.
The reading of A/4/16535: a feature for the abbreviation "P." as it appears in legal citations. The same character carries a different role here than in prose.

terms.term: PNAS, PSA, PLR, PZQ, PV, PBD
terms.definition: Assorted acronym tokens listed under the misc features A/2/7661 and A/3/2303. The figure gives them as raw examples without expansions; they are there to show these boxes are still mixed rather than to name particular topics.

terms.term: The rounded box grouping seven A/4 features
terms.definition: A thin outline enclosing A/4/22642, 13120, 32210, 16535, 29469, 43583 and 10255. It marks them as one cluster of narrow acronym-and-name features sharing a link back into the A/3 column, so the drawing does not have to run seven separate lines.

terms.term: Connecting lines and the vertical spine
terms.definition: Lines join a feature to its relatives in the neighbouring column. Where several connect, the lines join a shared vertical bar, which shows family membership across the two runs but not which individual feature descends from which.
The paper's name for what this figure shows: as the dictionary is made wider, one feature is replaced by several more specific features covering roughly the same territory.

The similarity score the paper uses elsewhere to link a feature to its relatives across runs, computed over only the tokens where at least one of the two fires. The text states it was not used here — the P relatives were found by manual inspection instead.

Each of these two identifiers is printed on two different boxes with different descriptions — A/2/4318 as both the P*N* acronym feature and the math/protein feature, A/4/32210 as both P450 and PDE. The paper does not comment; read as printed, it is most likely a labelling slip in the diagram.

numbers.meaning: The dictionary size of run A/0. It equals the number of neurons in the MLP layer being decomposed, an expansion factor of 1×, so this dictionary has exactly as many features as the layer has neurons and no capacity to separate contexts.
The dictionary size of run A/1, an 8× expansion. This is the run the paper analyses in most depth elsewhere, and here it is still coarse enough that only one P feature exists.
The dictionary size of run A/2, a 32× expansion. The figure shows the P family first dividing at this width.
The dictionary size of run A/3, a 64× expansion, twice A/2.
The dictionary size of run A/4, a 128× expansion, twice A/3 and the widest run in this figure.

The number of P-feature boxes drawn in each column, left to right. Doubling the dictionary from A/3 to A/4 does not double the family, and the growth is what the paper points at rather than any exact count — this is a hand-assembled diagram, not an exhaustive census.
The size of A/5, the next run in the same sequence and a 256× expansion. It lies beyond this figure's rightmost column, so the splitting shown here is not the end of the sequence.

The masked cosine similarity threshold above which the paper draws a link between features in the neighbouring mathematics-and-physics figure, chosen to keep that graph small enough to read. It does not apply here: the text says these P relatives were identified manually.
Part of the enzyme family name cytochrome P450, from the wavelength in nanometres at which the pigment absorbs. It is a fragment of a token string, not a measurement the paper made.

Numbers from the companion example in the same section, where one base64 feature in A/0 splits into three in A/1. They are not in this figure but are the paper's other worked case of the same splitting claim.

Arbitrary positions inside each dictionary, running from 0 up to the run's size minus one. An index in the tens of thousands can only come from A/3 or A/4, which is a quick consistency check on the labels; the numbers carry no ordering or importance.

items.caption: But in A/1, that feature splits into three different features whose activations seem to jointly cover those of A/0/45:
items.title: One base64 Feature Becoming Three
items.takeaway: In the 512-feature dictionary A/0, a single feature (A/0/45) fires across a whole base64 string. In the 4,096-feature dictionary A/1, three features share that job — one leaning on letters, one on digits, one on base64 that decodes to ASCII — and between them they light up roughly the same tokens the parent did. The figure is the paper's picture of feature splitting at the level of individual tokens, shown on one example.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Four rows, all showing the same piece of text. The left column names a [[feature]] — one direction in the MLP activation space, learned by the [[sparse-autoencoder]]. The right column is a dataset example, a YouTube URL, with each token shaded by how strongly that feature fired on it. Darker orange means a larger activation. No shading means the feature was off.

Read a name like A/0/45 in three parts: model A, [[dictionary-learning-run]] 0, feature number 45 inside that run. Run A/0 learned 512 features; run A/1 learned 4,096, with the same sparsity penalty. The arrows drop from the A/0 feature to three A/1 features. That downward branching is [[feature-splitting]].

### How to read it

Compare where the shading sits, row against row.

The top row runs continuously from `?v=` to the final `A`. A/0/45 treats the whole base64 tail as one undifferentiated thing.

Now the children. [[base64-feature|A/1/2357]] shades the letters — `qap`, `a`, `O`, `z`, `A` — and skips the digits. [[base64-digit-feature|A/1/2364]] does the reverse: `5`, `5`, `4`, `9` are dark, the letters bare. A/1/1544 barely fires here at all, a few pale tokens near the start.

### What it shows

No single child reproduces the parent. Taken together they cover most of the parent's span, and they are dark roughly where it was dark. That is what "jointly cover" means here: the union of firing positions, with total activation roughly preserved.

Why three and not two: the paper reads the digit/letter distinction as a tokenizer artifact ([[tokenization-artifacts-in-features]]), since two adjacent digits would have merged into one token, so a lone digit token is informative about what comes next. The third child responds to base64 that decodes to printable ASCII text; this video id is random, so it stays pale.

The evidence in this panel is one example, compared by eye. The paper says the activations "seem to jointly cover" the parent's and gives no coverage score alongside the picture.

The consequence the paper draws is that dictionary width behaves like a zoom level ([[dictionary-resolution]]), and that [[multiple-features-for-one-context|several features for one apparent concept]] is refinement rather than a bug.

terms.definition: Labels the column holding feature names. In this paper a feature is a single direction in the transformer's MLP activation space that the sparse autoencoder learned, not a neuron of the transformer.

terms.term: Activations on Dataset Example (right column header)
terms.definition: Labels the column showing text with per-token shading. Each row shows how strongly that row's feature fired at each token of the same example.
The transformer the features come from — the paper's main one-layer model. A second model, B, is used elsewhere for universality checks but does not appear here.
The dictionary learning run the feature was found in. Runs A/0 through A/5 hold the sparsity penalty fixed and increase the dictionary size, so a higher run number means a wider autoencoder.
The index of the feature inside its run. The numbering carries no meaning; it is just a slot in the autoencoder's hidden layer.
The parent feature, from the 512-feature dictionary. The paper describes it as activating on all tokens of base64-encoded strings — the only base64-related feature that run has.

One of the three children, from the 4,096-feature dictionary. It fires preferentially on the letter tokens inside base64 strings, and is the feature the paper studies in detail earlier as its base64 case study.
The second child, firing preferentially on single-digit tokens inside base64 strings. Its logit weights predict base64 tokens like the others but push down on digits.
The third child. The paper argues it responds to base64 strings that decode into printable ASCII text rather than to base64 in general, which is why it is nearly silent on this random video id.
The interpretation attached to each row — every one of these four features is about base64 context. base64 encodes arbitrary bytes as characters drawn from [a-zA-Z0-9+/].
The authors' shorthand for what distinguishes this child: within a base64 run it fires on letter tokens and mostly not on digit tokens.
The shorthand for the complementary child: it fires on the digit tokens the letter feature skips.
The shorthand for the third child: it prefers base64 whose bytes decode to readable ASCII text over base64 that is random-looking.

Per-token activation strength for the row's feature. Deeper orange is a larger activation; an unshaded token means the feature did not fire there. It is a relative scale within the row, not an absolute number.
The unit each shaded block covers. The shading here lands on pieces of the video id such as qap, a lone 5, and a lone 4, which is what lets a letter/digit split show up at all.
A snippet of real text from the model's training distribution, chosen to display a feature's behaviour. The paper's activation visualizations are drawn from a 100-million-token subset of that data.
The example text. The query string after ?v= is a base64-style video id, so the base64 features fire on its tail and not on the plain-English domain that precedes it.

The link from the A/0 feature down to the three A/1 features, asserting a parent-child relation between dictionary sizes. The paper elsewhere notes this refinement structure is not strictly a tree — features can also merge going up in size.
Ordinary printable text bytes. Because base64 decodes groups of characters back into bytes, a base64 string can carry readable ASCII or arbitrary binary, and A/1/1544 keys on the difference.

The claim the figure is making: the set of tokens where at least one child fires approximates the set where the parent fired, with comparable strength. It is asserted here by visual comparison, not by a stated metric.

numbers.meaning: The number of learned features in run A/0, the parent's dictionary. At this width the run has room for exactly one base64-related feature, A/0/45.
The number of learned features in run A/1, the children's dictionary — eight times A/0. The sparsity penalty is held fixed between the two runs, so width is the variable that changes.
The width of the next run, A/2. The paper says the base64 features there are 'many more' still, though A/2 is not shown in this figure.
The count of base64-specific features in A/0, A/1 and A/2. This progression is the paper's headline evidence for feature splitting; the figure shows the first step of it, 1 into 3.

The number of children in this panel. The paper's answer to 'why three?' is that the split separates letters from digits, and separately separates base64 that decodes to ASCII from base64 that does not.
The parent's index within A/0's 512 slots. Arbitrary — it is the position in the autoencoder's hidden layer, with no ordering by importance.
The children's indices within A/1's 4,096 slots. That 2357 and 2364 are seven apart carries no meaning; features are not sorted by similarity.
Run identifiers, ordered by dictionary size. A/0…A/5 form a sequence of increasing width at fixed L1 coefficient, so a larger run number means a finer decomposition of the same activations.
The size of the base64 character alphabet, [a-zA-Z0-9+/]. The paper models base64 strings as random draws from these 64 characters when building its computational proxy for the base64 feature.

base64 packs four encoded characters into three bytes. This is why the paper says deciding whether an example decodes to ASCII is subtle — it can only be decoded in groups of four — and why it selects substrings maximizing printable ASCII characters when checking A/1/1544.

The tokens A/1/2364 shades and A/1/2357 skips. Each appears as a lone digit because the BPE tokenizer would have merged two adjacent digits into one token, which is the tokenization artifact the paper says this feature exploits.
The length of the base64-ish string in the example. It is short and random-looking, which is consistent with A/1/1544 — the decodes-to-ASCII feature — staying nearly unshaded here.

The sampling behind the paper's activation visualizations: examples are drawn from a 100-million-token subset of the training data, taking only 10 tokens from each context. It sets the pool this dataset example came from.

Stated elsewhere for A/1/2357: the Pearson correlation between the feature's activations and the base64 computational proxy. The paper attributes the low value mostly to the proxy being too broad — it also counts hexadecimal strings, which have their own feature — rather than to the feature being impure.

items.caption: Put another way, if the present token is made of digits, the model will predict that the next token is a non-digit base64 token.
items.title: The Digit Feature That Won't Predict Digits
items.takeaway: Two base64 features from the same dictionary push almost the same tokens up, except that the feature firing on single digits gives the ten digit tokens far less of a boost than its letter-firing sibling does. The paper reads this not as a broken feature but as the tokenizer showing through: byte-pair encoding merges adjacent digits, so a lone digit token is evidence the next token is not a lone digit.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

A scatter plot with one dot per vocabulary token. The two axes are two [[logit-weight]] vectors, one per learned [[feature]]. A feature's logit weight for a token says how much that feature, when it fires, pushes that token's next-token logit up or down. The paper computes it by multiplying the feature's direction through the MLP output weights, a linearized layer norm, and the [[unembedding-matrix]].

The x-axis feature is A/1/2357, the [[base64-feature]], which fires preferentially on letter-run tokens inside base64 strings, such as `dN`. The y-axis feature is A/1/2364, the [[base64-digit-feature]], which fires on single-digit tokens such as `7`. Both come from the same [[dictionary-learning-run]], A/1 — see [[feature-notation]]. They exist as a pair because one coarser base64 feature in a smaller run divided into three, an instance of [[feature-splitting]].

### How to read it

Zero on each axis carries no absolute meaning. Softmax is shift-invariant, so the paper slides each feature's weights until its median lands at zero ([[logit-weight-median-centering]]). The dashed grey lines mark that median.

What matters is position relative to the diagonal. A token on the diagonal is boosted equally by both features; a token below it is boosted less by the digit feature.

Three groups are drawn. The blue cloud is the bulk of the vocabulary, clustered near zero, which the paper reads as [[weight-interference]] rather than deliberate behavior. The red cloud, up and to the right, is base64 tokens both features promote. The small pink island is the ten single-digit tokens.

### What it shows

The digit island sits far right but low. Read it off the axes: the letter feature gives digits roughly $+0.25$ to $+0.45$, while the digit feature gives those same tokens roughly $0.0$ to $+0.15$. A feature that fires only on digits declines to predict digits.

That looks like a bug, or a mislabeled feature. The paper's explanation is the tokenizer. Under [[byte-pair-encoding]], two adjacent digits merge: `[Bq][8][9][mp]` never occurs, because it is tokenized as `[Bq][89][mp]`.

So a lone digit token is itself evidence that the next token is not a lone digit, even in a random base64 string. The feature has picked up that statistic. The paper hedges — "likely an artifact of tokenization" — and this display is a linear approximation to a feature's effect rather than a measured one, but it stands as an example of [[tokenization-artifacts-in-features]].

terms.term: Logit Weights of Two Different base64 Features (title)
terms.definition: The plot's title. It announces that both axes are logit weight vectors, and that the two features being compared both live in base64 contexts.

For one feature and one vocabulary token, how much that token's output logit moves when the feature is active. The paper obtains it by tracing a linear path: feature direction, then the MLP output weights, then an approximation of layer norm, then the unembedding matrix.
The horizontal position of a token is A/1/2357's logit weight for it. Far right means this feature strongly raises that token's probability when it fires.
The vertical position of a token is A/1/2364's logit weight for it. Low height means this feature does little to raise that token's probability.
The feature on the x-axis. It fires preferentially on letter-containing base64 tokens, and is the base64 feature studied in detail earlier in the paper.
The feature on the y-axis. It fires preferentially on single-digit tokens inside base64 strings.
The dictionary learning run both features come from. In the paper's naming scheme, 'A' is which transformer, '1' is which autoencoder run, and the last number picks the feature within that run.
Not plotted here, but the reason this pair exists: the single base64 feature in the smaller A/0 run, whose territory the three A/1 base64 features jointly cover.
The third base64 feature in A/1, also not plotted. It responds to base64 strings that decode to readable ASCII text.
An encoding that writes binary data using 64 printable characters, [a-zA-Z0-9+/]. The paper models base64 strings as random sequences over that alphabet.
A sample of the kind of token A/1/2357 fires on: a short run of base64 letters with no digit in it.
A sample of the kind of token A/1/2364 fires on: a single digit standing alone as its own token.

terms.term: Other base64 tokens (red label and ellipse)
terms.definition: The upper-right group of dots: base64-specific tokens that both features push up. These are the tokens on which the two features agree.
The ten single-digit tokens, drawn as their own group. They sit far right on the x-axis but near zero on the y-axis, which is the whole point of the plot.
The bulk of the vocabulary, spread along the diagonal around zero. The paper treats this central mass as interference forced by superposition rather than as intended behavior by either feature.
The zero reference on each axis. Zero is not absolute: because softmax is shift-invariant, the paper shifts each feature's weights so its median weight is zero.

terms.term: The diagonal trend of the point cloud
terms.definition: The two features' logit weights are positively correlated across the vocabulary, which is the visual form of the claim that they predict largely the same tokens.
Hand-drawn boundaries marking the three groups. They are annotation, not fitted confidence regions with a stated coverage level.
The byte-pair-encoding tokenizer merges two adjacent digits into one token, so a pair of separate single-digit tokens never appears in the training data.
As the dictionary is made wider, one broad feature is replaced by several narrower ones covering roughly the same ground. This pair of features is a product of that process.
A direction in the MLP activation space that the sparse autoencoder learns, together with the scalar activation saying how strongly it is present on a given token.
The final linear map from the residual stream to one logit per vocabulary token; the last factor in the logit weight computation.

numbers.meaning: The range of both axes, in logit weight units. The same range on both makes the diagonal a fair comparison line.
The tick spacing on both axes. Ticks run at -0.6, -0.5, ... 0.5, 0.6.
The dashed reference line on each axis. It is the median logit weight for that feature, set to zero by the paper because softmax is shift-invariant and logit weights have no absolute scale.

The horizontal extent of the digit island: how much A/1/2357, the letter feature, raises the digit tokens. Digits are ordinary base64 characters, so the letter feature promotes them along with the rest of the alphabet.

The vertical extent of the digit island: how much A/1/2364, the digit feature, raises those same digit tokens. Close to its own median, meaning close to no boost at all — the gap of roughly 0.25 below the diagonal is the figure's finding.
Where the red 'other base64 tokens' group sits. Both features raise these tokens by a similar amount, which is why the group lies on the diagonal.
Roughly where the blue bulk is centered — slightly below zero on both axes. The paper reads this mass as interference, not as either feature deliberately suppressing those tokens.
The number of tokens in the pink group: the single-digit tokens '0' through '9'.

The size of the base64 alphabet, [a-zA-Z0-9+/]: 26 lowercase, 26 uppercase, 10 digits, plus '+' and '/'. Digits are 10 of those 64, so under the paper's random-string model a digit would be the next character about 16% of the time were it not for tokenization.
The number of features in A/1 that fire on subsets of base64 text: A/1/2357, A/1/2364, and A/1/1544. Two of the three are plotted here.
Feature indices within their dictionary learning runs. The numbers are arbitrary identifiers assigned during training and carry no ordering.
The dictionary sizes of runs A/0, A/1 and A/2. Base64-specific features go from 1 to 3 to many across that sequence, which is why the coarse A/0 feature has two of its refinements plotted here.

The paper's tokenization example. The first bracketing never occurs in the data because byte-pair encoding merges the 8 and 9 into a single token 89, which is why a lone digit token predicts a non-digit successor.

items.caption: If we look at the top dataset examples for each feature, we find that examples for A/1/1544 contain substrings which decode as ASCII, while none of the top activating examples for A/1/2357 or A/1/2364 do:
items.title: Base64 That Decodes to Text
items.takeaway: Three features in run A/1 all fire on base64, and this figure shows what separates the third one: the strings A/1/1544 fires hardest on decode into readable source code and markup, while the best available decoding of A/1/2357's and A/1/2364's top examples is unreadable bytes. That turns a set of features that looked like a redundancy in the dictionary into a distinction the model is apparently making — between base64 that encodes text and base64 that does not.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Three rows, one per feature, all drawn from the same [[dictionary-learning]] run.

That run is A/1. In the paper's [[feature-notation]], "A/1/2357" means model A, run 1, feature number 2357.

Each row shows four [[top-dataset-examples]] for one feature — the windows of text, out of the sampled corpus, on which that feature fired hardest.

Every example is printed twice. The upper line is the raw base64 as the model read it. The boxed line underneath is what that base64 decodes to.

### How to read it

Orange shading behind a token is the feature's activation on that token, and darker means stronger. Bold marks the peak token. Each example is nine token-blocks wide: the peak token plus four tokens on either side.

The bracket under the string marks the substring that was decoded, and the tick points at where the peak token sits inside it.

Base64 carries $6$ bits per character, so four characters decode to $3$ bytes, and a decode only lines up on a group of four. The authors therefore tried different offsets and substrings and kept whichever output held the most printable ASCII characters. Hence the column header: *best* ASCII decoding. Bytes with no printable character are shown as `\xNN` escapes.

That choice is what gives the figure its force. If even the best available decoding is unreadable, the string is not encoded text.

### What it shows

Row 1 is the [[base64-feature]] A/1/2357, labelled "prefer letters". Row 2 is [[base64-digit-feature]] A/1/2364, "prefer digits".

Their boxes are almost entirely escapes — `z\x07\xe7|H\xbb\xbe\x00\xc8`, or `M\x9e\xaf\xe2-f`. Best case, these strings decode to bytes rather than to text.

Their shading also separates them from each other. A/1/2364 peaks on a lone digit — 9, 9, 5, 4 — with the surrounding letters left pale, while A/1/2357 peaks on a letter token in all four examples.

Row 3 is A/1/1544, "prefers encoded ASCII". Its boxes read `|\n        nul`, `xport def`, `-State1!0` and `>        </g` — fragments of source code and markup.

Its peak token is `ICAgICAg` in two of the four examples. Those eight characters decode to six spaces, the indentation of an encoded text file. The paper says that token was the first clue.

So the third feature is not a duplicate of the other two ([[multiple-features-for-one-context]]). It cuts base64 by what the base64 contains, which is the reading that makes [[feature-splitting]] look like refinement rather than a bug.

One limit: this compares four maximal examples per feature. It is a claim about the top of each feature's activation range, not about everywhere the features fire.

terms.definition: Labels the left column, which names the learned sparse-autoencoder feature whose examples are shown in that row. A feature here is a direction in the MLP activation space that the autoencoder learned, not a neuron of the transformer.

terms.term: Top Dataset Example, With Best ASCII Decoding (right column header)
terms.definition: Announces that each cell holds one of the corpus windows where the row's feature fired most strongly, printed above the most readable decoding the authors could extract from it. "Best" is literal: they searched over substrings and offsets and kept the decoding with the most printable ASCII characters.

The dictionary learning run these three features come from: model A, autoencoder run 1, which has 4,096 learned features. The paper's runs A/0 through A/5 hold the sparsity penalty fixed and increase the dictionary size.
The feature in row 1, the one the paper studies in depth earlier as its base64 case study. Within base64 contexts it fires preferentially on letters.

The feature in row 2, which fires preferentially on single digits inside base64. Its logit weights suppress digit continuations, which the paper attributes to the BPE tokenizer merging adjacent digits into one token.
The feature in row 3, and the one this figure exists to explain. The paper's reading is that it fires on base64 which encodes ASCII text.
The italic sub-label under A/1/2357, stating the paper's hypothesis for that feature. It marks a preference within base64 contexts, not a claim that the feature fires on letters generally.
The italic sub-label under A/1/2364. Its evidence is visible in the row: the strong shading sits on digit tokens and the letters around them stay pale.
The italic sub-label under A/1/1544, meaning it prefers base64 strings whose decoded bytes are readable ASCII text. This is the interpretation the figure is offered as evidence for.

An encoding that writes arbitrary bytes using the 64 characters [a-zA-Z0-9+/], packing 6 bits into each character. The model sees only these characters, never the bytes underneath, so any distinction between kinds of base64 has to be computed from the character sequence.

The byte values that correspond to ordinary readable characters — letters, digits, punctuation, space. A decoded byte outside that set has no character to print, so the figure prints its hex escape instead.

The dark-red items inside the decoding boxes, each standing for one decoded byte with no printable character, written as two hex digits. A box that is mostly escapes means the decoding produced binary, not text.
The feature's activation on that token, with darker orange meaning a larger activation. This is the paper's standard activation display, used throughout its feature visualizations.
The token in the window with the highest feature activation — the token the example was selected around. The paper's interpretability rubric refers to these as the "high-activation (bolded) tokens".
A token on which the feature is at or near zero. In row 2 these are the letters sitting next to the digit the feature actually responds to.

terms.term: Bracket and tick beneath a string
terms.definition: The bracket spans the substring that was fed to the decoder, and the tick drops from the peak token to the box, connecting the activation above to the decoding below. The bracket is usually shorter than the printed example because decoding needs a four-character-aligned window.
The bordered monospace box under each example holding the decoded output for the bracketed substring. Printable characters are dark, non-printable bytes appear as red escapes.

The peak token in two of A/1/1544's four examples, and the token that first suggested the ASCII interpretation to the authors. It decodes to six consecutive spaces, which is what indented source code looks like once encoded.
The peak token in A/1/1544's second example, sitting inside a stretch that decodes to "xport def". It is a two-character fragment of the encoding, not a unit with meaning of its own.
The peak token in A/1/1544's third example. It falls inside "LVN0YXRl", which decodes to "-State".
The peak token in all four of A/1/2357's examples, a capital letter. It is consistent with the row's "prefer letters" label, though the figure does not claim the feature is specific to the letter E.

terms.term: Row 1 and row 2 example strings (yegfnfEi7vgDI, /eqkllEjyFa65e, dtDcVfEytMoriKs, 2ilSLlfEvlE4011, /z6fj9Vjbncv, aReHHh9C3V84, 6Rwut5/aOib, mTZ6v4i1mR)
terms.definition: The eight top-activating windows for the letters feature and the digits feature. They read as arbitrary base64, and their decodings confirm it.
The four top-activating windows for A/1/1544. Each contains a run that decodes cleanly into text.

The four decoded fragments in row 3, which look like pieces of source code and markup — an escape sequence and "null", part of "export def...", a hyphenated identifier, and the close of an SVG group tag. They are fragments because the decoding starts mid-file, not at a token boundary of the original text.
A unit of the transformer's BPE vocabulary; the shaded blocks are tokens, not characters. This is why a single block can hold eight base64 characters (ICAgICAg) while another holds one digit.

numbers.meaning: Rows, one per feature. The paper found exactly three features in run A/1 that fire on base64, and the figure puts all three side by side because the question being answered is why there are three rather than one.

Top dataset examples shown per feature, for 12 examples in total. Four is a display choice, and it is also the figure's main evidential limit: "none of the top examples decode" is a statement about four windows apiece.
The feature indices inside run A/1. The numbers are arbitrary labels assigned by the autoencoder's initialization, and carry no ordering — 1544 is not earlier or more important than 2357.
Token blocks per example. The paper's visualization appendix says it displays a window of four tokens on each side of the selected token, so four plus the peak plus four.
Dictionary sizes for runs A/0, A/1 and A/2. The count of base64-specific features goes 1, then 3, then many across these runs, which is what feature splitting means in this case.
The single base64 feature in the 512-feature run, which appeared to fire on all tokens of base64 strings. The three features in this figure jointly cover roughly what that one feature covered.
Information carried by one base64 character, since the alphabet has 64 = 2^6 symbols. This is why decoding is only defined on groups of four characters.

The base64 block size: 4 x 6 = 24 bits = 3 bytes. Because of it, a decode attempt has to be aligned, so the authors sweep the alignment and keep the substring whose decoding has the most printable characters.

The size of the token ICAgICAg and of its decoding — two aligned blocks, giving six bytes that are all the space character. Six spaces in a row is a strong sign of indented text rather than random data.

The peak tokens across A/1/2364's four examples, all single digits. This is the visible evidence for the row's "prefer digits" label; the digits are single because the tokenizer would have merged two adjacent digits into one token.

The range of hex byte escapes appearing in the row 1 and row 2 decoding boxes (\x07, \xe7, \xbb, \xd0, \xf1, \xff, \x9f, \xdd and others). Each is a decoded byte with no printable ASCII character, and their density is the figure's measure of "this is not encoded text".
Ordinary base64 characters that happen to be digits, appearing in the raw example strings. They carry no numeric meaning — base64 uses 0-9 as 10 of its 64 symbols.
Decoded output characters in row 3's third box, not activations or indices. They are part of whatever text was encoded, which the fragment does not reveal in full.

items.caption: These two notions of similarity correspond to the correlations of the points in the two scatter plots we used when analyzing individual features earlier. We've reproduced the plots for the Arabic feature below:
items.title: Activation Similarity vs Logit Weight Similarity
items.takeaway: The figure sets out the paper's two model-independent ways of asking whether the same feature was found twice, and shows that for the Arabic script feature they disagree: activation correlation between A/1/3450 and B/1/1334 is 0.91, logit weight correlation only 0.23. The gap comes from a large central cloud of small, near-uncorrelated logit weights, which the paper hypothesizes is interference forced by superposition rather than anything either model is trying to compute.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Two scatter plots, side by side. Each compares the [[arabic-script-feature]] A/1/3450 against B/1/1334, the feature that a separate [[dictionary-learning-run]] found on a separate transformer trained with a different random seed.

The plots are reused from the earlier case study. Here they serve to make the [[universality]] question concrete: is this the same feature in both models?

### How to read it

In the left panel, each dot is one token position sampled from the dataset. Its x-coordinate is what B/1/1334 fired at on that token, its y-coordinate what A/1/3450 fired at. Stack those per-token values into a vector for each feature, take the [[pearson-correlation]] between the two vectors, and you have [[activation-similarity]]. The orange badge prints it: 0.91.

In the right panel, each dot is one vocabulary token instead. Its two coordinates are the two features' [[logit-weight]]s on that token, the linear estimate of how much that token's logit moves when the feature is on. Correlating those vectors gives [[logit-weight-similarity]], here 0.23.

Colours follow the earlier activation figures: red for tokens the paper's Arabic-script proxy scores as Arabic script, blue for everything else. The bars hugging each axis are marginal histograms of that axis alone.

### What it shows

On the left, a broad red diagonal ridge runs from roughly 2 up to 7–8 in both runs. The two features switch on together, on Arabic script, at comparable strength.

Note the ">0" tick squeezed against the origin and the annotation "most probability mass is at zero". Both features are off on nearly every token, and that pile-up is compressed rather than drawn to scale.

On the right there are two clouds. A small red cluster sits at the top right, labelled Arabic Token Logits: characters both models push up when their feature fires. A much larger blue blob sits at the centre, roughly circular and roughly uncorrelated.

That central blob is what drags the correlation down to 0.23. The label carries a question mark, and so does the paper's reading of it: these small weights may be [[weight-interference]], the residue of [[superposition]] packing features into non-orthogonal directions, which the model would prefer to be zero but cannot make zero.

On that reading, the shared outlier mode is the finding, and the distance from 0.91 to 0.23 overstates the disagreement.

terms.definition: The left scatter plot compares how strongly the two features fire, token by token, over sampled dataset text. Each axis is one feature's activation value.
The right scatter plot compares the two features' effects on the model's output distribution. Each axis is one feature's logit weight, one point per vocabulary token.
The paper's naming scheme: transformer A, dictionary learning run 1, feature number 3450. This is the Arabic script feature that the paper studies in depth, and it supplies the y-axis in both panels.

Feature 1334 from run 1 of the dictionary learned on transformer B, a second one-layer transformer trained on the same data with a different random seed. It is the feature in B whose activations correlate most with A/1/3450, and it supplies the x-axis in both panels.

Shorthand for the two independent pipelines being compared: a transformer plus the sparse autoencoder trained on its MLP activations. A is the main model studied in the paper, B exists mainly to test whether features recur.

terms.term: Feature Activations (Run A) — y-axis, left panel
terms.definition: The activation of A/1/3450 at a given token, in the units the autoencoder learned. Zero means the feature is off there. (The figure's axis label carries the typo 'Activaitons'.)

terms.term: Feature Activations (Run B) — x-axis, left panel
terms.definition: The activation of B/1/1334 at that same token. Points far from the diagonal are tokens where the two runs' features disagree about how strongly to fire.

terms.term: Logit Weight (Run A) — y-axis, right panel
terms.definition: How much A/1/3450, when active, raises or lowers the logit of a particular vocabulary token, computed by multiplying the feature direction through the MLP output weights, a linearized layer norm, and the unembedding.

terms.term: Logit Weight (Run B) — x-axis, right panel
terms.definition: The same quantity for B/1/1334 on that same vocabulary token. The two are on comparable scales because each feature's logit weights are shifted so the median weight is zero.
The Pearson correlation between the two coordinate vectors plotted in that panel. It is the single number the panel exists to produce.

The paper's first model-independent measure: represent each feature as a vector of its activations over a fixed set of tokens, then correlate the two vectors. Two features are similar if they respond to the same data in the same amounts.

The paper's second measure: represent each feature as a vector indexed by vocabulary tokens holding its logit weights, then correlate. Two features are similar if activating them changes the model's predictions in the same way.

terms.term: Arabic Token Logits (eg. 'ي', 'ع') — pink annotation, right panel
terms.definition: The small cluster at the top right: vocabulary tokens in Arabic script, plus byte tokens like \xd8 and \xd9 that form the first half of Arabic UTF-8 characters. Both features push these up strongly, so they land high on both axes.

terms.term: Interference Weights? — blue annotation, right panel
terms.definition: The large, roughly circular central cloud of small logit weights. The paper's hedged guess is that these are not weights either model wants, but leftovers from packing many features into few dimensions.

terms.term: 'Most probability mass is at zero' — annotation, bottom left
terms.definition: A note that the overwhelming majority of tokens sit at exactly zero activation for both features, so the visible scatter is a small minority of the data.

A separate compressed band just above 0 on both activation axes, holding tokens with small but nonzero activation. It exists so the zero spike does not swamp the plot; distances near the origin are not to scale.

The one-dimensional distribution of each axis on its own, ignoring the other. In the left panel they show most mass at zero with a red tail; in the right panel they show the bimodal logit weight distribution the paper described earlier.
Tokens the paper's Arabic script proxy scores as Arabic, using the estimated log likelihood ratio log(P(s | Arabic script) / P(s)). In the right panel, red marks Arabic-script vocabulary tokens.
Everything the proxy does not call Arabic script: other-language and Latin-script tokens. These dominate by count in both panels.
Hand-drawn guides marking the two modes in the right panel — the Arabic outlier cluster and the central interference cloud. They are annotation, not fitted contours.

The claim the figure serves: that the same features arise across models trained with different seeds, which would suggest dictionary learning finds something about how these transformers represent the data rather than an artifact of one run.

The hypothesis that a model represents more features than it has dimensions, storing them as non-orthogonal directions. It is what the paper appeals to when explaining why the central logit weight cloud exists at all.

numbers.meaning: Pearson correlation between the activation vectors of A/1/3450 and B/1/1334. B/1/1334 was selected as the feature in run B/1 with the highest such correlation, so this is a maximum over that run, not a random pairing.

Pearson correlation between the two features' logit weight vectors over vocabulary tokens. The paper says it is 'more modest' than 0.91 because the distribution is dominated by the near-uncorrelated central mode, not because the Arabic tokens disagree.

numbers.value: 0 to 9.0 (left panel axis range, ticks every 1.0)
numbers.meaning: The span of feature activation values. The paper elsewhere treats activations above about 5 as the high-confidence region, where the feature is 98% specific to Arabic script; the dense diagonal ridge sits between roughly 2 and 8.

numbers.value: -0.6 to 0.6 (right panel axis range, ticks every 0.1)
numbers.meaning: The span of logit weights plotted. The scale has no absolute meaning because softmax is shift-invariant; the paper fixes it by shifting each feature's weights so the median is zero, which is why the interference cloud sits centered on the origin.
The number of tokens over which activation correlations are computed in the paper's definition of 'activation correlation'. It is the sample the left panel's points are drawn from.

The median activation correlation, across all A/1 features, with each one's closest counterpart in B/1. It is the context for reading 0.91 as high: the Arabic feature is well above the typical feature's match.
The same median computed for neurons rather than features, matching each A neuron to its closest B neuron. Features match across models better than neurons do, which is the point of the comparison.

The number of learned features in the A/1 dictionary, and the size of the pool B/1's counterpart search runs over. Of these, 168 are dead and 292 ultralow-density and are excluded from global analyses.
The fraction of training tokens that are Arabic script by the proxy. This is why red is a small minority of tokens overall, even though red dominates the region where the feature is strongly active.

The fraction of tokens on which A/1/3450 is active at all that are Arabic script, rising to 98% when activation exceeds 5 and falling to 25% at the weakest activations. It explains why red concentrates at the top-right of the left panel and blue near the origin.

numbers.value: 0.98 (mentioned in the same section, for contrast)
numbers.meaning: The activation correlation of the most extreme disagreeing pair, A/1/3949 and B/1/3321, which nevertheless have a negative logit weight correlation. The Arabic feature's 0.91 / 0.23 gap is a mild version of the same effect.

sections.title: Comparing features between two one-layer transformers

items.caption: Feature vs Neuron Universality: histograms of the activation correlation between each A/1 feature (or A neuron) and its most similar counterpart in the independently trained B run, with features (median 0.72) far more universal than neurons (median 0.46).
items.title: Feature vs Neuron Match Histograms
items.takeaway: When you look for each item's closest counterpart in a second, independently trained one-layer transformer, autoencoder features match far better than raw MLP neurons: the typical feature's best match has activation correlation 0.72, the typical neuron's only 0.46. The paper reads this as evidence that dictionary learning recovers something reproducible about how these models represent the dataset, rather than an artifact of one particular run.
items.walkthrough:
You are looking at one plot with two histograms drawn over each other, four example cards sitting above it, and two legend chips to the right.

### The measurement on the x axis

Both histograms come from the same recipe. Take one item from the A model — either a [[feature]] learned by the [[sparse-autoencoder]] in run A/1, or a raw MLP neuron of transformer A. Record how strongly it fires on each of roughly 41 million tokens of text.

Now do the same for every candidate in B, a second transformer trained on the same data with a different random seed, plus its own separately trained dictionary. Compare A's activation vector against each B vector with a [[pearson-correlation]], and keep only the single highest value. That best-match score is the paper's [[activation-similarity]], and it is the x axis, running from 0 to 1.

So each item contributes exactly one number: how well its nearest twin in the other model tracks it.

### Reading the bars

The y axis is density, so each histogram's bars enclose an area of 1. The bins here are about $0.02$ wide, which means a bar at height 4 holds roughly $4 \times 0.02 = 8\%$ of that population.

Crimson is features, teal is neurons, and dark navy is where the two histograms overlap. The teal mass is a single hump centred near 0.4, peaking around density 4.1 at $x \approx 0.38$, with little left past 0.7. The crimson mass is spread across the whole axis and climbs to its own peak near 0.95.

The chips on the right give the summary: median 0.72 for features, 0.46 for neurons.

### What the cards add

The four cards show text where each pair fires, so a correlation value gets an anchor. At $0.06$ two [[polysemanticity|features]] barely correspond — one fires on "motor", its best match on "road". At $0.38$, the median-ish neuron pair, the top examples share nothing readable, which is why the card is titled "??". At $0.61$ both fire on Russian surnames, and at $0.91$ both fire on Arabic script.

The crimson left tail is real and the paper does not explain it away; it suggests those cases may be different [[feature-splitting|splittings]] of the same underlying [[true-features]], or different features learned by the two base models.

terms.definition: The question the figure answers: whether the same units reappear when you train a second model and a second dictionary from scratch. "Universality" here means reproducibility across independently trained runs, not across architectures or datasets.

terms.term: Activation Correlation to Most Similar Feature/Neuron (x axis)
terms.definition: For each A-model item, the Pearson correlation of its activations with those of its single best-matching counterpart in the B model, computed over a fixed large sample of tokens. It is a best-match score, so it is by construction near the top of that item's whole correlation distribution.

Histogram counts normalized so that the bars of each colour enclose unit area. It lets the feature population and the neuron population be compared even though they contain different numbers of items.
The population of directions learned by the sparse autoencoder on run A/1's activations, each matched against the features of run B/1. This is the paper's proposed unit of analysis.
The population of raw MLP neurons of transformer A, each matched against the MLP neurons of transformer B. This is the baseline the paper is arguing against as a unit of analysis.
Not a third population: it is the colour where the crimson and teal histograms overlap on the same bin. Reading it, both feature and neuron mass is present at that correlation.
Four thin dotted droppers connecting each example card to the x position of that pair's correlation. Their colour matches the card: crimson for the three feature pairs, teal for the neuron pair.

terms.term: Maximally correlated pairs of features or neurons (side note)
terms.definition: The caption for the row of cards, saying that each card shows an item together with its single best match in the other model, not an arbitrary pairing.
The activation correlation for that specific pair, i.e. the pair's position on the x axis. Same quantity as the histogram is built from.
Two one-layer transformers trained with identical hyperparameters and data, differing only in the random initialization seed. B exists in this paper mainly so features can be compared across models.

Feature notation: model / dictionary learning run / feature index within that run. Here they are the low-correlation example, where the A feature fires on "motor" and its nearest B counterpart fires on "road" and "roadways". (These same two labels are also printed on the Russian-names card in this rendering, which looks like a labelling slip rather than a claim about the same pair.)
Neuron notation, used so MLP neurons can be named without being mistaken for learned features. This pair is the "??" example, sitting near the middle of the neuron histogram.
The card title for the failed match: the two features are each other's best available counterpart, yet they respond to different things. It shows what a low score on this axis looks like in practice.

The card title for the neuron pair, with the question marks standing in for an interpretation the authors do not offer. The highlighted tokens are a mix of biology text, escaped Unicode bytes and Japanese characters, which is the sort of mixed response the paper calls polysemantic.

A middling-correlation feature pair, where both members fire on transliterated Russian surnames such as "Mikhaylov" and "Blazevich". The two agree on the concept but not tightly enough on the exact tokens to score high.
The high-correlation feature pair, matching the paper's lead case study: A/1/3450 and its counterpart B/1/1334 both fire on Arabic script.

Short text excerpts from the dataset with orange shading behind each token, where darker shading means a stronger activation. They are the paper's standard way of showing what a feature or neuron responds to.

The 50th percentile of each histogram: half that population's items match their counterpart better than this value, half worse. The paper reports medians rather than means because both distributions are skewed.

numbers.meaning: Median activation correlation for features: the typical A/1 feature has a counterpart in B/1 whose firing pattern tracks it at 0.72. This is the figure's headline number and the paper's quantitative claim of feature universality.

Median activation correlation for neurons, from the same procedure applied to the two transformers' MLP neurons. The gap to 0.72 is what the figure exists to show; the paper calls the neuron similarity 'significantly less'.
The motor/road pair's correlation, an example from the crimson left tail. It means even the best available B feature barely co-fires with this A feature.
The ?? neuron pair's correlation, placed near the mode of the teal histogram and just below the neuron median of 0.46. It is offered as what a typical cross-model neuron match looks like.
The Russian-names pair's correlation, below the feature median of 0.72 despite the two features being recognizably about the same thing.

The Arabic pair's correlation, matching the value reported for A/1/3450 and B/1/1334 in the case study earlier in the paper. Note the paper reports the same pair's logit weight correlation as only 0.23, so a high activation match does not automatically mean a matching output effect.
The x axis range. A Pearson correlation could in principle be negative, but since each item is paired with its most correlated counterpart, no best match lands below 0 here.
Approximate bin width, giving roughly 50 bins across the axis. With density on the y axis, a bar of height 4 therefore covers about 8% of that population.
The teal histogram's peak density: neuron matches pile up in a narrow band around 0.4, so about 8% of neurons land in that single bin.
The crimson histogram's peak density, at the far right of the axis. Feature matches are spread widely but their heaviest concentration is at near-identical firing.
The top of the y axis, chosen to clear the tallest teal bar.

The sample over which the activation correlations are computed, per the paper's definition of activation correlation. A sample this large is what makes a best-match search over thousands of candidates meaningful rather than noise-driven.
The dictionary learning run identifier. A/1 and B/1 are matched runs: same dictionary size and same L1 coefficient, trained on activations from different transformers and different tokens.

Arbitrary position numbers within a run or within the MLP, assigned by training order. They carry no meaning beyond identifying a unit, and index sizes here reach into the low thousands for features versus the hundreds for the 512-neuron MLP.
Three feature pairs and one neuron pair, chosen to span the axis from 0.06 to 0.91 so each region of the histogram gets a concrete illustration.
One per population, overlaid on shared axes so the shift between them can be read directly rather than across two panels.

sections.title: Comparing features between two one-layer transformers

items.caption: In the scatterplot below, we find that this kind of disagreement is widespread.
items.title: Matched Features That Fire Alike But Write Differently
items.takeaway: For thousands of feature pairs matched across two independently trained models, agreement on *when* the features fire is much higher than agreement on *what* they push the next-token logits toward. The paper reads this gap not as the features being different, but as the logit weight vector being a noisy way to compare them, because superposition fills it with interference.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

One point per matched pair of features. For every feature in dictionary run A/1, the authors find the single most similar feature in run B/1 — a dictionary trained on a second one-layer transformer that differs only in random seed, with all other hyperparameters held fixed ([[feature-notation]] explains the slash naming). A/1 holds 4,096 features, so the cloud holds roughly that many points. The question behind the plot is [[universality]]: do two separately trained models learn the same things?

The horizontal axis is [[activation-similarity]] — the correlation between the two features' activation values over a fixed set of dataset tokens. The vertical axis is [[logit-weight-similarity]] — the correlation between the two features' [[logit-weight]] vectors, which have one entry per vocabulary token and say how much the feature's firing pushes each next-token logit up or down.

The two axes ask different questions of the same pair. One asks whether the features turn on together. The other asks whether they write the same thing to the output.

### How to read it

The pairing is chosen to maximise the horizontal coordinate, so each point sits as far right as that A/1 feature can get. The vertical coordinate is then whatever falls out.

The marginal histograms give each axis on its own. Along the bottom, activation correlations pile up near $1.0$, with a median of $0.72$. Along the left, logit weight correlations bunch around $0.5$–$0.6$ and stop short of about $0.87$.

### What it shows

The cloud rises from left to right, so the two measures do agree in direction. But it sits well under the diagonal. A pair matched at $0.9$ activation correlation typically lands near $0.6$–$0.7$ on logit weight correlation.

The circled point at the lower right is the sharpest case, expanded in the inset. Each inset point is one vocabulary token, its logit weight in run B against run A. Only the period token sits far from the origin. Everything else forms a round, roughly isotropic blob — [[weight-interference]], the near-zero noise the paper attributes to [[superposition]] rather than to anything the model intends.

So the disagreement is systematic, and the paper's stated reading is that logit weight correlation understates a real match. It backs that reading with a third measure, [[attribution-similarity]], rather than with this plot alone.

terms.term: Why do Activation Correlation and Logit Weight Correlation Disagree? (title)
terms.definition: The figure's own heading, posed as a question. It presumes the gap shown below is real and asks for its cause; the side panel supplies the paper's proposed answer.
The Pearson correlation between the two matched features' activation vectors, each indexed by a fixed set of dataset tokens. High values mean the two features fire on the same text.

The Pearson correlation between the two matched features' logit weight vectors, each indexed by vocabulary token. High values mean the two features push the model's next-token prediction in the same direction.

For one feature, a vector with one entry per vocabulary token, computed by pushing the feature's direction through the MLP output weights, a linearised layer norm, and the unembedding. It says how much the feature's firing raises or lowers each token's logit.
One matched pair of features: an A/1 feature and the B/1 feature most correlated with it in activation. Its position records how well that pair agrees on each of the two measures.
The bar plots along the left and bottom edges, showing the one-dimensional distribution of each axis on its own. They let you read the typical level of each measure without eyeballing the cloud.
The dictionary learning run the paper analyses throughout: 4,096 learned features, trained on MLP activations from transformer A.
The matched dictionary learning run on transformer B — same hyperparameters, different random seeds, different activations. It exists so features can be compared across independently trained models.
Feature 3949 in run A/1, the A-side member of the circled outlier pair. It fires on PLoS journal abbreviations inside citations.
Feature 3321 in run B/1, the B-side member of the circled pair, found independently in the second model and firing on the same PLoS citation contexts.
The highlighted outlier at far right and slightly below zero: the A/1/3949 – B/1/3321 pair. The dotted line ties it to the inset that unpacks it.
In the inset, the logit weight A/1/3949 assigns to a given vocabulary token. Each inset point is one token.
In the inset, the logit weight B/1/3321 assigns to the same token. Plotting the two against each other shows token-by-token where the pair agrees.
The period token, the one point far from the origin in the inset. Both features strongly raise its probability, because a period follows the citation abbreviation.

The dense, roughly circular mass of tokens near the origin in the inset, where the two features' weights are small and unrelated. It swamps the single agreeing token when a correlation is taken over all vocabulary.

The paper's hypothesis that the near-zero central mass of logit weights is unwanted cross-talk forced by superposition, not a deliberate prediction the model is making. It is the side panel's explanation for the disagreement.

Representing more features than there are neurons by giving each feature its own non-orthogonal direction. Because the directions cannot all be perpendicular, each feature's weights pick up small contributions from others.
The side panel's phrase for the handful of tokens a feature genuinely acts on — the second, far-right mode of its logit weight distribution — as opposed to the bulk sitting at noise level.
An example token sequence where both features fire, shown with the orange activation highlight the paper uses throughout. "pone" is the PLoS ONE abbreviation in a citation identifier.
The Public Library of Science, a scientific publisher. Its journal abbreviations (pone, pgen, pcbi) appear in citation strings frequently enough in the Pile for a dedicated feature to form.

The route from token embedding straight to the unembedding, skipping attention and the MLP. The paper offers it as one reason the model may not care about a feature's weights on tokens that were already implausible.

The follow-up measure the paper introduces after this figure: correlate vectors of activation times the logit weight on the token that actually came next. It agrees with activation similarity far better than logit weight similarity does.

numbers.meaning: Range of the horizontal axis, activation correlation, tick-marked every 0.1. It starts at zero because a feature's best match in the other run is essentially never anticorrelated.
Range of the vertical axis, logit weight correlation. It dips below zero only to accommodate the single circled outlier pair, whose logit weight correlation is slightly negative.
The number of features in run A/1, and so roughly the number of points in the main scatter, since each A/1 feature contributes one matched pair.

The median activation correlation between an A/1 feature and its closest B/1 counterpart. This is the centre of the bottom marginal histogram and the paper's headline evidence that features are largely universal across models.

The median activation correlation when the same matching is done between the two transformers' MLP neurons rather than their learned features. Lower than 0.72, which the paper takes as features being more universal than neurons.
Where the left marginal histogram peaks: the typical logit weight correlation for a matched pair. Well below the activation correlation of the same pairs, which is the figure's point.
The approximate upper edge of the left marginal histogram. No matched pair reaches near-perfect logit weight agreement, even though many reach near-perfect activation agreement.
The activation correlation between the Arabic script feature A/1/3450 and its B-run counterpart, quoted in the surrounding text as the first sign of the gap.
The logit weight correlation for that same Arabic pair — far below its 0.91 activation correlation. The agreeing tokens are the Arabic-script ones; the rest is near-isotropic noise.
The activation correlation of the circled pair A/1/3949 and B/1/3321. Almost perfect agreement on when the two features fire.
The logit weight correlation of that same circled pair. The paper calls it the most dramatic case of the disparity: near-identical firing, no agreement at all in the linear output weights.
Range of both inset axes, tick-marked every 0.2, in units of median-centred logit weight. The scale is set by the one token that escapes the central blob.
The approximate inset coordinates of the period token, read off the plot — the sole token both features strongly upweight, sitting far outside the interference cloud.

The fraction of tokens on which A/1/3949 fires. The paper notes this means at least 1 in 10,000 Pile tokens is a PLoS citation abbreviation, which it offers as evidence of the dataset's bias toward scientific text.
The digits in the example citation @pone.0114343 shown in the side panel — a PLoS ONE article identifier, included to show the context in which both features activate.

sections.title: Comparing features between two one-layer transformers

items.caption: We find that the attribution similarity correlates quite highly with the activation similarity, meaning that features that were coactive between models were useful at predicting the same tokens.
items.title: Attribution vs Activation Correlation
items.takeaway: For each feature in one dictionary and its best-matching feature in a dictionary learned from a separately trained transformer, the plot compares how similarly the pair fires with how similarly the pair contributes to predicting the tokens that actually came next. The two agree closely, with the points hugging the diagonal. The paper reads this as saying that features which are coactive across models are also doing the same predictive job, so the activation correlation it uses everywhere else is a reasonable stand-in for both notions of sameness.
items.walkthrough:
You are looking at one scatterplot with a histogram along each of its two edges.

Each dot is a **matched pair of features**. One member comes from [[dictionary-learning-run]] A/1; the other is the feature in run B/1 that best matches it. B is a second [[one-layer-transformer-testbed|one-layer transformer]] with the same architecture, data and hyperparameters as A, differing only in random seeds — so agreement across the pair is evidence for [[universality]] ([[transformer-a-and-b]]).

### The two axes

The horizontal axis is **activation correlation**. Write each [[feature]] as a vector of its activations over a fixed set of dataset examples, then take the [[pearson-correlation]] between the two models' vectors; that is [[activation-similarity]]. This is also the quantity used to *choose* the partner, so horizontal position is by construction "how good the match was."

The vertical axis is **attribution correlation**, and it takes more unpacking.

Feature $f_i$ has a [[logit-weight]] $v_{ik}$ for every vocabulary token $k$: how much its firing pushes that token's logit up or down. At a given position $t_j$ you compute the feature's activation $f_i(t_j)$, and multiply it by the logit weight $v_{i,t_{j+1}}$ of the token that *actually* came next.

That product $f_i(t_j)\,v_{i,t_{j+1}}$ is the **attribution score**. Stack it over a random sample of datapoints and you get the [[attribution-vector]]. Correlating those vectors across the pair gives [[attribution-similarity]].

The paper says this approximates the standard attribution method of multiplying gradient by activation, differing in that the denominators of the softmax and the layer norm are ignored.

### Why not just compare logit weights

The obvious alternative, [[logit-weight-similarity]], correlates the raw vocabulary-indexed weight vectors — and it disagreed badly with activation similarity. Most entries of a logit weight vector are small [[interference]] noise on tokens that would never have occurred anyway. Weighting by whether the feature fired, and by which token really followed, strips most of that out.

### Reading the plot

The cloud runs along the diagonal from bottom-left to top-right, densest near the top-right corner. The bottom histogram is the marginal distribution of activation correlation, rising towards 1.0; the left histogram is the marginal for attribution correlation, piled up near 1.0 with a thin tail running down.

A handful of dots sit well below the band — the annotation calls them "only a few outliers."

One caution the paper does not state: the attribution vector has the activation vector as a factor, so the two measures are not independent, and some of the agreement on display follows from how attribution is built.

terms.definition: The Pearson correlation between a feature's activation vector in model A and its matched feature's activation vector in model B, over a fixed set of dataset examples. It is also the criterion used to pick the match, so every dot sits at its pair's matching score.

The Pearson correlation between the two matched features' attribution vectors. It measures whether the pair contributed to predicting the same actual next tokens, not merely whether they fired together.
For one feature, the list of its attribution scores across a random sample of datapoints, stacked into a vector. It is the model-independent representation being correlated on the vertical axis.

For feature $i$ at position $t_j$, the product $f_i(t_j)\,v_{i,t_{j+1}}$ of the feature's activation there and its logit weight on the token that actually came next. It is large only when the feature was both active and pushing towards the correct continuation.
The $i$-th learned feature, treated as a function from a token position to a scalar activation.
The activation of feature $i$ at token position $t_j$ — how strongly that feature fired there.

The logit weight of feature $i$ on vocabulary token $k$: how much this feature firing raises or lowers that token's next-token logit, computed by tracing the linear path from the feature direction through the MLP output weights and unembedding.
The one entry of that logit weight vector picked out by the token that empirically followed position $t_j$ in the dataset.
A sampled token position and the token that actually comes after it in the corpus. The next token is taken from the data, not from the model's prediction.
The index over vocabulary tokens on which logit weights are defined; $n_\text{vocab}$ is the size of the byte-pair vocabulary.

A standard attribution method that scores a unit's contribution by multiplying its activation by the gradient of the output with respect to it.
