The attribution score here is that quantity with the softmax and layer-norm denominators dropped, which makes the logit weight a fixed vector rather than an input-dependent one.

The normalizing terms that make the true gradient depend on the current input. Ignoring them is what turns the exact gradient into the constant logit weight $v_{ik}$, and is the stated approximation in this measure.

Named in the plot's annotation as the thing attribution correlation is being contrasted with: correlating the two features' full vocabulary-indexed logit weight vectors directly. That measure agreed poorly with activation correlation.

Two dictionary learning runs with identical hyperparameters, one on activations from transformer A and one from transformer B, which differ only in random seeds. Every dot pairs an A/1 feature with its closest B/1 feature.
The bar charts along the bottom and left edges, showing the one-dimensional distribution of each axis on its own. They let you read how the matches are distributed without the scatter's overplotting.
The scattered dots that fall well below the main diagonal band: pairs that fire together closely but whose attributions agree much less. The annotation states there are only a few of them.
The plot's own heading, naming the two quantities being cross-plotted, in the order x then y.

numbers.meaning: The range of both axes. Both are Pearson correlations, which could in principle run to -1, but the plotted matches are all positive because each pair was selected as the best available match.
The spacing of the labelled ticks on both axes — eleven gridline labels from 0.0 to 1.0.
One dot per feature in run A/1 that has a counterpart. A/1 has 4,096 learned features, of which 168 are dead and 292 are ultralow density, so roughly 3,600 remain as live candidates.
Context from the surrounding text: the median activation correlation between an A/1 feature and its best B/1 match. It is the centre of mass of the bottom marginal histogram in this plot.

Context: the same median when matching individual MLP neurons across the two transformers instead of features. Features match across models far better than neurons do, which is the paper's universality claim.

Context from the Arabic script feature: activation correlation 0.91 but logit weight correlation only 0.23. This gap between the two earlier measures is the reason attribution similarity was introduced.

Context: the activation correlation of A/1/3949 with B/1/3321, a pair with a negative logit weight correlation despite firing almost identically. It is the extreme case that the attribution measure is meant to handle.
Where the scatter is thickest. Most matched pairs both fire alike and attribute alike, which is the figure's point.
The bottom end of the band: pairs whose match was poor on activations also agree poorly on attributions. The relationship holds at the low end as well as the high end.

sections.title: Comparing features between two one-layer transformers

items.caption: For example, a base64 feature increases the probability of tokens like Qg and zA – plausible continuations which would continue to activate it.
items.title: Single-Node Feature Loops
items.takeaway: Four features from the smallest dictionary each raise the probability of exactly the kind of token that would make them fire again one position later, so each one behaves as a one-state machine that keeps re-entering itself. The paper offers this as the simplest case of its "finite state automata" motif. The evidence shown is a list of top-promoted tokens, not a measured transition rate.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Four one-state diagrams, side by side, independent of each other. Each is a single box, and each box is one [[feature]] from [[dictionary-learning-run]] A/0, labelled with its index and with the name the authors gave it by hand: A/0/45 base64, A/0/489 Uppercase DNA, A/0/14 French, A/0/209 SQL.

### How to read one panel

Inside a box are dataset snippets on which that feature fires. The orange background marks where it is active, darker meaning a larger [[feature-activation]]. Each row is a window of four tokens either side of one selected token, shown in bold ([[activation-visualization-sampling]]). So the box is the input side: all four are [[context-features]], active across a whole stretch of text of one kind rather than on one word.

The arrow is the output side. It leaves the box and comes straight back into the same box, and the tokens above it are among those the feature most promotes when it fires. Those come from the [[logit-weight]] — the [[feature-direction]] pushed through the MLP output weights, a linearised layer norm, and the [[unembedding-matrix]], one number per vocabulary token, shifted so the median is zero. The figure prints the top of that list and no magnitudes.

### What it shows

Take A/0/45. It fires on base64 text. The tokens it raises are Qg, zA, YW, MQ — fragments that occur in almost nothing but base64. If the model samples one of those, the text at the next position is still base64.

So A/0/45 fires again there, on a token it helped put there itself.

The feature's output re-supplies its own input. One state, one transition back to itself; the paper calls this a single-node loop ([[self-exciting-feature-loop]]). The other three panels repeat the shape with different material.

Two hedges the paper states itself. Nothing wires the feature to itself inside the network — the loop closes through the emitted token stream, and the model never learned the pieces to cooperate ([[finite-state-automata-features]]). And A/0 holds 512 features, exactly the MLP width, so it is not overcomplete; in wider runs [[feature-splitting]] turns each node here into a family and the tidy one-state picture becomes a larger system.

Note also what is not shown: no sampled continuations, no ablation, no probabilities. The loop is read off a ranked token list.

terms.definition: The first panel's feature: feature number 45 of dictionary learning run 0 on transformer A, which the authors label as a base64 feature because it fires on strings of the base64 alphabet. It is a different, coarser feature from the base64 feature the paper case-studies in depth (A/1/2357).
The second panel's feature, which fires on long uppercase runs of A, T, C and G. The label is the authors' own reading of the dataset examples, not an output of the method.
The third panel's feature, which fires across passages of French prose rather than on any single French word.
The fourth panel's feature, which fires across SQL query text — table names, clauses, aliases.
The transformer the features were learned from. The paper trains two one-layer transformers differing only in random seed, calls them A and B, and studies A throughout.
The dictionary learning run. A/0 is the smallest run in the A/0…A/5 sequence, which holds the sparsity penalty fixed and grows the dictionary.
The position of the feature inside that run's dictionary. The numbers are arbitrary identifiers with no ordering meaning.
One node of the state machine — a single feature, shown together with a sample of the text on which it activates.

A transition from a feature back to itself, drawn leaving the box and re-entering it. It stands for: this feature promotes these tokens, and those tokens would put the model in a state where this same feature fires again.

terms.term: The token list above each arrow
terms.definition: The tokens whose next-token logits the feature raises most when it is active, taken from the feature's logit weight vector. The figure shows the top of the list only, with no values attached.

For one feature, a vector with one entry per vocabulary token saying how much the feature's firing pushes that token's logit up or down. It is computed by multiplying the feature direction by the MLP output weights, an approximation of the layer norm, and the unembedding matrix, then shifting so the feature's median weight is zero (softmax is shift-invariant, so only differences matter).
Marks tokens on which the feature is active in that snippet; darker orange means a larger activation. Uncoloured text is where the feature is off.
The token the snippet is centred on. The paper's visualisations sample tokens from the dataset and show four tokens either side of the sampled one.
A rendered newline character in the source text, drawn as a symbol so line breaks stay visible inside a one-line snippet.

terms.term: Leading spaces inside quoted tokens (" dans", " WHERE")
terms.definition: Part of the token itself. Under byte-pair encoding a word preceded by a space is usually a different token from the same word without one, so the paper prints the space.

The base64 feature's promoted tokens. They are short mixed-case letter fragments drawn from the base64 alphabet [a-zA-Z0-9+/]; several of them are near-meaningless in ordinary English text, which is why emitting one keeps the context reading as base64.
The DNA feature's promoted tokens — uppercase groupings of the four nucleotide letters, as the tokenizer happens to chunk them. Any of them continues a nucleotide string.

terms.term: "à", " dans", " avec", " qui", " pour", " des", " été", " é", " les"
terms.definition: The French feature's promoted tokens: common French function words plus accented fragments. " é" is a partial token that appears inside accented French words, so it is French-specific in a way that " les" alone is not.

The SQL feature's promoted tokens: query keywords, a column type, and the bare string SQL. "SQL" is printed without a leading space, so it is the token that appears inside identifiers such as mySQL rather than as a standalone word.
Text following the end of the nucleotide run in that snippet. Its pale shading shows the feature dropping off once the DNA stops, which is the visual signature of a context feature switching off.
A feature that fires across a whole region of text of a given kind — base64, DNA, French, SQL — rather than on one particular token. All four panels here are of this type.
The paper's second reading of any feature in a one-layer model: as well as responding to base64, a base64 feature acts to make base64 more likely. This figure is that reading drawn as a diagram.

Its name for assemblies of features where one feature raises tokens that cause another feature to fire at the next position. The paper is careful that these are not circuits: the features interact through the emitted token stream, and were never trained to work together.

As the dictionary is made wider, one broad feature divides into several narrower ones covering roughly the same territory. The paper notes this is why the single nodes here would become multi-node systems in a larger run.
A dictionary with more directions than the dimension of the space it decomposes. The paper flags that A/0 is not overcomplete, which is what keeps these diagrams as small as they are.

numbers.meaning: The dictionary learning run index. A/0 is the smallest run the paper trains on transformer A; the figure draws its features specifically because that run is coarse enough for the loops to have one node each.
The feature indices inside run A/0 for the base64, Uppercase DNA, French and SQL features. They are arbitrary slot numbers assigned during training and carry no order or magnitude.

The number of features in A/0 — equal to the transformer's MLP width, also 512. Because the dictionary is the same size as the layer it decomposes, A/0 is not overcomplete, which the paper gives as the reason these systems stay so simple.

The dictionary sizes of A/1 and A/2, the next runs in the sequence. Not shown in this figure, but they are the reason for the caveat: the base64 features go from 1 in A/0 to 3 in A/1 to many more in A/2, so the single node splits.

How many promoted tokens are printed above each panel's arrow (base64, DNA, French, SQL respectively). These are display counts — the top of a ranked list — not a property of the features; the full logit weight vector has one entry per vocabulary token.
The number of tokens shown on each side of the selected token in every snippet row, per the paper's visualisation settings. It is why the rows are short and cut off mid-word.

The visualisations draw from a 100-million-token subset of the training data, taking only 10 tokens from any one context. Sampling sparsely across contexts is meant to stop the displayed examples all coming from a handful of documents.

The size of the base64 alphabet, [a-zA-Z0-9+/], which is how the paper models base64 strings. Six bits per character means base64 text looks like uniform random draws from those 64 symbols, which is exactly what makes fragments like Qg and zA base64-specific rather than English.

numbers.value: Digits inside the base64 snippets (ILNdCxmNt1pPtV5, pWK2bVrV7PRd, 15P8Vr/sc7m, 7wFLfcSJT43JD6)
numbers.meaning: Raw dataset text, not measurements. Digits are part of the base64 alphabet, so they appear interleaved with letters at roughly one character in six; the strings have no meaning to decode.

numbers.value: Numbers inside the SQL snippets (246, table1, parent_id, tableid, tablealias1)
numbers.meaning: Also raw dataset text — literal values and table identifiers scraped from SQL in the training corpus. They are there to show what the feature fires on, not to be read as quantities.

The residual stream width of the transformer under study and the number of Pile tokens it was trained on. The paper deliberately overtrains this small model, hypothesising that many training tokens give cleaner representations in superposition.

items.caption: Let's now consider a two-node system for producing variables in "all caps snake case" (e.g. ARRAY_MAX_VALUE). One node (A/0/207) activates on the all caps text tokens, the other (A/0/358) on underscores:
items.title: The All-Caps Snake Case Loop
items.takeaway: Two features from the smallest dictionary — one firing on all-caps word pieces, one on underscores — each raise the probability of the tokens that switch the other on, so alternating between them produces variable names like ARRAY_MAX_VALUE. The paper offers it as its simplest two-node case of a feature assembly that behaves like a state machine, with the hand-off happening through the sampled token stream rather than through weights.
items.walkthrough:
**What you are looking at.** Two boxes, three arrows, and the figure's own note in the right margin. Each box is one learned [[feature]] from [[dictionary-learning]] run A/0, named in the paper's [[feature-notation]]: model A, then the run index, then the feature's index inside that run ([[dictionary-learning-run]]). Inside each box are dataset examples where that feature fires. Orange shading marks the per-token [[feature-activation]]; darker orange and bold mean a larger value. The snippets follow the paper's usual display: text drawn from a 100-million-token subset, four tokens of context shown on each side ([[activation-visualization-sampling]]).

**How to read the arrows.** They are not weights running between the two features. A/0 decomposes a [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]], where two features in the same MLP have no path to each other within one forward pass. An arrow means something slower. The feature at its tail pushes up the next-token logits for the tokens written on the arrow ([[logit-weight]]) — the "action" reading of a feature ([[action-features]]). That token then gets sampled. At the next position it switches on the feature at the arrow's head. The loop closes through the generated text, which is why the paper calls these assemblies [[finite-state-automata-features]] and says plainly that they are not [[circuit]]s.

**What it shows.** A/0/207 fires on all-caps word pieces — BOT, TAC, the ST in AC_SUBST, the SPA in SPACER. It upweights caps continuations ("ING", "ES", "ABLE", …), which land back on itself: that is the self-loop at top left, the same shape as the single-node case the section opens with ([[self-exciting-feature-loop]]). It also upweights "_", the arrow across the top.

A/0/358 fires on exactly those underscores. In FORWARD_ADAPTER_MAX the underscores are shaded and the letters are not. It upweights openings of fresh caps segments — "MEM", "MAX", "END", … — the bottom arrow back into 207.

Alternate the two: caps, more caps, underscore, caps again. That is ARRAY_MAX_VALUE.

One qualification the paper states: A/0 holds 512 features, equal to the MLP width, so it is not overcomplete ([[overcompleteness]]). In wider runs the caps node undergoes [[feature-splitting]] and this tidy two-node picture becomes a larger system.

terms.definition: The left node: a feature in run A/0 that activates on all-caps text tokens, especially pieces of words inside all-caps identifiers. In the figure it is the source of both the caps self-loop and the underscore arrow.
The right node: a feature in run A/0 that activates on the underscore character between all-caps segments. It is what fires immediately after 207 has emitted an underscore.
The dictionary learning run these two features come from — model A, run index 0, the smallest dictionary in the A sequence. Its features are coarse, which is why the diagram has only two nodes.

The paper's naming scheme for features: the letter is the transformer (A or B), the middle number is the autoencoder run, the last number is the feature's index within that run. Neurons get written A/neurons/32 instead.
Here a node is one feature, drawn as a box containing sampled text where it fires. It is a state of the informal automaton the two features implement together.

A transition: the feature at the tail raises the probability of the tokens labelling the arrow, and once such a token is sampled, the feature at the head fires on it at the next position. No weight connects the two features directly.
The activation display: shading intensity on a token shows how strongly that feature fired there, with the darkest, bolded tokens carrying the largest values and unshaded tokens carrying zero.
The naming convention the two features jointly model — words written in capitals and joined by underscores, as in variable and macro names.
The paper's worked example of the pattern; not text from the dataset panels but an illustration of what running the loop produces.
The label on the self-loop: tokens A/0/207 upweights that continue an all-caps word, so the next token re-activates 207 itself.
The label on the top arrow from 207 to 358: the underscore token, which 207 upweights as an alternative to continuing the current word, and which is exactly what 358 responds to.
The label on the bottom arrow from 358 back to 207: tokens A/0/358 upweights after an underscore, each of which starts a new all-caps segment and so re-activates 207.
A dataset example in the 207 panel, with BOT most strongly shaded — a caps identifier fragment of the kind that drives this feature.
A dataset example in the 207 panel from shell or autoconf-style code, peaking on TAC.
A dataset example in the 207 panel; the feature peaks on the ST piece of SUBST, showing it fires on sub-word caps tokens, not whole words.
A dataset example in the 207 panel, peaking on OTED inside UNQUOTED.
A dataset example in the 207 panel, peaking on SPA inside SPACER.
A dataset example in the 358 panel where the shading sits on the underscores and not on the capital letters — the cleanest read of what separates 358 from 207.
A dataset example in the 358 panel; again only the underscores are shaded.
A dataset example in the 358 panel, including a leading underscore at the start of the shown window.
A dataset example in the 358 panel, from what looks like a C preprocessor guard for ARM NEON.

terms.term: Margin note ("Two features interact to model …")
terms.definition: The figure's own annotation, stating that the first feature activates on all-caps tokens and predicts continuations or an underscore, and the second activates on the underscore and predicts the start of new all-caps components.
Reading a feature by what it makes more likely next, not only by what makes it fire. The arrows in this diagram are the action reading; the shaded panels are the input reading.

The paper's loose label for a set of features that hand off to each other through the token stream, each firing state predicting tokens that move the model into the next state. It stresses these are unlike circuits, since the model never learned the parts to work together — they interact only because of patterns in the data.
The effect that widening the autoencoder divides one feature into several narrower ones. Named here as the reason this two-node picture holds only for the small A/0 dictionary.
A dictionary with more entries than the dimension of the space being decomposed. A/0 is not overcomplete, which the paper flags when presenting these diagrams.

numbers.meaning: The index of the all-caps feature within run A/0. It is an arbitrary label from the training run, carrying no ordering meaning; with 512 features in A/0 the indices run 0 to 511.
The index of the underscore feature within run A/0, likewise arbitrary.

The run index: the first and smallest dictionary in the A/0…A/5 sequence, which holds the L1 coefficient fixed and increases dictionary size. The section explains its examples come from A/0 because the systems are simplest there.
The number of features in A/0, stated in the section text as equal to the transformer's MLP dimension — which is why the paper calls this run not overcomplete.
The number of nodes, one per feature. The paper presents this as the next step up from the single-node self-exciting loop shown just before it.
The number of arrows drawn: a self-loop on 207, a 207-to-358 transition on the underscore, and a 358-to-207 transition on caps openings. The two-node description counts states, not transitions.
The count of continuation tokens listed on the self-loop label ("ING" through "LE"). A sample of what 207 upweights, not an exhaustive list.
The count of segment-opening tokens listed on the bottom arrow ("MEM" through "BEGIN"). Again a sample of the tokens 358 upweights.
The number of dataset snippets shown inside the A/0/207 panel.
The number of dataset snippets shown inside the A/0/358 panel.
The size, in tokens, of the training-data subset the paper draws all its activation visualizations from, with only 10 tokens taken from each context.
The display window used throughout the paper: four tokens either side of the selected token, which is why the snippets here are short fragments rather than full lines.
Literal text from the dataset example, part of an identifier — not a measurement.
Literal text from the dataset example, an argument value following the identifier.
Literal text from the dataset example, a numeric argument in the sampled code — no interpretive weight.

items.caption: Thus, we observe two features, one of which fires on either complete characters or the suffix (predicting either a new complete character, or a prefix), while the other only fires on the prefixes and predicts suffixes.
items.title: Unicode Prefix–Suffix Feature Loops
items.takeaway: Where a script's characters are tokenized as a prefix byte plus a suffix byte, the paper finds a pair of features that hand off to each other: each one's top predicted tokens are exactly the tokens the other one fires on. Chinese adds a wrinkle — because a complete single-token character sits in the same position as a suffix, one feature covers both, and it also predicts back into itself.
items.walkthrough:
Four boxes, arranged as two independent panels that share a layout. Tamil on the left, Chinese on the right.

Each box is one [[feature]] found by the [[sparse-autoencoder]]. It carries the feature's identifier, a hand-written name, and a strip of [[top-dataset-examples]] — snippets of text where it fires, with orange shading for the [[feature-activation]] and darker orange for stronger firing.

The arrows are not weights and not wires. Each arrow is labelled with the tokens the source feature most raises in the next-token distribution — its largest positive [[logit-weight]] entries. It points at the feature those tokens would activate on the following step.

So a path through this diagram is a path through generated text, not through the network. That is the claim behind [[finite-state-automata-features]]: no circuit joins these features, they meet only through the token stream.

### The token vocabulary

The tokenizer is [[byte-pair-encoding]] over bytes, so a non-Latin character often arrives as several tokens ([[utf8-multi-token-characters]]). Tamil ண (U+0BA3) is UTF-8 bytes E0 AE A3, tokenized as `\xe0\xae` then `\xa3`.

Call `\xe0\xae` a **prefix token** and `\xa3` a **suffix token**. The prefix roughly fixes the Unicode block; the suffix picks the character inside it.

### Left panel: the plain two-node case

A/1/2499 fires on suffix bytes. Its top logit weights are the two Tamil prefixes `\xe0\xae` and `\xe0\xaf` — precisely what A/1/522 fires on.

A/1/522 fires on prefixes, and its top logit weights are continuation bytes `\x8d`, `\x81`, and so on — precisely what A/1/2499 fires on. Two arrows, one cycle, alternating forever ([[unicode-token-state-machines]]).

### Right panel: Chinese

Common Chinese characters get their own single token; rarer ones split. The paper's observation is that a complete character occupies the same position as a suffix — either can be followed by a whole new character or by a new prefix.

So one feature covers both. A/0/397 fires on complete characters *and* on suffix bytes, and its top logit weights fall into two groups, drawn as two arrows. Whole-character tokens (是, 的, 在) loop straight back into itself. Prefix tokens (`\xe5\x8f`, `\xe4\xbe`) land on A/0/101.

A/0/101 fires only on prefixes and predicts suffix bytes, which land back in A/0/397. Three arrows, two nodes, one self-loop.

Two caveats the paper states. A/0 holds 512 features while A/1 holds 4,096, and wider runs make these systems messier through [[feature-splitting]] — so the tidiness depends on dictionary size. And the diagram is read off top examples and top logit weights, not measured by intervention.

terms.definition: The top-left node: a feature from model A, dictionary learning run 1, index 2499, which fires on the second (suffix) byte token of a split Tamil character. Its name is the authors' own label, not an output of the method.
The top-right node of the left panel: a feature that fires on the first (prefix) byte token of a split Tamil character, the token that names the Unicode block.

The left node of the right panel: a feature that fires both on complete single-token Chinese characters and on the suffix byte of a split Chinese character. The paper argues these two cases are equivalent for prediction purposes, which is why one feature covers both.
The right node of the right panel: a feature that fires only on the prefix byte token of a split Chinese character, never on complete characters.
Which transformer the features come from. The paper studies two one-layer models, A and B; every feature here is from A.
Which sparse autoencoder training run produced the feature. Runs A/0 through A/5 share an L1 coefficient and increase in dictionary size, so the run index is effectively a resolution setting.
The index of the individual feature within its run. The numbers are arbitrary labels assigned by training; nothing is encoded in their magnitude.

The first byte token of a multi-token character, such as \xe0\xae for Tamil or \xe5\x8f for Chinese. It roughly determines which Unicode block the character sits in, but leaves the character itself undetermined.
The trailing continuation byte, such as \xa3 or \x93, which selects the specific character inside the block the prefix opened. It only makes sense following a prefix.
A Chinese character frequent enough that the byte-pair tokenizer gave it a single dedicated token, such as 是 or 的. No prefix or suffix is involved.

Not a connection inside the network. It runs from a feature to the feature that would fire next, and its label lists the tokens the source feature raises the probability of — tokens that happen to belong to the target's firing set.

The tokens with the largest positive logit weight for the source feature: those it most pushes up when it fires. Logit weight is computed by pushing the feature direction through the MLP output weights, a linearized layer norm, and the unembedding.

terms.term: Orange highlight in the example strips
terms.definition: How strongly the feature activates on that token, from a 100-million-token sample of the training data. Darker orange means a larger activation; unshaded tokens are context only.

terms.term: Bolded byte token inside a snippet
terms.definition: In the A/1/522 and A/0/101 panels, the bolded byte sequence marks the prefix token the feature is firing on, distinguishing it from the neighbouring bytes shown for context.

terms.term: Grey byte text above rendered glyphs
terms.definition: The raw token sequence the model actually sees, written as escaped hex bytes, with the human-readable characters those bytes decode to shown beneath. The two rows are the same text at two levels.

terms.term: Dotted circle glyph (◌ followed by a mark)
terms.definition: A Tamil combining vowel sign rendered with a placeholder circle because it has no standalone form. It appears where the decoded character is a diacritic rather than a base letter.
The two Tamil prefix tokens, the only ones the block needs. \xe0\xae opens the lower half of the Tamil block and \xe0\xaf the upper half.
Six of the Chinese prefix tokens A/0/397 predicts. There are many of them because Chinese characters are spread across large Unicode blocks that do not line up with byte boundaries.

terms.term: 是, 的, 在, 。, 不, 有, 一, 到, 为
terms.definition: High-frequency Chinese characters and punctuation that each have a single dedicated token. They are what A/0/397 predicts on the self-loop arrow, and they land back in its own firing set.

A set of features that behave like states in a state machine: each raises the probability of tokens that then trigger the next feature. The paper is explicit that the model never learned these to work together — they interact only because of patterns in the text.

terms.term: Feature splitting (named in the surrounding text)
terms.definition: As the autoencoder dictionary is widened, one feature divides into several more specific ones. The paper warns that these two-node systems become more complicated systems at larger dictionary sizes.
A direction in the MLP's activation space recovered by the sparse autoencoder, treated as an interpretable unit in place of a neuron. The scalar attached to it on a given token is its activation.

numbers.meaning: The two Tamil feature identifiers. Both come from run 1, which has 4,096 features — noticeably wider than the run used for most other examples in this section.
The two Chinese feature identifiers, both from run 0. The section notes run 0 is the one where these systems stay simple.

The number of features in run A/0, and also the number of neurons in the transformer's MLP. The paper flags this: A/0 is not overcomplete, so its dictionary has exactly as many directions as the space has dimensions.
The number of features in run A/1, eight times the MLP width. The Tamil pair is drawn from this wider run, so it already reflects some feature splitting relative to A/0.
The Unicode block for Tamil, given in the surrounding text. It is 128 code points wide, which is why two prefix tokens suffice to cover it.
The code point of ண, the worked example in the text. It sits in the lower half of the Tamil block.
The UTF-8 encoding of U+0BA3 as three bytes. The tokenizer merges the first two into \xe0\xae and leaves \xa3 alone, which is the split the two Tamil features track.
The byte range every suffix token falls in, because UTF-8 continuation bytes all start with the bits 10. Every value on the two bottom arrow labels — \x81 through \xa7 — lies inside it.
The leading byte range of the Chinese prefix tokens shown, reflecting that CJK characters occupy the three-byte UTF-8 range starting around U+4E00. All six labelled prefixes begin \xe4, \xe5 or \xe9.
How many tokens label the Tamil top arrow: \xe0\xae and \xe0\xaf. Two is the whole set of Tamil prefixes, so this feature's prediction covers the block completely.

How many suffix bytes label each bottom arrow — the Tamil one lists \x8d through \x9f, the Chinese one \x93 through \x94. These are truncated top-logit lists, not exhaustive: many more continuation bytes exist.
How many complete-character tokens label the Chinese self-loop arrow. They are the most frequent single-token characters, which is why they dominate the logit weights.
How many prefix tokens label the arrow from A/0/397 to A/0/101. Fewer than the suffix list, but far more than Tamil's two, because Chinese spans many Unicode blocks.
How many activating dataset examples the figure shows for each Tamil feature. It is an illustrative sample from the interface, not a measured statistic.
How many Chinese text snippets are shown for that feature. They contain no escaped bytes, illustrating the complete-character half of its firing set.
The size of the token subset the example strips are drawn from, with only 10 tokens kept per context. Each highlighted token is displayed with four tokens of context on either side.

items.caption: The full system can be seen below:
items.title: The Four-Node HTML Automaton
items.takeaway: Four features in the smallest dictionary hand off to each other through the token stream — open bracket, tag name, closing bracket, newline-and-indent, back to open bracket — so that together they behave like a small state machine that emits well-formed HTML such as `<div>\n\t\t<span>`. The paper stresses that nothing tied these four together during training: each learned its own job, and the loop exists because HTML in the training data has that shape.
items.walkthrough:
Four boxes, one per feature, with labelled arrows running between them.

Each box is a feature from the A/0 [[dictionary-learning-run]]. Under the paper's [[feature-notation]], the "A" names the transformer, the "0" names the autoencoder run, and the last number is the feature's index inside that run.

Inside a box sit rows of text sampled from the dataset, four tokens on each side of the selected token ([[activation-visualization-sampling]]). Orange shading marks how hard the feature fires on a token — darker is stronger, pale tan is weak.

The arrows are not weights between features. Each arrow is labelled with the tokens the source feature pushes hardest in the next-token distribution, its top [[logit-weight]] entries, and points at the feature that those tokens then switch on one step later. The handoff travels through the emitted text, not through the network. That is all [[finite-state-automata-features]] means here.

Now the loop. A/0/20 fires on the bracket that opens a tag — `<`, `</`, `><`, `></`. Section 5.1 calls it the "`<` in HTML" feature, one of the paper's [[token-in-context-features]]. It predicts tag names: div, td, span, li, tr, thead, tbody, section, table.

Those tag-name tokens are what A/0/0 fires on, most strongly on ul, also li, div, nav, entry. It predicts closes: `>`, `></`, `/>`, `><`, and `>` glued to punctuation.

A/0/30 fires on that closing `>` or `/>`, and predicts whitespace — the three quoted strings over the third arrow are a newline glyph followed by different amounts of indentation.

A/0/494 fires on exactly that newline-plus-indent token and predicts ` <`, ` </`, ` <!--`, `</`. The long arrow along the bottom carries it back to A/0/20 and closes the cycle. Run the loop once and you get `<div>\n\t\t<span>`.

The diagram adds two things beyond that four-step story. First, shortcuts: A/0/0 and A/0/30 also predict `></` and ` </`, skipping the whitespace node. Second, an exit — the dashed arrow dropping out of A/0/0, labelled ` xmlns`, ` href`, ` class`. If the model emits an attribute name, these four features say nothing about what follows. The paper names that gap itself.

One caveat carries the weight. A/0 has 512 features, the same width as the MLP, so the dictionary is not overcomplete. The simplicity here is a property of that resolution: in a wider run each node undergoes [[feature-splitting]] into a family, and the paper says the system becomes much more complex.

terms.definition: The open-tag node. It fires on the bracket tokens that begin an HTML tag — `<`, `</`, `><`, `></` — as the orange highlights in the leftmost panel show, and its top predicted tokens are tag names. Section 5.1 describes it as the 'angle bracket in HTML' feature.

The tag-name node. It fires on tag-name tokens (ul most strongly, then li, div, nav, entry) and predicts the tokens that close a tag. It is also the node from which the automaton leaks: it predicts attribute names too.
The tag-close node. It fires on the closing `>` and on the self-closing `/>`, wherever they end a tag, and predicts a newline followed by indentation.
The whitespace node. It fires on a newline-plus-indentation token that follows a closed tag, and predicts the bracket tokens that open the next tag — which returns control to A/0/20.

The dictionary learning run these four features come from: the smallest autoencoder in the A series, with 512 learned features. The paper picks it here because at this size the HTML system is only four nodes.

terms.term: A (first component of the feature name)
terms.definition: The transformer the features were extracted from — the one-layer model with a 512-neuron ReLU MLP that the paper studies throughout. A second model, B, is used only for universality checks.

A direction in MLP activation space recovered by the sparse autoencoder, standing in for a neuron as the unit of analysis. Each box in this diagram is one such direction, shown by the tokens it responds to.
Marks a token where the feature is active, with darker orange meaning a larger activation value. This is the paper's standard way of showing when a feature fires.
The same activation scale at its low end: a token where the feature fires weakly. In the A/0/494 panel, for example, `class=` and `PyTorch` get tan while the newline token gets full orange.

A handoff. The label lists tokens the source feature raises in the next-token distribution; the arrowhead points at the feature those tokens activate on the following step. It is a claim about the token stream, not a learned connection between features.

The one arrow that leaves the system. A/0/0 also predicts attribute-name tokens, and no node in this four-feature picture covers what happens after one is emitted, so the arrow points off the diagram.
The vector, one entry per vocabulary token, giving how much a feature's firing raises or lowers that token's next-token logit. The token lists on the arrows are the top positive entries.

The visualization's printed stand-in for a newline character inside a token, so that whitespace tokens are visible. It appears both inside the panels and in the whitespace strings labelling the A/0/30 to A/0/494 arrow.

terms.term: div, td, span, li, tr, thead, tbody, section, table
terms.definition: The tag names A/0/20 predicts once an opening bracket has been emitted. They are ordinary HTML element names, listed in the label above the first arrow.
The tokens A/0/0 predicts after a tag name — all of them close the tag, some with the following character already merged into the same token by the tokenizer.
The three whitespace tokens A/0/30 predicts: a newline followed by differing amounts of indentation. The differing widths in the label are differing indent depths, not different characters.
The tokens A/0/494 predicts after whitespace: an open bracket for a new element, a closing-tag bracket, or the start of an HTML comment. These are what re-activate A/0/20.
A shortcut edge. A/0/30 also predicts a closing bracket directly, so the model can move from a tag close straight back to an open-bracket state without emitting whitespace in between.
A second shortcut edge. These tokens both close the current tag and open the next one, so emitting one sends the system from the tag-name node back to the open-tag node in a single step.
Attribute-name tokens that A/0/0 also predicts. Emitting one leads to attribute syntax, which is the state the paper says these four features fail to describe.

The prototypical sample the paper says this loop generates: open bracket, tag name, close, newline and two tabs, then a new open bracket and tag name. Reading it left to right walks the four nodes in order.

The paper's loose label for an assembly of features that hand off through generated tokens rather than through weights. It flags explicitly that these are not circuits, and that the model was never trained to make the pieces cooperate.
The reading of a feature by what it predicts rather than what it responds to. This diagram depends on that reading: each node is named by both its firing condition and its output tokens.

The observation that widening the autoencoder divides one feature into a family of more specific ones. The paper invokes it to say this four-node picture is a property of A/0's coarseness and would fragment in a larger run.

Having more dictionary directions than the dimension of the space they live in. A/0 is not overcomplete — 512 features for a 512-dimensional activation space — which the paper notes when introducing these examples.
A feature that fires on one specific token but only in a particular kind of surrounding text. A/0/20 is the paper's own example: the `<` character, in HTML.

numbers.meaning: The feature indices of the four nodes within run A/0. They are positions in the autoencoder's hidden layer and carry no meaning of their own — the ordering is whatever training produced. They are quoted so a reader can look each one up in the published feature interface.
The index of the dictionary learning run. A/0 through A/5 form a sequence at fixed L1 coefficient with increasing dictionary size, so 0 is the smallest and coarsest of them.

The number of features in A/0, and also the width of the transformer's MLP. Because these are equal, the dictionary is exactly 1x expansion and not overcomplete; the paper cites this as the reason the HTML system here is only four nodes.

The number of nodes in this system. The paper contrasts it with the one-node base64 loop and the two-node snake-case and Unicode systems shown just before, presenting this as the more complex end of what A/0 offers.
The visualization convention: each row shows the selected token with four tokens before and four after. This is why the snippets in the panels are short and cut off mid-word.

The sampling behind every panel in the paper. Activating examples are drawn from a 100-million-token subset of the training data, taking only 10 tokens from any one context so the displayed rows are not all from the same document.
How many predicted tokens each arrow lists. These are top entries of the source feature's logit weight vector, truncated for display, not the complete set of tokens the feature promotes.
The indentation in the prototypical sample. The exact depth is incidental — A/0/494 fires on newline-plus-indent tokens of several different widths, as the three strings on the third arrow show.

The size of A/1, the next run up and the one the paper analyses in detail. The text points at it as where this system would stop being simple, since each node would split into a family of narrower features.

items.caption: It's important to note that these features can be quite contextual. There are several features related to IRC transcripts which form a totally different finite state automata like system:
items.title: The IRC Transcript Automaton
items.takeaway: Four features from run A/0 hand off to each other across an IRC transcript: one fires on the "<" that opens a nickname, one on the nickname's interior, one on the closing ">", and one across the message text that follows. None of them is keyed to a distinctive token — "<" and ">" are the same characters that drive the paper's HTML automaton — so what selects a feature here is the position inside an IRC line's format, not the token's identity.
items.walkthrough:
You are looking at four boxes and five arrows. Each box is one feature from [[dictionary-learning-run]] A/0. Together the paper reads them as a [[finite-state-automata-features]] assembly: no weights wire these features to each other, and they hand off only through the token stream, one feature raising the probability of tokens that make the next feature fire.

### Reading a box

The heading is the feature's name in the paper's [[feature-notation]]. Under it are five dataset examples where the feature fired. Orange shading is activation strength, darker meaning stronger. The bold token is the one the example was sampled at, with four tokens of context shown on each side ([[activation-visualization-sampling]]). The ⏎ glyph is a line break sitting in the token stream.

### Reading an arrow

An arrow's label lists the tokens the source feature pushes hardest toward — its largest [[logit-weight]] entries. The arrow claims that once such a token is emitted, the target feature fires on the next step. Two arrows return to their own box, the [[self-exciting-feature-loop]] case.

### Walking the cycle

A/0/178 fires on the "<" that opens a nickname right after a line break, as in "the better.⏎<Ayabara>". It promotes nick-opening pieces: "ubottu", "nick", "dav", "Blues".

Those land inside the brackets, where A/0/153 fires and shades the whole nickname — "rostayob", "hardwarenoob", "jnoob22". A/0/153 promotes more nick fragments ("ob", "onia", "oke"), which re-excite it, so a nick can run to any length. It also promotes ">" and "_>", which close the nick and switch on A/0/151.

A/0/151 activates most strongly on that ">". It promotes message openers: " hmm", " lol", " ok". One of those turns on A/0/46, which shades the entire message line and promotes " ubuntu", " linux", " sudo", " :)" — keeping itself on.

Chained, the paper says this generates something like `<nickonia_> lol ubuntu ;)`.

### What makes it contextual

The "<" and ">" here are the same characters that drive the [[html-feature-automaton]], where different A/0 features claim them. A/0/46's bold tokens include plain words like "on" and "given", so it behaves like one of the paper's [[context-features]] rather than a topic detector. Position in the IRC line format is what selects the feature — the reading the paper offers for [[token-in-context-features]].

Two caveats the paper states: A/0 is not overcomplete, so wider runs would split these into more states ([[feature-splitting]]); and the Ubuntu vocabulary is presumed to be a fact about the [[pile-dataset]].

terms.definition: The feature drawn leftmost; it fires on the "<" character that opens a nickname at the start of an IRC line, immediately after a line break. Its top predicted tokens are nickname-opening fragments.

The nickname-interior feature; it activates across the characters between "<" and ">", and its examples show the whole nick shaded. It predicts both further nick fragments (feeding itself) and the closing ">".
The nick-close feature; its strongest activation is on the ">" that ends a nickname, with weaker activation on the colon after an addressed nick. It predicts the first word of a chat message.
The message-body feature; it shades whole lines of IRC message text and switches off at the line break. It predicts Linux/Ubuntu vocabulary and emoticons, which keep it firing.
The paper's identifier scheme: "A" is the transformer, "0" is which sparse autoencoder run the feature came from, and the final number indexes the feature inside that run.
The dictionary learning run used for this whole finite-state-automata section; it is not overcomplete, learning 512 features for a 512-neuron MLP.
One node of the automaton: a single feature, named at the top, with dataset examples of it firing underneath.

A transition. It does not represent a weight between features; it represents the source feature raising the probability of the labelled tokens, which then cause the target feature to fire on the next step.
The tokens the source feature most increases the logits for — the top entries of its logit weight vector. Leading spaces are shown where the token itself carries one, as in " hmm" or " ubuntu".
An arrow that leaves a box and returns to the same box, meaning the feature predicts tokens that reactivate itself. Two appear here, on A/0/153 and A/0/46.
Activation strength of that feature on that token, with darker orange meaning higher activation and no shading meaning the feature is off.
The token the example window was sampled at; the display shows four tokens on either side of it as context.
A newline character in the token stream, rendered as a glyph so the line boundaries of the transcript are visible.

terms.term: Row marker at the left of A/0/178's first example
terms.definition: A small interface marker at the start of that row, part of the visualization chrome rather than part of the transcript text.
A log of Internet Relay Chat, in which each line has a fixed shape: a speaker's nickname in angle brackets, then the message text. That fixed shape is what the four features carve up.

The speaker's handle in an IRC line, written between "<" and ">". Examples in the figure include wastrel, Ayabara, matu, MasterShrak, xtknight, Amarilis, rostayob, hardwarenoob, nikunjlahot, jnoob22, in_mario, Porkepix2, onetinsoldier, dontm and beilabs.
The token A/0/178 fires on. Here it opens a nickname; in the paper's HTML automaton the same character opens a tag and a different feature fires on it, which is the contrast the figure is making.
The tokens A/0/153 predicts to end a nickname, and the ones A/0/151 fires on. "_>" is a single token covering an underscore followed by the closing bracket, common in nicks ending in an underscore.
A/0/178's top predicted tokens: subword pieces that commonly start an IRC handle. "ubottu" is the name of a well-known Ubuntu support bot.
A/0/153's top predicted tokens: subword pieces that extend a handle in progress. "ob" recurs because "noob" is a frequent ending in this corpus.

terms.term: Message openers (" hmm", " yeah", " hey", " ok", " hello", " heh", " yep", " ah", " lol")
terms.definition: A/0/151's top predicted tokens: the words that typically start a chat message once the nickname has closed.

terms.term: Body vocabulary (" ubuntu", " linux", " Ubuntu", " :)", " sudo", " gnome", " install", " ;)")
terms.definition: A/0/46's top predicted tokens: Linux support vocabulary plus emoticons, which the paper attributes to the training corpus containing many Linux IRC channels.
The convention of starting a message with another user's handle plus a colon to address them. A/0/151 shows weaker activation on these, alongside its strong activation on ">".
Chat emoticons appearing both in the dataset examples and in A/0/46's predicted tokens; they occur at message ends, where they keep the message-body feature firing.
A feature that stays on across a whole region of text of a certain kind rather than on one token. A/0/46 behaves this way, shading entire message lines including ordinary words like "on" and "given".
A feature that fires on a specific token but only in a particular surrounding context. A/0/178 and A/0/151 are of this kind: they take "<" and ">" only in IRC lines, not in HTML.
The paper's name for a group of features that pass control to each other through emitted tokens rather than through weights, so the model steps between states as it generates.

The tendency of a single feature to divide into several more specific ones as the dictionary is made wider. The paper notes it would turn each of these four nodes into a larger sub-system in bigger runs.

numbers.meaning: The feature indices inside run A/0. They are arbitrary identifiers assigned by the autoencoder's hidden-unit ordering, so their size carries no meaning and their ordering left-to-right in the figure is the paper's choice, not the run's.

Which dictionary learning run the features come from. The paper says explicitly that these automaton examples are drawn from A/0, the run that is not overcomplete, because the systems there are simple enough to draw.

The dictionary size of run A/0, equal to the transformer's MLP width. Because there is one learned feature per neuron, the run has no room to split states finely, which is why the paper says larger runs would turn each node here into a more complex sub-system.

The number of nodes drawn: A/0/178, A/0/153, A/0/151, A/0/46. Four is what the paper found sufficient to cover one IRC line — nick open, nick body, nick close, message — the same node count as its HTML automaton, but with different features and different transitions.
The number of arrows: three forward transitions (178→153, 153→151, 151→46) plus two self-loops (153→153, 46→46). The self-loops are what let a nickname and a message each run to arbitrary length.
The number of dataset examples shown per feature. This is a display choice in the paper's feature visualization, not a measurement; the underlying interface shows many more.

The number of tokens of context shown on each side of the bold sampled token, per the paper's activation visualization settings. Counting them confirms which token each example was selected for — in "makes a diff to driver performance⏎<baz", there are exactly four tokens either side of the bold "driver".
The number of tokens listed on each arrow. These are truncated top-of-list logit weights; the paper shows enough to make the transition legible rather than the full vocabulary-length vector.

The visualization examples are drawn from a 100-million-token subset of the training data, taking only 10 tokens from any one context. Sampling sparsely across contexts stops the five example rows from all coming from the same chat log.

Digits that are part of IRC handles rather than quantities. They matter only as evidence that A/0/153's shading extends over the numeric tail of a nickname, so the feature tracks the bracketed span, not a specific word.

The number of Pile tokens the one-layer transformer was trained on. The paper leans on that scale of exposure when it says the Pile presumably contains a great many Linux IRC transcripts, which is its explanation for why A/0/46 predicts " ubuntu" and " sudo".

items.caption: This is a relatively standard legal language, and notably occurs in the file headers for popular open source software licenses, meaning the model likely saw it many times during training.
items.title: The License-Boilerplate Chain
items.takeaway: Three narrow features from the large A/4 dictionary fire in sequence — on the "A", then on "PARTICULAR", then on "PURPOSE" — with each one raising the probability of the token that triggers the next. Together they reproduce the tail of the standard licence phrase "MERCHANTABILITY or FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE", which the paper offers as apparent memorization of a string the model saw many times in training.
items.walkthrough:
You are looking at three [[feature|features]] from a single [[dictionary-learning-run|dictionary learning run]], drawn as a chain of boxes and arrows.

Each grey box is one feature, named in the paper's [[feature-notation|feature notation]]. "A/4/11432" means feature number 11432, found by run 4 of [[dictionary-learning]], on the transformer called A. The lines inside a box are [[top-dataset-examples|top activating dataset examples]]: short windows of training text where that feature fired hardest.

To read a box, look for the orange highlight. It marks the one token the feature fired on; the surrounding words are printed only so you can see what that token was sitting in. A darker, bolder highlight means a larger activation.

To read an arrow, read its label. The label is a token whose [[logit-weight]] this feature pushes strongly up — the thing the feature votes for as the next token. The arrowhead points at the feature that fires once that token is actually there.

Now the chain. A/4/11432 fires on the "A" in "…FITNESS FOR A", and predicts " PARTICULAR". A/4/58888 fires on " PARTICULAR", and predicts " PURPOSE". A/4/56745 fires on " PURPOSE", which ends the phrase.

Nothing joins these three in the weights. This is a [[one-layer-transformer-testbed|one-layer model]], so each step is a fresh forward pass, and the only channel from one feature to the next is the token that got emitted in between. The paper calls such assemblies [[finite-state-automata-features|finite state automata]] and stresses they are not circuits: the model never learned the parts to cooperate, they line up because the text does.

The paper reads this particular chain as [[memorization-features|sequence memorization]], and notes it shows up only in dictionaries with many features — a small dictionary spends its budget on broad contexts instead, which is [[feature-splitting]].

Then the caveat. This sentence is licence boilerplate sitting in the file headers of popular open-source projects, and the training corpus is [[pile-dataset|the Pile]], so the model saw it many times. Heavy repetition is a plausible reason the chain exists at all — which is the [[model-vs-data-question|model-or-data]] worry in miniature, since a feature this narrow may be tracking a quirk of the corpus more than a computation.

The paper keeps both readings open. It links the chain to a mechanistic account of [[memorization-in-superposition|memorization in superposition]] and to [[mechanistic-anomaly-detection]], calls it surprising that something so specific fits inside 512 neurons at all — an illustration of what [[superposition]] can pack in — and then adds that mechanisms buried this deep in superposition are likely very noisy.

terms.definition: The left-hand feature: number 11432 in dictionary learning run A/4. It fires on the token "A" inside the licence phrase, and its top logit weight is on " PARTICULAR".
The middle feature: number 58888 in the same run. It fires on the token " PARTICULAR" in this phrase, and predicts " PURPOSE".
The right-hand feature: number 56745 in the same run. It fires on " PURPOSE", the last token of the memorized phrase, and closes the chain shown here.
Which transformer the activations came from. A is the main one-layer model the paper studies; B is its seed-twin, used for universality checks and not shown here.
Which dictionary learning run produced the feature. Runs A/0 through A/5 share an L1 coefficient and grow in dictionary size, so A/4 is one of the wide ones.
One learned feature, presented as a card of evidence: its name at the top, and beneath it the dataset snippets on which it activates most.

Marks the token the feature fired on in that snippet. Darker and bolder shading indicates a stronger activation, so the pale highlight on "A" in the left box is a weaker firing than the solid ones in the other two boxes.

A step in the automaton: the source feature raises the probability of the labelled token, and if the model emits it, the target feature fires on the next position. The arrow is a path through the token stream, not a weight connection.
The token A/4/11432 most strongly promotes. The leading space is part of the token, which is how this tokenizer writes a word that begins a new word rather than continuing one.
The token A/4/58888 most strongly promotes, and the token the third feature fires on.
One dataset example inside a box: a window of training text centred on the token where the feature fired, shown in monospace so the tokenization is legible.

terms.term: MERCHANTABILITY or FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE
terms.definition: The warranty disclaimer this chain reconstructs. It is standard legal wording carried in the file headers of common open-source licences, so it recurs verbatim across large amounts of public code.

Two variants of the same boilerplate visible across the boxes — "MERCHANTABILITY or FITNESS" in the left box, "AND FITNESS" in the middle one. Different licence texts word the connective differently, and the features fire across both.
Not a token of interest, just the snippet window cutting off mid-word. It shows the display truncates context rather than the feature responding to a fragment.

The paper's loose name for this shape: features as states, emitted tokens as transitions between them. The label is an analogy, and the paper is careful that the model did not learn the states to work together.

numbers.meaning: The number of features drawn. Three states are enough to carry the phrase from "A" to its end, because each one only has to predict the single next token.
The number of arrows, one fewer than the number of boxes. The last feature's own predictions are not shown here, so the diagram stops rather than closing a loop.
Snippet lines shown per box. It is a display choice, not a count of how often the feature fires; the paper draws its visualizations from a 100-million-token subset of the training data.

Feature indices within run A/4. The numbers themselves carry no meaning or ordering — features come out of the autoencoder unordered — but their five digits indicate a dictionary with tens of thousands of entries.
The run index. The paper says this phrase memorization can be seen only in runs with relatively large numbers of features, which is why the example is drawn from A/4 rather than a small run.

Two things at once. It is the number of neurons in the model's MLP, which is what makes the paper call it surprising that a mechanism this narrow fits inside the model at all; it is also the dictionary size of run A/0, which is why A/0 shows broad context automata and no phrase memorization.

The dictionary sizes of runs A/1 and A/2. The sequence 512 to 4,096 to 16,384 and upward is the axis along which feature splitting happens, with narrower and more specific features appearing as the dictionary widens.

The number of features in A/4 that respond mainly to the token "the" in different contexts. The paper gives it as a sign of how finely a dictionary this wide slices its territory — the same wideness that lets a single phrase get its own chain.
Tokens the one-layer transformer was trained on, deliberately far past compute-optimal. A corpus that large seen for that long is what makes many repetitions of a licence header plausible.
The size of the Pile, the public corpus used for training. Its heavy code content is the reason open-source licence headers are well represented.

The width of the model's residual stream. It is the bottleneck the 512 MLP neurons write back into, and part of why the paper describes these mechanisms as buried deep in superposition and therefore likely noisy.

items.caption: Moreover, it isn't clear that features need to be one-dimensional objects (encoding only some intensity). In principle, it seems possible to have higher-dimensional "feature manifolds" (see earlier discussion here).
items.title: Three Pictures of Feature Geometry
items.takeaway: A hand-drawn contrast between three ways features might be arranged in activation space: evenly spread one-dimensional directions, clumped one-dimensional directions, and continuous higher-dimensional patches. The last panel is the one that bites: if a model uses feature manifolds rather than rays, dictionary learning can only ever approximate them with discrete directions, and asking for the "correct number of features" stops being a well-posed question.
items.walkthrough:
Three grey circles sit side by side. Each is a cartoon of the activation space the [[sparse-autoencoder]] decomposes — the 512-dimensional space of MLP neuron activations, squashed onto the page. A dot inside a circle is one [[feature]] direction. The boundary carries no meaning; it just fences in the drawing. Nothing here is measured. The panels are three competing pictures of how features held in [[superposition]] sit relative to each other.

**Left: "isotropic superposition."** The dots are scattered roughly evenly. This is the picture inherited from [[toy-models-of-superposition]], and the caption says features "repel and spread as far apart as possible" because overlap costs [[interference]]. Discrete and one-dimensional is the key assumption here. One-dimensional means a feature's entire range is a single ray: a fixed unit direction $d$, and a scalar activation $a \ge 0$ contributing $a\,d$. That scalar carries intensity or confidence and nothing else.

**Middle: "anisotropic superposition."** Same dots, but several are gathered into tight clumps. The paper says its own results push it toward this picture, since related features come out with small angles between their dictionary vectors. It offers two reasons: the features fire together ([[correlated-features]]), or they push up the same next tokens ([[action-sharing-features]]). It suspects the second matters more.

Neither of these two panels threatens completeness. Features are still rays, so one dictionary entry per ray finishes the job; the entries are just spread unevenly in the middle case.

**Right: "[[feature-manifolds]]."** Beside the loose dots are three shaded shapes — a crescent, a wedge, an ellipse. Each stands for a continuous, higher-dimensional patch of directions the model actually uses, rather than a single ray. [[dictionary-learning]] can only place discrete vectors, so it would cover a patch by sprinkling rays across it.

That is the consequence the panel is built to deliver. If some manifolds admit no unique description in terms of finitely many one-dimensional features, extra dictionary entries keep buying finer resolution and never terminate — so the [[correct-number-of-features]] is not well posed, and the [[feature-splitting]] already observed may be that approximation in progress. The paper puts this forward as a hypothesis, not a finding, and notes it is not exclusive of the other two.

terms.definition: The bounding outline of each panel, standing in for the whole activation space in which feature directions live — here the 512-dimensional space of MLP neuron activations. The circular shape is drawing convention; only the arrangement of things inside it is meant to carry information.

One feature direction: a single unit vector in activation space, drawn as a point. A dot represents a feature whose activations lie along one ray, so the only thing that varies is how strongly it fires.

A feature whose whole set of possible contributions is a ray — a fixed direction scaled by a non-negative activation. The activation encodes only intensity, so the feature has no way to express which of several related things is present.

What the scalar activation of a one-dimensional feature is taken to mean: how strongly, or with how much confidence, the feature's property is present. The paper elsewhere says its features do look like this, which it counts as evidence for superposition.

The name the paper gives, retrospectively, to the picture it inherited from its earlier toy-models work: discrete one-dimensional features that repel each other into a roughly evenly spaced arrangement. Isotropic means the arrangement looks statistically the same in every direction.

The hypothesis that a network represents more independent features than it has neurons, by assigning each feature its own direction in activation space rather than its own neuron. All three panels are pictures of how those directions might be laid out.
The behavior that produces the left panel's even spread: because non-orthogonal directions cross-talk, the training pressure pushes feature directions apart from each other.
The authors' own earlier work, Toy Models of Superposition, which produced the isotropic picture from small synthetic models. This figure is the paper revising that inheritance.

The tight groups of dots in the middle panel: sets of features whose directions sit at small angles to each other rather than spreading out. The paper reports seeing this in its actual dictionaries, via UMAP projections of the learned directions.

The middle panel's picture: features are still one-dimensional, but their directions are distributed unevenly, dense in some regions and sparse elsewhere. Anisotropic means the arrangement is not the same in every direction.

The right panel's shaded shapes: continuous, higher-dimensional sets of directions that the model might use as a single unit, instead of one isolated ray. The paper raises this as a possibility it cannot rule out, not as something it has demonstrated.

Three drawn manifolds, differing in shape only to suggest that such patches need not be simple or convex. A curved crescent, in particular, is a patch that no finite set of rays can describe uniquely.

The claim that when the true object is a continuous patch, the learned dictionary does not recover it — it lays discrete directions across it and returns those. The learned features are then artifacts of resolution rather than the model's real units.

Writing each activation vector as a sparse weighted sum of directions drawn from a fixed, over-large set. The set is discrete by construction, which is exactly why a continuous manifold is a problem for it.

The paper's observation that widening the autoencoder turns one feature into several more specific ones covering the same territory. The right panel offers a possible cause: the extra features are finer samples of a manifold.
Features that tend to be active at the same time — one of the two explanations the paper offers for why directions clump in the middle panel.

Features that push up roughly the same next-token predictions and therefore need to produce similar neuron activations, ending up at similar directions. The paper suspects this, rather than correlated firing, is the main cause of clumping.
The dictionary size at which every feature the model uses has been recovered and no more. Under the manifold hypothesis this quantity may not exist.

numbers.meaning: The number of panels, and so the number of competing hypotheses drawn: isotropic superposition, anisotropic superposition, and feature manifolds. The paper states these are not mutually exclusive, so three panels are three ingredients rather than three alternatives you must choose between.
The dimensionality of a feature under the first two panels. A one-dimensional feature is a ray: direction fixed, one scalar free. This is the assumption the third panel drops.

The dimensionality of a feature manifold in the right panel. The shapes are drawn as 2-D patches only because the page is 2-D; the hypothesis is just that the dimensionality exceeds one, and the paper names no specific value because it has not measured one.

The number of loose feature directions drawn in each panel. This is illustrative crowding, chosen so the eye can compare spacing across panels — it stands for nothing measured, since a real dictionary here holds thousands of directions.
The size and count of the tight groups. Again illustrative: the paper reports clusters of related features in its UMAP projections but does not attach these counts to any of them.
Three manifolds drawn alongside the loose dots, indicating the hypothesis is that some features are manifolds and others remain ordinary rays — not that every feature becomes a patch.

The dimension of the space each circle abstracts: the one-layer transformer under study has a 512-neuron ReLU MLP, and each learned feature is a 512-dimensional column of the decoder matrix $W_d$. The circle is that space flattened to two dimensions for drawing.

The dictionary sizes of the paper's three main autoencoder runs (A/0, A/1, A/2). They matter to this figure because it is the increase across these sizes that produces feature splitting — the phenomenon the right panel proposes to reinterpret as ever-finer sampling of a manifold, with no size at which sampling would be complete.

items.caption: Two schematic alternatives to one-dimensional features: a feature manifold that may be equivalent to a set of correlated features, and a manifold that can be approximated by 1-dimensional features but admits no "correct" set of them.
items.title: Two Alternatives to 1-D Features
items.takeaway: A pair of sketches arguing that "features are higher-dimensional manifolds" is not one hypothesis but two. One version — the convex hull of a few features that fire together — is just correlated one-dimensional features under another name. The other — a closed ring of directions — can still be approximated by one-dimensional features, but has no uniquely correct set of them, which the paper offers as a possible reason feature splitting never stops.
items.walkthrough:
Two schematic drawings sit side by side, each with its sentence of text printed to its right. They continue the drawing convention of the previous figure: a dot is one [[feature-direction]], meaning a unit vector in the model's activation space along which a feature writes when it fires. The drawings are cartoons of that space, not plots of measured data.

**Left panel.** Three dark dots are joined by three curved edges, and the region they enclose is shaded. That shaded patch is the convex hull of the three directions: every activation vector you can build by firing the three features together, in varying proportions, lands somewhere inside it.

The printed text says some versions of hypotheses describing [[feature-manifolds]] may be equivalent to [[correlated-features]]. Read the patch one way and it is a single continuous two-dimensional feature. Read it the other way and it is three separate one-dimensional features that happen to co-occur. The paper's point is that these are descriptions of the same object, so this version of the manifold idea is not a rival to the ordinary picture of [[superposition]] at all.

**Right panel.** Here the structure is a closed ring drawn as an ellipse, with eight dots on it. Four are solid — top, bottom, left, right. Four are hollow, sitting halfway between the solid ones.

The two sets are the whole argument. The solid four are one choice of four one-dimensional features approximating the ring. The hollow four are another choice, rotated by half a step. Both approximate the ring equally well, and nothing about the ring picks out either one, because a circle has no distinguished points. So the printed text says such a structure can be approximated by one-dimensional features while having no "correct" set of them.

**Why it is here.** The sentence this figure hangs off is a hedge: *perhaps* this accounts for the continued [[feature-splitting]] observed earlier. Widening the dictionary from 512 to 4,096 to 16,384 features kept dividing features into finer ones, and the paper found no width at which the dividing stopped. If some structures really are rings, then giving [[dictionary-learning]] more capacity would simply scatter more points around the ring, without end — and asking for the [[correct-number-of-features]] would not be a well-posed question. No experiment here tests this; it is a picture offered as one possibility.

terms.definition: One feature direction — a single unit vector in activation space that a feature writes along when it fires. In the right panel the four filled dots are one candidate set of one-dimensional features approximating the ring.

A second, alternative set of feature directions on the same ring, sitting halfway between the filled ones. They are drawn hollow to mark them as an equally valid competing choice, not as weaker or secondary features.

The convex hull of the three plotted feature directions: the set of activation vectors reachable by firing those three features together in different proportions. It is what the figure is calling a feature manifold in this panel.
The boundary of that hull, drawn as arcs rather than straight lines because the directions live on a sphere of unit vectors. The curvature carries no separate meaning beyond that.

A closed one-parameter loop of activation directions, drawn as a continuous curve. It stands for a structure with no distinguished points anywhere along it, which is exactly why no set of dots on it is the right one.
The hypothesis that a feature might not be a single direction with an intensity, but a higher-dimensional continuous family of related directions. Both panels are versions of this hypothesis.
Ordinary one-dimensional features that tend to fire at the same time. The left panel's claim is that a hull of correlated features and a feature manifold can be the same thing described two ways.
The paper's default picture of a feature: a fixed direction plus a scalar activation encoding intensity or confidence. Both panels ask what happens when the underlying structure is not of this form.
A privileged, uniquely right decomposition that dictionary learning could in principle recover. The right panel is a case where no such set exists, only many equally good approximations.
The paper's term elsewhere for the idealized features a model actually uses, which dictionary learning approximates. The right panel is a scenario in which that notion breaks down.

The observed effect where widening the autoencoder makes one feature divide into several more specific ones covering the same territory. The figure's closing sentence offers ring-like structures as a possible cause of splitting that continues at every width tried.

numbers.meaning: The number of panels, and the number of distinct hypotheses the figure separates: manifolds that reduce to correlated features, and manifolds that admit no correct feature set.
Filled dots in the left panel. Three is the smallest number that encloses a two-dimensional patch, so it is the cheapest way to draw a hull that could be mistaken for a manifold.
The dimension of the shaded hull in the left panel, one less than the three features spanning it. It is what makes the patch a candidate 'higher-dimensional' feature rather than a line.

Filled dots on the right panel's ring, and separately the number of hollow dots. Four is just enough to make a visibly even placement around a loop; nothing in the figure argues that four is the right count.
Total dots on the ring, four filled plus four hollow, alternating. They are two overlaid answers to the same question, not eight features.

numbers.value: half a step (90 degrees apart, offset by 45 degrees)
numbers.meaning: The rotation separating the hollow set from the filled set. Any rotation would do equally well, which is the panel's entire argument — the offset is arbitrary because the ring has no distinguished point.
The dimensionality of the standard feature: one direction, one scalar activation. Both panels are framed as departures from this.

The dictionary sizes from the earlier feature-splitting results, cited here as the 'continued feature splitting' this figure is trying to account for. Each roughly eightfold or fourfold widening produced more, finer features rather than a stable set — for instance base64-specific features went from 1 to 3 to many more.

items.caption: Despite this, kurtosis shows the neuron basis is still privileged.
items.title: Decoder Sparsity in the Neuron Basis
items.takeaway: In an outside replication, 92% of the learned feature directions turn out to be spread across many MLP neurons rather than concentrated in one neuron or ten. The scatter plot sorts every feature by how much of its decoder vector's squared length sits in its single largest neuron and in the next nine. The sentence attached to it adds a claim the plot itself does not display: that kurtosis still shows the neuron basis is privileged.
items.walkthrough:
