This is the one figure in the paper's [[external-replication]] section, where an invited outside researcher trained his own [[sparse-autoencoder]] on a different open-source one-layer transformer and reported what he got. It is commentary appended to the paper, not one of the authors' own results.

He asks a narrow question. When a learned feature writes into the MLP layer, does it write through a handful of neurons, or through nearly all of them?

### How the axes are built

Each point is one feature from his dictionary. Take that feature's column of the [[dictionary-decoder]] — its [[feature-direction]] — and square every entry. Each neuron now holds a non-negative share of the direction's squared length. Sort the shares and divide by their total.

The x-axis, *Frac Explained by Top Neuron*, is the largest single share. The y-axis, *Frac Explained by Next 9 Neurons*, is the shares ranked 2 through 10 added up. So $x + y$ is how much of the direction lives in its ten biggest neurons.

Two mechanical facts help you read it. Both are fractions of the same total, so $x + y \le 1$. And no neuron in the next nine can beat the top one, so $y \le 9x$. That inequality is the straight diagonal edge slicing the upper-left of the blue cloud; nothing can sit above it.

Colour is a label he assigned: *1-sparse* (red) for features whose top neuron alone explains most of the direction, *10-sparse* (green) for those needing the top ten, *dense* (blue) for the rest. The cutoffs are not printed. The histograms on the top and right edges are the marginal distributions of $x$ and $y$, split by the same three labels.

### What it shows

Blue swamps everything. He reports 4% 1-sparse, 4% 10-sparse, 92% dense, and says he finds this surprising. Features are not neurons wearing a different name — the bulk version of the paper's own case-by-case finding about [[neuron-basis-coefficients]] and [[features-invisible-in-the-neuron-basis]].

The attached sentence then hedges the other way, and note that the plot does not show it: he says kurtosis — heavy-tailedness of the decoder weights measured in the neuron basis, versus randomly rotated bases — still comes out high. That is the [[kurtosis-privileged-basis-test]] for a [[privileged-basis]]. Heavy tails mean a few neuron coordinates are unusually large, which a random rotation would smear out. So the neuron basis is not arbitrary; features just refuse to line up with single neurons, which is what [[superposition]] predicts.

terms.term: Fraction of Squared Decoder Sum Explained by Top Neuron vs Next 9 Neurons
terms.definition: The plot's title. For each learned feature it compares two quantities: how much of the squared length of that feature's decoder vector is carried by its single biggest neuron coordinate, and how much by the next nine.

The x-axis. The squared value of the feature's largest decoder coordinate, divided by the sum of squares of all its coordinates. A value of 0.8 means one neuron holds 80% of the direction's squared length.
The y-axis. The same quantity for the coordinates ranked second through tenth by magnitude, summed. Adding it to the x-value gives the share held by the top ten neurons together.

The total $\sum_j (W_d)_{ji}^2$ over all neurons $j$ for feature $i$ — the squared L2 length of the feature's decoder column. Both axes are shares of this total, which is why they are comparable and why they cannot together exceed 1.

The output matrix $W_d$ of the sparse autoencoder. Its column for feature $i$ is the direction in MLP activation space that the feature writes along when it fires; the paper uses "decoder" and "dictionary" interchangeably.

The coordinate system given by the MLP's individual neurons — the axes you get for free from the architecture. Expressing a feature direction in this basis is what produces the per-neuron shares plotted here.

The legend title. It names the three-way classification the commenter applied to each feature according to how concentrated its decoder vector is in the neuron basis. The plotting library's raw column name, printed as-is.
Legend entry, red. Features whose decoder direction is well explained by a single neuron — points far to the right and low on the y-axis. He reports 4% of features fall here.
Legend entry, green. Features well explained by their top ten neurons but not by the top one alone — the top neuron carries some but the next nine carry a comparable amount. Also 4% of features.

Legend entry, blue. Features whose direction is spread across far more than ten neurons, so neither the top neuron nor the top ten account for much. The remaining 92%, and visibly the bulk of the points.

The small bar panels along the top and right edges. The top one is the distribution of x-values, the right one the distribution of y-values, each stacked by sparsity_label. They show how many features sit at each value, which the overplotted scatter cloud hides.

A measure of how heavy-tailed a distribution is. Applied here to decoder weight values expressed in the neuron basis: high kurtosis means a few coordinates are much larger than typical, rather than all coordinates being of similar size.

A basis the architecture itself singles out. The MLP's elementwise activation function acts on neurons one at a time, so the neuron basis is not just an arbitrary rotation of activation space, and features have some tendency to align with it.

The control the kurtosis test compares against. Rotate the activation space by a random orthogonal matrix and recompute the weight distribution; if the neuron basis were nothing special, its kurtosis would look like the rotated ones. Higher kurtosis in the neuron basis is the evidence that it is special.
One hidden unit of the sparse autoencoder, treated as a candidate interpretable direction in the model's MLP activation space. Each dot in the scatter is one such unit.

The one-hidden-layer autoencoder with a wide ReLU hidden layer and an L1 penalty on that layer, trained to reconstruct MLP activations. The commenter trained his own on a different model rather than reusing the paper's.

The open-source subject model the commenter used, distinct from the two one-layer transformers ("A" and "B") the paper itself trains. Because the model differs, the numbers here corroborate the paper's qualitative claim rather than reproducing its exact figures.
The paper's section 8, where invited external researchers who had seen preliminary results contribute their own commentary. This figure sits there, not in the main results.

numbers.meaning: Share of the commenter's learned features labelled dense — neither one neuron nor ten neurons explains their decoder direction. He calls this surprising, since it means the overwhelming majority of features are spread thin across the neuron basis.
Share of features well explained by a single neuron. These are the red points at high x. It is the fraction of features that are, in effect, just neurons.
Share of features well explained by neurons 2 through 10 together but not by the top one — the green points. Adding all three labels gives 4 + 4 + 92 = 100%.
The number of neurons on the x-axis: the single largest coordinate. It is 1 because the sharpest test of "this feature is a neuron" is whether one coordinate alone carries the direction.

The number of neurons on the y-axis (ranks 2 through 10). It is also the slope of the hard upper bound $y \le 9x$: nine coordinates each no larger than the top one cannot together exceed nine times it. That bound is the straight diagonal edge on the upper-left of the blue cloud.
The top-ten cutoff, $x + y$. Chosen as a loose threshold for "a small handful of neurons" — sparse enough that a human could still read the feature off a short list of neurons.

The x-axis gridline labels, running from no concentration to almost total concentration in one neuron. Points reach roughly 0.9 at the far right, where a single neuron holds nearly the whole direction.
The y-axis gridline labels. The top of the visible range is around 0.67, so no feature has its next-nine neurons carrying much more than two thirds of the squared length.
Both axes are fractions of the same squared total, so $x + y \le 1$ for every point. This is why no dot appears in the far upper-right corner.

Where the dense features sit. A typical dense feature has its top neuron holding a few percent of the squared length and its next nine holding perhaps 15% — so about a fifth of the direction is in its top ten neurons, and four fifths is spread over everything else.
Where the 1-sparse features sit. A high x with a low y is the signature of one dominant neuron with no close runners-up: the feature really is close to a single neuron.
Where the 10-sparse features sit — a broad band sloping down from upper-left to lower-right, because as the top neuron takes more, less is left for the next nine.

The reference value the dense cloud should be compared against. If a direction were spread perfectly evenly over $n$ MLP neurons, the top neuron would hold $1/n$ of the squared length and the next nine would hold $9/n$. For a model with hundreds or thousands of neurons that is a fraction of a percent, well below where the blue cloud actually sits — so even the dense features are more concentrated than a uniform spread, which is the direction the kurtosis claim points.

items.caption: Many of the feature density histograms are bimodal. For example, consider the feature density histogram for A/16:
items.title: The Two Density Modes of A/16
items.takeaway: Plotting how often each learned feature fires, on a log axis, splits the features of run A/16 into two humps: a spike of features that fire on roughly one token in ten million, and a broad bulk centred near one token in a hundred thousand. The paper reports that almost all of the right-hand features are interpretable and almost none of the left-hand ones are, and treats the left hump — which it names the ultralow density cluster — as a suspected artifact of autoencoder training rather than anything in the transformer.
items.walkthrough:
You are looking at one chart that summarises a whole [[dictionary-learning-run]]. The run is A/16, one of the ninety [[sparse-autoencoder]]s the paper trained on the same one-layer transformer. Every learned [[feature]] in that run contributes one count to one bar, so the chart is a census of the dictionary rather than a picture of any single feature.

The x axis is [[feature-density]]: the fraction of tokens in the training set on which a feature has a nonzero activation. It is plotted as $\log_{10}$ of that fraction. The tick at $-7$ therefore means a density of $10^{-7}$, one token in ten million; the tick at $-2$ means one token in a hundred. Note where that leaves the whole chart — even the busiest feature shown is silent on more than 99% of tokens.

The y axis is a plain count of features per bin. The tallest bar says roughly 7,500 features sit in the bin nearest $10^{-7}$.

Now the shape. Two humps make the histogram bimodal, which the paper says is typical rather than peculiar to this run. The left hump is drawn in purple and labelled "Ultra Low Density Cluster". The right hump is the grey mass, peaking around $10^{-5}$ and thinning out past $10^{-3}$; the paper calls it the [[high-density-cluster]], while noting that the name is relative and the density there is still very low.

The split matters because the two humps behave differently. Anecdotally, the paper says, almost every feature in the right hump is interpretable and almost none in the left hump is. It reads the [[ultralow-density-cluster]] as an artifact of autoencoder training, not a property of the transformer; those units fire so seldom that they are [[de-facto-dead-neurons]], invisible to a plain count of [[dead-neurons]]. In the smaller run A/1, 292 of 4,096 features fell below one in a million and were dropped from later analyses.

Two hedges travel with the figure. The right mode may itself be two modes, near $10^{-5}$ and $10^{-3}$, which the authors say they are still investigating. And the clean gap here does not always appear: for wide dictionaries with a large [[l1-coefficient]] the clusters overlap, and separating them then needs extra statistics.

terms.definition: Names what is being counted (feature density) and which trained dictionary the features come from (run A/16). Every bar in the chart belongs to that single run.

An identifier for one dictionary learning run under the paper's naming scheme: 'A' is the transformer the activations came from, and '16' indexes one of the autoencoders trained on it, each with its own dictionary size and sparsity penalty. The paper keeps a separate table of runs; the text here does not restate A/16's size or L1 coefficient.

The horizontal position of a feature is the base-10 logarithm of its density, so each unit step to the right is a tenfold increase in how often the feature fires. The log scale is what makes both the $10^{-7}$ spike and the $10^{-3}$ tail visible on one chart.

The paper's definition: the fraction of tokens on which a given feature has a nonzero activation. It is used as a cheap proxy for autoencoder quality during iteration, not as a measure of anything the feature means.
The number of features whose density falls in that histogram bin. It counts features, not tokens and not activations.

terms.term: Ultra Low Density Cluster (purple annotation and purple bars)
terms.definition: The left mode, made of features that fire on around one token in ten million. The paper reports that almost none of these are interpretable and suspects they are an artifact of the autoencoder training process rather than a real property of the transformer.

terms.term: High density cluster (the grey mass, unlabelled in the image)
terms.definition: The right mode, named in the surrounding text rather than on the chart. The paper says almost all of its features are interpretable, and points out that the name is comparative: an absolute density near $10^{-5}$ is still very rare firing.
Having two separated peaks. Here it means the dictionary's features do not sit on one smooth spread of densities but fall into two distinguishable populations.

One narrow interval of $\log_{10}$ density; the bar's height is how many features landed in it. Because binning is done in log space, each bar covers a fixed ratio of densities rather than a fixed difference.

An autoencoder hidden unit with zero activation across a large number of datapoints. Such units are counted separately and would not appear anywhere on this chart, since their density is zero and has no logarithm.

The paper's description of ultralow density units: alive by the strict test, since they do fire occasionally, but so rare that they contribute nothing usable. This is why the paper prefers counting the high density cluster over counting dead neurons.

The scalar weighting the sparsity penalty against reconstruction error in the autoencoder's loss. It is not shown on this chart, but it matters for reading it: with a large coefficient and many autoencoder neurons, the paper says the two clusters stop separating cleanly.

numbers.meaning: The x axis ticks, in $\log_{10}$ of density. They correspond to one activation per 10 million tokens, per million, per 100,000, per 10,000, per 1,000 and per 100 respectively. The axis stops near $-7$ on the left because that is about the rarest firing the paper can estimate, and near $-2$ on the right because no feature in this run is busier than roughly one token in a few hundred.
The centre of the left mode, stated in the text. A feature there fires on about one token in ten million.
The centre of the right mode, stated in the text. A feature there fires on about one token in a hundred thousand — the paper's point that the 'high density cluster' is high only by comparison.
The location of a possible second peak inside the right mode, which the paper flags in a note and says it is still investigating. About one token in a thousand.
The y axis ticks, in features per bin. The scale reaching into the thousands is itself informative: a dictionary this large has tens of thousands of features in total.
The height of the tallest purple bar, at the far left. It is the single most populated density bin in the run, and all of it sits in the cluster the paper distrusts.

The heights of the successive purple bars moving right from the spike. Each is roughly half the one before, so the ultralow cluster is a sharp peak with a short decaying shoulder, not a broad population.
The plateau height of the grey mass between roughly $10^{-5.5}$ and $10^{-4}$. Spread over dozens of bins, this is where the bulk of the run's usable features live.

The transformer's MLP width and the largest autoencoder width the paper trains, from its setup table — an expansion of 256×, against the 8× expansion used for the main run. A/16's own width is not given in the text, but bar counts totalling tens of thousands place it well up that range.
The number of learned dictionaries the paper trained and published visualizations for. A/16 is one of them, and the appendix shows density histograms for all the Seed A runs.

For the smaller run A/1, the number of learned features, the number that are dead (active on none of 100 million dataset examples), and the number classed as ultralow density. Both latter groups are excluded from the paper's later analyses. The 292 is about 7% of the dictionary; the numbers are quoted here because the paper gives no equivalent breakdown for A/16.
The density threshold the paper uses in its global analysis to call a feature ultralow. On this chart that is the tick at $-6$, which falls just right of where the purple bars end.

The number of dataset examples over which A/1's feature activity was checked. A count of this order is what lets densities as small as $10^{-7}$ be estimated at all, since a feature at that density fires on only about ten of them.

The activation vectors used for autoencoder training out of the collected dataset, sampled without replacement over 1 million steps. It sets the scale of 'training set' in the definition of feature density.

items.caption: In many preliminary small-scale experiments, the two clusters are often perfectly separable. However, for runs with a large number of autoencoder neurons and a large L1 coefficient these two clusters often overlap.
items.title: Overlapping Density Clusters in Run A/5
items.takeaway: The paper's quick diagnostic — read two separated humps off a log-scale histogram of how often each feature fires — stops working at the largest autoencoder sizes. In run A/5, with 131,072 hidden units, the ultralow-density features run continuously into the rest of the distribution instead of sitting apart, so density alone no longer tells the uninterpretable leftovers from the real features. The paper reports this as a pattern it has seen, not as a measured effect.
items.walkthrough:
You are looking at a single histogram, for the single [[dictionary-learning-run]] named in the title bar: A/5. A run is one trained [[sparse-autoencoder]]; runs differ in how many hidden units it has and in how hard the sparsity penalty pushes ([[feature-notation]] spells out the naming). A/5 is the widest run in the paper's A/0…A/5 sequence, with 131,072 hidden units fitted to a 512-neuron MLP.

Each hidden unit is one candidate feature. For each, the paper computes its [[feature-density]]: the fraction of tokens on which that unit has a nonzero activation. Densities are tiny, so the x axis is $\log_{10}$ of density — $-6$ means the feature fires on about one token in a million. The y axis, Counts, is how many features land in each bin.

So the bars should add up to A/5's 131,072 features, minus one group: units that never fire have density exactly $0$, which has no place on a log axis and simply cannot be drawn.

### What the paper wants to see here

A [[feature-density-histogram]] is read for its shape. Two separated humps is the good case: a left hump near $10^{-7}$, the [[ultralow-density-cluster]], whose features are almost never interpretable and which the paper treats as a training artifact; and a right hump, the [[high-density-cluster]], whose features anecdotally almost all are interpretable. Where the two split, you can count the run's usable features by cutting at the valley.

### What this one shows

There is no valley. Left of about $-6.2$ sit a few short isolated bars, a few hundred to about 1,500 features each. From there the counts climb without a break into one tall mass peaking around $10^{-5.7}$ at roughly 9,650 features, then fall away in a long tail that fades out near $10^{-2.6}$. (The sawtooth around the peak is most likely binning against whole-token counts at these densities; the paper does not comment on it.)

Nothing here marks where the ultralow features stop. The paper's stated pattern is that the clusters separate cleanly in small preliminary runs and overlap when the autoencoder is wide and the [[l1-coefficient]] is large — an anecdotal report, with no threshold or criterion given. Its fallback is [[density-cluster-separation]]: add each feature's bias and its encoder-decoder dot product, and the high-density cluster pulls apart again in three dimensions.

terms.definition: Names what is plotted and for which run: the distribution of feature densities for the dictionary learning run A/5. Nothing else in the image identifies the run's settings.
One trained sparse autoencoder, in the paper's run notation: seed/model A, run index 5. Reported elsewhere in the paper as 131,072 hidden units with an L1 coefficient of 0.004.
The base-10 logarithm of a feature's density, so each unit step is a factor of ten. A log axis is used because all the densities are small and they span several orders of magnitude.
The number of features whose density falls inside a given bin. Summed over all bins it is the number of features that fire at least once.

The fraction of tokens in the training set on which a feature has a nonzero activation. The paper uses it as a cheap proxy for how well an autoencoder run is doing, because measuring interpretability directly is slow.
Here, one hidden unit of the autoencoder together with its decoder column — a candidate interpretable direction in the MLP's activation space. The histogram gives one count to each such unit.

The left mode of a density histogram, features firing on the order of one token in ten million or rarer. Almost none of them are interpretable, and the paper reads them as an artifact of autoencoder training rather than something in the transformer.

The right mode of the histogram — still very rare in absolute terms, but dense compared to the left mode. The paper reports that almost all of these features are interpretable, which is why the split matters.
Having two humps. The paper's expected histogram shape, and the thing that fails in this figure.

terms.term: Number of autoencoder neurons ("N learned sparse")
terms.definition: The width of the autoencoder's hidden layer, i.e. the size of the learned dictionary. It is one of the two hyperparameters the paper varies across runs, and one of the two conditions it names for the clusters overlapping.

The scalar weight on the sparsity penalty in the autoencoder's loss, trading reconstruction error against how many features fire. The other hyperparameter varied across runs, and the other named condition for overlap.
One trained autoencoder with a fixed dictionary size and L1 coefficient. The paper trained ninety of them and identifies features by run.
The model producing these features: a wide ReLU hidden layer trained with MSE reconstruction loss plus an L1 penalty, fitted to the transformer's MLP activations.

Autoencoder hidden units with zero activation across a large number of datapoints. Their density is exactly zero, so they cannot appear anywhere on this log axis; the paper resamples them during training.

The three numbers the paper reads off histograms like this one: how many live features sit outside the ultralow cluster, the lowest density at which real features still appear, and how many features exceed 1% density. Overlap makes the first two hard to read.

terms.term: Separating the clusters by bias and encoder-decoder dot product
terms.definition: The paper's fallback when density alone fails: plot each feature's bias and the dot product between its encoder and decoder vectors alongside its density. It reports the high density cluster is clearly separable in those three dimensions.

numbers.meaning: The number of hidden units in A/5, and so the number of features whose densities are binned here. It is the largest dictionary the paper trained, 256 times the 512 MLP neurons being decomposed.

The number of ReLU neurons in the one-layer transformer's MLP, i.e. the dimension of the activations the autoencoder reconstructs. It is also the size of the smallest dictionary, A/0, at 1x expansion.
The L1 coefficient the paper reports for A/5. In the appendix's grid of all Seed A runs, this is one of five values swept, from 0.001 to 0.01.
The span of the x axis, so densities from roughly one token in 10 million up to a few tokens in a thousand. Every feature in the run that fires at all falls in this range.

Where the ultralow density cluster sits in the well-behaved case. In the companion histogram for run A/16 it is a tall isolated spike there, separated by a visible gap from the rest; here the far-left bars are short and no gap follows them.

Roughly where the high density cluster's mode sits in the A/16 example the paper gives as its picture of a clean split. The paper notes that mode may itself be two modes, one near 10^-5 and one near 10^-3, and says it is still investigating that.
Read off the plot: the point left of which the bars are short and isolated, and right of which the counts climb continuously. It is the closest thing to a boundary here, and it is not a clean one.

Approximate heights of the scattered bars at the far left, between about 10^-7 and 10^-6.2. These are the surviving ultralow-density features; there are few enough of them, spread widely enough, that they do not form a distinct hump.
The tallest bar, near 10^-5.7 — approximate, read off the axis. Around 7% of the run's features land in that single bin.
The top of the Counts axis, set just above the tallest bar. Note this is a linear axis while the density axis is logarithmic.
Where the right tail reaches zero. No feature in A/5 fires on more than roughly a quarter of a percent of tokens.

The density above which the paper treats a large number of features as a warning sign that the L1 coefficient is too low. Nothing in this histogram comes close, so by that particular check A/5's penalty is not too weak.

The dictionary sizes along the paper's main sequence of runs, at fixed L1 coefficient. A/1 is the run the paper's detailed analysis focuses on; A/5 is the extreme end where this histogram's overlap appears.

The five L1 coefficients grouping the appendix's full grid of Seed A histograms, one panel each. Within a panel the curves are dictionary sizes from 512 up to 131,072, so the grid varies exactly the two knobs named as causing overlap.

The fraction of the MLP's log-likelihood loss contribution recovered when the autoencoder's reconstruction is spliced in, for A/5 and for A/1 respectively. A/5 reconstructs the model better, which is the reason to train dictionaries this wide even though their density histograms are harder to read.
The number of MLP activation vectors used to train each autoencoder. Densities are fractions of tokens; the paper does not state the size of the token sample used to estimate them for these plots.
The average number of features active per token (the L0 norm) that the paper generally targets. It is a separate sparsity check from the density histogram, and the two are read together.

items.caption: Along these three dimensions, the high density cluster is clearly separable.
items.title: Three Diagnostics That Isolate the High-Density Cluster
items.takeaway: In a run where feature density alone leaves the two modes overlapping, plotting each feature's density together with its encoder bias and its decoder-encoder dot product pulls the high-density cluster out as a compact, separate blob. That separation is what lets the paper draw a line around the ultralow-density features and set them aside as a training artifact rather than as things the transformer actually computes.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

One 3-D scatter plot. Every point is one feature — one hidden unit of the [[sparse-autoencoder]] — from a single [[dictionary-learning-run]]. The run is not named. From the surrounding text it is one of the hard cases: a large dictionary trained with a large [[l1-coefficient]], where the ordinary [[feature-density-histogram]] no longer shows two clean modes.

Three numbers are computed per feature, one per axis.

*Density* is the [[feature-density]]: the fraction of tokens on which the feature's activation is nonzero. It is plotted as $\log_{10}$, running $-10$ to $-3$. So the plotted features fire on somewhere between one token in $10^{10}$ and one in $10^{3}$.

*Bias* is that feature's entry of the encoder bias $\mathbf{b}_e$ in $\mathbf{f} = \mathrm{ReLU}(W_e\bar{\mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{b}_e)$ ([[autoencoder-encoder]]). Every plotted value is negative, roughly $-3$ down to $-22$. Read it as a firing threshold: the input's projection onto the feature's read-in direction has to clear that magnitude before the ReLU passes anything.

*D/E projection* is the dot product of the feature's decoder column with its encoder row. The decoder column is the [[feature-direction]] the feature writes along, held at unit norm ([[dictionary-decoder]]); the encoder row is the direction it reads with. The two are learned independently ([[untied-decoder-weights]]), so they can drift apart. The axis runs $-3$ to $+3$.

Point color tracks the density coordinate — dark navy at the rare end, crimson in the middle, orange at the top.

### What it shows

A compact orange blob, tagged by a dashed leader as the [[high-density-cluster]], sits off on its own. The large crimson mass is the [[ultralow-density-cluster]].

Take the axes one at a time. In density the blob is orange and the mass crimson — higher, but the mass reaches up into the same range. In bias the blob occupies a narrow band; the mass fans out both above and below it. In D/E projection the blob sits at positive values near $+1$, while the mass spreads across most of the axis, including that band.

No single axis cuts cleanly. Together they do: the blob is an island.

That is the claim, and its limit ([[density-cluster-separation]]). Separability is not itself evidence of an artifact. It gives the paper a rule for drawing the boundary; the artifact reading rests on the separate observations that almost none of those features are interpretable, and that longer training kills them off. The paper says the ultralow cluster "appears to be" a training artifact, and says it is still investigating why. The darkest points, at the least negative biases, are the extreme end — units that fire so rarely they are [[de-facto-dead-neurons]].

terms.definition: The single entry of the autoencoder's encoder bias vector $\mathbf{b}_e$ belonging to this feature. It sits inside the ReLU, so it acts as the threshold that the feature's read-in projection must exceed before the feature fires at all.

The feature's density: the fraction of tokens in the dataset on which its activation is nonzero, plotted on a base-10 log scale. It is the paper's quick proxy for whether an autoencoder run is working.

The dot product of this feature's decoder column with its corresponding encoder row — the direction the feature writes along, dotted with the direction it is read out with. Large positive values mean read-in and write-out agree.
The right mode of the feature density histogram, drawn here as the compact orange blob. Anecdotally almost all of its features are interpretable, even though their absolute densities are still tiny.

The ultralow density cluster — the left mode of the histogram, made of features that fire on fewer than roughly one token in a million. Almost none of them are interpretable, and the paper treats them as an artifact of autoencoder training.
One feature, i.e. one hidden unit of the sparse autoencoder in this run, positioned by its own three diagnostic numbers.

A continuous scale carrying the same quantity as the density axis: dark navy for the rarest-firing features, crimson through the middle of the range, orange for the densest plotted here. There is no printed color legend.

terms.term: Dark navy tip (top of the mass)
terms.definition: The rarest features in the plot, at densities near the $10^{-10}$ end of the axis and at the least negative biases. These are units that fire so seldom they are effectively dead without registering as dead by a zero-activity check.
The output weight vector for one feature, constrained to unit L2 norm. The paper calls it the feature's direction, or its dictionary vector, and it is one half of what the D/E projection multiplies.

The input weight vector for one feature — the direction along which the activation vector is projected before the bias and the ReLU. It is learned independently of the decoder column, which is why their dot product carries information.
The claim the plot is offered for: no one of these three numbers cuts the two clusters apart in this run, but taken jointly they place the high-density cluster in a region of its own.

numbers.meaning: The plotted range of $\log_{10}$ feature density: features firing on one token in $10^{10}$ up to one in $10^{3}$. The axis is logarithmic because densities span many orders of magnitude, and every feature in this autoencoder is rare in absolute terms.
The labeled encoder-bias values; the plotted points run roughly from −3 down to −22. All are negative, meaning every feature needs a positive input projection of at least that size to fire.
The plotted range of the decoder-encoder dot product. Since decoder columns are unit norm, the magnitude here is set by the encoder vector's length and by the angle between the two.

Roughly where the high-density blob sits on the D/E projection axis in this view — positive, i.e. the feature reads along approximately the direction it writes along. The ultralow mass, by contrast, spreads over most of the axis including negative values.
The density of the histogram's right mode, i.e. the high-density cluster, as stated in the text accompanying this appendix. It is why the blob here falls at the orange end of the color scale.
The density of the histogram's left mode, the ultralow density cluster — about a hundred times rarer than the high-density mode, and where the bulk of the crimson mass sits.

A possible third mode the paper notices in one histogram, splitting the right mode; the authors say they are still investigating whether that split is real. It marks the dense end of the density axis here.

The number of per-feature diagnostics combined in this plot: density, bias, and the decoder-encoder dot product. The paper reaches for the second and third only because the first alone stops separating the clusters in large runs.
The MLP width of the one-layer transformer being decomposed, and so the input and output dimension of the autoencoder. It is the baseline against which a dictionary counts as large.

The largest dictionary the paper trains, at 256 times the MLP width. Runs of this size, paired with a large L1 coefficient, are the ones where the two density modes overlap and this three-way plot is needed.

items.caption: As we increase the number of autoencoder neurons (or “N learned sparse”), we continue to discover not only more features but also rarer features, suggesting that we have not exhausted the features in our one-layer transformer.
items.title: Density Histograms Across Dictionary Sizes
items.takeaway: Across five sparsity settings, each panel overlays the feature-density histograms of six autoencoders whose dictionaries run from 512 up to 131,072 units. Widening the dictionary does not just yield more features: it keeps pushing the left edge of the distribution further left, so rarer features keep appearing. The paper reads this as a sign that no dictionary size tried so far has exhausted the one-layer transformer's features, and states it as a suggestion rather than a result.
items.walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Five panels, one per setting of the weight on the sparsity penalty — the [[l1-coefficient]] $\lambda$, printed in each panel's corner as `L1=`, running 0.001, 0.004, 0.006, 0.008 and 0.01.

Inside each panel sit six curves. Each curve is one trained [[sparse-autoencoder]], and the legend value "N Learned Sparse" gives its dictionary width: 512, 4096, 16384, 32768, 65536 or 131072 hidden units. The transformer's MLP has 512 neurons, so those widths span 1× to 256× ([[expansion-factor]]). All runs shown are on the "A" transformer.

### How to read one curve

Each curve is a [[feature-density-histogram]]. The x axis is $\log_{10}$ of a feature's [[feature-density]] — the fraction of training tokens on which its activation is nonzero. A feature at $-4$ fires on one token in ten thousand; one at $-7$ fires on one in ten million.

The y axis is a raw count of features per density bin. It is not normalised by dictionary size. A wider run therefore starts with an advantage, since more units means more counts, so height alone is not the evidence.

### What each panel shows

The broad right-hand mode is the [[high-density-cluster]], whose features the paper reports are almost all interpretable. The narrow spikes jammed against the left edge near $10^{-7}$ are the [[ultralow-density-cluster]]: almost none are interpretable, and the paper treats them as an artifact of autoencoder training rather than a property of the transformer — [[dead-neurons]] in all but name.

Raising $\lambda$ shifts everything left. At $\lambda=0.001$ the bulk sits near $10^{-4}$ and a second bump sits right of $10^{-2}$; those are features firing on more than 1% of tokens, which the paper's own checklist reads as the penalty being too weak ([[feature-density-diagnostics]]). By $\lambda=0.01$ nothing survives above $10^{-2}$.

### The argument

Within a panel, read the curves in order of width. Two things happen at once, and the second carries the claim.

The curves get taller, which is just more features. And their left edge keeps sliding left, which means the rarest feature recovered keeps getting rarer.

Were the 512-neuron layer's [[true-features]] exhausted, extra capacity should go dead or produce duplicates. Instead new mass appears in the rare tail at every size tried. The caption says "suggesting", and the hedge is earned: the plot counts features and cannot separate a genuinely new one from [[feature-splitting]] of an existing one. The paper also warns that at large width and large $\lambda$ the two density clusters overlap, so the tall spikes in the $\lambda=0.008$ and $\lambda=0.01$ panels should not be read as all real features.

terms.definition: The quantity every panel histograms: for one feature, the fraction of tokens in the training set on which that feature's activation is nonzero. It is the paper's cheap proxy for how well an autoencoder run is doing.
The base-10 logarithm of that fraction, used because densities span many orders of magnitude. A value of -5 means the feature fires on one token in 100,000.
The number of autoencoder features whose density falls in a given histogram bin. It is an absolute count, not a share of the dictionary, so curves for larger dictionaries sit higher by construction.
The number of hidden units in the sparse autoencoder, i.e. how many dictionary directions it can learn. The paper uses it interchangeably with autoencoder size or dictionary width.
The dictionary with exactly as many units as the transformer's MLP has neurons, run A/0. It is not overcomplete, and its curve is the lowest and shortest-tailed in every panel.
The 8x dictionary, run A/1, which is the run most of the paper's individual feature analysis uses. Here it is one of the smaller curves.
A 32x dictionary. Its curve sits between the small and large runs in both height and leftward reach.
A 64x dictionary, one step up the size ladder.
A 128x dictionary, second largest in the sweep.
The largest dictionary in the paper, 256x the MLP width. Its curve is the tallest in every panel and reaches furthest into the rare tail, which is the figure's main evidence.

The coefficient multiplying the L1 penalty on the autoencoder's hidden activations in its training loss. Each panel holds it fixed while varying dictionary size, so the six curves in a panel are comparable.

One hidden unit of the trained autoencoder, understood as a direction in MLP activation space that fires on some interpretable condition. Each feature contributes exactly one entry to one histogram bin.

The left mode, the narrow spikes near 10^-7, made of units that fire on fewer than roughly one token in a million. The paper says almost none are interpretable and treats them as a training artifact, not as features of the transformer.
The broad right mode of each curve, which the paper says is anecdotally almost all interpretable, even though its absolute densities are still tiny.

Autoencoder hidden units with zero activation across a large number of datapoints. Training resamples them, but ultralow-density units that fire just barely enough to escape the check remain effectively dead.

All dictionaries plotted here were trained on the MLP activations of the paper's main one-layer transformer, called A. A second transformer B, differing only in initialization seed, is used elsewhere for universality checks.
Dictionary width divided by the 512 MLP neurons: how many times more feature directions than neurons the autoencoder has. The legend values correspond to 1x, 8x, 32x, 64x, 128x and 256x.
The features the transformer actually uses, as opposed to the ones a particular dictionary happens to learn. The figure's claim is about whether the dictionaries have covered them yet.

The observation that widening the dictionary makes a single feature divide into a family of more specific ones covering roughly the same territory. It is the main reason more curve mass does not automatically mean genuinely new features.

numbers.meaning: The six dictionary widths overlaid in every panel, as given in the legend. They form the sequence of runs the paper calls A/0 through A/5, trained with matched settings so that size is the only variable within a panel.
Also the width of the transformer's MLP layer. The smallest dictionary equals it exactly, so that run is not overcomplete and can at best relabel the neuron basis.
The same six widths expressed as multiples of 512. The paper's headline sweep runs from 1x up to 256x, and most of its individual feature work is at the 8x run.

The five L1 coefficients, one per panel. They are shown because the sparsity penalty and the dictionary width interact: raising the penalty makes each feature fire on fewer tokens and shifts every curve left.
Densities from one token in ten million up to one in ten. The right end only has occupants at low L1, where the penalty is weak enough to leave some features firing very often.
At the two strongest penalties nothing is left above 1% density, so the axis simply stops earlier. The distributions have been pushed entirely into the rare region.
One token in ten million: the density at which the ultralow spikes sit, and roughly the resolution floor of the measurement. The paper reads features here as almost never interpretable.
One token in ten thousand: roughly where the high density cluster peaks in the weakest-penalty panel. Even this, the paper notes, is a very low absolute rate.

The diagnostic threshold from the paper's hyperparameter checklist. A substantial number of features above 1% density is taken to mean the L1 coefficient is too low, which is visible as the secondary bump right of -2 in the L1 = 0.001 panel.
The tallest bin in that panel, on the 131,072-unit curve near a density of 10^-4.4. It is around 2.6% of that dictionary's units landing in a single bin.
The tallest bin at the second penalty setting, again on the largest dictionary, with the mode having shifted slightly left compared to L1 = 0.001.

A spike at the extreme left edge, near 10^-7, on the 131,072-unit curve. Unlike the other panel maxima this one is ultralow density cluster mass, not interpretable features, and a second spike of roughly 3,900 sits just to its right.

A tall narrow pile-up near 10^-5.6 on the largest dictionary. The paper cautions that at large width and large L1 the ultralow and high density clusters overlap, so density alone cannot say how much of this spike is real features.
The largest count anywhere in the figure, near 10^-5.7 on the 131,072-unit curve, with the corresponding 65,536-unit peak around 4,500. The same overlap caveat applies.

The number of MLP activation vectors the autoencoders are trained on. Feature density is a fraction of tokens in this training set, so it is measured over a very large sample, which is what makes densities as low as 10^-7 meaningful at all.
The number of Pile tokens the one-layer transformer itself was trained on. The paper overtrains it deliberately, hoping this yields cleaner representations in superposition.

items.caption: The $L^0$ norm and Reconstructed Transformer NLL metrics, taken together, display a human-interpretable tradeoff between sparsity and explained behavior:
items.title: Sparsity Against Explained Behavior
items.takeaway: Plotting how sparse each trained dictionary is against how much of the MLP layer's loss contribution it recovers turns hyperparameter choice into a visible tradeoff: a weaker sparsity penalty explains more of the model's behavior, but only by letting more features fire on every token. The four L1 coefficients sit as four separate vertical bands, so the penalty largely fixes the sparsity level, while widening the dictionary climbs the band by raising explained behavior at nearly constant sparsity.
items.walkthrough:
Each dot here is one finished [[sparse-autoencoder]] — one [[dictionary-learning-run]] against the same one-layer transformer, whose MLP layer has 512 neurons. The sweep varies two things: how wide the dictionary is, and how hard the sparsity penalty pushes.

### The two axes

The horizontal axis is the average [[l0-norm]], written $L^0$: the mean number of features with a nonzero activation on a token. Left is sparser. Runs here land between about 4 and 20 active features per token.

The vertical axis is the share of the MLP's loss contribution the features account for — the paper's [[loss-recovered-by-features]] measure. To compute it, run the transformer, pass the MLP activations through the autoencoder, splice the reconstruction back in place of the real activations, and see how much the loss rises.

That rise is then divided by the rise you get from deleting the MLP outright, the [[zero-ablation-baseline]]. One minus that ratio is what is plotted. For the paper's main run the substitution costs 21% of what full ablation costs, so 79% is recovered.

### The four lines

The legend lists four values of the [[l1-coefficient]] $\lambda$, the weight on the [[l1-sparsity-penalty]] in the training loss. Each colored line joins six dictionary sizes trained at that one $\lambda$.

Within a line the movement is almost vertical. Going from 512 to 131,072 dictionary entries at $\lambda=0.004$ lifts explained behavior from roughly 0.80 to 0.945 while $L^0$ only drifts from about 16 to about 20. Size buys explanation cheaply in sparsity terms.

Across lines the movement is horizontal. Halving $\lambda$ from 0.008 to 0.004 shifts a run's $L^0$ from around 8.5 to around 20, and buys about 3.5 points of explained behavior at the largest size. That is the tradeoff the paper reads off the plot, and it is the plot's whole point.

### Cautions the paper attaches

The percentage is called an overestimate, because zero-ablating the MLP may be an unusually bad baseline ([[reconstructed-nll-overestimate-caveat]]). The lowest coefficient tried, 0.001, is left out because its $L^0$ would stretch the axis. And no point here is chosen as best: the paper only says it targets $L^0$ below 10 or 20 and distrusts codes as dense as a large fraction of 512, which is why this chart is a guide rather than a verdict ([[l0-nll-tradeoff]]).

terms.definition: The chart's title. It names the two quantities being traded against one another: how few features fire per token, versus how much of the MLP layer's effect on the loss the features reproduce.

The mean, over tokens, of the number of features with a strictly nonzero activation. It is the paper's direct measure of how sparse a learned code actually is, as opposed to how much sparsity pressure was applied.
The count of nonzero entries in a vector. It is not a norm in the usual sense, but the name is standard; here the vector is the autoencoder's hidden activations on one token.

terms.term: Percent of MLP Loss Contribution Explained (y axis)
terms.definition: The fraction of the loss improvement the MLP layer provides that survives when the layer's activations are replaced by the autoencoder's reconstruction. Higher means the learned features carry more of what the MLP was doing.

The amount by which having the MLP layer lowers the transformer's next-token loss, measured as the gap between the intact model and the model with that layer zeroed out. It is the denominator that turns a raw loss increase into a percentage.

The name the surrounding appendix gives the y-axis metric: the negative log-likelihood of the transformer when it runs on autoencoder reconstructions instead of true MLP activations. The plotted number is that loss increase, normalized by the zero-ablation gap and subtracted from one.

The scalar $\lambda$ multiplying the sum of feature activations in the autoencoder's training loss, alongside the reconstruction error. It is the knob that sets how strongly the model is pushed to leave most features at exactly zero.
The weakest sparsity penalty shown. Its runs are the densest on the plot, sitting near an average of 16 to 20 active features per token, and also the highest in explained behavior.
The second-weakest penalty shown. Its runs sit around 8 to 12 active features per token, with explained behavior from about 0.74 to 0.93.
The second-strongest penalty shown. Its runs sit around 5 to 8.5 active features per token, with explained behavior from about 0.71 to 0.91.
The strongest sparsity penalty shown. Its runs are the sparsest, near 4 to 7 active features per token, and explain the least of the MLP's loss contribution, from about 0.67 to 0.89.
All the runs sharing one L1 coefficient, joined in order of dictionary size. The connecting line is not a fitted curve; it just marks which points belong to the same penalty setting.

The unlabeled variable moving along each line: the number of hidden units in the autoencoder, which is the number of candidate features it can learn. The companion feature-density figure names the six sizes used, from 512 up to 131,072.
One trained autoencoder, identified in the paper as A/0 through A/5 and so on. Every dot on this plot is one such run.

Setting the MLP layer's output to zero and finishing the forward pass, to measure how much the layer was worth. The paper flags this as possibly an unusually weak baseline, which would inflate every y value here.

numbers.meaning: The span of average L0 norm across all plotted runs, i.e. how many features fire on a typical token. The floor is set by the strongest penalty (0.01) and the ceiling by the weakest one shown (0.004).
The x-axis tick marks, in features active per token. There is no unit beyond a count of features.

The span of explained MLP loss contribution across all plotted runs. The worst point is the smallest dictionary under the strongest penalty; the best is the largest dictionary under the weakest penalty shown.
The y-axis tick marks. Note the axis is labelled 'Percent' but the values are fractions, so 0.95 means 95%.
The four L1 coefficients in the legend. They are the four sparsity-penalty weights whose runs are drawn; each defines one colored series.

The fifth L1 coefficient the paper trained but excluded from this plot. With so little sparsity pressure its runs had far higher L0, and including them would have stretched the x-axis; the appendix says it was dropped 'to create a reasonable scale'.
The number of points per line, one per dictionary size. The feature-density appendix lists those sizes as 512, 4,096, 16,384, 32,768, 65,536 and 131,072.

Two things at once: the smallest dictionary size, and the number of neurons in the transformer's MLP layer. A 512-entry dictionary is therefore not overcomplete, and 512 is also the dimensionality the paper compares L0 against when deciding a code is too dense.
The largest dictionary size, 256 times the MLP's 512 neurons. Its runs are the top point of each line.

For A/1, the 4,096-feature run at L1 = 0.004 that the paper studies most, the features recover 79% of the MLP's loss contribution, because substituting the reconstruction costs only 21% of what zero-ablating the MLP costs. The blue series has a point near 0.80, consistent with this run.
The explained fraction the paper quotes for A/5, the 131,072-feature run at L1 = 0.004. It matches the top-right blue point at roughly (19.8, 0.945), the best explained behavior anywhere on the plot.

numbers.value: purple: about 3.9 to 6.6 on x, 0.67 to 0.89 on y
numbers.meaning: The extent of the L1 = 0.01 series. Sparsity barely changes across a 256-fold increase in dictionary size, while explained behavior climbs about 22 points.

numbers.value: green: about 5.2 to 8.5 on x, 0.71 to 0.91 on y
numbers.meaning: The extent of the L1 = 0.008 series. Loosening the penalty from 0.01 to 0.008 shifts the whole band right by roughly 1.5 features per token and up by about 2 points at the top end.

numbers.value: red: about 7.8 to 11.9 on x, 0.74 to 0.93 on y
numbers.meaning: The extent of the L1 = 0.006 series. Its top end explains about 0.93, roughly 2 points more than the 0.008 band, at the cost of about 3.4 more active features per token.

numbers.value: blue: about 16.0 to 19.8 on x, 0.80 to 0.945 on y
numbers.meaning: The extent of the L1 = 0.004 series. Compared with 0.006 it gains only about 1.5 points of explained behavior at the top but roughly doubles L0, which is the sharpest illustration of diminishing returns on the plot.
The gain in explained behavior from halving the L1 coefficient from 0.008 to 0.004 at the largest dictionary size, going from roughly 0.910 to 0.945. It costs a jump in L0 from about 8.5 to about 20.

The L0 range the appendix says the authors generally target when picking hyperparameters. It is stated as a rule of thumb with no principled derivation, and it places the blue (0.004) band right at the edge of what they accept.

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Hyperparameter Selection

items.caption: The distributions and overall conclusions are almost identical to Spearman.
items.title: Pearson vs Spearman Scoring Panel
items.takeaway: The paper re-runs its automated interpretability scoring with Pearson correlation alongside the Spearman correlation used throughout the main text, and the two give visibly the same distributions and the same ordering: dictionary-learning features score well above transformer neurons, while features from a randomized model sit awkwardly high. This is a check that the headline gap does not depend on which correlation coefficient was chosen, not a new measurement.
items.walkthrough:
You are looking at a 4x3 grid of histograms. Each of the four stacked blocks is one *way of scoring* a unit. Each of the three columns is one *population* of units being scored.

### Reading the grid

The columns are fixed all the way down. Left: features from [[dictionary-learning-run]] A/1 ([[feature-notation]] — model A, autoencoder run 1). Middle: the MLP neurons of that same transformer, the [[polysemanticity]] baseline. Right: features learned by running the same autoencoder on a [[randomized-transformer]], whose weights were shuffled so that any structure comes from the data rather than from training.

Row 1 is the [[manual-interpretability-scoring]] result: a count of scored activation intervals at each value of the 0–14 [[feature-interpretability-rubric]]. Rows 2–4 plot density, so bar heights integrate to one and panels are comparable even though the populations differ in size.

Rows 2 and 3 are the same [[automated-interpretability]] experiment scored twice. Claude writes an explanation of a unit from examples, then uses only that explanation to predict the unit's activations on unseen tokens; the score is the correlation between predicted and true activations. Row 2 uses [[pearson-correlation]]. Row 3 uses [[spearman-correlation]], the rank-based version reported everywhere in the main text. Row 4 is [[automated-logit-scoring]], an accuracy rather than a correlation.

The triangle under each panel marks that distribution's median. The dotted vertical line marks the null value: zero correlation in rows 2–3, chance accuracy of $0.5$ in row 4.

### What it shows

Compare row 2 against row 3, panel by panel. The shapes track each other closely: the same spike at zero, the same long climb toward $1.0$ for features, the same narrow pile-up at zero for neurons. Medians move by a few hundredths and never change the ranking.

That is the whole point of the figure. Pearson is included only so the numbers can be set beside Bills et al., whose autointerp scores are Pearson correlations; the paper's own conclusions were computed on Spearman.

The comparison the reader should carry away is between columns, not rows. Features beat neurons under either coefficient. The randomized column beating features on correlation is discussed separately, and the paper attributes it to easy single-token features rather than to real interpretability.

terms.definition: The left column: features learned by the sparse autoencoder run labelled A/1, meaning transformer A and dictionary learning run 1. This is the run whose features the paper studies throughout the main text.

The middle column: the ordinary MLP neurons of transformer A, scored by exactly the same procedures as the features. They are the baseline the paper wants to beat, because individual neurons are expected to be polysemantic.

The right column: features from running the same dictionary learning on a version of transformer A whose weight matrices have had their entries shuffled. It tests how much of the structure found comes from the dataset alone rather than from a trained model.

The top row's title: scores assigned by a blinded human annotator who formed an interpretation of each unit and rated it on a fixed rubric. The paper treats human judgment as the metric it trusts most.

The x-axis of the top row: the total score on the paper's interpretability rubric, summing confidence in the interpretation, consistency of high activations with it, consistency of the logit weights with it, an effect-size separation point, and specificity.
The y-axis of the top row: the raw number of scored activation intervals falling in each rubric bin. It is a count rather than a density because the human sample is small.

The scoring pipeline behind rows 2, 3 and 4: a language model (Claude) writes an explanation of a unit from examples, and that explanation alone is then used to predict behaviour the model has not seen.

Row 2's metric: the ordinary linear correlation between Claude's predicted activations and the true activations, across the scored tokens for one unit. Included only for comparability with Bills et al., who scored this way.

Row 3's metric: the same comparison computed on ranks instead of raw values, so it measures whether Claude gets the ordering of activations right rather than their magnitudes. This is the metric used throughout the paper's main text.
The x-axis of rows 2 and 3: one unit's score, ranging from -0.4 to 1.0 as plotted. Each bar counts units, not tokens; every feature or neuron contributes exactly one correlation value.
The y-axis of rows 2, 3 and 4: a normalised histogram height, so the area under each panel is one. It lets panels with different numbers of units be compared directly.

The bottom row's metric: from the same explanation, Claude labels each candidate output token yes or no for whether the unit firing should make that token more likely. It cross-checks the explanation against what the unit does, not just when it fires.
The x-axis of the bottom row: the fraction of logit tokens Claude classified correctly for one unit, on a set that is half true top-positive logits and half random tokens.

The legend entry for the small triangles beneath each panel, each marking the median score of that panel's distribution. Medians are used rather than means because several distributions are strongly skewed or bimodal.
The reference line drawn in rows 2 through 4. In the correlation rows it sits at zero correlation; in the logit row it sits at 0.5, which is chance for a balanced yes/no task.

One of eleven evenly spaced bands between zero and a unit's maximum activation, sampled from so that scoring covers the whole activation spectrum rather than only the top examples. The top row counts intervals, not units.

The tall thin bar exactly at 0 in rows 2 and 3. When Claude predicts a constant value, most often all zeros, no correlation is defined and the paper assigns a score of zero, which piles units up at that point.
The language model used as the automated interpreter: it produces the explanations and then makes the activation and logit predictions that rows 2 through 4 score.
The prior automated-interpretability work whose scoring protocol this paper adapts. Its scores are Pearson correlations, which is why row 2 exists at all.

numbers.meaning: The grid layout: four scoring methods (manual rubric, Pearson autointerp, Spearman autointerp, logit-weight accuracy) crossed with three populations (A/1 features, A neurons, randomized-model features).
The range of the manual rubric x-axis. The maximum is 14 rather than 15 because a perfect score on the effect-size-separation item makes the following item inapplicable.
The median rubric score for A/1 features (row 1, left triangle). The paper reads this as the annotator having a confident, specific, consistent hypothesis that also matched the logit weights.
The median rubric score for neurons (row 1, middle triangle), and the location of their tall spike. A zero means the annotator could not even form a hypothesis about what the neuron represents.

The approximate median rubric score for randomized-model features (row 1, right triangle). It sits between features and neurons because the randomized set is bimodal: a cluster at 0 plus a non-zero cluster.

The tallest bars in the top row: roughly 23 counts at rubric 13-14 for features, 23 at rubric 0 for neurons, and 23 at 0 for randomized features. Counts are small because human scoring is labour-intensive.
The total human workload behind row 1: 412 activation intervals scored across 162 features and neurons combined. This is why row 1 is plotted as counts, not density.
The plotted x-range of the two correlation rows. Correlations can in principle reach -1, but almost nothing falls below -0.4 in practice.
The median autointerp score for A/1 features under the two coefficients. They differ by a few hundredths, which is the figure's whole claim.
The median autointerp score for neurons under the two coefficients. Both sit far below the feature medians, so the feature-versus-neuron gap survives the change of metric.

The median autointerp score for randomized-model features, above the A/1 features under both coefficients. The paper attributes this to easy single-token features in the randomized model, not to genuine interpretability.

The height of the zero-correlation spike in the neuron panels of rows 2 and 3. It is the largest density in either correlation row, and reflects how often Claude's explanation of a neuron yields a constant prediction.

In the randomized-feature panels, the height of the spike at zero and the height of the peak near correlation 0.9 (about 3.2 under Pearson, about 2.85 under Spearman). That right-hand peak is the single-token cluster that is trivially easy to predict.
The evidence behind each single correlation value in rows 2 and 3: per unit, Claude predicts activations for 60 held-out dataset examples of nine tokens each.

The number of examples Claude is shown when writing an explanation: ten top-activation, two from each of the other 12 intervals, five random, and ten showing the top tokens in other contexts. These are kept separate from the 60 scoring examples.
The integer range activations are quantized to before Claude sees or predicts them, following Bills et al. It is why row 3's rank-based correlation is a natural fit for this data.
Chance accuracy in row 4, marked by the dotted line, because the logit set is a 50/50 mix of true top-positive logits and random tokens.

The medians in row 4 for A/1 features, neurons and randomized features. The randomized median sits exactly at chance, which follows from its weights being shuffled so its logit effects carry no structure.

The main text's version of the same logit result, quoted as averages across features and across neurons rather than medians. The average for neurons is higher than their median of 0.53 because the neuron distribution has a tail above chance.
The logit set scored per unit in row 4: 50 random vocabulary tokens plus the 10th through 60th largest positive logits. The top 10 are excluded because they were used to generate the explanation.

The height of the spike at accuracy 0.5 for randomized features in row 4, far taller than anything else in that row. Random weights give Claude nothing to be right or wrong about, so nearly every unit lands at chance.

items.caption: It turns out that the randomized transformer features are distinctly bimodal, consisting of single token and polysemantic clusters which are separated out in the inset at the bottom of the following figure.
items.title: The Randomized-Transformer Control
items.takeaway: On the paper's automated activation score, features found in a random-weight transformer get a slightly higher median than the real features do. Splitting the randomized features on whether they are "single token" shows where that advantage comes from: the single-token half is trivially easy to score, and on everything else the real features win while the randomized ones sit about where polysemantic neurons sit. The panel is the paper's own warning that a good automated interpretability score, taken alone, is not evidence that a decomposition found real structure.
items.walkthrough:
Two populations of features are compared, score by score. Magenta is run A/1, the [[dictionary-learning]] run whose [[feature]] set the paper studies throughout. Yellow is the same autoencoder procedure applied to a [[randomized-transformer]] — a copy of the one-layer model whose weight matrices have had their entries shuffled in place, so the weight distributions are preserved and only the learned structure is destroyed ([[weight-shuffling]]).

Where the two histograms overlap, the bars render dark orange. The small triangles below each axis mark each group's median, per the legend at top right.

### The three scores in the top row

Left is [[automated-interpretability]] on activations: Claude writes an explanation of a feature, then uses only that explanation to predict activations on unseen text, and the score is the [[spearman-correlation]] between predicted and true. Middle is the same explanation used to judge unseen high-logit tokens, scored as accuracy against a half-real, half-random mix, so $0.5$ is chance ([[automated-logit-scoring]]). Right is a blinded annotator's [[feature-interpretability-rubric]] score.

Two of the three go the way the paper expects. The randomized model's logit accuracy piles up on chance, which is unsurprising given its output weights are shuffled. On the rubric, magenta sits higher.

The left panel does not. Its banner says so: "Randomized Seems Better??"

### The inset

The inset splits that awkward panel in two, on one binary property. A feature counts as single token if, across all twenty examples in its top [[activation-interval]], the same token carries the largest activation ([[single-token-features]]).

On the left half, the randomized features dominate, with a tall spike of near-perfect scores. Predicting "fires on this one token" is easy to explain and easy to score.

On the right half the ordering reverses, and the paper notes the randomized curve there resembles the distribution for [[polysemanticity|polysemantic]] neurons.

So the randomized model's apparent win is composition, not quality ([[randomized-feature-bimodality]]). It learns more, and more strictly, single-token features — which the paper reads as dictionary learning picking up regularities of the dataset rather than of the model ([[model-vs-data-question]]) — and those inflate its median on a score that rewards easy explanations.

terms.definition: The magenta population: features from dictionary learning run A/1, the run trained on the real (trained) one-layer transformer that supplies nearly all the paper's examples. Here it is the reference group the control is measured against.

The yellow population: features from running the same sparse autoencoder on MLP activations of a one-layer model whose weights were randomly shuffled. It is an ablation asking how much feature structure survives when the model has learned nothing.

Used interchangeably in this figure for the same control. The randomization shuffles the entries within each weight matrix of the trained model rather than drawing fresh random values, so each matrix keeps its distribution of weights and loses only its structure.
The legend at top right explains that each small triangle under an axis marks the median of the same-colored distribution. Medians are the summary the appendix's comparisons are stated in.
The left top panel. It scores how well Claude, given only its own written explanation of a feature, can predict that feature's activations on text it has not seen.

The score for that panel: correlation of predicted and true activations computed on ranks rather than raw values. It runs from -0.4 to 1.0 here, with 1.0 meaning the predicted ordering of activations matches the true one exactly.

The histograms in the two automated panels and both insets are normalized to integrate to one within each group. This lets the magenta and yellow populations be compared even though they contain different numbers of features.
The manual panel plots raw counts instead of density, because human scoring produced only a few hundred scored intervals in total.
The yellow banner over the left top panel, flagging that on this one score the control group has the higher median. The question marks signal that the authors do not take the result at face value.
The middle top panel. Using the same generated explanation, Claude is asked whether an unseen token with a high output logit is one this feature should promote.
Fraction of those binary logit judgments that are correct, scored against a 50/50 mix of genuine top-logit tokens and random tokens. Chance is therefore 0.5.
The magenta banner appearing over the middle and right top panels and over the right inset, marking the comparisons where the real features come out ahead.

The right top panel. A blinded human annotator (one of the authors) formed an interpretation of each feature and scored it, sampling examples across the full activation spectrum rather than only the top ones.

The annotator's total score on the paper's five-part rubric: confidence in the interpretation, consistency of high activations with it, consistency of the positive logit effects, effect-size separation, and specificity.
Not a third group. Where the magenta and yellow histograms cover the same bin, the bars are drawn over each other and read as dark orange.
A reference line on the correlation axes marking zero correlation — the score assigned when Claude's prediction carries no information about the true activations.

The narrow yellow column sitting on the zero line in the left panel and, larger, in the right inset. When Claude predicts a constant value — usually all zeros — no correlation can be computed and the paper assigns a score of zero, which stacks features at that one point.

The subset of features whose top activation interval is dominated by one and the same token in every example. The paper calls this behavior trivial, because an explanation of such a feature is just the name of a token.
The complementary subset: features whose strongest activations do not always land on the same token. This is where the paper says the interesting comparison lives.
The yellow banner over the left inset, stating that on single-token features the randomized model's features score higher.
The same Spearman activation score as the left top panel, redrawn on each half of the split. The insets sum to that panel, which is what the "+" between them denotes.
A reminder that the two inset populations are a partition of the left top panel's yellow and magenta distributions, not two new experiments.

One of eleven evenly spaced bands between zero and a feature's maximum activation. Both the human and automated evaluations draw examples from across all of them, so that a feature is judged on weak activations as well as its top ones.

Ordinary MLP neurons that fire for several unrelated things at once; they are the paper's baseline for uninterpretable. The appendix says the not-single-token randomized features have a score distribution close to theirs.
The shape claimed for the yellow population: two separated clumps rather than one spread. The inset shows the clumps are the single-token and non-single-token groups.

numbers.meaning: Range of the Spearman correlation axis in the left top panel and both insets. It stops well short of -1 because predictions that are actively anti-correlated with the truth are rare.

Medians in the left top panel, read off the triangles: magenta (A/1) at roughly 0.57, yellow (randomized) at roughly 0.62. The yellow triangle sitting to the right of the magenta one is the entire anomaly the figure exists to explain.
Height of the yellow spike sitting on zero correlation in the left top panel. It is the accumulation of features for which Claude gave a constant prediction, which the paper scores as zero.
Height of the yellow peak near correlation 0.9-1.0 in the left top panel — the pile of near-perfectly-scored randomized features that the inset attributes to single-token behavior.
Range of the accuracy axis in the middle top panel, since accuracy on a binary judgment is a fraction of correct answers.

Chance accuracy in the middle panel, because the tokens shown are a 50/50 mix of genuine top-logit tokens and random ones. The yellow median sits exactly here, which the appendix calls unsurprising: the randomized model's output weights carry no learned structure for an explanation to predict.
Height of the yellow density spike at accuracy 0.5 in the middle panel. Randomized features cluster tightly on chance rather than spreading around it.
Median logit accuracy for A/1 features, stated in the main text and matching the magenta triangle at about 0.75. The comparison values are 0.53 for neurons and 0.5 for the randomized transformer.
Range of the manual rubric axis. The maximum is 14 rather than 15 because a perfect score on the effect-size-separation item (worth 1) implies the specificity item is not applicable.

The five component ranges of the rubric that sum to the Rubric Value: confidence in the interpretation, consistency of high-activation tokens, consistency of positive logit effects, whether inconsistent logit effects were separated by effect size, and specificity.

Medians in the manual panel: yellow (randomized) at about 7, magenta (A/1) at about 12. The main text gives 12 as the median scored feature interval, meaning a confident, specific hypothesis consistent with the logit weights.

The tall yellow bar at zero in the manual panel: randomized features the annotator could not form any hypothesis about. Zero is also the median score the annotator gave polysemantic neurons in the main text, which is why the appendix reads this bar as one mode of a bimodal distribution.
The tallest magenta bars in the manual panel, at the top of the scale. Most A/1 feature intervals land near the rubric maximum.
Number of examples in a feature's top activation interval. A feature is labeled single token only if the largest activation falls on the same token in all twenty.

Medians in the left inset (single-token features): magenta about 0.65, yellow about 0.83. The gap is the paper's evidence that the randomized model's single-token features are not merely more numerous but more strictly single-token, firing on the same token even in weak intervals, which makes them easier to score.
Height of the yellow peak just below correlation 1.0 in the left inset — the high-scoring peak the appendix points to as trivially earned.
Medians in the right inset (not single token): yellow about 0.18, magenta about 0.39. Here the ordering reverses, and the randomized distribution is said to resemble that of polysemantic neurons.
Height of the yellow zero-correlation spike in the right inset. Constant, uninformative explanations are concentrated in the non-single-token randomized features.
Per feature, Claude predicts activations for 60 dataset examples of nine tokens each, giving 540 predictions from which the Spearman correlation on the left panel is computed.
Number of evenly spaced activation intervals between zero and a feature's maximum activation, used by both the human and automated evaluations so that weak activations are tested too.
Total activation intervals scored (412) across features and neurons (162) in the manual analysis. The small sample is why the right top panel plots counts rather than density.

For the logit score, Claude judges 100 tokens per feature: 50 random ones and the 10th through 60th largest positive logits. The top 10 are withheld because they were used to generate the explanation.

items.caption: Empirically, taking an average over features, 88% of their true activations from the random examples are zero versus 54% for the neurons (the medians are ~91% and 58%, respectively).
items.title: Importance-Weighted Interpretability Scores
items.takeaway: Once the automated-interpretability scores are reweighted to what random text would have given, features still beat neurons (median 0.28 vs 0.04) but both distributions collapse toward zero. The paper's explanation is that a feature's true activations on random text are almost all zero — 88% on average, versus 54% for neurons — so the reweighted correlation mostly rewards predicting zero rather than predicting when the unit fires.
items.walkthrough:
This is the scorecard for [[automated-interpretability]] with one correction applied. In that procedure Claude reads examples where a unit fires, writes a short explanation, and then — seeing only that explanation — predicts the unit's activation on fresh tokens.
