A unit's score is the [[spearman-correlation]] between predicted and true activations, so 1.0 is a perfect ranking and 0 is chance.

### How to read it

The x-axis is that score; the y-axis is density, so each histogram integrates to 1 and the two populations can be compared despite very different sizes. Magenta is the 3,676 scored [[feature]]s of the A/1 [[dictionary-learning-run]]. Teal is the 512 MLP neurons of the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]]. Where the two overlap the fill turns dark navy — navy is not a third group. The dotted line at 0 is labelled random chance, and the two small triangles under the axis mark the medians.

### What the correction does

Half the scored examples were drawn on purpose from the unit's own [[activation-interval]]s rather than from random text, which oversamples tokens where the unit fires. [[importance-scoring]] undoes that: random-text tokens get weight 1, interval tokens get weight feature_density × interval_probability.

### What it shows

Features still score above neurons — median 0.28 against 0.04, mean 0.35 against 0.11. But both have slid toward zero: unweighted, the same features sat at median 0.58 and the neurons at 0.2. The bin at zero now reaches about 9 density units for features and about 7.6 for neurons; with bins roughly 0.03 wide, that is on the order of a quarter to a third of each population.

The paper attributes this to [[feature-density]], typically $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-6}$. Almost all the weight lands on random text where a feature never fires, so an explanation predicting zero everywhere already matches most of the truth.

The supporting measurement is stated in the text, not plotted here: averaged over units, 88% of a feature's true activations on random examples are zero, against 54% for neurons, with medians of ~91% and ~58%. The paper reads the gap as [[polysemanticity]] — a neuron firing for many things offers more non-zero values on which an explanation can be tested. That is the [[importance-scoring-degeneracy]]: the unweighted score is inflated by oversampling firing tokens, but the corrected one rewards explanations that say what a feature does not fire for.

terms.definition: The plot title. It means the automated-interpretability scores shown here have been recomputed with importance weights, rather than taken raw from the deliberately unbalanced sample of examples.

The x-axis quantity: for one unit, the rank correlation between the activations Claude predicted from its explanation and the unit's true activations on the same tokens. Ranks are used rather than raw values, so only the ordering of activations matters.
The y-axis. Each histogram is normalized so its bars integrate to 1, which lets 3,676 features and 512 neurons be compared on the same panel; bar height is therefore not a count.
The dotted vertical line at Spearman correlation 0, marking the score an explanation would get if its predicted ordering were unrelated to the true activations.
The magenta population: directions learned by the sparse autoencoder over the MLP activations, here the A/1 run's features that survived the paper's exclusions.
The teal population: the 512 individual ReLU units of the transformer's MLP layer, scored the same way as a baseline for comparison.
The dark blue region where the magenta and teal histograms cover the same area. It is a drawing artifact of the two translucent fills, not a separate set of units.
The middle score of that population: half its units score below this value. Reported separately for features and neurons in the two coloured boxes.
The arithmetic average score over that population. It sits above the median for both groups here, which tells you the distributions have long right tails.
The count of units for which no score could be produced at all, written as a fraction of the units attempted. Both read 0, so every feature and every neuron is represented in the histogram.
The legend for the two small triangles below the x-axis; each triangle sits at its population's median score, in that population's colour.

The reweighting shown here. Tokens from completely random examples get weight 1; tokens from a feature's own activation intervals get a smaller weight, so the correlation approximates what a fully random sample would have given.
The fraction of tokens over a large slice of the dataset on which a unit has a non-zero activation. It is one of the two factors in the weight given to an interval example.
The other weighting factor: the non-zero activations of a feature are bucketed into activation intervals, and this is the probability mass of the interval an example came from.
One of the evenly spaced bands between zero and a unit's maximum activation. The paper samples examples across all of them rather than only the top band, so that weak activations are tested too.
The paper's main dictionary learning run: 4,096 learned features trained on the MLP activations of the one-layer transformer. The magenta population comes from it.
The unit's actual values on the scored tokens, held out from Claude when it makes its predictions so that nothing but the explanation carries information about the activation pattern.
Scored examples drawn uniformly from the dataset rather than from a unit's activation intervals. Under importance weighting they carry almost all the weight.

numbers.meaning: Median importance-weighted Spearman score for features. Half the 3,676 features score below it; the magenta triangle under the axis sits here.
Mean importance-weighted score for features. It exceeds the median because a long tail of features scores between 0.5 and 1.0.
Median importance-weighted score for neurons — barely above the random-chance line at 0, which is why the teal triangle nearly touches the dotted line.
Mean importance-weighted score for neurons. Higher than their median for the same reason: a thin right tail pulls the average up.

Failures among features: no feature failed to receive a score. 3,676 is the number of A/1 features scored, the run's 4,096 features minus those excluded as dead or ultralow-density (the paper elsewhere gives 168 dead and 292 ultralow, so the filtering here is close but not identical).
Failures among neurons: none. 512 is the full MLP width of the one-layer transformer under study, so every neuron is scored.

Mean over features of the fraction of a feature's true activations on random examples that are exactly zero. This is the paper's evidence that the importance-weighted correlation is being computed against a mostly-zero target.
The same mean zero-fraction for neurons. It is much lower because a neuron responds to many unrelated things, so it fires on a far larger share of random tokens.
Median over features of the per-feature zero-fraction on random examples. Close to the 88% mean, so the feature distribution is not being driven by a few extreme cases.
Median over neurons of the per-neuron zero-fraction. Again close to the 54% mean, so the feature/neuron gap of roughly 34 percentage points holds at the centre of both distributions.
Median and mean feature score before importance weighting, from the main-text activation figure. Comparing with 0.28 and 0.35 here shows how much the correction moves features.
Median and mean neuron score before importance weighting. Falling to 0.04 and 0.11 here, neurons are moved less than features, which is the asymmetry the appendix is explaining.

Approximate heights, in density units, of the feature and neuron bars in the single bin containing zero — read off the plot, not stated in the text. The magenta cap above the navy region is what makes the feature bar the taller of the two.
Approximate bin width, from about 40 bins spanning roughly -0.25 to 1.0. Multiplying by the bar heights puts roughly 29% of features and 24% of neurons in the bin at zero.
The x-axis range. Neurons reach the negative end; features essentially do not go below about -0.05, so no unit's explanation predicts strongly in the wrong direction.
The y-axis range in density units, with labelled ticks at 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8. The scale is set by the spike at zero; everywhere else both histograms stay under about 2.
The typical range of feature densities in this run — the fraction of tokens on which a feature fires. This is the quantity that makes almost all importance weight fall on random examples.
The importance weight assigned to every token from a completely random example, against which interval examples are downweighted by feature_density × interval_probability.
The scoring sample per unit: 60 examples of nine tokens each, giving 540 individual activation predictions from which one Spearman correlation is computed.

The composition of those 60 examples: six from the top activation interval, two from each of the other 12 intervals, ten completely random, and twenty top-activating tokens shown out of context. Half being interval-drawn is exactly the sampling bias importance scoring corrects.
The number of examples Claude is shown when writing the explanation, in a separate interaction from the scoring one, with no overlap between the two sets of examples.

items.caption: Most importantly, it does not result in significantly different scores when we split out the performance of those with long explanations from short ones.
items.title: Explanation Length Distributions
items.takeaway: A prompting bug sometimes let Claude's whole chain of thought stand in as a feature's explanation, producing explanations several hundred tokens long instead of a few dozen. This figure shows that the long tail appears in all three scored populations at similar rates — 19% for neurons, 15% for the randomized model, 13% for the A/1 features — and the appendix reports that splitting scores into long-explanation and short-explanation groups does not change them significantly. It is a caveat check the authors ran, not a result about features.
items.walkthrough:
Three histograms stacked in one column, sharing a single horizontal axis: the length of the natural-language explanation that Claude 2 wrote for one unit. Each row is a different population of units. Magenta on top is the learned [[feature]] set of the A/1 [[dictionary-learning-run]]. Teal in the middle is the 512 MLP neurons of the same transformer ([[neuron-notation]]). Yellow at the bottom is the features fit to the [[randomized-transformer]] baseline. The vertical axis is density, so each row sums to one and the three can be compared even though the populations differ in size.

Why length matters at all. In [[automated-interpretability]], Claude first writes an explanation of a unit from examples of where it fires, and then, in a fresh interaction with the true activations hidden, uses only that written explanation to predict activations on new text. The score is [[activation-prediction-scoring]], a [[spearman-correlation]] between predicted and true activations.

The prompt asks Claude to reason first and place the finished explanation inside `<answer>` tags. Sometimes it fails to close them. The whole chain of thought is then kept as the explanation — the [[explanation-length-caveat]] — and that reasoning names specific tokens the unit fires on. A longer explanation could therefore make the prediction step easier and inflate the score.

How to read the rows. Each has two modes. The tall left mode, roughly 50–150 tokens, is well-formed short answers. The low, broad right mode, spread from about 500 to 1300 tokens, is leaked chain of thought.

What it shows. The right mode is present in every row, so the bug is not specific to features. By the appendix's count it is most common for neurons at 19%, then the randomized model at 15%, then features at 13% — slightly more inflation, if any, for the baselines the paper is beating.

One limit worth naming. This panel plots lengths only. The score split it is cited for is asserted in the text, with no distribution and no test statistic shown here, and the surrounding paragraph describes the measure as characters while the axis reads tokens.

terms.definition: The figure's title. It plots how long Claude's written explanations were, for each of the three populations of units that the automated interpretability pipeline scored.

The horizontal axis, shared by all three rows: the number of tokens in the text taken as a unit's explanation. Short values are properly tagged answers; long values are cases where the untrimmed chain of thought was used instead.

The vertical axis of each row: the histogram is normalized so its total area is one, rather than showing raw counts. This lets the three populations be compared even though they contain different numbers of units.
The top row, in magenta. Its units are the features learned by the A/1 sparse autoencoder on the main one-layer transformer's MLP activations.
The paper's naming scheme: model "A" and dictionary learning run "1", the run whose 4,096 features are used throughout the global analyses.
The middle row, in teal. Its units are the raw MLP neurons of transformer A, scored by exactly the same pipeline so features and neurons can be compared.

The bottom row, in yellow. Its units are features learned by dictionary learning on a version of the transformer whose weight matrices have had their entries shuffled — a control for how much of the structure comes from the model rather than the data.
A direction in activation space recovered by the sparse autoencoder, treated by the paper as the interpretable unit that should replace the neuron.

The short natural-language description Claude 2 writes of what a unit fires for, given examples of its activations. It is the only channel through which information about the unit reaches the prediction step.
The delimiters the prompt asks Claude to wrap its final explanation in, so the preceding reasoning can be stripped off. When Claude omits them, nothing gets stripped.

The step-by-step reasoning Claude produces before its final answer, demonstrated in the eight worked examples included in the prompt. When it is not stripped, it becomes part of the explanation and names concrete tokens the unit fires for.
The left annotation, pointing at the tall mode near the origin. It marks the intended behaviour: a brief answer, with the reasoning cut away.

terms.term: "Sometimes explanations are longer due to a bug..."
terms.definition: The right annotation, pointing at the low second mode. It states the authors' reading: the leakage is uncommon, occurs at similar rates in all three rows, and does not appear to move scores.
The number this caveat is about: the Spearman correlation between Claude's predicted activations and the true ones, computed per unit from the explanation alone.
Correlation computed on ranks rather than raw values, used here so a prediction only has to order tokens by activation strength correctly.
The language model that writes the explanations and then predicts activations from them. It is the explainer, not the model under study.
The shape every row has here: one narrow peak of short explanations, plus a separate low, wide bump of long ones. The second mode is the bug, not a different kind of feature.

numbers.meaning: The horizontal axis ticks, in tokens. The axis is cut at 1400 because essentially no explanation runs longer than that.
Where the tall left peak sits in every row: the length of a correctly tagged explanation, after the prompt asks Claude to be succinct and to avoid listing specific tokens.
The span of the low right mode: explanations that are really untrimmed chain of thought, roughly an order of magnitude longer than intended.
How often the long-explanation bug fires for neurons — the highest of the three rows, per the appendix text.
How often it fires for the randomized transformer's features.
How often it fires for the A/1 features — the lowest rate, so if leaked reasoning inflates scores it inflates the two comparison groups slightly more than the paper's own features.
The number of rows: A/1 features, neurons, randomized-transformer features. These are the three populations compared throughout the automated interpretability section.
The number of features in the A/1 dictionary, of which 168 dead and 292 ultralow-density features are excluded from the global analyses before any scoring.
The number of MLP neurons in the one-layer transformer, the size of the population in the middle row.

Examples shown to Claude when it writes an explanation: 10 from the top activation interval, 2 from each of the other 12 intervals, 5 random, and 10 where the top-activating token appears in other contexts.
Examples Claude then predicts activations for, using only its own explanation; at nine tokens each this gives 540 predictions per unit, which the Spearman score is computed over.
The range activations are quantized to before Claude sees or predicts them, following Bills et al. so the task is a small integer prediction.
Human-written demonstration features included in both prompts, each showing chain-of-thought reasoning — the reasoning style that leaks into the long explanations plotted here.

items.caption: Linear feature decomposition of the MLP activation vector (unnumbered display in "Features as a Decomposition", Section 2.1)
items.title: Activations as a Sum of Features
items.takeaway: The paper defines a decomposition of a layer as writing each token's MLP activation vector as a fixed bias plus a weighted sum of unit directions, one direction per feature. The weights are the feature activations, and the sum runs over many more features than the vector has dimensions, which the paper says is only workable because the weights are sparse.
items.walkthrough:
This is the paper's statement of what "decomposing a layer" means. It is an unnumbered display in Section 2.1, written down before any autoencoder is trained. Everything later in the paper is an attempt to fill it in.

Start on the left. $\mathbf{x}^j$ is the MLP activation vector at one token position, with $j$ indexing the datapoint. In the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]] that vector has $d_{\rm MLP} = 512$ entries, one per hidden neuron. Those 512 numbers are the thing the paper says it cannot avoid interpreting.

Now the right side, term by term. $\mathbf{b}$ is a single bias vector, the same for every token, absorbing a constant offset so that the sum only has to explain what varies. Each $\mathbf{d}_i$ is a [[feature-direction]]: a unit vector in that same 512-dimensional space, fixed once and shared across all tokens. Each $f_i(\mathbf{x}^j)$ is a [[feature-activation]]: a scalar, read off this particular token's activation, saying how strongly [[feature]] $i$ is present here.

So the direction says what a feature is, and the scalar says how much of it is there. A token's activation is then a weighted sum of directions, plus the bias. Note the $\approx$ — this is a reconstruction, not an identity, and the paper does not claim the leftover is zero.

Then the count. The sum over $i$ runs over far more features than the 512 dimensions the vectors live in: 4,096 at the 8× expansion the paper mostly uses, and 131,072 at its largest. More directions than dimensions is not a basis in the usual sense, and the paper calls such a set [[overcompleteness|overcomplete]]. The directions cannot all be orthogonal, so recovering the coefficients is not a matter of projecting onto an orthogonal basis.

What makes recovery possible at all is that $f$ is sparse — on any one token, nearly every $f_i$ is exactly zero. That is the same assumption [[superposition]] rests on, and it is what makes this display an instance of [[dictionary-learning]]. The paper is plain that the equation itself is not new: it is an ordinary linear matrix factorization.

One thing it leaves open on purpose. Whether models are in some sense composed of features, or whether this is a convenient after-the-fact description, is a question the paper says it takes an agnostic position on.

terms.definition: The MLP activation vector for datapoint $j$ — the hidden-layer values of the transformer's MLP at one token position. It is what the paper sets out to decompose.
The datapoint index, meaning one token in one context. The decomposition is written per token, and $f_i$ is recomputed for each.
The decomposition is approximate, not exact. Some part of the activation vector is left unexplained by the bias and the sum.

A bias vector in activation space, shared across all datapoints, that carries the constant part of the activations. In the autoencoder this is the tied bias, subtracted before the encoder and added back at the output.
The sum over features. It runs over the whole dictionary, which has many more entries than the activation vector has dimensions.
The feature index. It identifies one feature, which owns both a direction $\mathbf{d}_i$ and an activation function $f_i$.

The activation of feature $i$ on datapoint $j$: a single non-negative number saying how strongly the feature is present. In the sparse autoencoder it is the ReLU hidden-layer value, $\text{ReLU}(W_e(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{b}_d)+\mathbf{b}_e)_i$.

The direction of feature $i$: a fixed unit vector in the 512-dimensional activation space along which the feature writes when it fires. In the autoencoder these are the columns of the decoder weight matrix $W_d$.
A basic interpretable direction in activation space, which the paper wants to use as the unit of explanation in place of a neuron. A feature can point anywhere and need not align with any neuron.
The length of the activation vector $\mathbf{x}^j$, i.e. the number of neurons in the MLP hidden layer. In this paper's transformer it is 512.
The $d_{\rm MLP}$-dimensional space that $\mathbf{x}^j$, $\mathbf{b}$ and every $\mathbf{d}_i$ live in. Its coordinate axes are the MLP neurons.
Each $\mathbf{d}_i$ has length one, so it carries direction only. All of a feature's magnitude is pushed into the scalar $f_i$, which makes activations across features comparable.

Having more dictionary directions than the dimension of the space they sit in. The paper says this is what separates its setting from ordinary disentanglement methods, and it forces the directions to be non-orthogonal.
On any given token only a small number of the $f_i$ are non-zero; the rest are exactly zero. Sparsity is what makes recovering many coefficients from a low-dimensional vector possible at all.

Writing every activation vector as a sparse weighted sum of directions drawn from one fixed, larger-than-necessary set. The paper notes the form of the equation is standard and not its own contribution.

The hypothesis that a network represents more features than it has neurons by giving each feature its own direction in a lower-dimensional space, tolerating some interference. It is the reason the sum here is allowed more terms than the vector has dimensions.

numbers.meaning: $d_{\rm MLP}$: the number of entries in $\mathbf{x}^j$ and the dimension every $\mathbf{d}_i$ lives in. It is the MLP hidden width of the one-layer transformer the paper studies.
The length of each $\mathbf{d}_i$. The directions are constrained to be unit vectors, so scale is carried entirely by $f_i$ rather than being split between the two.
The expansion factor the paper mostly works at: eight times as many features as neurons, so the sum over $i$ has 4,096 terms against 512 dimensions.
The largest dictionary the paper trains: 256 times more features than neurons. It is the extreme of the same sum, with 131,072 terms in 512 dimensions.
The full range of dictionary sizes reported, from 512 features (as many as neurons, so not overcomplete) up to 131,072. Widening the dictionary is what produces feature splitting later in the paper.
The value nearly all $f_i$ take on any given token. The ReLU in the encoder plus the L1 penalty push most feature activations to exactly zero, which is the sparsity the decomposition depends on.

items.caption: Sparse autoencoder encoder / feature activation f_i(x) = ReLU(W_e(x - b_d) + b_e)_i (unnumbered display, Section 2.1)
items.title: The Encoder Equation
items.takeaway: This fixes what a "feature activation" concretely is in this paper: one non-negative number per dictionary element, produced by a single linear readout of the MLP activation vector followed by ReLU, computed after a learned offset has been subtracted from the input. Everything the paper later says about a feature firing, weakly or strongly, is a statement about this quantity.
items.walkthrough:
This is the encoder half of the paper's [[sparse-autoencoder]] — the rule that turns one activation vector into a list of [[feature]] activations.

The output $f_i(\mathbf{x})$ is the [[feature-activation]] of feature $i$ on datapoint $\mathbf{x}$. Here $\mathbf{x}$ is the MLP activation vector of the one-layer transformer being studied, a vector of 512 numbers ([[mlp-activations-as-target]]).

Read the operations in order. A fixed vector $\mathbf{b}_d$ is subtracted from the input. The matrix $W_e$ multiplies what is left. The vector $\mathbf{b}_e$ is added. ReLU clips anything negative to zero. The subscript $i$ then picks out the $i$-th entry of the resulting vector.

$W_e$ has one row per feature. Row $i$, dotted with the centred input, is a raw score for feature $i$ — large when the input points along that row's direction. So each row works as a detector. Having more rows than the input has dimensions is deliberate; the paper calls this [[overcompleteness]], and it follows from expecting the MLP to carry more features than neurons through [[superposition]].

$\mathbf{b}_e$ is an ordinary learned threshold. A negative entry means that feature needs a stronger match before it fires at all.

ReLU makes every activation zero or positive. A feature is therefore absent, or present with some intensity — it cannot fire negatively. Paired with the [[l1-sparsity-penalty]], which pushes most entries to exactly zero, this makes "did the feature fire here?" a plain yes-or-no question.

$\mathbf{b}_d$ is the [[pre-encoder-bias]], and its name comes from the decoder. The decoder reconstructs $\hat{\mathbf{x}} = W_d\mathbf{f} + \mathbf{b}_d$, adding back the same vector that was subtracted here; the paper ties the two rather than learning them separately. The effect is that the autoencoder fits the activations after a fixed offset is removed, so the [[feature-direction]]s stored in $W_d$ describe deviations from that offset instead of spending capacity on the offset itself.

Appendix 18.1 gives the reason it is there. On toy problems with a bias, the autoencoder failed to produce the expected [[bounce-plots]] unless a learned bias sat at both the encoder input and the decoder output. The bias is initialised to the geometric median of the activation dataset ([[geometric-median-initialization]]). The paper ranks this first among its architecture modifications, while saying plainly that it ran no rigorous ablations — the support offered is toy-model behaviour and intuition.

terms.definition: The activation of feature $i$ on datapoint $\mathbf{x}$: a single non-negative number saying how strongly that feature fires there. It is the $i$-th hidden unit of the sparse autoencoder.
The full vector of feature activations for one datapoint, of which $f_i$ is one entry. Its length equals the number of dictionary elements, not the number of neurons.
The input to the encoder: one datapoint's MLP activation vector from the transformer under study. This is the thing the paper is trying to decompose.
The centred input $\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}_d$, written explicitly in the appendix version of the same equation. It is what the encoder matrix actually multiplies.

The encoder weight matrix, with one row per feature and one column per input dimension. Each row is the detector for its feature; the dot product of that row with the centred input is the feature's raw score before bias and ReLU.
The pre-encoder bias, subtracted from the input before encoding and added back by the decoder on the way out. It is a single learned vector shared by both ends, not two independent biases.
The encoder bias, one learned number per feature, added to the raw scores before ReLU. A negative entry raises the bar the input must clear for that feature to fire.
The elementwise non-linearity applied last, replacing every negative entry with zero. Here its role is to make feature activations non-negative, so a feature is either off or on with some intensity.
An index selecting one coordinate of the vector the ReLU produced. It runs over the dictionary elements, so $i$ names a feature rather than a neuron.

The decoder weight matrix, named in the sentence following the equation. Its columns are the feature directions, and the same $\mathbf{b}_d$ that is subtracted here is added after multiplying by $W_d$.

The direction of feature $i$: the unit vector in activation space that feature $i$ writes along when it fires, equal to column $i$ of $W_d$. The encoder produces the coefficient, this is what the coefficient multiplies.
The input and output dimension of the autoencoder in the appendix notation, equal to the transformer's MLP width. $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{b}_d$ have $n$ entries.
The autoencoder's hidden width in the appendix notation: how many features the dictionary has. $W_e$ has $m$ rows and $\mathbf{b}_e$ has $m$ entries, with $m \geq n$.

numbers.meaning: The floor ReLU imposes on every feature activation. Any raw score that comes out negative becomes exactly zero, which is what makes a feature's state readable as absent versus present.
The MLP width of the one-layer transformer the paper studies, so the number of entries in $\mathbf{x}$, in $\mathbf{b}_d$, and in each row of $W_e$. Table 1 lists it as the transformer's MLP size.
The expansion factor the paper focuses on: eight times more dictionary features than neurons. With a 512-wide MLP that makes $W_e$ 4,096 rows tall, so 4,096 values of $f_i$ per datapoint.

The range of expansion factors across the paper's dictionary learning runs, from as many features as neurons up to 256 times as many. The same equation applies at every size; only the number of rows in $W_e$ changes.
The largest hidden width used, being 512 x 256. It is the upper end of how many $f_i$ values a single activation vector can be decomposed into here.

The number of MLP activation samples the autoencoder is trained on. $W_e$, $\mathbf{b}_e$ and $\mathbf{b}_d$ are all learned by gradient descent over this dataset, so it is what fixes the equation's numbers.

The L2 norm the columns of $W_d$ are constrained to. It matters for reading $f_i$ as an intensity: with directions pinned to unit length, the encoder cannot shrink a direction to inflate its activation, or vice versa.

items.caption: Full sparse autoencoder forward pass and training objective, MSE reconstruction plus lambda * L1 sparsity penalty (unnumbered aligned display, Appendix 18)
items.title: The Sparse Autoencoder's Two-Term Loss
items.takeaway: This is the entire method in four lines: a ReLU encoder turns one MLP activation vector into feature activations, a linear decoder rebuilds the activation from them, and training minimizes squared reconstruction error plus an L1 penalty on those activations. The two loss terms pull against each other — reconstruction forces the dictionary to keep the information, L1 forces most features to be off — and the coefficient lambda sets the exchange rate between them.
items.walkthrough:
This block is the whole [[sparse-autoencoder]] written out: three lines defining a forward pass, and one line defining what training minimizes.

Read the first three lines as a round trip. The input $\mathbf{x}$ is a single MLP activation vector taken from the transformer under study — the activations are the only thing the autoencoder ever sees ([[mlp-activations-as-target]]).

Line one subtracts $\mathbf{b}_d$ from the input. The same bias is used at the input and at the output, so the whole autoencoder works in coordinates recentred on the data. The paper calls this the [[pre-encoder-bias]] and lists it as its single most important modification to a standard autoencoder.

Line two is the [[autoencoder-encoder]]: a linear map, a bias, then ReLU. Its output $\mathbf{f}$ is the vector of [[feature-activation]]s. ReLU matters here because it makes entries that are exactly zero possible, not merely small.

Line three rebuilds the activation. $W_d\mathbf{f}$ is a weighted sum of the columns of $W_d$, with $\mathbf{f}$ supplying the weights. Each column is one [[feature-direction]], which is why the paper calls $W_d$ the dictionary ([[dictionary-decoder]]).

Line four is the loss, and it has two terms pulling opposite ways.

The first, $||\mathbf{x}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}||_2^2$, is squared reconstruction error ([[mse-reconstruction-term]]). It is what forces the dictionary to keep the information: drop a direction the activations actually use, and this term rises.

The second, $\lambda||\mathbf{f}||_1$, sums the feature activations ([[l1-sparsity-penalty]]). What the paper actually wants is a small count of nonzero entries, which it measures separately as the [[l0-norm]] — but a count gives gradient descent nothing to push on. The L1 sum is the differentiable stand-in, and sitting above a ReLU it drives most entries to exactly zero.

$\lambda$ sets the trade between the two ([[l1-coefficient]]). Raise it and the code gets sparser but reconstructs worse; lower it and the reverse ([[l0-nll-tradeoff]]).

One detail keeps the L1 term honest. Nothing stops a network from halving every entry of $\mathbf{f}$ and doubling the matching column of $W_d$ — same reconstruction, half the penalty. So the columns of $W_d$ are constrained to unit L2 norm ([[unit-norm-dictionary-columns]]).

Finally, note $m \geq n$: the hidden layer is wider than the input ([[overcompleteness]]). That is what lets the decomposition have more features than the MLP has neurons, as [[superposition]] would require.

terms.definition: One MLP activation vector from the transformer being decomposed — a single datapoint the autoencoder is asked to reconstruct. It lives in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
The input after the decoder bias has been subtracted, $\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}_d$. This recentred vector, not the raw activation, is what the encoder sees.
The hidden-layer activations, which the paper calls its learned features. Entry $f_i$ says how strongly feature $i$ fires on this datapoint; most entries are zero.

The autoencoder's reconstruction of the input, built as a weighted sum of dictionary directions plus the bias. The gap between $\mathbf{x}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ is what the first loss term punishes.
The encoder weight matrix, shape $m \times n$. It maps a recentred activation vector up into the wider feature space.
The decoder weight matrix, shape $n \times m$, also called the dictionary. Its columns are the feature directions, and they are constrained to unit norm.
The encoder bias, a vector in $\mathbb{R}^m$ added before the ReLU. It sets each feature's firing threshold.
The decoder bias, a vector in $\mathbb{R}^n$. It appears twice: subtracted from the input in line one and added back in line three, so the input and output biases are tied.
The training objective, minimized by Adam over the activation dataset. It is reconstruction error plus the sparsity penalty, with nothing else in it.
The input and output dimension of the autoencoder — here the width of the transformer's MLP layer, since MLP activations are what is being decomposed.
The autoencoder's hidden-layer dimension, i.e. the number of features in the dictionary. The paper takes $m \geq n$.
The dataset of MLP activation vectors the autoencoder is trained on. Each $\mathbf{x}$ in the sum is one such vector.
The number of activation vectors in the dataset, used to turn the summed loss into a mean. In practice this is a batch average.

The elementwise nonlinearity on the hidden layer. Here its role is specifically to allow feature activations that are exactly zero, so the L1 penalty produces genuine sparsity rather than many small values.
Squared L2 reconstruction error between the true activation and its reconstruction. The paper notes this is taken as a mean over vector elements.
The L1 norm of the feature activations, the sum of their absolute values (all non-negative here, after ReLU). Unlike the MSE term, this is a sum rather than a mean over elements.

The L1 coefficient, a scalar weighting the sparsity penalty against reconstruction error. It is one of the two hyperparameters the paper varies across its dictionary learning runs, the other being $m$.

The constraint that every column of $W_d$ has L2 norm exactly 1. Without it the network could shrink $\mathbf{f}$ and grow the matching column, cutting the L1 penalty without changing the reconstruction.
Having at least as many dictionary directions as the dimension of the space they live in, usually many more. The paper treats this as what separates its setting from ordinary disentanglement work.
The paper's alternate name for the decoder $W_d$, taken from sparse dictionary learning, where a signal is written as a sparse combination of a fixed set of directions.
The paper's framing of what $W_e$ is doing: a single linear-plus-ReLU stand-in for a multi-step, non-linear sparse coding algorithm that would otherwise have to be run per datapoint.

$W_e$ is learned independently rather than being fixed to the transpose of $W_d$. The paper reports the learned encoder ends up tilted away from the decoder, which it says increases representational capacity.
The average number of nonzero feature activations per datapoint. This is the paper's direct measure of sparsity, and the quantity the L1 term is standing in for during training.

numbers.meaning: The subscript names the L2 norm and the exponent squares it, making the first term ordinary squared error. The paper says it uses an MSE loss, and elsewhere notes that MSE — unlike the cross-entropy the transformer was trained with — does not itself reward polysemantic representations, so sparsity can inhibit superposition forming inside the learned dictionary.
The L1 norm, the plain sum of the feature activations. It is used instead of a count of nonzeros because a count gives no gradient.
The fixed L2 length of every column of $W_d$. It is set to 1 purely to remove the rescaling degree of freedom that would otherwise let the L1 penalty be gamed.
The averaging factor over the dataset, so the loss does not scale with batch size.
The overcompleteness condition. The paper wants more features than neurons because it believes the MLP layer uses superposition to represent more features than it has dimensions.
The value of $n$ in this paper — the transformer's inner MLP dimension, and hence the dimension of the activation vectors being decomposed.
The residual stream dimension of the one-layer transformer. It is not part of this equation, but it is the space the MLP reads from and writes back into.
The range of $m$ across the paper's runs, i.e. expansion factors from 1x (no overcompleteness at all) to 256x.
The value of $m$ in run A/1, the 8x expansion the paper focuses its detailed analysis on.
The value of $\lambda$ in run A/5, given as the paper's example of a low L1 coefficient paired with the largest dictionary. It is the one numeric $\lambda$ the text names.

The $L^0$ norm the paper generally targets when choosing $\lambda$ — the average number of features it wants active per token. The paper says it has no principled way to pick this level, and distrusts solutions where $L^0$ is a large fraction of 512.

For run A/1, the fraction of the MLP's log-likelihood loss contribution recovered when the autoencoder's $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ is spliced in for the real activations, and the fraction lost. This is the reconstruction side of the trade $\lambda$ controls.
The same measure for A/5, the largest dictionary with the low $\lambda$ of 0.004. The paper offers it as the extreme showing that reconstruction improves as $\lambda$ falls and $m$ grows.
The feature density above which the paper reads a $\lambda$ as too low. A feature firing on more than 1% of tokens is treated as a sign the sparsity penalty is not biting hard enough.
The number of activation vectors used to train the autoencoder, drawn from a pool of 10 billion. The paper reports that more data made features subjectively sharper.
The autoencoder's batch size and its number of update steps, sampled without replacement. Multiplied together these give the just-over-8-billion activation vectors seen.

items.caption: Computational proxy as a log-likelihood ratio log(P(s|context)/P(s)), with P(s) the unigram product (unnumbered inline display, Section 3 and Appendices 12.1-12.2)
items.title: The Log-Likelihood-Ratio Proxy
items.takeaway: The paper scores every string with a hand-built number: how much more likely that string is under a guessed context (base64, Arabic script, DNA) than under the data as a whole. Because the score is computed from Unicode blocks and character counts, and never from the autoencoder, it gives an outside yardstick for checking whether a feature's proposed interpretation holds.
items.walkthrough:
This is an unnumbered display, written inline in Section 3 and unpacked in Appendix 12. It defines the [[computational-proxy]] — the score the paper puts next to a feature's activations to test an interpretation.

Read the ratio first. The numerator $P(s|\text{context})$ is the probability of the string $s$ if $s$ really came from the hypothesised context. The denominator $P(s)$ is its probability under the data distribution generally. A ratio above one means the hypothesis explains the string better than the general distribution does; the [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]] takes the log, so "better explained" becomes a positive number.

Now the two pieces, each estimated crudely and on purpose.

The denominator is [[unigram-p-s-estimate]]: $P(s)=\prod_{t\in s}p(t)$, the product of independent per-token unigram probabilities. No context, no ordering — just how common each token is.

The numerator depends on the hypothesis. For the [[base64-proxy]], every base64 character gets probability $1/64$ and everything else $10^{-10}$, multiplied across characters. The [[dna-proxy]] does the same with A, T, C and G at $1/4$ each. The [[arabic-script-proxy]] instead goes through Bayes' rule, using the fact that Arabic script occupies known Unicode blocks: a string of only Arabic characters gets $P(\text{Arabic}|s)=1$, one with any other character gets $10^{-10}$.

Two adjustments matter. A feature may fire more strongly deep into a long string, so the paper maximises the ratio over prefixes ending at the final token. And the paper says it chose log-likelihoods on the intuition that features interact linearly with the logits, so they are pushed to track log-likelihoods — an intuition, not a result.

What this buys: a number computed without touching the [[sparse-autoencoder]]. Feature and proxy can then be correlated — 0.74 for Arabic, 0.8 for DNA once binarised, 0.38 for base64 — and a feature that fires only where a rare, specific proxy fires is hard to call [[polysemanticity|polysemantic]].

The limits are the paper's own. It admits these contexts were cherry-picked because they are easy to model, and where feature and proxy disagree it usually concludes the proxy, not the feature, is wrong.
items.latex:
\begin{gathered}
\log\!\left(P(s|\text{base64}) \,/\, P(s)\right) \qquad \log\!\left(P(s|\text{Arabic Script}) \,/\, P(s)\right) \\[6pt]
P(s) = \prod_{t\in s} p(t) \\[6pt]
P(s|\text{base64}) = \prod_{c\in s} P(c), \qquad
P(c) = \begin{cases} 1/64 & c \text{ is a base64 character} \\ 10^{-10} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \\[6pt]
P(s|\text{Arabic}) = P(\text{Arabic}|s) \cdot P(s) \,/\, P(\text{Arabic})
\end{gathered}

terms.definition: The string being scored — in practice a token, or a run of tokens ending at the token whose feature activation is under examination. Everything in the proxy is a probability assigned to this string.

The probability of the string under the hypothesised context, i.e. if the text really were base64, Arabic script, DNA or Hebrew. This is the numerator, and it is estimated with a deliberately simple hand-written model of that context.

The context-free probability of the string under the full empirical data distribution. Estimated as a product of independent per-token unigram probabilities, so it carries no information about word order or context.

The proxy itself: the log of how much more likely the string is under the hypothesis than under the general distribution. Positive means the hypothesis explains the string better; the paper picks the log form on the intuition that features, interacting linearly with logits, are pushed to track log-likelihoods.
A token in the string, and its marginal frequency in the training data. The denominator multiplies $p(t)$ over every token of $s$.
A character in the string, and the probability that character gets under the context model. Used for the base64 and DNA numerators, which are products over characters rather than tokens.

The proposed interpretation of a feature, stated as a kind of text the feature is claimed to respond to. The paper builds proxies only for contexts that are easy to model from Unicode blocks or a small character alphabet.
The encoding whose alphabet is [a-zA-Z0-9+/]. The paper models a base64 string as a uniform random draw from those 64 characters.

Sequences of the uppercase letters A, T, C and G, modelled as uniform random strings over that four-letter alphabet. Because single tokens like CAT occur in ordinary text, the DNA proxy is only evaluated on groups of at least two tokens.
Text in the Arabic writing system, detected by whether characters fall in the Arabic Unicode blocks. The numerator is obtained through Bayes' rule rather than a character model.

The probability that a string is Arabic given the string itself, assigned by a rule rather than learned: 1 if every character is in an Arabic Unicode block, and a tiny value otherwise. Shared punctuation and whitespace count as non-Arabic, which makes the proxy miss some genuine Arabic text.
The base rate of Arabic script in the data, estimated by applying the same Unicode-block rule to a random sample of the dataset. It appears as the normaliser in the Bayes-rule form of the numerator.
The distribution of tokens taken independently, ignoring all context. The paper uses it for the denominator of every proxy.

Because a feature may fire more strongly late in a long stretch of the context, the paper computes the ratio for several prefixes ending at the final token and keeps the largest. This also softens the harsh penalty a single stray character imposes on the Unicode-block rule.
Reducing the continuous proxy to a yes/no value based on its sign, done for the DNA feature because the log-probabilities turned out strongly bimodal.
The single number the paper reports when comparing a proxy against a feature's activations, combining specificity and sensitivity while taking activation magnitude into account.
The claim that when the feature is on, the hypothesised context is usually present. The proxy is what makes this checkable at scale.
The claim that when the context is present, the feature is usually on. The paper finds this is often imperfect, with gaps covered by other features.
A unit responding to several unrelated things at once. A feature that fires only where a rare and specific proxy fires cannot be polysemantic in that usual sense.

numbers.meaning: The probability the base64 model gives to each character in the base64 alphabet [a-zA-Z0-9+/], which has 64 members. Uniform, because the paper models base64 as a random string over that alphabet.

The tiny probability assigned to a character outside the base64 alphabet, and likewise to $P(\text{Arabic}|s)$ when a string contains any non-Arabic character. It is a stand-in for zero, chosen so the product stays finite and the log stays defined while still crushing the score.
The probability given to each of A, T, C and G in the DNA model, four letters treated as equally likely.
The value of $P(\text{Arabic}|s)$ when the string consists entirely of Arabic characters — full certainty, by rule rather than by estimate.
Two of the Unicode blocks the paper checks membership in to decide whether a character is Arabic script. They are given as examples, not as the complete list.
The minimum number of tokens the DNA proxy is evaluated over, because single tokens such as CAT occur both in DNA and in ordinary English.

The Pearson correlation between the Arabic script proxy (thresholded at 0) and the activity of feature A/1/3450, over 40 million tokens. The paper calls this substantial while noting the feature misses some Arabic tokens that other features cover.
The Pearson correlation between the binarised DNA proxy and the DNA feature A/1/2937 — the highest of the four, helped by the proxy's clean bimodal split.
The Pearson correlation between the Hebrew script proxy and A/1/416. The paper attributes part of the shortfall to a companion feature, A/1/1016, that covers the \xd7 byte.

The Pearson correlation between the base64 proxy and A/1/2357 — the weakest of the four. The paper reads this as the proxy being too broad, since hexadecimal strings also score highly under it while having a feature of their own.
The number of tokens over which the Arabic feature-proxy correlation was computed.
The share of training tokens that are Arabic script, according to the proxy. Its rarity is what makes a high-specificity result meaningful.
The share of tokens on which A/1/3450 is active that the proxy calls Arabic — against a 0.13% base rate.

How that 81% varies with activation level: 25% where the feature is barely on, rising to 98% above activation 5. The paper uses this spread to argue that specificity holds where it matters, since larger activations have larger effects on predictions.
The activation level for A/1/3450 above which the proxy agrees 98% of the time; the paper treats this as the boundary of the feature's clean upper spectrum.

items.caption: Bayes-rule estimate of P(s|Arabic) = P(Arabic|s)P(s)/P(Arabic) for script proxies (unnumbered display, Appendix 12.3)
items.title: Inverting the Script Probability
items.takeaway: To score how Arabic-like a string is, the paper needs $P(s|\text{Arabic})$, which would otherwise require a generative model of Arabic text. Bayes' rule replaces it with three quantities that are cheap to compute: a character-level script check, a unigram probability, and the corpus rate of Arabic script. The same construction is reused for Hebrew and any other script with its own Unicode blocks.
items.walkthrough:
This is one unnumbered line of algebra in the appendix, printed without a caption. It supplies one ingredient of the paper's [[computational-proxy]] for Arabic script.

### Why this quantity is needed

Every proxy in the paper has the same shape, a [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]]: $\log(P(s|\text{Arabic Script}) / P(s))$. It asks how much more likely a string $s$ is under the hypothesis "this is Arabic script" than under the corpus in general.

The denominator is easy. $P(s)$ is the [[unigram-p-s-estimate]] — multiply the frequency of each token in $s$.

The numerator is the awkward one. Writing $P(s|\text{Arabic})$ directly would mean building a generative model of Arabic text.

### How to read the line

Read it right to left. $P(\text{Arabic}|s)$ runs the conditioning the other way: given the string, is it Arabic script? That is a classification question, and characters answer it.

Each of the three right-hand terms is cheap. $P(\text{Arabic}|s)$ is set by checking whether every character of $s$ sits in an Arabic Unicode block, such as U+0600–U+06FF or U+0750–U+077F. All Arabic gives $1$; any character outside those blocks gives $10^{-10}$, a tiny value rather than a hard zero.

$P(s)$ is the unigram estimate again. $P(\text{Arabic})$ is measured by running the same character heuristic over a random sample of the dataset.

### What it buys

Substitute the line into the proxy and the unigram term cancels: $\log(P(\text{Arabic}|s)/P(\text{Arabic}))$. The score becomes a script check divided by the base rate of that script, and since Arabic is around $0.13\%$ of training tokens, a confidently-Arabic string scores high.

Two wrinkles. A token that is not a complete Unicode character — common, because [[utf8-multi-token-characters]] split across byte tokens — gets its script share estimated by sampling random occurrences instead. And the proxy is evaluated over several prefixes ending at the token in question, taking the maximum, which is [[prefix-maximization]].

The construction is generic. The paper applies it to Hebrew as well, where the [[hebrew-script-proxy]] correlates $0.55$ with the [[hebrew-feature]].

One acknowledged cost: shared characters like punctuation and whitespace count as non-Arabic, so the proxy misses tokens the feature fires on. The paper lists this first among [[proxy-limitations]].

terms.definition: The probability of observing the string $s$ given that the text is in Arabic script. This is the numerator of the Arabic proxy and the quantity the equation is solving for.
The probability that text is Arabic script given the string $s$. Here it is not learned but assigned by a rule: 1 if every character of $s$ lies in an Arabic Unicode block, $10^{-10}$ otherwise.
The probability of the string under the corpus as a whole, computed as the product of independent per-token unigram probabilities, $P(s) = \prod_{t \in s} p(t)$.
The prior rate of Arabic script in the data, estimated by applying the same Unicode-block character heuristic to a random sample of the dataset.
A string of tokens ending at the token being scored. The proxy is computed over several such prefixes and the maximum is taken.
The identity $P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B)$, used here to swap a hard conditional for an easy one in the opposite direction.
A cheaply computable score standing in for "is this string of the hypothesized kind", used as an independent yardstick to compare against a feature's activations.
The form every proxy in the paper takes, $\log(P(s|\text{hypothesis})/P(s))$. The paper's stated reason is that features interact linearly with the logits and so should track log-likelihoods.
A contiguous range of Unicode codepoints assigned to a writing system. Arabic script occupies several, including U+0600–U+06FF and U+0750–U+077F.
The writing system used by Arabic, Farsi, Urdu and other languages. The proxy detects the script, not any one language.
The empirical frequency of each token in the training corpus, treated as independent across positions when forming $P(s)$.

A token that is only part of a multi-byte UTF-8 character, so its script cannot be read off directly. Its script probability is estimated by sampling random occurrences and measuring how often it appears in that script.
The section title flags that Arabic is only the worked example; the same Bayes construction produces proxies for Hebrew and any script with distinctive Unicode blocks.

numbers.meaning: The value assigned to $P(\text{Arabic}|s)$ when the string consists entirely of characters from Arabic Unicode blocks. It is a certainty by construction, not an estimate: the rule treats an all-Arabic string as definitely Arabic script.

The value assigned to $P(\text{Arabic}|s)$ when the string contains any character outside the Arabic blocks. It is a tiny probability rather than zero, so the log-likelihood ratio stays finite; the paper notes the proxy is maximized over multiple prefixes, so a heavily penalized prefix simply loses to a cleaner one.
The main Arabic Unicode block, one of the ranges used to decide whether a character counts as Arabic script.
The Arabic Supplement block, a second range included in the same character test. The paper writes "including e.g.", so the list it prints is not exhaustive.

The share of training tokens that are Arabic text, reported in the Arabic feature section. It is the scale of $P(\text{Arabic})$: because the base rate is this low, dividing by it makes a confident Arabic classification produce a large proxy score.

The Pearson correlation between the Arabic feature A/1/3450 and this proxy thresholded at 0, measured over 40 million tokens. It is the paper's headline evidence that the proxy and the feature track the same thing.
The number of tokens over which that correlation was computed.

The Pearson correlation of the Hebrew script proxy — built by the same Bayes construction — with the Hebrew feature A/1/416. Lower than the Arabic figure; the paper attributes part of the gap to a complementary feature that fires on the leading byte token of Hebrew characters.

items.caption: Attribution score f_i(t_j) * v_{i,t_{j+1}} used to build the attribution-similarity vector (unnumbered display in footnote, Section 5.3.1)
items.title: Attribution Score for the Observed Next Token
items.takeaway: This footnote formula defines one number per datapoint: a feature's activation there, multiplied by its logit weight on the token that actually came next. Stacking those numbers over sampled datapoints gives an attribution vector, which the paper uses as a cheap stand-in for measuring a feature's real effect on the loss instead of running an ablation everywhere.
items.walkthrough:
This is a formula from a footnote, not a numbered equation. It defines a single number: how much [[feature]] $i$ contributed to predicting the token that actually followed, at one position in one piece of text.

Read it in pieces. $f_i(t_j)$ is the feature's activation at token $t_j$, which is how strongly feature $i$ fired at position $j$. $v_{ik}$ is the feature's [[logit-weight]] on vocabulary token $k$, meaning how much the logit for token $k$ moves when this feature is on. There is one such weight for every token in the vocabulary, which is what $k \in \{1,\ldots,n_{\text{vocab}}\}$ says.

The formula then picks out exactly one of those weights. $t_{j+1}$ is the token that empirically came next in the dataset, so $v_{it_{j+1}}$ is the feature's push on that one token and no other.

Multiplying the two gives a large score only when the feature was firing *and* was pushing up the continuation that in fact occurred. A feature that was silent contributes nothing. A feature that fired but pushed on tokens that did not appear also contributes nothing.

Stack that score across a random sample of datapoints and you get the [[attribution-vector]] for feature $i$, with one entry per sampled position. Correlating two such vectors, one per model, is the paper's [[attribution-similarity]].

The reason for introducing it is that the two earlier measures disagree. [[activation-similarity]] asks whether two features fire on the same tokens; [[logit-weight-similarity]] asks whether they push the same vocabulary. For the Arabic feature the first is 0.91 and the second only 0.23, because the logit weight vector is dominated by a cloud of near-zero entries the paper reads as [[weight-interference]] rather than deliberate behaviour.

Weighting by activation and by the observed next token suppresses that cloud.

The more direct alternative would be [[feature-ablation]] for every feature at every datapoint, which the paper says is too expensive computationally. The authors name what they do instead: the classic gradient-times-activation attribution, differing in that the softmax and layer norm denominators are ignored. It is an approximation, and the paper says so.

terms.definition: Feature $i$ from a dictionary learning run, treated here as a function that assigns an activation value to each token position. The subscript $i$ indexes which learned feature is being scored.

The activation of feature $i$ at token $t_j$: the value that feature's hidden unit takes in the sparse autoencoder when the model processes that position. It is zero whenever the feature is not firing there.
The token at position $j$ in a sampled piece of text, i.e. the datapoint at which the feature's activation is read off.
The token that actually follows $t_j$ in the dataset. The formula uses the observed continuation, not the model's most likely prediction.

The logit weight of feature $i$ on vocabulary token $k$: how much the logit of token $k$ rises or falls when feature $i$ is active, computed by pushing the feature direction through the MLP output weights, a linearized layer norm, and the unembedding.
The single entry of feature $i$'s logit weight vector corresponding to the token that actually came next. This is the term that ties the score to what the model was supposed to predict.
The index over vocabulary tokens, running over the whole vocabulary. It labels which output token a logit weight refers to.
The size of the transformer's vocabulary, so the logit weight vector $v_i$ has $n_{\text{vocab}}$ entries, one per token.
The product $f_i(t_j)v_{it_{j+1}}$ at one datapoint: the paper's estimate of how much this feature helped push up the token that in fact occurred.
The stack of attribution scores for a random sampling of datapoints, giving one vector per feature with indices corresponding to sampled positions rather than to vocabulary tokens.

The correlation between two features' attribution vectors, one feature from each model. It is the paper's third way of asking whether two features are the same, after activation similarity and logit weight similarity.
Correlation between two features' activation vectors over a fixed set of datapoints, which asks whether the features fire in the same places.
Correlation between two features' logit weight vectors, indexed by vocabulary token, which asks whether the features push the same output tokens.

The standard attribution method of multiplying a unit's activation by the gradient of the output with respect to it. The paper says its score approximates this, differing by ignoring the softmax and layer norm denominators.

The normalizing terms that a full gradient computation would include: the softmax's partition function over the logits, and layer norm's division by the activation's standard deviation. Dropping them keeps the score linear and cheap, at the cost of exactness.
The alternative the paper rejects on cost grounds: for every feature and every datapoint, the change in the model's prediction when that feature's contribution is subtracted.

The paper's reading of the large mode of near-zero logit weights as noise forced by superposition rather than deliberate behaviour. It is why raw logit weight correlations are low even for matching features.

numbers.meaning: The lower end of the vocabulary index range $k \in \{1,\ldots,n_{\text{vocab}}\}$; the logit weights are simply indexed from the first vocabulary token.
The upper end of that range: the number of tokens in the transformer's vocabulary, and hence the length of each feature's logit weight vector. The paper does not state the value here.

The offset in $t_{j+1}$. The activation is read at position $j$ but the logit weight is read for position $j+1$, because a next-token predictor's output at $j$ is a prediction about the following token.
Activation correlation between the Arabic script feature in run A/1 and its closest match in run B/1. It is high, so the two features fire in the same places.
Logit weight correlation for that same pair, far below the 0.91 activation correlation. The gap is the disagreement that motivates building the attribution vector.

Activation correlation for the paper's most extreme case, features A/1/3949 and B/1/3321, whose logit weight correlation is nonetheless negative. The paper attributes this to interference, since only the '.' token has high logit weight in both models.

items.caption: Feature ablation, replacing x^j with x^j - f_i(x^j) d_i (unnumbered display, Appendix 13)
items.title: Subtracting One Feature's Contribution
items.takeaway: Ablating a feature means subtracting exactly that feature's own contribution — its activation times its dictionary direction — from the MLP activation at every token, then finishing the forward pass. Because everything else in the activation is left alone, the resulting change in the model's predicted log-likelihood is evidence that the model actually uses the feature, not merely that the feature co-occurs with the text.
items.walkthrough:
This is the one-line edit behind every ablation result in the paper. It is not part of training and not a measurement of the activations. It is a surgical change made to the model's internals in the middle of a forward pass, so that the rest of the model runs on activations with one thing removed.

### How to read it

$\mathbf{x}^j$ is the MLP activation vector at token position $j$ — the vector the [[sparse-autoencoder]] was trained to reconstruct. That reconstruction writes the vector as a bias plus a sum of terms, one per [[feature]]: each contributes its own activation $f_i(\mathbf{x}^j)$, a scalar, times its own unit direction $\mathbf{d}_i$ in activation space.

The expression on the right removes exactly one of those summands. Nothing is scaled, clipped or renormalised. The coefficient subtracted is the feature's own activation on that very token, so feature $i$ ends up at zero there.

The full procedure: run the model up through the MLP layer, run the encoder to get feature activations, apply this subtraction on every token in the context, then complete the forward pass as normal.

### What it shows

Notice what survives the edit. Every other feature's term stays. The bias stays. Whatever the autoencoder failed to reconstruct stays. Only the component along $\mathbf{d}_i$ moves. [[directional-ablation]] matters because under [[superposition]] feature directions are not orthogonal — zeroing a neuron, or blanking the activation, would knock out things you did not mean to test.

The reported effect is the change in the model's predicted log-likelihood for each token, drawn as a coloured underline in the paper's displays. [[ablation-effect-visualization]]

This is what makes ablation a causal test. The [[dictionary-learning]] procedure only ever saw MLP activations; what those activations do to the output was never an input to it. So if removing a feature makes a prediction worse, the model was using it.

The test is narrow, though. It shows the feature was load-bearing for those tokens in that context. It does not by itself confirm the feature's interpretation, which is why the paper reads ablations alongside [[logit-weight]] estimates and pinned sampling. [[feature-downstream-effects]]

terms.definition: The MLP activation vector at datapoint $j$ — that is, at one token position in one context. It has length $d_{\rm MLP}$, the width of the transformer's MLP layer, and it is the vector the autoencoder was trained to reconstruct.
The index over datapoints, meaning token positions in the context being run. The ablation is applied at every $j$ in the context, not just where the feature is strongest.
The index of the single feature being ablated. It is held fixed for the whole intervention: one feature is removed, everywhere.

The activation of feature $i$ at token $j$ — a single non-negative number, produced by the autoencoder's ReLU encoder, $f_i(x) = \text{ReLU}(W_e(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}_d) + \mathbf{b}_e)_i$. It is zero wherever the feature is not firing, so the ablation changes nothing at those tokens.

The direction of feature $i$: a unit vector in MLP activation space, taken as a column of the autoencoder's decoder weight matrix $W_d$. This is the sense in which a feature is a direction rather than a neuron.

The article prints the subscript as $j$, but $j$ indexes datapoints, not features. The direction subtracted is the ablated feature's own direction, $\mathbf{d}_i$; read the printed $\mathbf{d}_j$ as a slip for $\mathbf{d}_i$.

The feature's contribution to this particular activation vector: how strongly it fired, times where it points. This whole product is what ablation removes, which is why the feature ends up at exactly zero rather than merely reduced.
The number of neurons in the transformer's MLP layer, and hence the length of $\mathbf{x}^j$. The dictionary has many more directions $\mathbf{d}_i$ than this, which is what overcomplete means here.
The bias term in the decomposition $\mathbf{x}^j \approx \mathbf{b} + \sum_i f_i(\mathbf{x}^j)\mathbf{d}_i$. Ablation does not touch it; only one summand is removed.
The intervention this equation defines: subtract one feature's contribution from the MLP activations and let the rest of the model run, to see which token predictions depended on that feature.

After the subtraction, the edited activation is fed through the remainder of the model — the MLP output weights, layer norm and unembedding — so the effect shows up in real output probabilities rather than in a linear approximation.
The quantity reported for each token: the log-probability the model assigns to the token that actually comes next, after ablation minus before. A drop means the feature was helping that prediction.
In the paper's displays, shading behind a token marks where the feature was active, with intensity tracking $f_i(\mathbf{x}^j)$.
Marks the ablation effect on a token's prediction. Blue means ablation decreased the likelihood, so the feature was helping; red or orange means ablation increased it, so the feature was hurting.
The point that only the component along $\mathbf{d}_i$ is taken out; every other feature's contribution to the same vector survives intact.

A separate, linear estimate of a feature's downstream effect, obtained by pushing $\mathbf{d}_i$ through the MLP output weights, a linearised layer norm and the unembedding. Ablation is the on-data check of what that estimate predicts.

numbers.meaning: Index families, not quantities. $i$ ranges over the learned dictionary features (thousands to over a hundred thousand, depending on the run); $j$ ranges over token positions in the context being run.

The value feature $i$ is left at after the subtraction. Because the coefficient removed is the feature's own activation at that token, the removal is exact rather than approximate, and the feature is off across the entire context.

The implicit multiplier on the removed term. Ablation subtracts one times the feature's contribution — the paper is not scaling the feature down or turning it up, which are separate interventions it reports elsewhere (pinned sampling sets a feature to its maximum observed value instead).

The schematic three-token context the appendix uses to explain the display. A feature active on [B] whose ablation lowers the probability of [C] gets an orange background on [B] and a blue underline on [C]: it was helping predict [C].

The feature identifier in the worked ablation example: model A, dictionary learning run 1, feature number 3450 — the Arabic script feature. Ablating it lowered the likelihood of Arabic script tokens and raised that of a period.

Two activation ranges the visualisations sample from. Examples in interval 5 have roughly half the feature activation of those in interval 0, and the paper notes the ablation effects there are correspondingly smaller — the effect size scales with $f_i(\mathbf{x}^j)$, as the equation implies.
